ABSTRACT Public safety and security have become major concerns in today’s world due to the growing number of criminal activities and missing person incidents. Traditional surveillance systems often lack real-time intelligence and automated identification capabilities, which limits their effectiveness in critical situations. To address these challenges, this project introduces a Smart Surveillance System for Missing Person and Criminal Detection with [NAME]. The proposed system integrates computer vision, artificial intelligence (AI), and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies to create an intelligent monitoring solution. Using facial recognition algorithms based on YOLO (You Only Look Once) and deep learning models, the system can automatically identify known criminals and missing individuals from live CCTV or camera feeds. When a match is detected, the system instantly generates real-time alerts to authorized personnel through connected devices, ensuring quick response and action. Additionally, the system maintains a secure database of facial records, continuously learns from new data, and improves its accuracy over time. The combination of AI-based recognition and IoT-based alerting makes the system efficient, scalable, and practical for real-world deployment in public places, airports, railway stations, and other high-security areas. This project aims to support law enforcement agencies and enhance public safety by offering a proactive surveillance mechanism that operates with minimal human intervention and high precision. INTRODUCTION Preamble This chapter serves as the foundation for the project, "Smart Surveillance System for Missing Person & Criminal Detection with [NAME]." It introduces the critical domain of public safety and the pressing challenges faced by traditional surveillance methods. As criminal activities and missing person cases rise, the necessity for an intelligent, automated, and proactive security solution becomes paramount. This introduction outlines the core problem statement the project addresses, defines its specific objectives, and establishes the fundamental need for integrating advanced technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) into modern surveillance. The chapter will detail the project's aim, provide a comprehensive system overview, and explain the implementation concepts that drive the system's functionality. Overview The Smart Surveillance System for Missing Person & Criminal Detection with [NAME] is an AI-powered security solution designed to enhance public safety. Traditional CCTV systems act as passive recording devices with no intelligence or automated identification capabilities. This project integrates computer vision, facial recognition, and IoT technologies to convert standard surveillance into an active, automated monitoring system. The system uses YOLO-based face detection and CNN-based recognition to identify missing persons or criminals from live video feeds. When a match is detected, the system triggers IoT-enabled alerts to authorities instantly. It is designed for public places, smart cities, transportation hubs, and high-security environments where real-time monitoring is essential. LITERATURE SURVEY Preamble Before designing a novel solution, it is essential to understand the existing landscape of research and technology in smart surveillance. This chapter provides a comprehensive literature survey, critically reviewing previous studies and systems related to facial recognition, criminal detection, and [NAME]. The survey examines the evolution of surveillance technology, from traditional machine learning approaches like SVMs to modern deep learning models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), YOLO, and FaceNet. By analyzing the methodologies, successes, and limitations of prior work, this chapter aims to identify the current research gaps and establish a solid theoretical foundation for the proposed system's innovative approach. The findings summarized herein justify the technological choices made in this project.

2.1 Literature Survey Smart surveillance systems equipped with face recognition have gained prominence in security, law enforcement, and public safety applications. These systems integrate machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision techniques to detect faces in real-time, recognize individuals, and trigger alerts for identified persons of interest. Modern approaches leverage diverse inputs, including video frames, facial landmarks, and environmental metadata, aiming to maximize accuracy, reduce false positives, and provide timely alerts. Research in this domain has focused on improving face detection, recognition, tracking, and system efficiency under challenging conditions such as occlusion, crowding, and low-light environments. 2.1.1 Data Analysis and Machine Learning for Face Recognition Early studies explored traditional machine learning approaches for face recognition. For instance, J. Smith, A. Kumar, and R. Zhang (2018) proposed a hybrid system combining Haar Cascade Classifiers for face detection and Support Vector Machines (SVMs) for recognition. Using a dataset of 2,000 images from 50 individuals, the system achieved a recognition accuracy of 85% and a detection accuracy of 92%. The study highlighted challenges in handling occlusions, multiple faces, and low-resolution video frames, emphasizing the importance of preprocessing and feature engineering for robust performance. 2.1.2 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for Real-Time Recognition The adoption of CNN-based approaches revolutionized face recognition. M. Li, K. Tan, and P. Zhou (2019) developed a CNN model for real-time recognition on surveillance footage, achieving an accuracy of 91% under controlled conditions and 87% under low-light or crowded scenarios. CNNs automatically extract facial features, reducing the need for manual feature engineering and improving recognition robustness, especially in dynamic surveillance environments. 2.1.3 Hybrid Detection and Recognition Systems

Tan, and P. Zhou (2019) developed a CNN model for real-time recognition on surveillance footage, achieving an accuracy of 91% under controlled conditions and 87% under low-light or crowded scenarios. CNNs automatically extract facial features, reducing the need for manual feature engineering and improving recognition robustness, especially in dynamic surveillance environments. 2.1.3 Hybrid Detection and Recognition Systems Combining detection and recognition networks further improves system performance. H. Li, X. Wang, and J. Chen (2020) implemented a hybrid system using YOLOv3 for face detection and FaceNet embeddings for recognition, tested on 5,000 video frames containing multiple overlapping faces. The approach achieved 94% detection accuracy and 89% recognition accuracy, outperforming CNN-only models. Similarly, R. Banerjee, A. Ghose, and M. Mandana (2020) proposed a dual-input CNN-LSTM architecture for tracking and recognizing faces in video sequences, achieving 92% recognition accuracy. The temporal modeling in LSTM ensured robust tracking across frames despite motion blur or rapid movements. 2.1.4 Dimensionality Reduction and Feature Optimization To improve computational efficiency, researchers applied dimension reduction techniques. S. Verma, V. Awasthi, and S. Sahu (2021) used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce feature dimensions before feeding the data into a deep neural network. On a dataset of 2,000 high-resolution images, the system achieved 93% recognition accuracy while reducing computational requirements by 40%, demonstrating the importance of feature optimization for real-time surveillance applications. 2.1.5 Data Mining and Ensemble Learning

S. Sahu (2021) used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce feature dimensions before feeding the data into a deep neural network. On a dataset of 2,000 high-resolution images, the system achieved 93% recognition accuracy while reducing computational requirements by 40%, demonstrating the importance of feature optimization for real-time surveillance applications. 2.1.5 Data Mining and Ensemble Learning Data mining and ensemble approaches have been effective in identifying individuals in large datasets. N. Kumar, M. Sharma, and P. Gupta (2020) combined decision trees, SVMs, and random forests for criminal identification using 1,500 facial images, achieving 88% recognition accuracy. Ensemble methods reduced false positives and improved robustness. Additionally, A. Shahid, B. Roy, and M. Singh (2021) introduced a Hybrid Extreme Learning Machine (HELM) approach with feature selection, achieving 95% accuracy on 3,000 images. Feature selection enhanced both processing speed and recognition performance, making it suitable for large-scale, real-time surveillance. 2.1.6 Deep Learning and Hybrid Architectures Hybrid architectures combining CNNs with LSTMs or RNNs have shown significant promise in real-time surveillance. Temporal modeling through LSTM allows systems to track faces across consecutive frames, accounting for movement, occlusion, and partial visibility. These models have consistently outperformed traditional CNNs or machine learning classifiers, offering higher accuracy and reliability in dynamic environments. 2.1.7 IoT Integration for Smart Surveillance The integration of IoT platforms enables remote monitoring and instant alerts. Surveillance cameras connected to cloud or local servers can transmit face recognition results in real-time, allowing authorities or system administrators to respond promptly. Detection and Alignment Features This group of features answers the question, "Where is the face and how is it oriented?" Image Frame: The raw data (the picture itself). Bounding Box Coordinates: Defines the exact location of the face in the frame. Facial Landmarks: These are crucial for aligning the face (e.g., making sure it's upright and scaled) before creating the embedding. This dramatically improves accuracy. 2. Identification and Classification Features This group answers, "Who is this person?" Embedding Vector: This is the most important feature for recognition. It's a mathematical "faceprint" (often 128 numbers) that represents the unique features of the face. The system works by comparing this vector to a database of known vectors. Face ID: The unique name or ID linked to a known embedding vector in your database. Label (Known/Unknown): The final classification result after the system compares the embedding vector to its database. 3. Context and Action Features This group answers, "When, where, and what should we do about it?" Timestamp: Essential for logging and creating a timeline of events. Location ID: Tells you which camera made the detection. Alert Status: The final action. Introduction Biometric authentication systems verify identity using unique physiological traits, offering higher security than traditional password-based methods. Fingerprint recognition is the most commonly deployed biometric technique due to its permanence, uniqueness, and cost efficiency. However, conventional fingerprint authentication systems store biometric templates in databases that are vulnerable to theft and misuse. Unlike passwords, biometric data cannot be changed once compromised. In parallel, recent advances in quantum computing pose a serious threat to classical cryptographic algorithms such as RSA and ECC, which are widely used to protect biometric templates. Research papers in quantum computing demonstrate that quantum algorithms can break these cryptographic schemes, rendering current biometric security solutions inadequate for long-term protection. Recent research has also explored quantum-assisted biometric matching and quantum fingerprinting, showing promising computational advantages. However, most existing quantum biometric approaches directly encode raw biometric features into quantum states, leading to severe privacy and security concerns. The proposed project QuMetric aims to design a secure, privacy-preserving, and quantum-resistant biometric authentication system by integrating cryptographic hashing, post-quantum security, and quantum similarity computation. The motivation for this project is derived from the following research-driven observations: Uploaded studies on quantum biometric systems show feasibility but lack irreversible template protection Classical biometric template protection schemes are not designed to withstand quantum attacks Quantum cryptography and quantum similarity algorithms can enhance scalability if privacy is preserved Hence, there is a strong need for a hybrid biometric authentication framework that prioritizes security first and then leverages quantum computation safely.

Literature Review The literature survey is organized into three categories: (i) classical biometric authentication and template protection, (ii) quantum computing in pattern matching, and (iii) quantum-assisted biometric systems. 2.1 Classical Biometric Authentication and Template Protection Early fingerprint authentication systems relied on minutiae-based matching techniques. Jain et al. proposed a reliable fingerprint verification model achieving high accuracy under controlled environments. However, such systems store raw biometric templates, making them highly vulnerable to database breaches. Cancellable biometrics, proposed by Ratha et al., introduced non-invertible transformations to allow template revocation. Although effective to some extent, security depends on transformation secrecy, which can be compromised. Biometric cryptosystems such as the fuzzy vault scheme proposed by Juels and Sudan bind cryptographic keys with biometric features. While these systems tolerate biometric variability, they suffer from helper data leakage and correlation attacks. Hash-based biometric protection techniques provide strong irreversibility by storing only hashed templates. However, due to intra-class variations in biometric data, hash-based matching becomes challenging, motivating the need for similarity computation in protected domains. 2.2 Quantum Computing and Similarity Computation Several uploaded research papers discuss quantum similarity measures such as quantum cosine similarity, SWAP test–based fidelity estimation, and quantum kernel methods . These techniques demonstrate theoretical and experimental advantages in computing similarity between high-dimensional vectors. Quantum machine learning algorithms such as Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVM) have been applied to classification tasks and show competitive accuracy on small datasets. However, most studies assume direct access to raw feature vectors, which is unsuitable for sensitive biometric data. 2.3 Quantum-Assisted Biometric Authentication Recent works specifically explore quantum fingerprinting and quantum biometric matching. Papers such as those by Mogos et al. and Kipchirchir et al. demonstrate the feasibility of encoding fingerprint features into quantum states and performing matching using quantum algorithms. However, a critical limitation of these systems is that raw biometric features are directly encoded into quantum states, exposing biometric data to potential leakage during state preparation or measurement. Additionally, these approaches lack formal security models and do not consider post-quantum cryptographic protection for stored templates.

Problem Statement Biometric authentication systems, particularly fingerprint-based systems, are widely used due to their reliability and user convenience. However, traditional biometric authentication mechanisms store biometric templates in classical databases, making them vulnerable to template theft, replay attacks, and irreversible privacy loss. Once compromised, biometric data cannot be revoked or replaced like passwords or cryptographic keys. Furthermore, existing biometric security frameworks rely on classical cryptographic algorithms, which are increasingly threatened by advances in quantum computing. Recent research shows that quantum algorithms can potentially break commonly used public-key cryptographic schemes, rendering current biometric protection mechanisms inadequate for long-term security. Although recent studies have explored quantum-assisted fingerprint matching and quantum similarity computation, these approaches often directly encode raw biometric features into quantum states, leading to privacy leakage and lack of irreversible template protection. Additionally, many quantum biometric systems do not provide a complete end-to-end authentication pipeline that includes secure preprocessing, feature reduction, quantum encoding, matching, and verification. Therefore, there is a critical need to design a secure biometric authentication system that ensures irreversible biometric template protection, resists both classical and quantum attacks, and efficiently integrates quantum-assisted similarity computation without exposing sensitive biometric data.

Objectives The primary objective of this project is to design a secure fingerprint-based biometric authentication system using a hybrid classical–quantum approach that ensures privacy, robustness, and future quantum resistance. The system aims to implement effective data acquisition and preprocessing techniques to enhance fingerprint image quality, followed by feature extraction and dimensionality reduction to generate compact representations suitable for quantum encoding. Quantum feature encoding methods such as angle and amplitude encoding are employed to represent biometric features in quantum states, enabling quantum-assisted similarity computation through quantum circuits and measurement-based analysis. A threshold-based decision engine is developed to perform reliable identity verification while ensuring that raw biometric templates are neither stored nor directly exposed at any stage of the authentication process. The secondary objective of the project is to evaluate the feasibility and performance of the proposed framework using quantum simulators such as Qiskit. This includes analyzing authentication accuracy, security strength, and computational efficiency, as well as studying the impact of dimensionality reduction on quantum encoding fidelity and matching performance. The project also aims to compare the proposed quantum-assisted approach with conventional classical fingerprint authentication systems, assess resistance against common biometric attacks such as template theft and replay attacks, and design a scalable architecture capable of adapting to future advancements in quantum hardware and post-quantum security requirements.

Methodology The proposed QuMetric system follows a hybrid classical–quantum methodology designed to ensure secure biometric authentication while preserving privacy and future quantum resistance. The methodology strictly follows a layered pipeline starting from fingerprint acquisition to final identity verification. Phase 1: Data Acquisition and Preprocessing Fingerprint images are collected either through fingerprint sensors or publicly available datasets. Preprocessing techniques such as noise removal, normalization, binarization, and ridge enhancement are applied to improve image quality and reduce acquisition noise. Phase 2: Feature Extraction and Reduction Lightweight fingerprint features are extracted using pixel sampling and minutiae-lite techniques. Dimensionality reduction and normalization are applied to generate compact feature vectors suitable for quantum encoding and to minimize information loss. Phase 3: Quantum Feature Encoding The reduced feature vectors are encoded into quantum states using angle encoding or amplitude encoding methods. This step prepares classical biometric data for quantum-assisted similarity computation. Phase 4: Quantum Matching and Analysis Quantum circuits are executed to compute similarity between query and stored biometric templates. Measurement outcomes and probability distributions are analyzed to derive similarity scores using fidelity or distance-based metrics. Phase 5: Identity Verification A decision engine compares the similarity score with a predefined threshold and produces an authentication decision (Accept / Reject).

Conclusion The QuMetric project proposes a secure and future-ready biometric authentication framework that integrates classical image processing with quantum-assisted similarity computation. By avoiding direct exposure of raw biometric templates and leveraging quantum encoding techniques, the system enhances privacy, security, and scalability. The proposed approach addresses both current biometric security challenges and emerging quantum threats.

Future Scope Integration with real quantum hardware. Extension to multimodal biometrics (face, iris). Incorporation of post-quantum cryptographic storage. Optimization of quantum circuits for noise-resilient execution. Deployment in large-scale enterprise environments.

Introduction The rapid expansion of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has revolutionized modern healthcare by enabling real-time monitoring, remote diagnosis, personalized treatment, and continuous patient evaluation. IoMT represents the network of interconnected medical equipment along with applications that gather, transfer, and process health-related data. Medical devices deployed in hospitals and clinics continuously generate and transmit highly sensitive patient data, including vital signs such as heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, and SpO2 levels, diagnostic reports, medication records, treatment plans, and comprehensive monitoring information. The provision of effective diagnostics, individualized treatment regimens, and continuous evaluation for patients has been made possible by this interconnected ecosystem. Motivation The rapid growth of the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) has transformed modern healthcare by enabling real-time patient monitoring, remote diagnosis, and smart medical devices. However, this increased connectivity has also exposed healthcare systems to serious cyber security risks. Medical devices continuously transmit sensitive patient information such as heart rate, blood pressure, and diagnostic records, making them highly attractive targets for attackers. Most existing medical devices still rely on traditional cryptographic algorithms like RSA and ECC for security. These classical techniques are expected to become vulnerable with the emergence of quantum computers, which can break such encryption using advanced quantum algorithms. This creates a long-term threat where attackers may collect encrypted medical data today and decrypt it in the future, compromising patient privacy and hospital integrity.

Problem Statement The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) connects medical devices to enable real-time monitoring and data-driven healthcare, but it also exposes sensitive patient data to serious cybersecurity risks. Most existing devices rely on classical cryptographic algorithms such as RSA and ECC, which are vulnerable to future quantum computing attacks. This creates a “harvest now, decrypt later” threat where encrypted medical data may be compromised in the future. Replacing or modifying medical devices is costly due to strict regulatory and financial constraints. Therefore, a secure, affordable, and quantum-resistant protection mechanism is required to safeguard IoMT systems without altering existing hardware.

ABSTRACT The rapid proliferation of resource-constrained Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices has expanded the attack surface for large-scale botnets and Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) campaigns, creating an urgent need for lightweight, low-latency detection that can run on the network edge. This project designs, implements and evaluates a practical edge-deployable anomaly detection framework that combines a compact Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) front-end with Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) layers to capture spatial and temporal patterns in IoT network traffic. The system ingests live telemetry via MQTT, applies a robust, artifact-driven preprocessing pipeline (feature ordering, clipping, scaling and protocol mapping), and performs calibrated inference on devices such as a Raspberry Pi. A Streamlit dashboard provides live visualization, alerts and operational hooks for retraining or dataset upload. The multi-phase workflow covers reproducible preprocessing, class-imbalance aware training (weighted loss, mixup, early stopping), model calibration and an edge runtime path (ONNX/quantization) to minimize memory and latency. Experiments on standard IoT datasets (BoT-IoT, UNSW-NB15) demonstrate high detection performance (validation F1 ≈ 0.995) with real-time inference latency suitable for edge use (~8 ms/packet on Raspberry Pi) while keeping runtime memory and binary sizes compatible with constrained devices. The work highlights practical deployment considerations (health checks, thread limits, async logging) and points to future directions such as quantization/pruning, federated learning and attention mechanisms for improved generalization. Future Work The future of this edge-deployed system holds immense potential for further enhancements and 
applications. The following areas are identified as key directions for future research and 
development: • 
Advanced Model Optimization (Quantization & Pruning): A primary future goal is the 
full implementation of more aggressive model optimization techniques. By converting 
model weights from 32-bit floating-point numbers to 8-bit or even 4-bit integers 
(quantization), the model's memory footprint and computational cost can be drastically 
reduced. Further, pruning irrelevant connections or neurons can simplify the model. This 
would enable the deployment of this high-accuracy model on even more resource-
constrained devices, such as low-cost microcontrollers, making the solution more 
universally applicable across a broader spectrum of IoT devices. • 
Decentralized Collaborative Learning (Federated Learning): To enhance the model's 
ability to detect new threats without compromising user privacy, federated learning can 
be implemented. In this architecture, a fleet of deployed edge devices would 
collaboratively train a global model. Each device would train on its own local data, and 
only the model updates (weights), not the raw network traffic, would be sent to a central 
server. This allows the entire system to learn from new, evolving attack patterns seen by 
any single device, creating a more robust, adaptive, and privacy-preserving defense 
mechanism.

Introduction Children with dyslexia face unique challenges in early education, especially with letter recognition, sound-symbol associations, and reading fluency. Traditional classroom methods, which heavily rely on text and memorization, often fail to meet their needs—leading to frustration, low confidence, and slower academic growth.
To overcome these barriers, this project introduces [NAME] (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) as tools to create multi-sensory, interactive learning experiences. Instead of passive reading, dyslexic students can see, hear, and interact with letters and objects in a 3D environment. For instance, learning the letter “B” can be enhanced by viewing it in virtual space, hearing its pronunciation —reinforcing memory and understanding.
Developed using Unity 3D, and deployable on mobile AR and low-cost VR headsets, the platform promotes inclusive, adaptive learning by tailoring pace and content to individual needs. By reducing cognitive overload and replacing text-heavy instruction with visual and auditory cues, this project aims to empower dyslexic students with a more engaging, accessible, and confidence-building approach to foundational literacy. Motivation In today’s classrooms, not every student learns the same way—especially those with dyslexia, who often find it hard to keep up with traditional, text-heavy teaching. Struggling to recognize letters, connect sounds, or follow along can make learning frustrating and affect a child’s confidence early on. This project is about changing that. By using Augmented Reality (AR) and [NAME] (VR), we’re creating an interactive way for kids to actually see, hear, and explore what they’re learning. Imagine a student walking around a big 3D letter "A" and watching an apple appear beside it while hearing “A for Apple”—learning becomes more natural and fun. The best part? It works on everyday devices like mobile phones and affordable VR headsets, so it’s easy to use at school or home. This is about helping every child feel confident, supported, and excited to learn.

Problem Statement The core problem is that traditional educational methods and most digital learning tools are not designed to support the unique cognitive needs of dyslexic students. These approaches rely heavily on text, lack sensory engagement, and do not adapt to individual learning styles, making it difficult for dyslexic children to recognize letters, connect sounds, and retain information. As a result, many struggle with confidence, attention, and academic performance, especially in early literacy development where foundational skills are crucial. Sr.

Conclusion This project explores how Augemented Reality (AR) and [NAME](VR) can make a real difference in how children with dyslexia learn during their early years. Traditional methods that rely on text alone often leave these students feeling frustrated and left behind. By creating a more hands-on, interactive experience—where kids can see, hear, and play with letters and sounds—AR and VR turn learning into something more natural and engaging. The platform adjusts to each child’s pace, helping them learn in a way that feels comfortable and supportive. It’s also designed to be accessible, using mobile devices and affordable VR headsets so more students can benefit. Looking ahead, it can grow to include subjects like numbers or grammar. At its heart, this project is about helping dyslexic students build confidence and enjoy learning in a way that truly works for them.

Abstract
Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a serious blood cancer that causes too many
immature lymphocytes to form in the bone marrow. Detecting its stages early—beginner,
early, pre-leukemic, and pro-leukemic—is important for timely treatment and better
outcomes. Traditional methods, which involve manually examining blood smear images
under a microscope, can be slow and may lead to different results depending on who is
looking. In this project, we propose a deep learning-based framework for automated white
blood cell (WBC) classification and confidence estimation to identify the stages of ALL from
microscopic images. The methodology involves preprocessing a publicly available dataset
of labeled microscopic WBC images, followed by the implementation of (CNNs) for feature
extraction and stage classification. To ensure reliability in clinical decision-making, our
approach incorporates confidence estimation techniques. This enables the system not only
to classify the stages but also to provide confidence levels for each prediction, aiding in
trust and interpretability. Performance metrics will be evaluated to validate the model. This
study aims to assist medical professionals with a robust, interpretable, and reliable tool for
ALL diagnosis, ultimately contributing to faster and more accurate clinical workflows in
hematopathology. Future scope includes expanding the model to multi-class cancer
detection and real-time clinical deployment.
Keywords— Tensorflow, Python, Confidence estimation, softmax probability, Image

ABSTRACT Internal cracks in pipeline systems pose serious risks to industrial safety, environmental protection, and operational reliability, particularly in aging pipelines used for transporting oil, gas, water, and chemicals. Manual inspection of internal pipelines is often unsafe, time-consuming, and unreliable due to confined spaces, low visibility, and hazardous conditions. To address these challenges, this work presents an autonomous robotic system for internal pipeline crack detection using artificial intelligence. The proposed system utilizes a mobile in-pipe robotic platform equipped with a low-cost vision sensor to capture internal surface images during inspection. An image-based hybrid deep learning framework is employed, where YOLOv8 is used for real-time crack detection and localization, and an Attention U-Net model performs pixel-level crack segmentation for precise visualization. Image-processing techniques are further applied to estimate crack length and width, enabling quantitative defect assessment. The system is designed to operate reliably under practical internal pipeline conditions such as low illumination, surface noise, motion blur, and limited visibility. Experimental results demonstrate effective detection of small and fine internal cracks, along with structured visual outputs and measurements to support maintenance decisions. By integrating autonomous robotic mobility with robust AI-based vision models, the proposed approach provides a cost-effective, scalable, and reliable solution for automated internal pipeline inspection. Keywords: Internal Pipeline Inspection, Crack Detection, Autonomous Robotics, Artificial Intelligence, Deep Learning, YOLOv8, Attention U-Net. Page | 3

INTRODUCTION Crack formation in critical infrastructure has emerged as a major engineering concern due to aging materials, prolonged operational loads, corrosion, and harsh environmental conditions. Among various infrastructure elements, pipelines play a vital role in the transportation of water, oil, gas, and industrial fluids, making their structural integrity extremely important. Cracks in pipelines often initiate as micro-defects and gradually propagate under internal pressure and environmental stress, leading to leakage, contamination, economic loss, and in severe cases, catastrophic failure. In addition to pipelines, similar crack-related issues are also observed in roads, bridges, tunnels, and concrete structures, further emphasizing the need for reliable inspection systems. Traditional pipeline crack inspection methods largely depend on manual surveys, shutdown-based inspection, or contact-based sensing techniques, which are expensive, 
time-consuming, 
and 
sometimes 
unsafe. 
Pipelines 
located underground, underwater, or in hazardous industrial environments pose significant challenges for human inspectors. Moreover, manual inspection may fail to identify fine surface cracks or early-stage defects, and inspection outcomes often vary based on operator experience and visibility conditions. While automated inspection techniques such as ultrasonic and acoustic methods have been used, they require specialized equipment and are not always suitable for continuous monitoring. In recent years, image-based crack detection using computer vision and deep learning has gained attention as a non-contact and cost-effective alternative [1], Page | 4 [8]. However, many existing approaches rely on high-resolution images captured under controlled lighting and static conditions, limiting their effectiveness in real- world pipeline environments. Factors such as motion blur, uneven illumination, surface rust, and noise significantly reduce detection accuracy in practical scenarios. The proposed project addresses these limitations by developing an image-based pipeline crack detection system deployed on a mobile robotic platform. A low-cost camera is used to capture real-time images of pipeline surfaces during inspection. Deep learning models are employed to automatically detect, localize, and segment crack regions from captured images. The system is designed to operate under realistic field conditions and does not require manual image acquisition or shutdown of pipeline operations. By enabling early-stage crack detection and quantitative analysis, the proposed solution aims to reduce inspection risk, minimize maintenance costs, and enhance pipeline safety. Additionally, the framework can be extended to other

Additionally, the framework can be extended to other infrastructure systems such as tunnels and bridges, making it a scalable solution for automated structural health monitoring. Page | 5

PROPOSED SYSTEM 1. Data Collection: The methodology begins with the collection of crack images relevant to pipeline surfaces from publicly available datasets, along with real-time images captured using an ESP32- CAM mounted on an RC car–based mobile robotic platform. The collected data includes variations in crack size, orientation, lighting conditions, surface corrosion, and background noise to represent realistic inspection environments. 2. Image Preprocessing and Augmentation: The collected images are preprocessed to improve data consistency and visibility of crack patterns. Preprocessing steps include resizing images to a fixed input resolution, noise reduction, and contrast enhancement. To ensure robustness under real-world conditions, data augmentation techniques such as rotation, brightness variation, and motion blur simulation are applied, enabling the models to generalize effectively during live inspection. 3. Model Selection: Appropriate deep learning models are selected based on accuracy, computational efficiency, and suitability for real-time applications. An object detection model is chosen for fast localization of crack regions, while a segmentation model is selected for precise pixel-level extraction of cracks [8], [11]. The selection ensures a balance between detection performance and deployment feasibility on resource-constrained systems. 4. Model Implementation and Training: The selected models are implemented using a deep learning framework and trained on the prepared dataset. During training, annotated images are used to learn crack features, while validation is performed to prevent overfitting. Model performance is evaluated using standard metrics to ensure reliable crack detection and segmentation under varying conditions. Page | 6 5. Crack Detection and Segmentation Pipeline: During inference, the detection model first identifies potential crack regions and generates bounding boxes. These regions are then processed by the segmentation model to obtain detailed crack masks. This sequential approach improves accuracy while maintaining real- time processing capability [8]. 6. Crack Measurement and Analysis: The segmented crack output is further processed using image analysis techniques to estimate crack length and width. These measurements provide quantitative information useful for assessing crack severity and structural condition. 7. Integration with ESP32-CAM and Mobile Platform: The trained models are integrated with the RC car–based mobile robotic platform. The ESP32-CAM captures live images of pipeline surfaces during movement. These images are

and Analysis: The segmented crack output is further processed using image analysis techniques to estimate crack length and width. These measurements provide quantitative information useful for assessing crack severity and structural condition. 7. Integration with ESP32-CAM and Mobile Platform: The trained models are integrated with the RC car–based mobile robotic platform. The ESP32-CAM captures live images of pipeline surfaces during movement. These images are transmitted to the processing unit through wireless communication, enabling real-time analysis without manual intervention. 8. Live Detection and Data Transfer: Captured image frames are sent from the ESP32-CAM to the processing system for live crack detection. The detection results, including annotated images and crack measurements, are transmitted back and displayed in real time. This enables continuous monitoring during inspection. 9. Output Visualization and Reporting: The final system generates visual outputs with detected cracks, bounding boxes, segmentation masks, and crack dimensions. Structured inspection results are produced to support maintenance decision-making. Page | 7

CONCLUSION The project titled “Internal Pipeline Crack Detection Using Artificial Intelligence And Robot” demonstrates a practical approach to automated crack detection and measurement using deep learning and a mobile robotic platform. By combining image preprocessing with parallel detection and segmentation models, the system accurately identifies cracks under real-world conditions. The proposed solution offers a reliable and cost-effective alternative to manual inspection, supporting efficient infrastructure monitoring and maintenance. Page | 9 Page | 9

1. Introduction This project aims to implement a Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Authentication System that allows users to log in securely without revealing their password to the server. The system generates a random number and combines it with the password to create a proof, which is then verified by the server using a simple mathematical challenge. Traditional login systems require users to send and store passwords on the server, which exposes them to risks like hacking, phishing, and data breaches. Zero-Knowledge Proof is a cryptographic method where a user can prove they know a secret without actually revealing it, making it a promising solution for secure authentication. The purpose of this project is to build a secure and privacy- preserving authentication mechanism. It removes the need to store sensitive information on the server, reduces the risk of password theft, and enhances user trust. By using simple random numbers and mathematical operations, this system is easy to implement and demonstrates the core idea of ZKP in a practical way.

2. Literature Review Authentication and identity verification are critical aspects of secure communication in 
digital systems.Traditionally, password-based authentication has been the most commonly used method, where users’ passwords are stored (often encrypted) on the server. However, research has shown that even encrypted passwords are vulnerable to theft, brute-force attacks, and phishing. • 
To overcome these vulnerabilities, Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKP) have been proposed as a privacy-preserving authentication mechanism.In 1986, Amos Fiat and Adi Shamir introduced the Fiat-Shamir Identification Protocol, which allowed a user to prove knowledge of a secret without revealing the secret itself. This became one of the first practical applications of ZKP in authentication. • 
Later advancements, such as the zk-SNARKs and zk-STARKs frameworks, demonstrated ZKP’s applicability to blockchain and cryptocurrency (e.g., Zcash), showing that ZKPs could be deployed at scale while preserving privacy. More recently, Mysten Labs (2023) proposed zkLogin, a passwordless login method. These studies highlight that ZKP is a powerful tool for secure authentication, but existing implementations tend to be either highly complex (like in blockchain) or require third-party services (like OAuth in zkLogin). How This Project Adds to Existing Knowledge:- While prior research and systems have demonstrated the feasibility of ZKP-based authentication, most require: • Complex cryptographic libraries 
• Significant computational resources 
• Integration with blockchain or third-party services 
Our project simplifies ZKP authentication by: • Removing the need for blockchain or third-party 
identity providers. 
• Using a lightweight, web-based implementation 
with random numbers and basic mathematical 
operations (like addition or subtraction) to create 
and verify the proof. 
• Making ZKP authentication accessible and 
demonstrable on a standard client–server model, 
with clear educational value.

3. Problem Statement Primary Goals of the Project :- The primary goal of this project is to develop a secure authentication system that allows a user to prove their identity without 
revealing 
their 
password 
to 
the 
server. It aims to eliminate the need to store sensitive information on the server while maintaining a simple and user-friendly login process. In traditional login systems, passwords are sent to and stored on the server, which exposes them to risks such as: • Database breaches and password leaks 
• Phishing attacks 
• Replay attacks using previously captured login 
requests 
This project addresses these risks by applying the principles of Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP), where the user can prove knowledge of a password without transmitting it or having it stored on the server. What the Project Intends to Achieve :- • Design and implement a passwordless authentication system where: 1. The password is only held temporarily on the 
client device. 
2. The server verifies a proof without learning the 
password. 
• Incorporate a random number and mathematical challenge mechanism to generate and validate the proof. • Create a working web-based prototype to demonstrate the feasibility of ZKP authentication in a simplified manner.

Objectives :- 1. Develop a client–server authentication system using ZKP 
principles. 2. Generate a random number at login and combine it with 
the password to create a proof. 
3. Ensure that the proof is sufficient for the server to verify 
identity without knowing the password. 
4. Use simple mathematical operations (like addition or 
subtraction) as part of the server’s challenge. 
5. Demonstrate an authentication flow that enhances privacy, 
improves security, and reduces the risks associated with 
password storage.

4. Methodology Description of Methods and Procedures :- This project follows a client–server model where authentication is performed without sending or storing the user’s password on the server. Instead, the system uses a random number and a mathematical challenge–response mechanism, inspired by Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) principles, to validate the user’s identity securely. At login: • The user enters their password on the client device. 
• A random number is generated locally. 
• A proof is created by combining the password and 
random number using simple arithmetic. 
• The proof is sent to the server, which ignores the 
password and focuses on the random number. 
• The server issues a challenge (e.g., add or subtract 
the random number). 
• The user solves the challenge and sends the answer 
back. 
• The server verifies the answer and grants or denies 
access accordingly.

System Architecture :- The system is divided into: Client Side: • Password entry 
• Random number generation • Proof creation 
• Challenge solver Server Side: • Receives proof and random number 
• Sends challenge (add/subtract) 
• Verifies response Algorithm :- 1. User enters password. 
2. Client generates random number r. 
3. Client computes: 
 proof = password + r 
4. Client sends proof and r to server. 
5. Server chooses challenge: Add or Subtract r. 
6. User computes: 
 answer = password + r (if challenge = add) 
 or 
 answer = password - r (if challenge = subtract) 
7. Server verifies if the answer matches expected value → login 
success or failure. Tools, Technologies, and Resources Required :- • Languages: Python (for backend), HTML, CSS, JavaScript (for 
frontend) 
• Frameworks: Flask (web server) 
• Libraries: random, hashlib (optional), math functions 
• Development Tools: VS Code / PyCharm, Postman, browser 
DevTools 
• Hardware: Standard computer/server with browser support 
• Environment: Localhost or web server Data Collection and Analysis Techniques :- • Data is generated dynamically for each session; no sensitive data 
is permanently stored. 
• Server collects random number and proof per session for 
validation. • Verification involves comparing user’s response against the 
computed expected value. 5. Project Plan and Timeline Project Plan and Timeline for ZKP Authentication System A project plan for ZKP Authentication System involves several key stages. Month 1: Literature Review & Study In the first month, we will research the principles of Zero- Knowledge Proofs, study existing authentication mechanisms, and understand how challenge–response models work. This phase lays the foundation of theoretical knowledge for the project. Month 2: System Design During the second month, we will design the overall system architecture and workflows, create block diagrams, and define the interactions between client and server components clearly. Month 3: Frontend & Backend Setup In the third month, we will set up the technical environment. This includes building the Flask server for the backend and designing the user interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on the frontend. Month 4: Implementation In the fourth month, the main development work will take

create block diagrams, and define the interactions between client and server components clearly. Month 3: Frontend & Backend Setup In the third month, we will set up the technical environment. This includes building the Flask server for the backend and designing the user interface with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript on the frontend. Month 4: Implementation In the fourth month, the main development work will take place. The client-side logic for proof generation and the server- side logic for verifying the proof and issuing challenges will be implemented. Month 5: Testing & Debugging In the fifth month, we will conduct thorough testing of the system. This involves unit testing, integration testing, identifying and fixing bugs, and refining the system for better performance and usability. Month 6: Documentation & Reporting In the sixth and final month, the focus will be on preparing the complete project documentation and reporting. This includes writing a detailed project report covering all sections such as

methodology, implementation details, results, and conclusion. 6. Expected Outcomes The project is expected to deliver a functional Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Authentication System that demonstrates how users can authenticate securely without transmitting or storing their passwords on the server. The key expected outcomes of the project include: • A working client–server prototype where authentication is 
performed using random number generation, proof creation, and 
challenge–response verification. 
• A login system that is privacy-preserving, ensuring that the 
password remains on the client side and is never exposed to the 
server. 
• Demonstration of a secure and user-friendly authentication flow 
based on simple mathematical operations, making it accessible and 
easy to understand. 
• A documented implementation of ZKP principles in a web-based 
environment, which can serve as an educational reference for 
students and developers interested in cryptography. 
• Improved security over traditional password-based systems by 
eliminating risks such as password storage, phishing, and replay 
attacks. Potential Impact or Applications : • Can be applied in secure web portals or applications 
where privacy of user credentials is critical. • Acts as a learning model for implementing advanced 
cryptographic concepts in real-world scenarios. 
• Can inspire further research into lightweight, practical 
implementations of Zero-Knowledge Proofs in 
authentication systems.

Abstract Insider threats remain a critical challenge in organizational cybersecurity, given the trusted access insiders possess and the subtle nature of their malicious or negligent actions. This paper presents “A Behaviour-Driven Approach to Insider Threat Detection in Organizational Systems”, which leverages behavioural analytics to identify anomalies in user activity that may indicate potential insider threats. The

proposed system establishes dynamic behavioural baselines for individual users by monitoring patterns such as access frequency, file usage, login times, and resource interactions. Any significant deviation from these baselines is flagged through a risk- scoring mechanism that aids security teams in assessing and responding to threats in real time. The study includes a detailed evaluation of real-world insider threat incidents, with a focus on Indian organizations, and compares the effectiveness of current detection techniques across key metrics such as accuracy, false positive rate, and operational success. The integration of machine learning techniques further strengthens the system’s predictive capabilities and supports automated threat mitigation strategies. By aligning behavioural intelligence with adaptive detection mechanisms, this approach provides a scalable and proactive solution to safeguard organizational systems against insider threats. Introduction to Guardian: A Human-Risk Aware Security System for Proactive Breach Prevention In today’s digital and interconnected organizational environments, cybersecurity has become a critical concern, particularly with respect to insider threats. Insider threats originate from users who already possess authorized access to organizational systems, making their activities difficult to detect using traditional security mechanisms. With the increased adoption of cloud computing, remote work, and digital collaboration platforms, monitoring internal user behavior has become more complex. This project presents a conceptual AI-based insider threat detection dashboard that demonstrates how employee behavior can be observed, analyzed, and visualized to identify potentially risky activities. The focus of this work is on demonstrating the concept and visual interpretation of insider threat detection rather than full-scale system implementation. Motivation The rapid expansion of digital infrastructure, cloud services, and remote work has significantly increased the risk of insider threats in modern organizations. Insiders already possess authorized access, allowing malicious or unintentional misuse of systems without triggering traditional security controls. Rule-based detection mechanisms are ineffective against evolving and subtle insider behaviors, while dynamic work patterns make accurate behavior classification difficult. Although machine learning improves detection capabilities, many solutions operate as black boxes and fail to provide clear explanations. Security teams often face alert fatigue due to large volumes of low-context alerts, increasing investigation time and operational overhead. There is a strong need for systems that combine behavioral analysis with explainable insights to improve analyst trust. By presenting risks through clear visualization and ranked scoring, security teams can focus on high-risk users more efficiently. This project is motivated by the goal of enabling proactive, transparent, and human-centric insider threat detection.

Problem Statement Insider threats represent one of the most challenging cybersecurity problems faced by modern organizations. Since insiders already have legitimate access to systems and sensitive information, their malicious actions often go unnoticed by traditional security tools. Rule-based and signature-driven detection mechanisms fail to identify slow-moving, unknown, or changing insider behaviors. Although machine learning-based solutions offer improved detection capabilities, many of them operate as black-box systems and do not provide clear explanations for generated alerts. This lack of explainability reduces analyst confidence and increases investigation time. Furthermore, employees access systems from multiple locations, devices, and networks, making it difficult to accurately distinguish between normal and suspicious behavior. As a result, there is a need for a behavior-aware and explainable system that can effectively detect insider threats while reducing investigation effort and operational overhead. ABSTRACT Millions of people it is very difficult to apply for important government documents like income certificates, caste certificates, and proof of domicile, especially if they live in rural areas or have limited digital skills in India. Dispersed portals, unclear instructions, inconsistent state-by-state procedures, and district-level these all factors complicate the process. These problems often result in process errors, frequent office visits, and the exclusion of less technical expertized individuals. We have developed GovGuideBot, an AI-powered chat-bot that explains government documentation procedures, to address this issue. It provides easy-to-use, location-based, step-by-step assistance. In order to understand user intent, the system uses a Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline that is optimized with transform-er models like BERT. Named Entity Recognition (NER) is used to identify crucial information such as document type, state, and district. These specifics are arranged in structured JSON workflows that enable region-specific instructions. GovGuideBot also uses location entered by user query to adapt procedures for user locations, links to official government websites to guarantee accuracy, and uses the YouTube Data API to offer visual tutorials which are particularly useful for users who might have literacy issues or are using these services for the first time. With a precision of 91%, a recall of 93%, and an overall F1-score of 92% for identifying intents and entities, GovGuideBot performs well when tested on actual citizen questions. About half of the planned features were successfully implemented in the working prototype we created for Maharashtra, which includes workflows for income, caste, and domicile certificates. By supporting multiple languages and media formats, GovGuideBot demonstrates how chatbot technology can improve access for more people, decrease needless visits to service sites, and reduce procedural errors. Evolution of Chatbots Chatbots have evolved from simple rule-based systems to advanced AI-driven conversational models. Early chatbots like ELIZA (1966) and ALICE (1995) relied on keyword matching and handcrafted rules to generate responses. However, they lacked contextual understanding and adaptability. The emergence of transformer-based models such as BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) by Google and GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) by OpenAI marked a major breakthrough in language comprehension and text generation, leading to more natural, coherent, and human-like interactions. Chatbots in Public Service and E-Governance Recent years have seen increasing adoption of chatbots in the public sector to simplify citizen-government interactions. Several governments have introduced AI-powered assistants such as: a) Umang (India) – A unified mobile app providing access to central and state government services. b) AskDISHA (Indian Railways) – A conversational chatbot designed to assist users with ticket bookings and inquiries. c) Gov.sg WhatsApp Bot (Singapore) – Used to share verified government updates and GovGuideBot: AI Chatbot for Government Document Assistance GHRCEM, Department of [NAME], 2025 9 information with citizens. ABSTRACT Efficient accounts receivable management and cash-flow predictability continue to be major 
challenges for small and mid-sized manufacturing enterprises, even with the adoption of digital 
billing systems. Issues such as delayed customer payments, inconsistent credit terms, and lack 
of forward-looking insights often lead to liquidity constraints and reactive financial decisions. 
This paper presents “A Unified ETL Framework and Predictive Analytics System for Deal-
Level Risk Assessment in Manufacturing SMEs,” a data-driven framework that shifts 
traditional retrospective receivables analysis toward proactive financial intelligence. The system utilizes historical billing data, transaction records, payment delays, and deal-
specific attributes to develop predictive models that forecast receivable realization timelines 
and future cash inflows. By analyzing customer payment behavior, frequency of delays, and 
contractual terms, the model classifies deals based on payment reliability and cash-flow risk. 
It integrates time-series forecasting techniques along with financial indicators such as Days 
Sales Outstanding (DSO) and Cash Conversion Cycle (CCC) to improve visibility into working 
capital. Unlike conventional aging-based reporting, the proposed system dynamically adapts 
to changing payment patterns and enables early identification of high-risk receivables, allowing 
timely financial intervention. The framework has been validated using real-world manufacturing data from an Indian 
industrial context, demonstrating enhanced accuracy in cash-flow prediction and better 
decision support compared to traditional methods. Overall, MFG360 provides a scalable and 
cost-effective approach to improving liquidity management and financial resilience in 
manufacturing enterprises. Domain: Machine Learning, Data Engineering Keywords: Accounts Receivable Analytics, Cash-Flow Forecasting, Predictive Analytics, Financial Risk Classification, Manufacturing Finance iv TABLE OF CONTENTS Page No. CERTIFICATE

ALL arises from clonal expansion of immature lymphoid cells. While some genetic syndromes (e.g., Down syndrome, Fanconi anemia) and environmental factors (radiation, pesticides, viruses like EBV, HIV) increase risk, most cases are de novo [2]. The morphological differences between the stages of ALL are often subtle and not easily distinguishable by the human eye, especially in the early stages [3].

Leukemia (ALL) is a rapidly progressing and life-threatening blood cancer primarily affecting children but also present in adults. It disrupts normal blood cell formation by producing immature lymphocytes, leading to severe health complications if not diagnosed and treated early. The urgency for early and accurate diagnosis cannot be overstated, as treatment protocols and patient outcomes are highly dependent on correctly identifying the stage of disease progression. Traditionally, the diagnosis and staging of ALL rely on the manual examination of microscopic images of blood or bone marrow smears by trained hematologists. While effective, this process is inherently time-consuming, labor-intensive, and subject to inter-observer variability, especially in the early stages where morphological differences between subtypes are extremely subtle. These limitations can lead to delayed treatment, misclassification, and suboptimal care. With the increasing availability of digital medical data and advancements in artificial intelligence, particularly in deep learning and computer vision, there is now a promising opportunity to automate and standardize this diagnostic workflow. Deep learning models, especially Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), this project aims to bridge the gap between manual diagnosis and intelligent automation by developing a robust deep learning-based system that can accurately classify WBC microscopic images into four clinically meaningful stages: begining, early, pre, and pro. Incorporating confidence estimation techniques ensures not only high accuracy but also interpretability and trust.

ABSTRACT Insider threats, particularly those involving trusted users exploiting legitimate access credentials, remain one of the most difficult and costly security challenges facing organizations today. Early detection and continuous behavioral monitoring are essential to reducing the damage such threats cause before they are ever discovered. In response to this challenge, we present Guardian, a human-risk aware insider threat detection platform that integrates machine learning with Explainable AI to deliver a comprehensive and analyst-ready security solution. Guardian continuously monitors user activities by processing session-level telemetry including file access operations, data export volumes, and login timestamps. Each incoming event is scored in real time by a 100-tree Random Forest ensemble, which evaluates three behavioral signals to distinguish normal user patterns from suspicious activity that may indicate an insider threat in progress. What sets Guardian apart is its commitment to transparency — every risk score is accompanied by a SHAP-based explanation that tells an analyst not just that something is wrong, but precisely which behavioral features drove the suspicion and by how much. This transforms each alert from a verdict to second-guess into an investigation brief that any analyst can act on immediately. Validated against a live simulated corpus of 2,057 activity records spanning 200 employees over six days of continuous operation, Guardian flagged all 42 threat events with zero false positives and a median scoring latency of 5.795 ms per event — well within the threshold required for synchronous real-time scoring. Results are surfaced through a React 19 dashboard that provides live visibility into organizational security posture, prioritized alert feeds ranked by risk score, and per-user activity timelines accessible without leaving the interface. ABSTRACT Academic credential verification is fundamental to admissions, employment, and professional licensing across institutions and industries worldwide. Traditional verification methods — including manual checks, centralized databases, and direct institutional communication — are slow, costly, and critically vulnerable to document forgery, unauthorized modification, and administrative delays. The growing global mobility of students and professionals has further amplified the urgency for a reliable, fast, and trust-independent verification infrastructure. This project presents Vardox, a public-blockchain anchored academic credential verification architecture. Vardox leverages cryptographic hashing (SHA-256), Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), Ethereum smart contracts written in Solidity, and distributed off-chain storage via the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to deliver a complete credential lifecycle management system. Issuing authorities digitally sign documents, generate SHA-256 cryptographic hashes, and anchor these proofs immutably on the Ethereum blockchain. The original documents are stored off-chain via Pinata's IPFS pinning service, while the blockchain serves as the permanent, tamper-proof source of truth for authenticity verification. A file-upload-based verification interface abstracts blockchain complexity for non-technical verifiers, enabling instant document authenticity checks without blockchain knowledge or direct contact with the issuing institution. The system introduces a dual account model — organisations (issuers) and individuals (recipients) — each with distinct dashboard functionalities. An npm SDK (@yashodeep/vardox-sdk) and a versioned REST API (GET /api/v1/verify) enable seamless programmatic integration for external employers, HR systems, and regulatory bodies. Experimental evaluation on 200 test cases demonstrates 100% tamper detection accuracy, zero false positive rate, average end-to-end verification time of 2.8 seconds (compared to 3-7 days for traditional methods), and blockchain hash retrieval latency of 1.2 seconds on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet. The system is built using Next.js, Node.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Solidity, and PostgreSQL with Prisma ORM. Domain: Blockchain Technology, Cryptography, Decentralized Systems, Web Engineering

CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION 1.1 Overview Academic credential verification plays a critical role in admissions, recruitment, and professional validation globally. As student and professional mobility increases across institutions and national boundaries, the demand for reliable, timely, and trust-independent cross-institutional verification has grown significantly. Institutions, employers, and regulatory bodies require fast, accurate confirmation that academic credentials presented by individuals are genuine, unaltered, and issued by recognized authorities. Traditional verification practices rely on manual processes, centralized databases, or direct communication with issuing institutions — approaches that are slow, expensive, and inefficient. These methods are further compromised by vulnerability to document forgery, unauthorized modification, and administrative delays. Even where digital certificates and hashing techniques have been introduced, most systems store verification records in centralized repositories, requiring verifiers to trust the database administrator and creating single points of failure that undermine verification integrity. Vardox is a public-blockchain anchored academic credential verification architecture that addresses all of these challenges. By anchoring cryptographic document proofs immutably on the Ethereum blockchain, Vardox eliminates the need for any centralized authority in the verification process. Any verifier — employer, university, regulatory body — can independently confirm a document's authenticity by checking the blockchain, which is publicly auditable, tamper-proof, and permanently accessible without institutional permission. 1.2 Motivation The global prevalence of counterfeit academic certificates has caused enormous damage to institutions, employers, and legitimate credential holders. The International Qualifications Assessment Service estimates that credential fraud costs economies billions of dollars annually through misplaced hiring decisions, compromised academic integrity, and fraudulent professional licensing. Traditional verification methods fail in several critical dimensions. Manual verification through institutional communication typically takes 3–7 business days or longer for international credentials. Centralized digital verification portals, while faster, remain single points of failure: a database breach, administrative error, or institutional shutdown can permanently compromise verification capability. PKI-based digital signatures improve document integrity but still require verifiers to trust the issuing institution's key management infrastructure — an assumption that is difficult to guarantee across borders and over time.

Additionally, existing blockchain-based credential systems have focused heavily on technical implementation while neglecting usability and practical adoption. Complex blockchain interactions, wallet management, and smart contract knowledge create insurmountable barriers for most employers, HR professionals, and university admissions officers. Vardox is equally motivated by the need to abstract all blockchain complexity behind a simple file-upload verification interface and a one-command SDK, making the system immediately accessible to non-technical users. 1.3 Problem Definition and Objectives The increasing mobility of students and professionals has significantly raised the demand for reliable and timely academic credential verification. Traditional verification practices depend on manual checks, centralised databases, or direct communication with issuing institutions, which are often slow, costly, and inefficient. These methods are vulnerable to document forgery, unauthorised modification, and administrative delays, especially when verification is required across institutions, organisations, or national boundaries. Although digital certificates and document hashing techniques have been introduced to improve security, most existing systems store verification records in centralised databases. Such approaches still require verifiers to trust the issuing authority or database administrators, creating single points of failure and increasing the risk of insider manipulation or data breaches. Furthermore, verification processes are often fragmented, lacking a unified workflow that seamlessly connects credential issuance, storage, and third-party verification.

The problem is therefore to design a secure, scalable, and trust-independent academic document verification system that: (1) enables institutions to issue tamper-proof credentials anchored on a public blockchain, (2) allows any third party to verify document authenticity without institutional contact, (3) provides a user-friendly interface accessible to non-technical verifiers, and (4) delivers a programmable API and SDK for integration into existing employer and HR systems. 1.4 Project Scope and Limitations Vardox encompasses the complete lifecycle of academic credential management from initial document issuance through blockchain anchoring, IPFS storage, and third-party verification. The system supports two account types — organisations (issuers) and individuals (recipients) — with role-specific dashboards. An npm SDK and versioned REST API enable external system integration. The verification interface requires only file upload, with no blockchain knowledge needed by the verifier. Current limitations include: (1) Dependence on Ethereum gas fees for on-chain transactions, requiring wallets to be funded via testnet faucets during evaluation. Full mainnet deployment would require gas optimization through Layer 2 solutions. (2) IPFS content availability depends on active pinning via Pinata; the system includes a graceful fallback to hash-only verification if IPFS is unavailable. (3) Credential revocation is not yet implemented on-chain; a revoked credential would require off-chain registry marking. (4) QR-code-based document embedding and zero-knowledge proof selective disclosure are targeted as future work. 1.5 Project Aim

CHAPTER 2: LITERATURE SURVEY The literature survey examines four categories of prior work: (i) traditional academic document verification systems, (ii) blockchain-based credential management frameworks, (iii) decentralized identity and verifiable credential systems, and (iv) privacy-preserving and scalability-focused approaches. 2.1 Traditional Academic Document Verification Systems Early academic credential verification systems relied exclusively on centralised databases maintained by universities or third-party agencies. While effective in controlled institutional environments, such systems suffer fundamentally from single points of failure, delayed verification, and complete dependence on the issuing authority's continued operation and cooperation. To reduce fraud, several studies introduced digital signatures and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) for certificate authentication. Digitally signed PDFs significantly reduce tampering risks at the document level; however, these systems still require verifiers to trust the issuing institution's key management and database integrity, making them vulnerable to insider threats and database manipulation. Rifat and Hossain (2025) demonstrated that SHA-256 and ECDSA based certificate generation systems provide strong tamper-evidence at the document level but fail to guarantee global verifiability without an immutable public ledger — the verification record itself remains mutable. Hash-based verification methods were subsequently introduced, where document hashes are stored in centralized databases. Mehta and Kulkarni (2025) demonstrated that although hashing ensures document integrity at the time of issuance, centralized hash storage does not prevent unauthorized modification by database administrators and lacks global verifiability. An administrator with database access could silently alter or delete hash records, destroying verification integrity. Casino et al. (2025) conducted a systematic review of blockchain applications in education and identified that the majority of institutions still rely on legacy manual verification workflows that are neither scalable nor resistant to document fraud. 2.2 Blockchain-Based Credential Management Frameworks Recent research strongly emphasizes blockchain as a tamper-resistant ledger for credential verification, addressing the fundamental limitation of centralized hash storage. Zhang et al. (2025) proposed a blockchain-based degree certificate verification platform recording certificate hashes on Ethereum, demonstrating improved trust and significantly reduced verification time compared to centralized systems. Their work established the core architectural pattern of hash anchoring on public blockchains.
