ABSTRACT Insider threats, particularly those exploiting legitimate credentials, are a leading cause of organizational security breaches worldwide. Early detection and continuous monitoring of user behavior play a pivotal role in reducing the associated risks. In response to this challenge, we introduce a Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System, an innovative Machine Learning project that seamlessly integrates with Explainable AI to provide a comprehensive solution for organizational security management. The system continuously monitors user activities by utilizing endpoint and application event sensors. Real-time data are processed to notify security analysts of behavioral anomalies, distinguishing between normal user patterns and suspicious activities that may indicate insider threats. The system's real strength emerges in its hybrid detection capabilities, driven by AI. It leverages statistical analysis through Isolation Forest, behavioral modelling via Autoencoders, and graph-based relationship analysis to predict insider threats. What sets this system apart is its versatility, as it allows analysts to detect threats using statistical anomalies, behavioral deviations, or a combination of both, harnessing the power of Isolation Forest for statistical analysis, Autoencoders for behavioral patterns, and Graph Analytics for contextual relationships. The system achieves 89% accuracy with an 8% false positive rate, processing over 1,000 events per minute with sub-100ms latency. To make security management accessible and user-friendly, the system offers a dedicated real-time dashboard application built with Next.js. This application enables analysts to monitor risk scores and behavioral patterns continually, granting them the ability to gauge organizational security posture. Should analysts suspect an anomaly, the system's Explainable AI features step in to provide transparent insights into threat predictions. If insider threats are detected, the application facilitates seamless investigation and triage with security teams, ensuring timely intervention. Introduction The Internet of Things (IoT) has revolutionized connectivity across smart homes, industries, and healthcare. However, the rapid increase in IoT devices has introduced serious security vulnerabilities, making them easy targets for botnet and DDoS attacks. This project addresses these challenges by designing a real-time anomaly detection system optimized for edge devices. • IoT devices are vulnerable due to limited resources and weak security, often exploited in large-scale cyberattacks. [NAME] cloud-based detection systems are slow and internet-dependent, making them unsuitable for real-time protection. • Edge computing enables faster, offline detection by analyzing data locally on devices like [NAME]. • The system uses a CNN + BiLSTM hybrid model to detect anomalies in live IoT traffic ingested via MQTT. • Phase 1 focused on preprocessing the BoT-IoT dataset—cleaning, encoding, and normalizing it for deep learning model training. Motivation This project is motivated by the need for a lightweight, scalable, and offline-capable anomaly detection solution
tailored to the constraints of IoT ecosystems. By combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for spatial
feature extraction and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) for capturing temporal dependencies, the proposed hybrid deep learning model enables accurate analysis of IoT network traffic. In today’s interconnected world, the rapid growth of IoT devices across smart homes, healthcare, and industrial
environments has dramatically expanded the attack surface for cyber threats. Despite their increasing adoption,
many IoT devices operate with limited processing power and memory, often lacking essential security features. This makes them prime targets for botnet infections, DDoS attacks, and unauthorized access. Traditional
centralized anomaly detection systems are typically cloud-dependent, slow, or resource-intensive, limiting their
effectiveness in real-time and edge-based environments.

Problem Statement Despite advancements in machine learning and cybersecurity, IoT networks remain highly vulnerable due to a lack
of scalable, real-time protection mechanisms. Key challenges include: • IoT devices typically have limited processing power, making traditional anomaly detection models unsuitable.
• Many existing detection systems are cloud-dependent, introducing latency and reducing reliability in low connectivity environments.
• Current models often do not support real-time protocols like MQTT, which are widely used in IoT systems.
• Few existing solutions integrate detection, monitoring, and alerting in a lightweight, deployable package. 1 3 4 Sr.

1. Introduction In today’s increasingly digital education landscape, technological advancements are revolutionizing how students interact with and absorb knowledge. However, not all students benefit equally from these innovations. Children with learning differences—particularly those with dyslexia—often find it difficult to engage with traditional teaching methods and even many mainstream e-learning tools [2][4][6]. Dyslexic learners struggle with reading fluency, symbol recognition, and memory retention, leading to academic frustration, reduced confidence, and slower progress during early foundational stages such as alphabet and language learning. To bridge this gap, this project focuses on integrating Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) into early education environments, specifically targeting the learning needs of dyslexic students. These immersive technologies allow for multi-sensory learning experiences, enabling learners to see, hear, and interact with letters and objects in three- dimensional space. For example, instead of memorizing an alphabet from a book, a child can walk around a virtual letter, hear its correct pronunciation, and associate it with related visual cues—such as an animated object beginning with that letter [1][3][5]. This hands-on approach reinforces memory and comprehension through repetition and engagement. The system will be built using Unity 3D, with compatibility for affordable VR headsets and AR- supported mobile devices. This ensures broader accessibility and scalability in both urban and under-resourced educational settings [8]. Initial learning modules will include alphabets, phonics, shapes, and colors—critical elements for developing early language and cognitive skills [9]. This research-driven initiative promotes inclusive, accessible, and personalized education by embracing universal design principles. It demonstrates how AR/VR tools can be effectively utilized to adapt educational content to suit different learning styles. The project envisions a future where every child—regardless of learning ability—has the opportunity to thrive academically through engaging, supportive, and tailored learning environments [10].

Studies have shown that Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) can significantly enhance user experience when applied to conversational interfaces. However, when it comes to government documentation assistance, there is still a gap in creating region-specific, easy-to- follow systems. 3. Problem Statement Reading and writing are essential foundational skills in a child’s early education. However, children with dyslexia—who experience difficulties in processing written language—often find these stages overwhelming and discouraging. They may struggle to recognize letters, match sounds with symbols, or retain basic literacy concepts, leading to low confidence, frustration, and academic delays. Conventional teaching methods, which rely heavily on repetitive, text- based instruction, typically do not address the diverse learning styles of dyslexic students. While digital education has grown rapidly, most tools available today are not designed with learning disabilities in mind. Many existing solutions are passive, generic, and heavily text- oriented, lacking the interactivity and multi-sensory engagement that dyslexic learners require. This creates a gap in the educational ecosystem for tools that are both inclusive and adaptive. There is a strong need for immersive, technology-driven platforms that utilize Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) to make learning more engaging, accessible, and tailored to the unique cognitive needs of children with dyslexia.

Objectives: 1. Develop an immersive AR/VR platform that visually supports dyslexic students in learning core concepts. 2. Integrate multi-sensory methods combining visuals, sound, and interaction to enhance understanding. 3. Use tools like Unity and ARKit to build accessible, engaging, and child-friendly educational content.

4. Methodology The development of the platform will follow a modular and structured methodology that leverages Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Natural Language Processing (NLP) to create an inclusive and immersive learning experience for students with dyslexia. The system is designed to personalize instruction, simplify complex concepts through interactive media, and support neurodiverse learners with engaging, multisensory educational content tailored to their unique learning needs. 4.1 System Overview The project architecture is structured into three major layers: • User Interaction Layer (Frontend) • Processing Layer (Backend + ML/NLP Models) • Content & Integration Layer (Databases, APIs, AR/VR SDKs) 4.2 Step-by-Step Working Process 1. User Onboarding and Personalization: The learning journey begins with a simple and engaging onboarding process where students or their guardians provide basic information such as age, learning grade, language preference, and any special learning needs. The system also takes into account individual learning styles— whether the child responds better to visuals, audio, or interaction—to customize the educational experience. This personalized approach ensures that the content is not only appropriate for the learner's developmental level but also adaptable to specific cognitive and perceptual needs, particularly those associated with dyslexia. This data helps the system tailor its interface, voice instructions, pacing, and difficulty level. For instance, younger students might be presented with slower animations and simpler interactions, while older students may be provided with more vocabulary-focused challenges. The platform is designed to remember the user’s preferences, offering a seamless experience every time they return. 2. Module Selection and Immersive Activation: After onboarding, learners are directed to a clean and intuitive interface where they can choose from various subject modules such as alphabet learning, phonics, word recognition, or object association. Once a module is selected, the system activates the corresponding immersive experience depending on the user’s device. If the child is using a smartphone or tablet, the module launches in augmented reality, allowing virtual elements to blend with the physical environment—like animated letters appearing on a desk or floating in the room. For students using a headset, the module loads in full virtual reality,

Adaptive Learning and Progress Tracking: As the learner progresses through different activities, the system quietly monitors performance indicators like accuracy, completion time, and level of interaction. These data points allow the system to adjust the difficulty of future tasks, suggest additional practice, or even slow down instructions to match the student’s pace. At the same time, the system generates visual progress reports for educators and parents. These reports include charts, summaries, and suggestions—allowing adults to better understand the child’s learning journey and step in with support when needed. 6.Motivation, Feedback, and Parent Involvement: To maintain interest and reward effort, the platform incorporates a system of motivational elements such as badges, trophies, stars, and encouraging animations. After completing tasks, children are praised with cheerful visuals and friendly feedback, reinforcing their efforts and building a positive emotional connection to learning. Parents and teachers can view detailed reports that track improvement over time, highlight areas of concern, and offer recommended actions. These insights promote a collaborative approach between the student, family, and educators, making sure the support continues beyond the digital environment.

Abstract This project develops a Deepfake Detection System built on a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)–Vision Transformer (ViT) model, with the dual goals of robust detection and clear interpretability. The CNN branch concentrates on localized facial cues, capturing fine-grained texture irregularities and subtle inconsistencies, while the ViT branch models long-range dependencies and global relationships across different facial regions. In parallel, frequency- domain analysis using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) is applied to uncover manipulation artifacts that may remain hidden in the spatial domain alone.To make the model’s decisions understandable to end users, the system incorporates Explainable AI through Grad-CAM, generating visual heatmaps that highlight which facial areas most strongly influenced the predicted label. The proposed model is deployed as a web-based application, enabling convenient integration in academic environments as well as potential real-world security workflows. Experimental evaluation on standard deepfake benchmark datasets indicates that the hybrid architecture surpasses conventional single-model approaches in detection performance while simultaneously offering meaningful visual explanations. Consequently, this work provides a practical, scalable, and user- oriented approach to mitigating the growing risks associated with deepfake media in contemporary digital ecosystems. Keywords: Deepfake Detection, Hybrid CNN–ViT, Vision Transformer, Explainable AI, Grad-CAM, FFT, Cybersecurity

adversarial networks, or GANs. Here, we present a method for 
producing valid images using generative adversarial networks 
(GANs). Promising outcomes have been obtained from recent 
GAN-based methods for image to sketch translating issues. In 
this work, we develop a GAN-based framework for the automatic 
generation of photo-realistic faces from forensic sketches. The 
model is proposed using a U-Net generator and a PatchGAN 
discriminator to build more detailed and higher-quality images. 
The aim of this paper is to implement GAN architecture for 
sketch synthesis using a type of pix2pix GAN known as 
PatchGAN. Current approaches either depend on already taken 
pictures or require accurate edge maps. This research proposes a 
strategy that overcomes the shortcomings of existing approaches 
by utilising generative adversarial networks. The suggested 
approach aims at improving speed, accuracy, and usability of 
forensic sketches for real-world police investigators. Keywords— Artificial Intelligence, GAN, Image-sketch Synthesis,

The approach turns sketches into genuine visuals by 
combining several modern machine learning techniques. In 
addition to U-Net, CNNs, data augmentation, the Adam 
optimiser, and a number of custom loss functions, the system

create realistic results. • 
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): The system is based on Generative Adversarial Networks. 
The discriminator and generator neural networks are the two 
competing neural networks that make up a GAN. The 
discriminator acts as a critic, determining whether an image 
is authentic (from the dataset) or fraudulent (generated by 
the generator), while the generator oversees producing 
realistic images from hand-drawn sketches. The generator will progressively get improved at creating 
genuine and challenging images due to this adversarial 
training procedure. The distribution of the input data is 
denoted by G(z), the conversion of the input noise (z) into 
the input data by D(x), and the pattern of distribution of an 
actual image (x) by pdata(x). The best-case function for 
GANs is defined as minmax [5]. An overview of GAN

preserve low-level elements from the sketch and include

for translation of images to images use cases. The encoder 
reduces the input sketch to a lower order feature

full-size image. Contours and edges are among the crucial 
structural details that are transferred from the encoder 
towards the decoder layer via the skip connections. U-Net 
implements a skip-connection encoder-decoder design. • 
PatchGAN PatchGAN is a sort of picture discriminator used in generative 
adversarial networks (GANs). In image processing, a patch is a 
tiny, rectangular portion of a picture. Specific patches are 
reviewed by PatchGAN rather than the complete image. 
PatchGAN is used to operate a discriminator at the patch levels. 
The discriminator rates the small portions of the image 
according to how realistic they seem, rather than assessing the entire image as a single unit. This enables the discriminator to 
capture images with more detail. Instead of generating one 
outcome (real or fake) for all of the pixels, PatchGAN splits the 
picture into multiple smaller patches and applies a neural

METHODOLOGY 
1. User Input: The user uploads a facial sketch to the model to 
start the system. 
2. Preprocessing Module: In order to make them function with 
the deep learning model, uploaded sketches are resized, 
normalized and transformed into tensor format. 
• Data Preparation: For model training, the CUHK Face Sketch 
Database is utilised. The photos are downsized to 256x256 
pixels, it is crucial to remember that when photographs are 
resized, the original aspect ratio of the facial features is 
maintained. Based on the finding that style-transfer employing 
GANs can only learn to alter the texture and colour of a picture, 
it is unable to precisely alter the image's shape.[5] 
3. GAN Core (Pix2Pix): Generator: To produce genuine facial 
images, a U-Net-based architecture encodes and decodes the 
input image to latent features. consists of bottleneck, decoder 
layers (Transposed Conv + ReLU), skip connections, encoder 
layers (Conv + BatchNorm + LeakyReLU), and final Tanh 
activation. Discriminator: For improved local texture analysis, 
a PatchGAN model uses patch-wise scores (70x70) to 
differentiate between generated and real images. 
4. Loss Functions: Generator Loss: combines L1 loss and 
adversarial loss to preserve content and achieve pixel-level 
accuracy. Discriminator Loss: Develops the capacity to discern 
between real and fraudulent images. 
5. Model Execution & Output Handling: The image is generated, 
saved, and then postprocessed (converted, resized, and 
denormalised) before being sent back to the user. 
6. Post-Processing Step: Denormalise the values of pixels. 
Modify the output image's size or format. Convert tensor to a 
format that can be seen. 
7. Output to User: The user can access or save the reconstructed 
face using the sketch following the generation of the final image

CONCLUSION 
The method allows self-sufficient, genuine facial image 
reconstruction from sketches using Generative Adversarial 
Networks (GANs). This can be used to create human faces that 
look genuine for forensic analysis sketching. It can also be 
improved to generate higher resolution images and further 
applied to other tasks like face recognition. The GAN 
architecture discussed above can generate images that are 
perhaps more varied than, typical generative models. Despite 
this, there aren't many studies looking at how to make GAN 
network structures better. Better loss functions are the primary 
goal of GANs to provide genuine outcomes and stable 
training. We implemented a network structure for our 
generative challenge, and testing shown that it performed 
better than the current setups. XI. FUTURE SCOPE Future improvements to systems seek to improve model 
prediction accuracy, the process will obviously need to increase 
and broaden the datasets utilized with quality annotations as well 
as has the review of increasingly complex GAN types, such as 
Style-GAN, Star-GAN or more recent diffusion-based models to 
output images with even more detail. Additionally, harnessing 
high quality performance GPUs would be essential for effective 
training as it is much faster which would further ensure feasibility 
of deploying these models. Measuring more perceptual metrics 
like LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity) can 
improve quantitative strength.

1. Introduction In the modern financial technology (FinTech) world, security is the top priority. The standard "stateless" authentication model, known as JSON Web Tokens (JWT), relies heavily on mathematical formulas to create the secret keys that protect user accounts. While these mathematical numbers are very fast to generate, they are not truly random. Because they are based on math, they follow a pattern. Powerful future computers, known as Quantum Computers, could potentially analyze these patterns and guess the keys, putting user data at risk. This threat is often described as "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later," where hackers steal encrypted data today and wait for better computers to unlock it in the future. To solve this critical problem, we developed the Quantum-Seeded Dynamic JWT Framework. This project integrates a Quantum Entropy Source (QES) to create truly random seeds that have no mathematical pattern. These seeds are used to digitally sign JWTs. Furthermore, the system is dynamic: even if a hacker manages to steal a key, it becomes useless almost immediately because the system changes (rotates) the keys automatically. The ultimate goal is to make banking applications and APIs secure enough to withstand future quantum attacks without requiring everyday users to buy expensive or specialized hardware.

2. Literature Review Most standard security systems today rely on "computational hardness"—meaning the math is too hard for current computers to solve quickly. However, this approach might fail against new Quantum algorithms (like Shor's and Grover's algorithms) which can solve these specific math problems very fast. While researchers are working on "Post-Quantum Cryptography" (PQC), many of these proposed solutions require heavy processing power, making them too slow for mobile banking apps running on phones. 4. Problem Statement Primary Goals: Current authentication standards, specifically JSON Web Tokens (JWT), rely heavily on Pseudo-Random Number Generators (PRNGs) to create cryptographic secrets. While computationally efficient, these generators are deterministic, meaning they produce output based on mathematical patterns that can be predicted by advanced computing power. The emergence of quantum computing poses a significant "Harvest Now, Decrypt Later" threat, where adversaries collect encrypted data today to decrypt it once quantum hardware becomes sufficiently powerful. However, transitioning to Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNG) introduces a new engineering challenge: latency. Direct calls to quantum cloud services (like IBM Qiskit) are too slow for real-time web applications, often resulting in unacceptable login delays. Furthermore, most existing systems use static or long-lived keys, which creates a large "window of opportunity" for attackers if a key is compromised. There is a critical lack of frameworks that automate the injection of quantum entropy into high-speed authentication flows without sacrificing performance

Objectives: I. 
To replace deterministic algorithms with True Random Number Generation (TRNG) derived from quantum circuit measurements using IBM Qiskit. II. 
To implement a "Producer-Consumer" architecture using an Entropy Pooling mechanism (Redis) that decouples slow quantum generation from authentication, ensuring low-latency logins. III. 
Engineer a dynamic security policy that automatically adjusts the Time-To-Live (TTL) of keys based on real-time threat scores, strictly limiting the lifespan of compromised credentials. IV. 
To verify the quality of the generated quantum keys against the NIST SP 800-22 standard for cryptographic randomness

5.1 System Architecture The system uses a smart 3-tier "Producer-Consumer" architecture to ensure user logins are fast, reliable, and secure. I. 
Entropy Pooling (The "Speed Buffer") - [Implemented] What it is: Quantum computers on the cloud can be slow or have long waiting lines (queues). To prevent this from slowing down the app, we created a background system similar to a "Miner." How it works: This "Miner" works in the background, 24/7. It connects to the IBM Cloud, downloads random quantum bits before they are actually needed, and stacks them in a fast local database (Redis). Benefit: When a user clicks "Login," the system doesn't have to call the quantum computer. Instead, it grabs a ready-made key instantly from this local pool. This reduces the wait time from potentially seconds to just milliseconds. II. 
Key Vault (Redis) This acts as a temporary safe storage. It stores active keys and enforces a strict "Time- To-Live" (TTL). Once a key's time is up, the Vault automatically deletes it, ensuring no old keys are left lying around for hackers to find. III. 
API Gateway (FastAPI) This is the front door of the system. It connects the user to the backend. It handles the logic of fetching new keys to sign tokens for login and checking existing keys to verify users who are already logged in. IV. 
Hybrid Fail-Safe Mode - [Safety Mechanism] What it is: A robust backup plan designed to keep the system running no matter what. How it works: Real-world systems can have connection issues. If the connection to the IBM Quantum computer fails, or if the internet goes down, the system automatically detects the error and switches to standard mathematical (classical) random numbers. Benefit: This ensures the banking app is reliable. A user trying to buy groceries or pay a bill will never face a crash just because the quantum server is offline. 4.2 Algorithms and Logic I.

Quantum Circuit (The Randomness Source): Tool: Qiskit (Python). Logic: We create a quantum circuit and apply a Hadamard Gate (H) to a qubit. In simple terms, this puts the qubit into a "superposition" state where it is both 0 and 1 at the same time. When we measure it, nature forces it to choose 0 or 1 completely at random. This randomness is physical, not mathematical. II. 
Adaptive Quantum Rotation (AQR) - [Smart Security] What it is: A smart rule engine that adjusts the lifespan of a security key based on how much we trust the user at that moment. Logic: a. Safe User: If the user is logging in from their usual location and device, the key remains valid for 5 minutes, offering convenience. b. Suspicious User: If the user looks risky (e.g., logging in from a known hacker IP address or a strange location), the key is set to expire in just 5 seconds. Benefit: This creates a "moving target" for hackers. Even if they manage to intercept a key from a suspicious connection, it becomes invalid before they can use it to steal data. III. 
Threat Scoring Engine - [Risk Logic] What it is: A logic system that acts like a security guard, calculating a "Risk Score" (from 0 to 100) for every single login attempt. Factors: It analyzes multiple data points: the user's IP address, their geographical location (Geo-IP), and recent behavior like how many times they typed the wrong password. Usage: The output of this engine feeds directly into the Adaptive Quantum Rotation system, telling it exactly how long the key should last. High risk equals short key life. IV.

IP address, their geographical location (Geo-IP), and recent behavior like how many times they typed the wrong password. Usage: The output of this engine feeds directly into the Adaptive Quantum Rotation system, telling it exactly how long the key should last. High risk equals short key life. IV. Header Injection: To keep track of these changing keys, we inject a custom "Key ID" (kid) into the token header. This acts like a label so the verification server knows exactly which temporary key to check in the Vault. V. 
Data Collection and Analysis Techniques Entropy Analysis: We cannot just "look" at numbers to see if they are random. We use the NIST SP 800-22 test suite, a gold standard for cryptography, to statistically prove that our Quantum Keys have higher entropy (unpredictability) than standard Python keys. Latency Testing: We use tools to measure the speed of the login process. Specifically, we want to prove that the Entropy Pooling method keeps the total login time under 20ms, ensuring a smooth user experience. Attack Simulation: We run a custom script named "Eve" that acts like a hacker. It tries to brute-force or guess the key. We count how many attempts fail specifically because the key rotated (changed) before the attack could finish. 6. Project Plan and Timeline Fig 6.1: Project Plan and Timeline Work / Months

8. Conclusion The Quantum-Seeded Dynamic JWT Framework successfully moves authentication security from the realm of "Computational Hardness" (hoping the math is too hard to solve) to "Information-Theoretic Security" (where the data is physically unpredictable). By replacing static passwords with a stream of ephemeral, physically random keys that change constantly based on threat levels, this project demonstrates that high-security quantum concepts can be practically applied to today's banking infrastructure. The addition of the Speed Buffer ensures the system is not just secure, but also fast enough for everyday use.

9. Future Scope While the current system is robust, we have identified advanced features that could be added in future updates: I. 
Honey Tokens (Deception Technology): We plan to plant fake security keys in the code that look exactly like real ones. If a hacker finds and tries to use one of these "poisoned" tokens, the system will instantly recognize the attack, block the hacker's IP, and trigger a system-wide reset. This turns the defense system into an active trap. II. 
Quantum Watermarking: A method to embed a hidden "fingerprint" inside the digital token. We will hash the quantum number and insert it into the token header. This allows the server to mathematically verify that the key originated from a real Quantum Computer, providing a chain of trust without needing to query the database for every single request. III. 
Hardware Integration: Eventually, we aim to replace the Qiskit simulator with a real, cloud-connected Quantum Processing Unit (QPU) to derive randomness from actual hardware qubits rather than simulation. IV. 
Decentralized Verification: We plan to expand the Redis Vault into a distributed cluster. This would allow different banking microservices located in different countries to verify the same quantum-signed token instantly, enabling global scale.

ABSTRACT The automotive sector is rapidly advancing toward autonomous driving, with Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) acting as a major enabler. However, most ADAS solutions are designed for structured, rule-based traffic seen in developed nations and therefore perform poorly on India’s highly unpredictable roads, where mixed traffic, irregular lane markings, and infrastructure limitations are common. This project presents a Level-3 ADAS prototype tailored specifically for Indian road environments. The system integrates real-time lane, pothole, and traffic-sign detection along with a driver-drowsiness monitoring unit using a hybrid perception approach that combines classical computer vision with lightweight deep learning models such as YOLOv5 and Mask R-CNN. All models are trained on Indian road datasets to ensure contextual accuracy. The solution is deployed on a Raspberry Pi platform to maintain affordability and accessibility for wider adoption. The final outcome is a functional prototype and an

implementation roadmap demonstrating the feasibility of low-cost, scalable ADAS solutions suited for emerging markets like India. Lane Detection Module In this module, the lane boundaries are detected with the help of classical computer vision that makes sure the vehicle remains within the purpose of its course. • Purpose: To determine the location of the car concerning the middle of the lane and identify a future possible lane departure. • Methodology: Grayscale Conversion & Filtering: The frame of the video is turned to grayscale to make processing easier and more to remove noise. • Edge Detection: Canny Edge Detector is used to locate the steep variations in intensity, which represent the edges of the roads and the lanes. • Region of Interest (ROI): This is a trapezoidal mask, which is used to make processing only on the area of the road relevant to the vehicle ahead, minimizing computational load and false positives. • Perspective Transform: The Birdseye View (BEV) transform (or Inverse Perspective Mapping) is frequently used to straighten the curvilinear lane lines, so that they can be more readily identified mathematically. • Line Fitting: The Hough Line Transform will be applied to find the lines (lane markers) within the image that has been processed. These identified lane lines are fitted with polynomials (typically a second-order polynomial). Output and Alert: The computer performs calculations on the Lane Offset (the distance between the center of the lane) and activates a Lane Departure Warning (LDW) when the Lane Offset rises beyond a safety threshold that is preset. 8.1 Conclusion This project demonstrates that advanced driver-assistance features can be implemented effectively using affordable hardware and optimized AI models. By combining classical computer vision techniques with lightweight deep learning architectures, the system achieves real-time lane, pothole, and sign detection while also monitoring driver alertness. The results confirm that even low-cost embedded platforms like Raspberry Pi can provide meaningful safety enhancements suitable for Indian roads. Although environmental variability and hardware limitations remain challenges, the project establishes a strong foundation for future improvements such as multi-sensor fusion, adaptive learning models, and more advanced levels of driving automation.

Traditional security solutions often fall short in detecting sophisticated attacks, lack transparency in decision-making, and require constant manual intervention. Strengthening IoT security is essential to protect sensitive data, ensure system integrity, and maintain trust in smart environments. This project presents NetDefend IoT, an intelligent and resilient security framework designed to detect, explain, and autonomously recover from cyber threats targeting IoT ecosystems. Leveraging machine learning (ML) for real-time anomaly detection, explainable AI (XAI) for transparent decision-making, blockchain for immutable threat logging, and self-healing mechanisms for autonomous recovery, NetDefend IoT offers multi-layered protection without human dependence. The system continuously learns from evolving threats and adapts its defense strategies accordingly. Scalable, adaptive, and transparent, NetDefend IoT is tailored for smart cities, critical infrastructures, and enterprise IoT networks. By addressing the limitations of conventional security models, this project delivers a forward-thinking, all-in-one solution for robust and autonomous IoT defense.

NetDefend IoT is designed for deployment across smart cities, healthcare systems, industrial automation, and other critical infrastructure where security, reliability, and interpretability are essential. It aims to mitigate modern cyber threats through adaptive defence, making IoT systems more trustworthy and robust. MOTIVATION In today's cybersecurity landscape, the rapid growth of IoT devices has introduced new vulnerabilities and significantly expanded the attack surface across connected environments. Traditional security systems are often static, reactive, and incapable of addressing the dynamic nature of modern cyber threats. The absence of intelligent detection, explainability, and autonomous recovery mechanisms makes IoT ecosystems increasingly vulnerable to data breaches, unauthorized access, and persistent attacks. This project is motivated by the urgent need for a smarter, adaptive, and transparent IoT security framework that addresses these limitations. By integrating machine learning-based anomaly detection, explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as SHAP and LIME, blockchain-powered immutable threat logging, and self-healing capabilities, this project ensures robust, real-time protection without requiring constant human intervention. Moreover, the scalable architecture and modular design of NetDefend IoT make it well-suited for deployment across smart cities, healthcare, industrial control systems, and other critical IoT- driven infrastructures. By overcoming the shortcomings of conventional security solutions, this project offers a comprehensive and intelligent approach to safeguarding the next generation of connected systems.

PROPOSED SYSTEM The NetDefend IoT system is designed to provide an intelligent and automated security framework for IoT networks. Unlike traditional intrusion detection systems, our proposed system integrates Machine Learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), Blockchain, and Self-Healing Intelligence into a unified solution that can not only detect attacks but also explain decisions and automatically recover from threats. Key Components of the Proposed System Machine Learning-Based Detection ML models such as Random Forest, XGBoost, or LSTM are trained on IoT traffic datasets (e.g., CICIDS2017 and UNSW-NB15) to detect anomalies like DDoS, probing, or MITM attacks in real time. Explainable AI (XAI) We use SHAP and LIME to provide clear explanations for model predictions. This helps users and developers understand why a particular packet or flow was flagged as malicious. Blockchain-Powered Secure Logging Detected threats and events are recorded on an Ethereum-based blockchain ledger using smart contracts. This ensures tamper-proof logs and traceability for forensic investigations. Self-Healing Engine When a threat is detected, the system can quarantine the compromised node, reset its configuration, or reroute traffic. This reduces downtime and minimizes manual intervention. Workflow of the Proposed System IoT devices generate real-time network traffic and logs. Data is collected and preprocessed for the ML module. ML models classify traffic as either normal or suspicious. XAI methods (SHAP/LIME) explain the reasons behind a detection. Threat logs are securely recorded on the blockchain. The self-healing mechanism is activated for recovery or isolation. Advantages of the Proposed System Real-time anomaly detection with high accuracy. Transparent decision-making through explainable AI. Secure, tamper-proof logging using blockchain technology. Autonomous self-healing, reducing downtime and improving resilience.

IMPLEMENTATION The implementation phase of NetDefend IoT mainly focused on building a machine-learning- based intrusion detection system (IDS) that can detect abnormal network traffic patterns. To make the model more transparent, we also integrated Explainable AI (XAI) components. The key steps we followed are explained below: Dataset Collection and Preprocessing We used IoT traffic datasets like CICIDS2017 and UNSW-NB15 for training and testing our model. All the rows with missing or invalid values were removed to keep the dataset clean and reliable. Only numerical features were selected for the ML pipeline, while the "Label" column (attack type) was converted into numbers using LabelEncoder. Extreme and infinite values were clipped to a fixed range, and the dataset was normalized using StandardScaler so that all features were on a similar scale. Model Training We selected a Random Forest Classifier as our main ML algorithm because it is good at handling large datasets, avoids overfitting, and gives accurate results. The dataset was divided into 80% training data and 20% testing data using stratified sampling to maintain a proper class balance. The Random Forest model was trained with the following settings: n_estimators = 100 (number of decision trees) max_depth = 20 random_state = 42 After training, our model achieved 99.83% accuracy, as shown in the classification report. Code Pipeline We developed a Python-based pipeline using libraries such as pandas, numpy, and scikit- learn. This pipeline performed: Data cleaning and normalization. Model training and accuracy evaluation. Saving the trained model and scaler as .pkl files (using pickle) for future use. Explainability (XAI) We used SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) to show the importance of each feature in making predictions. This makes the model’s decisions easier to understand and helps us identify which parameters influence the detection of attacks. Model Evaluation A classification report was generated, which included metrics like precision, recall, and F1-score for different attack types. The evaluation proved that the Random Forest model is highly accurate and reliable for IoT threat detection. ABSTRACT The rapid expansion of satellite imaging technologies has transformed modern surveillance, defence analysis, and strategic intelligence operations. However, detecting and classifying military vehicles in satellite imagery remains a challenging task due to factors such as camouflage, noise, low resolution, terrain variations, and the subtle visual similarities between different vehicle types. Traditional deep learning models often fail under these constraints because they rely solely on pixel-level features, making them vulnerable to environmental distortions. To address these challenges, this project presents AMED (Advanced Military Equipment Detection) - a three-stage modular pipeline designed for accurate detection, segmentation, and classification of military vehicles from satellite imagery. In Stage 1, a fine-tuned YOLOv11m model acts as a high-recall detector to localize vehicle–shadow pairs. Stage 2 performs instance segmentation, beginning with classical image processing techniques and scaling toward a deep-learning based YOLO-seg model using synthetic and SAM-generated masks. Stage 3 introduces a robust geometric feature-based classifier that extracts shape descriptors such as aspect ratio, compactness, Hu Moments, and shadow correlation to achieve reliable class prediction under camouflage or varied lighting. The hybrid combination of deep learning and geometry-driven reasoning enhances interpretability, robustness, and adaptability. Experimental evaluation demonstrates strong performance, with Stage 1 achieving 87.1% recall, 88.4% precision, and 93.6% mAP@50, validating AMED as a reliable foundation for advanced military surveillance applications. This work establishes a structured, scalable, and computationally efficient system suitable for real-world defence intelligence workflows. INTRODUCTION Overview Satellite-based military surveillance plays a critical role in defense intelligence, border monitoring, and threat assessment. With increasing global tensions and advancements in reconnaissance technology, there is a rising demand for automated systems capable of analyzing large volumes of satellite imagery with accuracy and speed. The AMED (Advanced Military Equipment Detection) system is designed to detect, segment, and classify military vehicles from satellite imagery using a three-stage processing pipeline. These stages include: (1) high-recall object detection, (2) instance-level segmentation, and (3) geometric feature–driven classification. This multi-level approach ensures higher interpretability and robustness compared to single-model end-to-end deep learning solutions. 1.2 Motivation Military reconnaissance traditionally relies on manual inspection of satellite images, which is time-consuming and prone to human error. Modern battlefields involve camouflage, complex backgrounds, shifting shadows, and small-scale objects making traditional detection methods unreliable. The motivation behind AMED includes: The need for automation in defence imagery processing. The success of YOLO models in high-speed detection tasks. The importance of shadow correlation to reduce false detections. The need for explainable AI, where each prediction is backed by measurable geometric features. Problem Definition and Objectives The complexity of satellite data demands more than conventional object detection. Many images contain overlapping shadows, cluttered environments, agricultural patterns, industrial machinery, or civilian vehicles that resemble military assets. These factors increase false alarms, which can mislead intelligence operations or result in unnecessary threats. To address these issues, AMED’s objectives extend beyond typical detection tasks by incorporating shadow-vehicle correlation analysis, geometry-based reasoning, and a hybrid approach that balances deep learning with classical computer vision. The system aims to not only locate vehicles but also justify classifications through measurable features, making it suitable for strategic decision-making. Each objective was carefully chosen to ensure technical feasibility, defensive relevance, and reliability in real-world deployment scenarios. Problem Definition: Detecting military equipment in satellite imagery is challenging due to: small object sizes, terrain variations, camouflage, low image resolution, shadow distortion. Most deep learning models struggle to generalize, and their predictions lack interpretability.

Objectives of AMED: Develop a 3-stage detection–segmentation–classification pipeline. Achieve high recall using YOLOv11m detector for Stage 1. Extract accurate segmentation masks for vehicles and shadows. Compute robust geometric features (Hu Moments, aspect ratio, solidity). Classify vehicles into categories using a transparent and interpretable system. Build a real-time, computationally efficient workflow. 1.4 Project Scope & Limitations The scope of this project encompasses the design and development of a complete multi-stage framework capable of detecting, segmenting, and classifying military vehicles from satellite imagery. AMED focuses on processing high-altitude satellite images where vehicles appear small, low-contrast, and often blended with natural surroundings. The system is designed to handle such complexities through a modular architecture that separates detection, segmentation, and classification into distinct stages, allowing each component to be independently developed and optimized. The project covers the creation of a high-recall detection module using YOLOv11m, ensuring that all potential vehicle–shadow pairs are identified before further refinement. It extends into the development of a segmentation module that isolates vehicle shapes from varied terrains and lighting conditions, enabling deeper structural analysis even when texture information is unreliable. The final part of the scope includes constructing a geometric and CNN-supported classification module capable of discriminating between vehicle types based on shape descriptors, spatial relationships, and learned visual features. The system is intended for controlled experimental environments, using curated satellite datasets and synthetic augmentations. Its focus is to demonstrate proof-of-concept accuracy, robustness, and interpretability suitable for defence surveillance scenarios. While the project does not implement a full-scale operational intelligence system, it establishes a foundation that can be expanded with larger datasets, more advanced segmentation networks, and integration into broader military analysis tools. The scope ultimately emphasizes creating a functional, extensible, and research-oriented model tailored to real-world defence imaging challenges. Limitations: Shadow Dependency: The approach heavily relies on visible, distinct shadows cast by vehicles, thus its effectiveness diminishes in low-light conditions, heavy cloud cover, or environments where shadows are diffused or absent.

Limitations: Shadow Dependency: The approach heavily relies on visible, distinct shadows cast by vehicles, thus its effectiveness diminishes in low-light conditions, heavy cloud cover, or environments where shadows are diffused or absent. Segmentation Sensitivity: The accuracy of final classification is tightly linked to the performance of the instance segmentation model. Any errors or noise in mask generation may propagate into misclassifications. Advanced Camouflage and Decoys: Sophisticated decoys designed to mimic both shape and shadow patterns pose challenges for detection and could reduce system reliability without additional countermeasures. Environmental Constraints: Variability in atmospheric conditions, sensor resolution, and terrain features can affect detection quality, requiring site or sensor-specific adaptation. Computational Requirements: Although optimized for efficiency via cascading and patch-wise processing, processing very high-resolution satellite data in near real-time demands considerable computational resources and optimized hardware. 1.5 Methodologies of Problem Solving The AMED system adopts a structured and modular methodology to effectively address the challenges of detecting military vehicles in satellite imagery. The overall approach is divided into three sequential stages detection, segmentation, and classification each designed to overcome specific limitations observed in traditional end-to-end deep learning models. In the first stage, a fine-tuned YOLOv11m model is employed to achieve high-recall detection of vehicles and their corresponding shadows, enabling the system to reliably localize objects even under camouflage or low-contrast environments. The second stage focuses on segmentation, where regions of interest obtained from the detector are refined using classical computer vision techniques such as HSV thresholding, contour extraction, and morphological filtering. This helps in isolating vehicle bodies and shadows more accurately, while also laying the foundation for integrating advanced segmentation models such as SAM or YOLO-Seg in future expansion of the project.

LITERATURE SURVEY 2.1 Survey The development of a reliable military vehicle detection system requires a strong understanding of the technological progress made in object detection, segmentation, and classification within the broader computer vision domain. Over the years, numerous techniques have been proposed to address the challenges of small-object detection, variable lighting, camouflage, and noisy satellite imagery. A review of this existing literature is essential for identifying the limitations of present-day solutions and understanding how modern approaches—including YOLO-based detectors, segmentation architectures, shadow-aware processing, and geometric feature analysis, contribute to improved performance. This section provides an overview of the key research contributions, datasets, methods, and gaps that directly inform the design decisions behind AMED. 2.2 Efficient Small Object Detection for Aerial Images (2024) [Jie Luo, Zhicheng Liu,Yibo Wang,Ao Tang,Huahong Zuo and Ping Han] The study on ESOD-YOLO focuses on enhancing the performance of single-stage detectors for extremely small objects in aerial and satellite imagery. Building on the YOLOv8 architecture, the authors introduce improved multi-scale feature fusion and attention-driven refinement blocks to preserve high-frequency details that are typically lost during downsampling. Their findings demonstrate substantial improvements in recall and localization stability for objects that occupy only a few pixels in large satellite frames. The modifications allow the detector to better identify tiny vehicles that classical detectors often fail to capture, especially in cluttered terrains. Despite its improvements, ESOD-YOLO presents research gaps relevant to AMED. The model relies heavily on appearance cues and does not incorporate shadow-awareness or geometric reasoning, which limits reliability in camouflage-heavy defense environments. Additionally, while the architecture excels in detection, it does not propose solutions for segmentation or classification. 4.1 System Architecture The architecture of the AMED system is defined by a rigorous, three-stage cascaded pipeline designed to transform raw aerial data into actionable intelligence. As illustrated in the system flow design, the process initiates with the ingestion of a high-resolution Satellite Image. This input is immediately processed by the Detection Stage, which leverages the YOLOv11 Architecture. Unlike standard detectors, this stage is specialized to output not just Bounding Boxes but also correlated Shadow Pairs, achieving a validation accuracy of 93.60% mAP@50. The output of the detection phase feeds directly into the Segmentation Stage. Here, the system performs Instance Segmentation within the detected Regions of Interest (ROI). The primary objective of this stage is to generate precise Vehicle & Shadow Binary Masks, effectively isolating the geometry of the target from the background terrain. This pixel-level isolation is a prerequisite for the final stage. The pipeline concludes with the Classification Stage. This logic-driven subsystem extracts a vector of Geometric Features, specifically calculating Aspect Ratio, Compactness, Hu Moments, and Shadow Analysis metrics from the binary masks. These numerical descriptors are passed through a decision tree of Classification Rules, which definitively categorizes the object into one of four classes: Tank, APC (Armoured Personnel Carrier), MV (Military Vehicle), or SPG (Self-Propelled Gun). The final system output is consolidated into Annotated Results, comprising visual overlays and structured JSON Data. Vehicle & Shadow Detection: This is the first stage of AMED. When a satellite image is provided, the system first uses a YOLOv11m model to locate all possible vehicles and their shadows. YOLOv11m is chosen because it provides high recall and is capable of detecting very small objects such as vehicles that appear tiny in satellite views. The input image is resized, normalized, and passed through the YOLOv11m model. YOLO divides the image into regions and predicts bounding boxes wherever a possible vehicle or shadow is detected. The output of this module is a set of bounding boxes. Each bounding box contains coordinates showing where the object is located in the image. These boxes are then cropped and sent to the next module for more detailed pixel-level analysis. Segmentation: Once bounding boxes are received from the detection module, the segmentation module refines them to obtain the exact shape of the vehicle and its shadow. This module ensures that we do not rely on rough rectangular boxes but on accurate masks, which help analyze the geometry of the object. Each cropped region undergoes classical computer vision operations such as grayscale conversion, thresholding, edge detection, and morphological filtering. These steps help in identifying the actual boundaries of the vehicle. This coarse mask is then improved using modern segmentation models such as SAM-assisted segmentation or YOLO-Seg, which make the boundary more accurate. The output of segmentation is a pixel-level mask that shows the exact shape of the detected vehicle. These masks are essential for extracting geometric features used in the classification stage. Otsu Thresholding: Automatically selects an optimal grayscale threshold to separate foreground (vehicle) from background. Morphological Closing: Fills small holes inside the segmented vehicle region using dilation followed by erosion. Morphological Opening: Removes small noise and artifacts using erosion followed by dilation. Shadow Intensity Thresholding: Detects dark shadow regions by applying inverse binary thresholding on low-intensity pixels. Contour Detection: Finds the external boundary of the segmented vehicle mask for shape analysis. Geometric Feature Extraction: Computes numerical descriptors (area, perimeter, aspect ratio, compactness, solidity) from the contour. Hu Moments: Generates seven invariant shape features that remain consistent under rotation, scale, and translation. Rule-Based Classification: Classifies the vehicle into Tank, APC, SPG, or Military Vehicle using predefined geometric thresholds. Transfer Learning: Fine-tunes the YOLOv11m detector from pre-trained weights to improve accuracy with limited data. Data Augmentation: Applies transformations such as rotation, scaling, translation, and color shifts to improve model robustness. Early Stopping: Stops training automatically when validation accuracy stops improving to prevent overfitting. Alpha Blending: Overlays segmentation masks onto the original image by blending pixel values for visualization. Bilinear Interpolation: Smoothly resizes images by averaging neighboring pixel values for clean display grids.

8.1 Conclusion The AMED (Advanced Military Equipment Detection) system represents a complete and coherent attempt to automate the detection and identification of military vehicles from satellite imagery using a hybrid approach that blends modern deep-learning techniques with classical computer vision and geometric analysis. The primary objective of this project was to design a pipeline capable of detecting vehicles, isolating their visible structure and associated shadows, extracting meaningful visual and geometric descriptors, and finally categorizing them into standardized military equipment types. Across all stages, the project successfully met the defined problem statement and objectives. The Stage 1 detection module, powered by the YOLOv11m deep-learning architecture, demonstrated high accuracy in locating vehicles under varying illumination and terrain conditions. The fine-tuned model showed strong performance on both high-resolution and medium-resolution satellite images, proving its robustness and adaptability. Consistent detection accuracy, high precision, and effective non-maximum suppression illustrate the capability of the YOLOv11m backbone to handle complex backgrounds, camouflage patterns, and partially occluded vehicles—realistic challenges commonly present in defence-based imaging scenarios. The Stage 2 segmentation module further contributed to the system’s accuracy by generating clean binary masks of vehicles and shadows. Although built using classical thresholding and morphological operations, the segmentation pipeline proved effective in highlighting core structural regions of the vehicle. It captured essential contour shapes and shadow regions, enabling reliable measurement of geometry and enabling strong downstream classification performance. This stage demonstrated that hybrid pipelines can offer high interpretability without requiring computationally expensive models, making AMED more efficient and resource-friendly. The Stage 3 classification module introduced a feature-driven method based on contour analysis, geometric descriptors, and Hu Moments. This approach allowed the system to categorize vehicles into meaningful military classes such as Tanks, Armoured Personnel Carriers (APCs), Self-Propelled Guns (SPGs), and generic Military Vehicles. The interpretability of this rule-based classifier stands out as a major advantage, as analysts and defence personnel can understand exactly why a classification was assigned an important requirement for mission-critical applications. The consistency of classification results across diverse datasets confirms the stability and reasoning capability of this approach.

One of the most significant areas for improvement is the segmentation stage. Future versions of AMED could integrate advanced segmentation algorithms such as Segment Anything Model (SAM), Mask R-CNN, or YOLO-Seg. These deep-learning segmentation models can handle fine-grained object boundaries, camouflage, overlapping vehicles, and complex shadows more effectively than traditional thresholding. Integrating such models would significantly increase pixel-level precision and, in turn, strengthen the reliability of downstream feature extraction. Another important extension is the replacement of the rule-based classifier with a trainable machine learning model or a hybrid system that combines geometric analysis with neural classification. For example, a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) or a Random Forest classifier could be trained on the extracted features, providing probabilistic predictions based on data-driven learning rather than manually defined rules. Alternatively, a deep-learning classifier could be built using CNN-based shape encoders, enabling greater complexity and adaptability to diverse vehicle geometries.

1. Introduction 
Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, 
primarily affecting the lungs. Despite the availability of treatment, TB remains a major 
global health concern, especially in developing countries. Early diagnosis plays a crucial 
role in preventing the spread of the disease and improving patient survival rates. Chest X-
rays are one of the most widely used tools for TB screening due to their low cost and quick 
availability. However, accurate interpretation of X-rays requires trained radiologists, which 
may not be available in resource-limited regions. Automated systems can help reduce 
diagnostic delays and workload. Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning, has 
shown remarkable performance in medical image analysis. Convolutional Neural Networks 
(CNNs) can automatically extract complex patterns from images, making them suitable for 
disease detection tasks such as TB diagnosis. Many existing AI models operate as black 
boxes, making it difficult for medical professionals to trust their predictions. Additionally, 
most systems only provide raw classification results without generating structured medical 
reports or enabling meaningful interaction with users. This project is motivated by the need 
for an accurate, explainable, and intelligent TB diagnosis system that can automatically 
generate diagnostic reports and support interactive communication through a chatbot 
interface, thereby improving usability, transparency, and clinical support. This project is 
motivated by the need for an accurate, explainable, and interactive TB diagnosis system that 
not only detects the disease but also explains the reasoning behind its predictions.

molecular tests. Although effective, these methods are time-consuming and require 
laboratory infrastructure. 2.1. Deep Learning Approaches for TB Detection Recent studies have used deep learning models such as CNNs to classify chest X-ray 
images as TB-positive or TB-negative. These models have achieved high accuracy but 
often lack interpretability. CNN architectures like VGG, ResNet, and DenseNet have been 
widely used in medical imaging tasks. Their ability to learn hierarchical features makes 
them suitable for complex image classification problems. Explainable AI (XAI) 
techniques such as Grad-CAM and saliency maps help visualize the regions of an image 
that influence model decisions. XAI is essential in healthcare to build trust and support 
clinical decision-making. Conversational AI systems enable natural language interaction 
between users and machines. When integrated with medical systems, they can explain

Despite significant advancements in artificial intelligence and deep learning for medical 
image analysis, several critical gaps remain in existing tuberculosis (TB) detection systems. 
These gaps limit the practical adoption of AI-based solutions in real-world clinical 
environments 3.1. Limitations of Existing TB Detection Systems Most existing TB detection systems primarily emphasize achieving high classification 
accuracy using deep learning models. While accuracy is an important metric, these systems 
often fail to address real-world clinical requirements such as transparency, reliability, and 
clinical interpretability. In many cases, AI models provide only a binary output (TB-positive 
or TB-negative) without sufficient contextual information to support medical decision-
making. Furthermore, these systems are often developed and evaluated in controlled 
research settings, making them difficult to deploy in real healthcare environments with 
varying image quality, patient demographics, and operational constraints. As a result, 
healthcare professionals may hesitate to rely on such systems due to the lack of supporting 
evidence and explainable outputs. 3.2 Lack of Explainability in Deep Learning Models Deep learning models, especially Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), are widely 
considered black-box systems. Although they can learn complex visual patterns from chest 
X-ray images, they do not naturally explain how or why a particular decision was made. This 
lack of explainability poses a major challenge in medical applications where accountability 
and trust are essential. Without visual explanations such as heatmaps or region-based 
highlights, medical professionals cannot verify whether the model is focusing on clinically 
relevant areas of the lungs or on irrelevant artifacts. This makes it difficult to validate 
predictions, identify potential errors, and confidently use AI-assisted diagnosis in clinical 
practice.

4. Problem Statement 
To design and develop an automated system that accurately detects tuberculosis from 
chest X-ray images using deep CNNs, provides explainable visual insights for 
predictions, and enables user interaction through a conversational AI powered by 
LLaMA-3.

transparency and trust in model predictions. 
C. To design a generative AI module capable of producing structured, human-readable diagnostic reports that summarize prediction outcomes, confidence levels, and visual 
explanations. 
D. To create an interactive chatbot application powered by LLaMA-3 that assists users by explaining diagnosis results, answering TB-related queries, and improving user 
engagement and understanding.

using chest X-ray images by integrating deep Convolutional Neural Networks, explainable

critical challenges in traditional TB diagnosis, such as dependency on expert radiologists, lack of 
transparency in AI predictions, and limited user interaction. By incorporating explainability 
techniques like Grad-CAM, the system enhances trust and interpretability by visually highlighting

This work highlights how advanced AI technologies can assist early TB detection, improve 
healthcare efficiency, and support informed clinical decision-making, particularly in resource-
constrained environments.

ABSTRACT In today's fast-paced medical environments, doctors are often overwhelmed by a mountain of complex data. While AI has shown promise, many existing tools operate as "black boxes," offering answers without explanations. This project introduces a Multi-Disease Medical Diagnosis System a smart, end to-end collaborator designed to simplify clinical workflows and give doctors a clearer picture of patient health. Our system doesn't just look for one thing; it manages three critical health areas simultaneously: Respiratory Diseases (Lung Cancer and Pneumonia), Blood Disorders (Anaemia, Thalassemia and Malaria), and Metabolic Conditions (Diabetes). We start by cleaning and enhancing raw medical images and lab results to ensure the highest data quality. Using advanced Deep Learning and Transfer Learning, our engine identifies subtle patterns that might be missed by the human eye. What truly sets this project apart is its focus on trust and transparency. Instead of just giving a "yes" or "no" diagnosis, our Explainability AI agent generates visual heatmaps. This shows clinicians exactly where the AI sees an issue, providing the "why" behind every suggestion. To make it even more practical, the system includes a Decision Support Stage that acts as a digital consultant, offering tailored guidance for each condition. The final experience is delivered through an intuitive User Interface that keeps the human in control. By including a Feedback Loop, we allow medical professionals to correct or confirm findings, helping the AI learn from real-world expertise. Ultimately, this system isn’t about replacing doctors it’s about giving them a powerful, transparent tool to reduce errors and focus on what matters most: saving lives. 1.3 Problem Statement Medical diagnosis systems play a vital role in healthcare, particularly in the early detection and treatment of diseases. However, traditional diagnostic approaches rely heavily on manual analysis of medical images, clinical reports, and physician expertise. These methods can be time-consuming, resource-intensive, and prone to human error, especially when handling large volumes of patient data or diseases with overlapping symptoms. This often leads to delays in diagnosis and affects the overall quality of patient care. Furthermore, most existing AI-based diagnostic systems are designed to detect only a single disease, limiting their applicability in real-world healthcare scenarios where multiple diseases need to be evaluated simultaneously. Such systems lack flexibility and fail to integrate different types of medical data, including imaging data, clinical parameters, and symptom-based inputs, within a unified framework. Although recent advancements in machine learning and deep learning have improved the accuracy of disease prediction, many systems lack explainability and transparency. Predictions are often presented without clear reasoning, making it difficult for healthcare professionals to trust and adopt these systems in clinical decision-making. Therefore, there is a critical need to design an intelligent and scalable multi-disease diagnosis system that can integrate multiple AI models, handle diverse medical data formats, provide accurate predictions, and offer explainable insights. The system should function as a clinical decision support tool that enhances diagnostic efficiency, reduces human error, and assists healthcare professionals in making faster and more informed decisions.

1.4 Objectives The primary objective of this project is to design and develop an intelligent multi-disease medical diagnosis system using an agentic AI approach that ensures accuracy, scalability, and explainability. The system aims to implement effective data acquisition and preprocessing techniques for handling diverse medical data formats, including medical images, clinical parameters, and symptom-based inputs. Image preprocessing methods such as resizing, normalization, and noise reduction are applied to enhance the quality of medical images, while data cleaning and normalization techniques are used for structured clinical datasets. Feature extraction and selection methods are employed to generate meaningful representations that can be effectively utilized by machine learning and deep learning models. Disease-specific AI agents, including Convolutional Neural Networks for image-based diagnosis and machine learning classifiers for tabular and symptom-based data, are developed to accurately classify diseases such as malaria, diabetes, and migraine. An agent orchestration layer is designed to intelligently route inputs to the appropriate diagnostic agent and generate a unified prediction output with confidence scores. 1.5 Project Scope & Limitations The scope of the proposed MediAssist AI system is focused on designing and implementing an intelligent, agent-based multi-disease medical diagnosis framework that ensures accuracy, scalability, and explainability. The system operates on multiple types of medical data, including medical images, clinical parameters, and symptom-based inputs, and aims to provide a complete diagnostic pipeline from data acquisition to final disease prediction. The project utilizes publicly available datasets such as the malaria blood cell image dataset, the PIMA diabetes dataset, and migraine symptom datasets. Rather than treating each component in isolation, this methodology weaves together classical machine learning, ensemble-based transfer learning concepts, Explainable AI (XAI), and coordinated multi-agent orchestration. The idea is simple but powerful: instead of asking one model to do everything, the system breaks the problem into well-defined stages, each managed by a specialized agent, so that failures in one part do not bring down the whole pipeline. Each phase addresses specific gaps found in the literature review — most notably the fact that existing systems either diagnose only a single disease, lack transparency in their predictions, or rely on rigid monolithic architectures that are hard to maintain and extend. Data Collection and Dataset Preparation The first phase lays the foundation by identifying and collecting clinically relevant, publicly available datasets suitable for multi-disease classification. Before any model training begins, the dataset is carefully audited for quality issues: missing values are identified and quantified, class imbalance ratios are computed, outlier records are flagged using statistical thresholds, and label accuracy is cross-referenced against clinical literature. The dataset is then split into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) subsets using stratified sampling to ensure each disease class is proportionally represented in every split. This careful preparation prevents the common pitfall of inflated test accuracy caused by class leakage or distribution mismatch between train and test sets. 2. Feature normalization using min-max scaling standardizes numerical ranges so that biomarkers with naturally large values (such as platelet counts in the hundreds of thousands) do not overshadow features with smaller magnitudes (such as hemoglobin in single digits). Missing values are imputed using column-wise median values — a robust strategy that is less sensitive to extreme outliers than mean imputation.

A Random Forest ensemble classifier is trained on the preprocessed feature vectors to simultaneously distinguish between six disease classes: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, Iron-Deficiency Anemia, Malaria, Hepatic Dysfunction, and Coronary Artery Disease. The Random Forest was chosen deliberately over more complex deep learning alternatives because of its excellent balance of interpretability, robustness to overfitting, natural handling of mixed numerical feature types, and computational efficiency that makes real-time inference practical. The model uses 100 decision trees, each trained on a random subset of features and samples, with class_weight='balanced' to counteract the inherent imbalance in disease prevalence. After training, the model is serialized into a compact bundle file (mediscan_bundle.pkl) that packages the classifier, the fitted label encoder, the ordered list of 24 feature names, and the six class labels together. This is not just an aesthetic design decision — it addresses a genuine clinical need for modular, fault-tolerant systems where individual components can fail, be updated, or be replaced without bringing down the whole pipeline. The Intake Agent serves as the entry point, receiving and validating all patient inputs through a Pydantic model that enforces correct data types and provides safe defaults for missing fields. The Router Agent then analyzes what data was actually provided and intelligently selects the most appropriate prediction pathway — full ML inference for complete blood panels, rule-based heuristic inference for basic vitals, or a file processing pathway for uploaded lab reports. Finally, the Report Agent retrieves a curated set of condition-specific clinical recommendations tailored to the top predicted disease. Together, these five agents create a pipeline that is greater than the sum of its parts. 5. On the quantitative side, the Random Forest model is evaluated using accuracy, per-class precision, recall, and F1-score on the held-out test set. Macro-averaged versions of these metrics are computed across all six disease classes to give equal weight to minority conditions that might otherwise be drowned out in aggregate statistics. On the qualitative side, all 25 documented test cases are executed through the complete end-to-end pipeline to validate agent coordination, routing logic, fallback behavior, explanation quality, and recommendation relevance.
