LITERATURE SURVEY The rapid evolution of AI in healthcare over the past decade has produced a diverse body of research spanning deep learning for medical image analysis, agent-based clinical decision support, multi-label disease prediction from electronic health records, and hybrid intelligent systems that combine these approaches. Understanding what has already been tried, what has worked, and — critically — what gaps remain is essential context for the design of MedAssist AI. This literature survey is organized into three major categories that most directly inform the project: (i) agent-based clinical decision support systems, which motivate the multi-agent architecture; (ii) multi-label disease prediction using machine learning, which motivates the structured-data ML approach; and (iii) hybrid intelligent systems that combine agents with learning models, which reveals the core research gap that MedAssist AI aims to fill. The survey draws on 10 peer-reviewed works published between 2020 and 2024, with a focus on identifying concrete limitations in existing systems rather than simply cataloguing prior art.

2.1 Literature Review 2.1.1 Agent-Based Medical Diagnosis and Decision Support Systems Early research in clinical AI recognized that the complexity of medical diagnosis — involving multiple specialties, data sources, and decision-makers — maps naturally onto multi-agent system (MAS) architectures. Unlike monolithic models that attempt to capture all clinical knowledge in a single parameter space, agent-based systems distribute reasoning across specialized, cooperative components that mirror the roles in an actual clinical team. Oprea (2020) proposed MEDICAL MAS, one of the most cited early examples of a comprehensive agent-based medical diagnosis system. The architecture assigned distinct roles to physician agents (responsible for rule-based differential reasoning with weighted confidence factors), patient agents (maintaining individual health profiles), nurse agents (monitoring vitals and scheduling), and information retrieval agents (querying relational medical databases). What made MEDICAL MAS notable was its explicit modeling of the social structure of a clinical team rather than reducing diagnosis to a single inference problem. However, the system's dependence on hand-crafted clinical rules meant that adding a new disease required manual rule engineering, and the single-disease-at-a-time design limited its real-world applicability for patients with multiple conditions. Korolyova et al. (2021) tackled the rigidity problem by integrating Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) into a multi-agent CDSS, allowing the system to adapt its diagnostic reasoning based on historical patient cases rather than purely static rules. Evaluated on heart disease diagnosis, the system demonstrated improved accuracy and adaptability compared to pure rule-based systems. However, the CBR approach requires a well-curated case library that may not be readily available for all disease domains, and the system still operates on a single-disease basis, making it unsuitable for multi-morbidity scenarios that are increasingly common in aging patient populations. A clear pattern emerges from these early agent-based systems: they excel at distributed reasoning and explainability but consistently lack the data-driven learning capabilities needed to model complex, multi-disease clinical patterns. This limitation motivates the hybrid approach taken in MedAssist AI, where agent-based orchestration is combined with a trained machine learning model. 2.1.2 Multi-Label Disease Prediction Using Machine Learning

A clear pattern emerges from these early agent-based systems: they excel at distributed reasoning and explainability but consistently lack the data-driven learning capabilities needed to model complex, multi-disease clinical patterns. This limitation motivates the hybrid approach taken in MedAssist AI, where agent-based orchestration is combined with a trained machine learning model. 2.1.2 Multi-Label Disease Prediction Using Machine Learning The growing availability of structured electronic health records provided machine learning researchers with large-scale clinical datasets suitable for training multi-label classifiers — models that can predict multiple conditions simultaneously rather than treating each disease as a separate binary classification problem. This is clinically significant because multi-label modeling can capture statistical correlations between diseases, reflecting the real-world phenomenon of comorbidity. Zhou et al. (2021) conducted one of the most thorough comparative studies of multi-label classification approaches for clinical data, applying five different model families to the task of predicting four diabetic complications concurrently from large-scale EHR data. The key finding was that Ensemble Classifier Chains — which model disease labels sequentially, passing earlier predictions as features to subsequent classifiers — significantly outperformed independent binary classifiers by explicitly capturing correlations between conditions. This work established the statistical case for multi-label learning in clinical settings, though it acknowledged limitations in explainability and the absence of any interactive clinical interface. On the imaging side, Rajpurkar et al. (2021) demonstrated with CheXNet that a densely connected CNN could achieve radiologist-level accuracy for pneumonia detection from chest X-rays, marking a milestone for AI-assisted radiology. Wang et al. (2022) extended this to multi-label classification across 14 thoracic pathologies using the large-scale ChestXray8 dataset, modeling hierarchical disease dependencies to improve performance. While these imaging studies are technically impressive, their exclusive focus on a single data modality — chest X-rays — limits their applicability to the broader multi-disease, structured-data diagnostic challenge that MedAssist AI addresses.

CHAPTER 3 Software Requirements Specification 3.1 Assumptions and Dependencies 3.1.1 Assumptions The design and implementation of MedAssist AI rest on a set of explicit assumptions about the deployment environment and usage context. First and foremost, patient input data is assumed to arrive through the web dashboard in a structured digital format — whether that means a complete 24-feature blood panel from a laboratory system or just a few manually entered vital signs and checkbox symptom selections. All numerical values are expected in standard clinical units: glucose in mg/dL, blood pressure in mmHg, hemoglobin in g/dL, temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, and cholesterol in mg/dL. The trained model bundle file (mediscan_bundle.pkl) is assumed to be present in the models/ directory at the time of application startup. This bundle must contain a trained Random Forest classifier, a fitted scikit-learn LabelEncoder, an ordered list of 24 feature names, and a list of six disease class labels. If the bundle is missing or corrupted, the system's heuristic fallback engine is assumed to provide clinically reasonable outputs sufficient for decision support until the bundle is restored. The system is designed as a decision support tool, not a replacement for clinical judgment. It is assumed that all AI-generated predictions will be reviewed and acted upon only by qualified healthcare professionals. Users are expected to have basic familiarity with clinical terminology to correctly interpret the differential diagnosis output, biomarker heatmaps, and clinical recommendation panels. 3.1.2 Dependencies MedAssist AI has well-defined software and data dependencies. The primary model dependency is the mediscan_bundle.pkl file, which encapsulates the complete trained inference pipeline in a single serialized artifact. 4.1 Introduction The methodology of MedAssist AI is organized around a single governing objective: building a diagnostic system that is simultaneously accurate, transparent, and reliable. Accuracy means the system correctly predicts the most likely disease from available clinical data. Transparency means every prediction comes with a human-readable explanation tracing it back to specific biomarker evidence. Reliability means the system always produces a medically grounded output — even when the ML model fails, even when input data is incomplete, even when the deployment environment is degraded. These three objectives are not independent: they create genuine design tensions. Maximizing accuracy often pushes toward complex black-box models; maximizing transparency pushes toward simpler, rule-based systems; maximizing reliability requires redundant pathways that add architectural complexity. The methodology described in the following sections represents the design decisions made to balance these tensions within the specific constraints of a clinical decision support application deployed as a web service. 4.2 Overview of the Proposed System The system architecture flows through six sequential processing stages. Stage 1 is data ingestion and preprocessing, where raw patient inputs from the web form are validated, normalized, and structured into a consistent 24-dimensional feature vector. Stage 2 is intelligent routing, where the Router Agent analyzes input completeness and directs the request to the most appropriate inference pathway. Stage 3 is disease inference, executed by either the trained Random Forest model or the rule-based heuristic engine depending on the router's decision and the model bundle's availability. Stage 4 is explanation generation, where the Explanation Agent identifies the clinical evidence supporting the prediction. Stage 5 is recommendation retrieval, where the Report Agent provides condition-specific clinical guidance. Stage 6 is visualization rendering, where the dashboard transforms the JSON API response into interactive charts, heatmaps, and recommendation panels. 4.3 Dataset Acquisition and Model Training

The 24 biomarker features span five clinical domains: metabolic health (Glucose, HbA1c, Insulin, BMI, Triglycerides), hematological status (Hemoglobin, Hematocrit, RBC, WBC, Platelets, MCV, MCH, MCHC), cardiovascular function (Systolic BP, Diastolic BP, LDL, HDL, Cholesterol, Heart Rate, Troponin), hepatic function (ALT, AST, Creatinine), and inflammatory markers (C-reactive Protein). This multi-domain coverage is what enables the model to distinguish between conditions that may share surface-level symptoms but have distinct biomarker signatures. This sounds straightforward but requires careful handling of the wide variation in input completeness that characterizes real-world clinical settings. When a complete blood panel is submitted, all 24 feature slots are filled directly from the corresponding lab values. When only basic vitals are available (glucose, cholesterol, hemoglobin, BMI, blood pressure), five feature slots are filled and the remaining 19 default to 0.0 — a zero-imputation strategy consistent with the median-based imputation used during training. All features are min-max normalized to the [0, 1] range during training to prevent high-magnitude features from dominating the tree splitting criteria. Five-fold stratified cross-validation provides robust performance estimates across all six disease classes, ensuring that the model's reported accuracy reflects genuine generalization rather than fitting to a particular data split. 4.5 Heuristic Scoring Engine The heuristic scoring engine is arguably the most clinically important component of MedAssist AI from a safety perspective. Heuristic Scoring Engine The heuristic scoring engine is arguably the most clinically important component of MedAssist AI from a safety perspective. It ensures that the system provides diagnostically meaningful outputs under all conditions, including the scenario where the ML model is unavailable. Rather than a generic fallback that returns placeholder text, the heuristic engine implements a complete, medically validated scoring algorithm derived from established clinical diagnostic criteria. For Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, the engine applies ADA diagnostic thresholds: glucose above 126 mg/dL (fasting diagnostic criterion) contributes 0.35 to the diabetes score; pre-diabetic glucose of 100-125 mg/dL contributes 0.18; BMI above 30 contributes 0.20; thirst and urination symptoms each add 0.15 and 0.12. For Hypertension, systolic BP above 160 mmHg (JNC Stage 2) contributes 0.40; BP of 140-159 mmHg contributes 0.28; cholesterol above 240 mg/dL adds 0.20. For Iron-Deficiency Anemia, hemoglobin below 10 g/dL contributes 0.45; mild anemia (10-12 g/dL) contributes 0.28; fatigue and shortness of breath symptoms add 0.18 and 0.14. For Malaria, temperature above 103 degrees F contributes 0.40; fever symptom adds 0.22; headache and nausea each contribute 0.14 and 0.12. For Hepatic Dysfunction, jaundice symptom contributes 0.45 (reflecting its high specificity for liver disease); nausea and fatigue add 0.15 and 0.12. For Coronary Artery Disease, chest pain symptom contributes 0.35; shortness of breath 0.20; age above 55 adds 0.08. A Pandas DataFrame is constructed from the input dictionary, any missing columns are added with a value of 0.0, and columns are reindexed to exactly match the stored feature_names ordering. This approach is deliberately defensive: the model will always receive exactly 24 features in exactly the right order, regardless of how many or which features were actually provided by the user. Partial inputs simply result in zero-filled features for the missing dimensions. 4.7 Feature Representation The 24-dimensional clinical feature vector represents a comprehensive physiological snapshot spanning metabolic, hematological, cardiovascular, hepatic, and inflammatory domains. This multi-domain representation is what enables the Random Forest to distinguish between conditions that might share surface-level symptoms. For example, both malaria and anemia can present with fatigue — but their biomarker signatures are completely different: malaria is associated with elevated temperature and fever patterns, while anemia is defined by low hemoglobin and hematocrit values. The model learns these domain-specific discriminative boundaries from the training data in a way that no single-disease model can. 4.8 Feature Encoding and Model Inference

This design choice reduces application startup time and avoids loading the model bundle into memory if the application is started and then receives only non-prediction requests. Once loaded, the bundle's components are cached as instance attributes for all subsequent requests. At the routing level, the RouterAgent selects the inference pathway most likely to produce the best prediction given the available input: ML inference when rich blood panel data is available (higher accuracy from learned feature patterns), heuristic inference when only basic vitals are provided (clinically validated rules that work well with limited data). At the inference level, the PredictionAgent wraps ML execution in a try-except block that catches any runtime failure and seamlessly activates the heuristic engine as a fallback. The ExplanationAgent synthesizes insights across both inference modes. For ML predictions, it identifies which specific biomarker values cross clinical thresholds to contextualize the statistical prediction. For heuristic predictions, the clinical rules themselves serve as the explanation. This cross-mode consistency ensures that clinicians always receive actionable clinical reasoning regardless of which inference pathway was used. 4.10 Decision Making

The top class and its confidence percentage are presented as the 'Primary Diagnosis'. All remaining classes are displayed as the 'Differential Diagnoses' ranked by probability — a design choice rooted in clinical practice, where differential diagnosis lists are standard tools for managing diagnostic uncertainty. A high-confidence primary diagnosis (say, 85%+) with all others below 10% suggests a clear clinical indication. A more distributed probability mass (say, 45% primary with a 30% secondary) signals genuine diagnostic ambiguity that warrants further investigation, guiding the clinician to order additional tests rather than acting on the AI's top suggestion alone. 4.11 Performance Evaluation System evaluation uses a comprehensive set of metrics covering both prediction quality and operational performance. Prediction quality metrics include per-class precision, recall, and F1-score; overall accuracy; macro-averaged F1-score computed without class-size weighting to give equal voice to minority disease classes; and confusion matrix analysis to identify which disease pairs are most frequently confused. Model calibration is assessed by comparing predicted confidence levels against empirical accuracy — well-calibrated models give 80% confidence only when they are actually correct about 80% of the time. Operational performance metrics include end-to-end API response latency measured across 25 test cases, validated against the 2-second SRS requirement; concurrent request throughput tested under 10 simultaneous connections; heuristic fallback activation success rate (required: 100% in all model-unavailable scenarios); and cross-browser compatibility validated on Chrome, Firefox, and Edge. These dual evaluation dimensions reflect the project's commitment to building not just a statistically accurate model but a genuinely deployable clinical system.

5.1 System Architecture MedAssist AI is built on a clean three-tier architecture that enforces strong separation between the presentation, application, and model layers. The Presentation Tier is the multidisease_dashboard.html file — a self-contained, single-file web application that handles all user interaction and result visualization without any build tools or external dependencies. The Application Tier is app.py — the FastAPI backend that implements the five-agent orchestration pipeline, defines the API contract, and coordinates the flow of data between the model layer and the frontend. The Model Tier consists of model_bundle.py and heuristic.py — isolated inference implementations that can be updated, retrained, or replaced without touching any application-level code. The agent pipeline flows as follows: patient data enters through the Intake Agent, which validates and structures it; the Router Agent selects the prediction pathway; the Prediction Agent executes inference (ML or heuristic); the Explanation Agent generates clinical reasoning; the Report Agent retrieves recommendations; and the API response assembler packages everything into the JSON response that the dashboard renders. Every handoff between agents uses well-typed Python objects, making the data flow explicit and the pipeline easy to trace and debug. 5.2 Mathematical Model The formal prediction model is as follows. Let F be the 24-dimensional normalized feature vector representing a patient's clinical measurements. Let C = {Diabetes, Hypertension, Anemia, Malaria, Hepatic Dysfunction, CAD} be the six disease classes. The Random Forest RF consists of N = 100 decision trees. Each tree Ti maps F to a probability vector P_Ti over C. The ensemble posterior is the averaged class probability: P_RF(ck|F) = (1/N) * sum(P_Ti(ck|F)) for each class ck. The final ML diagnosis is D* = argmax over C of P_RF(ck|F).

This high-level view captures the system's fundamental purpose: transforming clinical inputs into structured diagnostic guidance. Level 1 DFD: Patient data flows into Process 1 (Intake Agent: validate and structure inputs) producing a Context Object. The Context Object flows to Process 2 (Router Agent: select prediction pathway) producing a Routing Decision. The decision directs data to either Process 3A (ML Prediction Agent: Random Forest inference) or Process 3B (Heuristic Prediction Agent: rule-based scoring), both producing a Prediction Object. Its process(req: PredictRequest, report_file: Optional[UploadFile]) method performs two operations: it determines the 'richness' of the input (is structured clinical data present? is a file attached?) and packages this context alongside the validated request object into a dictionary for downstream agents. Input richness is assessed by checking if req.blood contains any blood panel values or if any of the eight basic vital fields are non-zero. This boolean assessment drives the Router Agent's routing decision. If a file is attached, its metadata (filename, content_type) is extracted and stored in the context. The PredictRequest Pydantic model enforces type safety on all 24+ input fields — float values for all vitals with 0.0 as the safe default, list for symptoms with empty list as default, and dict for the blood panel with empty dict as default. Pydantic's strict type checking ensures that a string accidentally passed as a glucose value is caught and rejected before reaching the prediction pipeline. 7.1.2 Router Agent Module

Its route(context) method applies three ordered checks. First, if the blood panel dictionary is populated (indicating a lab system provided structured values for specific biomarker names), the request is sent to the ML inference pathway — this is where the full 24-feature Random Forest delivers its highest-accuracy predictions. Its run(req) method instantiates a ModelBundle object pointing to the model file path (configurable via the MEDISCAN_MODEL_BUNDLE environment variable for deployment flexibility). If the bundle exists, it constructs the feature dictionary — using the blood panel values directly when available, otherwise building from basic vitals with zero-padding — and calls bundle.predict_proba(). The entire ML inference block is wrapped in a try-except that catches any exception: FileNotFoundError if the bundle is missing, UnpicklingError if the file is corrupted, ValueError if required keys are absent, or any runtime error during prediction. When any of these occur, the except block immediately calls predict_with_heuristic() with the six basic vital parameters, returning a ModelPrediction with model_mode='heuristic_agent' to indicate the fallback was used. This unconditional fallback guarantee is the cornerstone of the system's availability requirement. 7.1.4 Explanation Agent Module

Input: Python dictionary mapping biomarker feature name strings to float values (up to 24 features, partial inputs accepted). Output: Top disease label string, top confidence float, full confidence dictionary with all six class probabilities. Steps: (1) Check bundle.exists(); raise FileNotFoundError if bundle file is absent (triggers heuristic fallback in caller). (2) Lazy-load bundle on first call: open pickle file, deserialize, extract rf_model, label_encoder, feature_names, class_names with multi-key fallback logic. (3) Construct pandas DataFrame with single row from input dictionary. (4) For each name in feature_names: if not in DataFrame columns, add column with value 0.0. (5) Reindex DataFrame columns to exact feature_names ordering. (6) probs = rf_model.predict_proba(df)[0] — probability vector of length 6. (7) pred_encoded = rf_model.predict(df)[0]; top_label = label_encoder.inverse_transform([pred_encoded])[0]. (8) Build confidence dict: {class_names[i]: probs[i] for i in range(6)}. (9) Normalize: divide each value by sum of all values. (10) Return top_label, max(probs), normalized confidence dict.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE Preamble: This chapter synthesizes the key contributions, performance outcomes, and broader clinical significance of the MedAssist AI Multi-Disease Medical Diagnosis System. It reflects on how the project addresses the research gaps identified through literature review, evaluates the system against its stated objectives, and outlines a future work roadmap that extends toward broader disease coverage, imaging modality support, and large-scale clinical deployment.

9.1 Conclusion MedAssist AI was conceived to answer a specific question: can a student team build a unified, deployable, multi-disease diagnostic AI system that is simultaneously accurate, transparent, and reliable — within a single academic year and using only open-source tools? The answer, as demonstrated by the working system, is yes. But the more interesting answer is in the how, because the architectural choices made along the way reveal principles that go beyond this specific project. The five-agent architecture is the most significant design decision in the project. By decomposing the diagnostic workflow into five specialized, independently testable agents, the system achieves a level of modularity and fault tolerance that is rare in student AI projects and uncommon even in commercial clinical tools. The RouterAgent's intelligent pathway selection and the PredictionAgent's unconditional fallback guarantee together ensure that the system never returns an error to a clinician — it always produces a medically grounded diagnostic output, even when the ML model is unavailable. This 100% availability property is not a nice-to-have in clinical settings; it is a fundamental safety requirement. The integration of transparent clinical reasoning through the Explanation Agent addresses what is arguably the deepest barrier to clinical AI adoption: the black-box problem. By anchoring every prediction to specific, named biomarker threshold violations and symptom flags, the system transforms an opaque statistical output into a clinical narrative that a physician can evaluate, accept, challenge, or extend. This is not post-hoc explainability added as an afterthought — it is built into the agent architecture as a first-class citizen of the diagnostic workflow. The heuristic scoring engine deserves special recognition as a contribution in its own right. It is not just a fallback — it is a transparent, auditable diagnostic system that implements established clinical knowledge in executable, reviewable code. A clinician who reads the heuristic scoring rules can directly verify whether the clinical thresholds are medically appropriate. This level of transparency is something that not even the most sophisticated explainable deep learning system currently achieves.

1.​ Introduction Academic credential verification is a fundamental requirement in modern education systems, supporting admissions, employment, and professional licensing across institutions and industries. Traditional verification methods depend on manual checks, centralized databases, or direct communication with issuing universities, which can be slow, costly, and vulnerable to document forgery, data tampering, and institutional dependency. Recent advancements in blockchain technology have demonstrated strong potential for building tamper-resistant and transparent record systems. However, many existing digital credential solutions rely on centralized storage or private databases, requiring verifiers to trust a single authority. Such approaches limit interoperability, introduce single points of failure, and reduce acceptance, especially when credentials must be verified across countries or organizations. The proposed Blockchain-Based Academic Document Verification System addresses these challenges by introducing a decentralized framework for issuing and validating academic credentials. In this system, educational institutions digitally sign student certificates, generate cryptographic hashes of the documents, and anchor these hashes immutably on a public blockchain. The original documents are stored securely off-chain, while the blockchain acts as a permanent source of truth for authenticity verification. Furthermore, the system incorporates QR-code-based access to simplify verification by third parties such as employers and universities. By scanning the QR code, verifiers can independently validate certificate integrity by comparing document hashes against blockchain records without relying on the issuing institution. Rather than replacing existing academic processes, the system functions as a trust infrastructure layer, reducing fraud, improving transparency, and enabling trust-less verification of academic credentials. 2.​ Literature Review The literature survey is organised into three categories: (i) traditional academic document verification systems, (ii) blockchain-based credential management frameworks, and (iii) decentralised identity and verifiable credential systems. 2.1​Traditional academic document verification systems Early academic credential verification systems relied on centralised databases maintained by universities or third-party agencies. While these systems can verify credentials within controlled environments, they require verifiers to trust the issuing institution and database administrators, making them vulnerable to insider manipulation, data breaches, and service unavailability. Gap: There is a lack of trust-independent verification mechanisms that allow third parties to verify academic credentials without relying on centralized authorities. 2.​ Limited Trust and Transparency in Hash-Based Verification Approaches Several studies propose hash-based integrity verification by storing document hashes in conventional databases. Although hashing ensures document integrity, the verification process still depends on the security and honesty of the database owner. Unauthorized modification or deletion of hash records cannot be independently detected by external verifiers. Such approaches restrict public verifiability and reduce the core benefit of decentralization, especially for cross-institutional or cross-border verification scenarios. Gap: There is no widely adopted framework that enables global, trust-less verification of academic credentials using public blockchain infrastructure. 4.​ Lack of Practical Verification Interfaces for Non-Technical Users A major limitation in existing blockchain-based solutions is the assumption that all stakeholders possess technical knowledge of blockchain systems, wallets, or smart contracts. This creates adoption barriers for employers, recruiters, and institutions unfamiliar with blockchain technology.

Comprehensive systems that integrate credential issuance, off-chain document storage, on-chain proof anchoring, and seamless third-party verification are relatively scarce. Gap: There is an absence of a complete end-to-end academic credential lifecycle framework that is secure, scalable, and practical for real-world institutional adoption. 4.​ Problem Statement The increasing mobility of students and professionals has significantly raised the demand for reliable and timely academic credential verification. Traditional verification practices depend on manual checks, centralised databases, or direct communication with issuing institutions, which are often slow, costly, and inefficient. These methods are vulnerable to document forgery, unauthorised modification, and administrative delays, especially when verification is required across institutions, organisations, or national boundaries. Although digital certificates and document hashing techniques have been introduced to improve security, most existing systems store verification records in centralised databases. Such approaches still require verifiers to trust the issuing authority or database administrators, creating single points of failure and increasing the risk of insider manipulation or data breaches. Furthermore, verification processes are often fragmented, lacking a unified workflow that seamlessly connects credential issuance, storage, and third-party verification. In addition, many blockchain-based credential solutions focus heavily on technical

implementation while neglecting usability and real-world adoption challenges. The absence of simple verification interfaces and end-to-end system integration limits their practical deployment in traditional academic environments. Therefore, the problem is to design a secure, scalable, and trust-independent academic document verification system that enables institutions to issue tamper-proof credentials and allows third parties to verify authenticity without relying on centralised databases. The system must provide an end-to-end issuance-to-verification workflow while maintaining usability for non-technical users and ensuring data integrity, transparency, and global verifiability. 5.​ Objectives The primary objective of this project is to design and implement a blockchain-based academic document verification system that enables secure issuance, immutable storage, and trust-less verification of academic credentials. The system aims to allow educational institutions to digitally sign certificates, generate cryptographic hashes, and anchor these proofs on a public blockchain, ensuring tamper resistance and long-term integrity. Off-chain storage mechanisms are used to securely store original documents while minimizing on-chain data overhead. Another key objective is to simplify the verification process for third parties such as employers and universities by providing a user-friendly verification mechanism using QR codes and web-based interfaces. This ensures that verifiers can independently validate document authenticity without requiring technical knowledge of blockchain systems or direct interaction with the issuing institution. The secondary objective of the project is to evaluate the effectiveness and practicality of the

proposed system by analyzing verification accuracy, resistance to document tampering, and reduction in verification time compared to traditional centralized approaches. The project also aims to study scalability, cost efficiency, and adaptability of the system for different academic institutions, while designing an extensible architecture that can support future enhancements such as decentralized identity frameworks and cross-border credential interoperability. 6.​ Methodology The proposed Blockchain-Based Academic Document Verification System is developed using a phased methodology to ensure structured design, secure implementation, and effective validation. Each phase focuses on a specific component of the system while maintaining seamless integration across the credential lifecycle. Phase 1: System Requirement Analysis and Design In this phase, system requirements are identified by analyzing existing academic verification processes, security challenges, and stakeholder needs. Functional and non-functional requirements are defined, followed by the design of the overall system architecture, including on-chain and off-chain components. Phase 2: Document Issuance and Digital Signing Educational institutions generate digital academic certificates and apply cryptographic digital signatures to ensure authenticity. A unique cryptographic hash of each document is generated, which serves as a tamper-evident fingerprint for verification purposes. Phase 3: Blockchain Hash Anchoring The generated document hash, along with essential metadata, is recorded on a public blockchain using smart contracts. This phase ensures immutability and public verifiability of credential proofs while preventing unauthorized modification of verification records. Phase 4: Secure Off-Chain Document Storage Original academic documents are stored securely in off-chain storage systems such as institutional servers or distributed storage solutions. The system maintains a logical link between stored documents and their corresponding blockchain records without exposing sensitive data on-chain. Phase 5: Verification and QR-Code-Based Access For verification, a QR code embedded in the certificate directs verifiers to a verification interface. The system recomputes the document hash and compares it with the blockchain-stored hash to confirm authenticity. This process enables fast and independent verification without requiring trust in centralized databases. ABSTRACT Dyslexia is a learning difficulty that significantly impacts a child’s ability to read, write, and recognize letters and sounds, often leading to emotional frustration and academic setbacks. Traditional teaching methods—centered on rote memorization, linear instruction, and heavy text usage—often fail to address the unique cognitive needs of dyslexic learners. This project aims to bridge that gap by developing an immersive educational platform that harnesses the power of Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) to support children with dyslexia in building foundational literacy skills. The platform offers a multisensory learning environment where children can interact with 3D letters, hear phonics through clear audio cues, and visually associate words with contextual objects. Built using Unity 3D, the system integrates AR Foundation and Vuforia for mobile-based AR experiences and utilizes the Oculus SDK to provide fully immersive VR interaction. Key features include gesture-based navigation via Unity XR Toolkit, voice feedback using Text-to-Speech APIs, and audio-assisted learning using Unity’s AudioSource component. The platform is designed for accessibility and affordability, optimized for Android devices and low-cost VR headsets, making it ideal for both school and home settings. By turning passive learning into an active, playful experience, the solution fosters engagement, builds confidence, and supports early literacy development in a way that’s tailored to the needs of dyslexic children. This approach not only makes learning more inclusive but also lays the foundation for scalable, technology-driven educational support that adapts to individual learning challenges with empathy and innovation. INTRODUCTION Children with dyslexia face significant challenges in early education, particularly in recognizing letters, forming sound-symbol associations, and processing text-heavy learning materials. Traditional classroom environments often rely on written instruction and memorization techniques that are not effective for neurodiverse learners. As a result, many dyslexic students experience reduced engagement, low confidence, and slower academic progress. To address these difficulties, this project proposes the use of immersive technologies such as Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) to transform how dyslexic students interact with foundational learning content. Instead of passive reading, students will engage in multi-sensory experiences—seeing, hearing, and interacting with letters and related objects in a 3D environment. For example, a child learning the letter "B" can view it floating in front of them, listen to its pronunciation, and associate it with an animated ball to reinforce learning. This method supports personalized learning, adapts to the student’s pace, and reduces cognitive overload by replacing complex text with visual and auditory cues. The platform will be developed using Unity 3D and deployed via accessible devices such as mobile phones (for AR) and low-cost VR headsets. By aligning with inclusive education principles, the project seeks to empower dyslexic learners and provide a supportive, engaging learning environment that enhances comprehension and retention through immersive, technology-driven experiences.

LITERATURE SURVEY SCOPE This project is all about creating a learning tool that truly supports young children with dyslexia. Instead of relying on traditional, text-heavy teaching methods, it uses AR and VR to turn early reading lessons into fun, interactive experiences. Kids can see letters in 3D, hear how they sound, and connect them to familiar objects—all in a way that feels more natural and easier to understand. The platform runs on affordable devices like Android phones and VR headsets, so it can be used both in classrooms and at home. Everything is designed with the child in mind—from the easy-to-use interface to the clear audio and dyslexia-friendly fonts. As it grows, the platform will also include grammar, different languages, progress tracking, and even emotional feedback. It’s a step toward making learning more inclusive, engaging, and built around how each child learns best. MOTIVATION Many students with dyslexia find it tough to keep up in traditional classrooms, where lessons are mostly text-based and follow a one-size-fits-all approach. This can lead to frustration, low confidence, and a lack of motivation—especially when it comes to learning the basics like letters and sounds. This project was inspired by the idea that learning should feel exciting and accessible for everyone. By using immersive technologies like Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR), we’re creating an experience where kids can actually see, hear, and interact with what they’re learning. Imagine a child walking around a giant letter “A,” hearing its sound, and seeing an apple appear beside it—all in 3D. With voice feedback, gesture-based controls, and support for affordable devices, this platform makes learning feel more natural and fun, whether at school or home. It’s about giving dyslexic students a learning space that works for them.

PROPOSED SYSTEM The proposed system is a comprehensive Extended Reality (XR) learning platform designed to directly support students with dyslexia by leveraging simultaneous Visual, Auditory, and Kinesthetic (VAK) stimuli. At the current 80% implementation stage, the core AR learning module is complete, demonstrating interactive, three-dimensional animal models in the user's space. Each model is fully integrated with audio narration for descriptive information, a linked web button for deeper research, and dynamic animations that activate upon touch. This multi-sensory framework is critical, as it bypasses traditional text-heavy difficulties and utilizes the spatial strengths and active engagement preferred by dyslexic learners, thereby promoting greater focus and memory retention. The technical architecture is built for maximum accessibility and performance. The system utilizes Unity 3D as the central game engine, guaranteeing robustness across multiple target devices. We have successfully integrated AR Foundation (and similar frameworks like [NAME]) for stable world tracking and XR Toolkit for seamless interaction handling in the immersive space. The specialized Audio Engine (using Text-to-Speech/AudioSource) ensures clear, low-distraction voice guidance to reinforce the visual and textual data. This ensures the platform is immediately deployable on affordable devices, including standard AR-enabled smartphones and low-cost VR headsets, making the solution highly scalable for educational settings. The final 20% of the project will focus entirely on validation and scalability. The established AR animal module will serve as the template for developing additional immersive content modules. The next steps include formal pilot testing of the current module with dyslexic students to gather quantitative feedback on engagement and effectiveness. Based on these results, we will finalize the system's architecture for stories and phonics-based poems and implement personalized learning features tailored to individual progress, ensuring the final deliverable is an inclusive, scientifically-grounded, and highly engaging educational tool ready for broad application.

IMPLEMENTATION The implementation of the AR module for dyslexic students was carried out in multiple stages, ensuring a structured and efficient development process aimed at maximizing accessibility and multi-sensory engagement. Environment & Asset Preparation Platform Initialization: The project was set up in the [NAME] platform (MyWebAR) using World Tracking, allowing the digital content to be seamlessly anchored onto real-world surfaces. 3D Model Acquisition: High-quality, animated 3D animal models (e.g., Lion, Elephant, etc.) were sourced and optimized for low latency and smooth rendering on mobile devices. Content Curation: Concise, dyslexia-friendly textual information (facts, habitat details) was prepared for each animal. Interface Layer: A clear, high-contrast User Interface (UI) overlay was designed with four primary buttons: Information, Audio, Animation, and Website. Information Linking (Visual Support): The 'Information' button was linked to a separate, dynamically appearing text panel that displays the animal facts in a clean, legible format. Audio Integration (Auditory Support): The core 'Audio' button was scripted to trigger the simultaneous playback of the associated voice-over track, reinforcing the textual information through sound. Kinesthetic/Interactive Feedback: The 'Animation' button was configured to trigger the model's key behavior (e.g., a lion roar animation or a monkey jump), satisfying the need for interactive, kinesthetic engagement. Web Link Integration: The 'Website' button was implemented to provide a deep learning pathway by launching an external resource URL for advanced students or further research. Virtual Reality Implementation The Virtual Reality (VR) module was successfully implemented as an immersive learning environment designed to enhance alphabet recognition and interactive engagement for dyslexic students. The VR system was developed and executed using Unity 3D and tested with the Oculus Quest 3s headset, offering a smooth and fully immersive experience. In this module, a virtual classroom setup was created featuring a bench with multiple cubes, each labeled with different alphabets. The student, represented by the VR user, can move around the environment using teleportation controls and interact with objects through drag-and-drop gestures. The primary learning task involves identifying and picking the correct alphabet cube and placing it into the corresponding box. Once the cube is correctly dropped inside the box, the system provides instant auditory feedback—a success sound along with a voice prompt such as “Correct! Well done!”—and the box automatically closes. This immediate reinforcement helps strengthen recognition and retention. If the cube is misplaced, gentle corrective feedback encourages retrying, promoting self-learning without frustration. The environment supports 360° interaction, realistic lighting, and physics-based object handling to simulate natural movement. The teleportation feature allows smooth navigation without motion sickness, making it comfortable even for young learners. The VR module effectively combines interactive motion, audio response, and spatial awareness to create an engaging, gamified learning experience. It enables students to actively participate rather than passively observe, bridging the gap between visual recognition and kinesthetic memory.

CONCLUSION This project highlights the transformative potential of Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) in addressing the challenges faced by dyslexic students during early education. Traditional, text-heavy teaching methods often fail to meet the cognitive needs of these learners, resulting in frustration and slow academic progress. By creating a multi-sensory, interactive environment, AR/VR enables students to visualize, hear, and engage with letters, sounds, and objects—making the learning experience more intuitive, memorable, and enjoyable.The platform promotes inclusive education by adapting to each learner’s pace and style while remaining cost-effective and accessible through mobile AR and low-cost VR headsets. Its scalable design supports future integration of subjects beyond literacy, such as numbers or grammar. In doing so, this project not only improves early reading skills but also contributes to a more empathetic and technologically enriched educational environment that empowers dyslexic students to learn confidently and independently.

Abstract The increasing sophistication of cyber threats and the rise of underground digital marketplaces have intensified the need for proactive cybersecurity measures. The Dark Web Threat [NAME] is a project designed to automate the process of monitoring and analyzing hidden web services (accessible via Tor) for the detection of potential cyber threats. The system focuses on gathering threat intelligence from darknet forums, marketplaces, and leak sites, which are often hubs for malicious activities such as data breaches, sale of stolen credentials, malware distribution, and discussions related to cyberattacks. This crawler utilizes web scraping and crawling techniques tailored to the anonymity and dynamic nature of dark web pages. By integrating natural language processing (NLP) and keyword-based filtering, the system extracts relevant data, classifies threat-related content, and stores it in a structured database. The collected intelligence can then be visualized or alerted through dashboards for real-time monitoring and decision-making. The project ensures ethical handling of data by avoiding engagement or interaction with illegal services, and it adheres to legal guidelines for passive data collection. It serves as a crucial tool for cybersecurity professionals, law enforcement agencies, and organizations aiming to enhance situational awareness and threat preparedness.By enabling early detection of emerging threats and vulnerabilities, the Dark Web Threat [NAME] contributes significantly to strengthening cyber defense mechanisms. It also demonstrates how automated systems can be leveraged for digital forensics and threat hunting in complex and opaque online ecosystems. Keywords: Dark Web, Threat Intelligence, Crawler, Cybersecurity, Tor Network.

Abstract
The Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System is designed to counter the primary disadvantage of
conventional drones with centralized control and manual triggering. Under high-risk
operations such as defense, surveillance, or disaster relief, such systems are extremely
susceptible to jamming or controller breakdown. This research proposes a next-generation
system where drones self-trigger based on onboard sensors (e.g., MPU6050) as soon as
they are deployed or enter into free-fall. This self-initiated mode permits instant mid-air launch
without human intervention, guaranteeing mission integrity even if mothership or command
station is lost. After taking off, every drone stabilizes and resumes autonomous flight,
applying onboard computer vision to spot and engage dynamically detected targets. Without
the requirement for external instructions, the system greatly improves responsiveness and
reliability in dynamic or communication-restricted environments. The project design involves
an industrial-strength latch and fallout system that allows safe dropping of multiple child
drones by a mother drone. The small drones are contained in latches that secure them until a
programmed trigger condition (e.g., free-fall or altitude level) is achieved. When released, the
drones automatically start and spread out for assigned functions. Created

Abstract The Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Authentication System is a cryptographic solution designed 
to verify user identities without revealing any sensitive information, such as passwords or 
personal data, during the authentication process. This system leverages the principles of zero-
knowledge proofs to enhance both security and privacy in digital communication and access 
control mechanisms. 
Traditional authentication systems often rely on password-based verification, which poses 
significant security risks, including phishing, credential stuffing, and data breaches. With the 
increasing concern over data privacy and the rising number of cyber-attacks, there is a growing 
demand for authentication methods that ensure high security while preserving user privacy. 
Zero-Knowledge Proofs, a concept from theoretical cryptography, provide a solution by 
allowing one party to prove to another that a statement is true without conveying any additional 
information. 
The primary purpose of the ZKP Authentication System is to develop a robust and privacy-
preserving authentication mechanism that eliminates the need for transmitting or storing 
sensitive user credentials. This system significantly reduces the attack surface for hackers and 
enhances user trust in digital platforms. Its significance lies in its potential application across 
various domains, including secure banking, blockchain-based systems, secure voting, and 
privacy-focused web applications. Keywords : Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Secure Authentication Privacy-Preserving Protocols Cryptographic Security Identity Verification

ABSTRACT This project demonstrates the successful implementation of the Advanced Military Equipment Detection (AMED) system, a modular, end-to-end system for detecting military equipment within satellite and aerial imagery that can specifically target camouflaged or hidden assets. The core innovation of this study is the multi-modal detection approach, as seen in the pipeline, which combines high-performing, direct object detection, with implicit shadow analysis. A customized YOLOv11m model was trained on a mixed dataset that included real-world and synthetic imagery (over 2000 images in total). The customized YOLOv11m model properly solved the "domain generalization" problem and is able to perform reliably on synthetic test data and real-world drone footage that was never seen by the model. The YOLOv11m model achieved a strong mean Average Precision (mAP50-95) of 68.1% on its main 'tank' class. The method generates synergistic evidence by associating shadows ultimately detected using a computer vision shadow algorithm with the vehicle found by YOLO. The outputs of the final product include marked images and structured JSON as evidence of a scalable and effective solution for advanced surveillance problem solving. Keywords: Satellite Imagery, Shadow Analysis, Deep Learning, Object Detection, YOLOv11, Domain Generalization, Synthetic Data, Data Fusion.

Abstract This project addresses the growing cyber-physical threats in Smart Cities by simulating and mitigating network-based and sensor-level attacks. These include Denial of Service (DoS), Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks, and ARP spoofing. The project utilizes [NAME] as the AV control module to emulate the communication and sensor interfaces typically found in real-world AV systems. Tools such as hping3, Scapy, and ARPSpoof are used to carry out these intrusions. As AVs rely heavily on continuous communication with cloud servers, control units, and GPS data for safe navigation, these communication pathways become critical points of vulnerability for malicious attacks. The aim is not only to evaluate the impact of these attacks but also to implement AI-based and rule-based real-time mitigation techniques using iptables. We will use Supervised and Unsupervised Learning to counteract these attacks. This approach provides a practical, low-cost framework for studying and defending AVs against real-time threats, contributing to the development of more secure smart transportation systems. The simulation highlights both technical vulnerabilities and effective prevention strategies. Keywords: Denial of Service, [NAME], ARP Spoofing, [NAME], Smart City.

Conventional security solutions mainly detect external attacks using
predefined signatures or rules. However, insider threats rarely follow
predictable patterns and often change over time. Therefore, there is a

The scope of Project Guardian focuses on developing an intelligent, behavior-based insider threat detection system that monitors user activities within an organization and identifies suspicious or abnormal behavior using advanced machine learning and data analysis techniques. The system aims to enhance cybersecurity by detecting potential insider threats at an early stage and assisting security teams in making informed decisions. The project covers the collection, simulation, and analysis of user activity data such as login behavior, file access, USB device usage, and email communication. By analyzing these activities, the system establishes normal behavioral patterns and identifies deviations that may indicate malicious or risky actions. The system also integrates graph-based relationship analysis to study interactions between users, files, and devices, helping to uncover hidden threat patterns. Furthermore, Project Guardian includes the development of an interactive visualization dashboard that allows administrators and security analysts to monitor risk levels, view anomaly alerts, and analyze suspicious activities in real time. The integration of explainable artificial intelligence techniques ensures transparency in detection results and improves trust in the system’s decision-making process. SCOPE MOTIVATION Many cybersecurity incidents are caused by trusted employees who misuse their access privileges. Organizations often lack systems to monitor behavioral anomalies effectively. Project Guardian was developed to provide organizations with an intelligent monitoring system that can detect suspicious activities before they lead to serious security incidents. The system aims to reduce manual monitoring efforts and improve overall cybersecurity awareness.

PROPOSED SYSTEM The proposed system, Project Guardian, is an AI-powered insider threat
detection platform designed to monitor, analyze, and identify suspicious
user activities within an organization. The system focuses on detecting
behavioral anomalies by analyzing user interaction with organizational
resources such as files, devices, and communication platforms. Unlike
traditional rule-based security systems, Project Guardian uses advanced
machine learning and graph-based analysis techniques to detect hidden and
evolving insider threats. Working Process
1.Data Collection and Log Monitoring
The system collects and simulates user activity logs, including login records, 
file access logs, USB device usage, and email communication data. These logs 
represent normal and suspicious organizational behavior patterns.
2. Feature Extraction and Behavioral Analysis
The collected data is preprocessed and transformed into meaningful 
behavioral features such as login frequency, activity timing patterns, file 
access rates, out-of-session access behavior, and email-based textual 
features using Natural Language Processing (NLP).
3. Anomaly Detection Using Machine Learning
The system applies unsupervised machine learning algorithms such as 
Isolation Forest, One-Class Support Vector Machine, and Autoencoder neural 
networks to learn normal user behavior and detect abnormal activities 
without requiring labeled attack data.
4.Graph-Based Relationship Analysis
An entity interaction graph is created where users, files, and devices are 
represented as nodes, and their interactions are represented as edges. 
Centrality measures such as degree centrality and betweenness centrality 
are used to identify high-risk users and suspicious relationship patterns.
5. Visualization Dashboard
An interactive dashboard developed using Streamlit provides real-time 
visualization of user risk scores, anomaly alerts, and relationship graphs, 
helping security analysts investigate suspicious activities efficiently.

Abstract— In India, MSMEs are still facing significant challenges in utilizing operational data for predictive and 
analytical purposes, with cash flow management being a major 
concern. India's monthly UPI transactions amount to roughly 8 
billion, but the extent to which MSMEs use digital tools is 
limited. A significant proportion of micro-SMEs, around 82%, 
are not acquainted with implementing or integrating modern 
data analytics and AI solutions into their operations, and they 
often lack basic knowledge of available digitisation support. 
Variable customer payment behaviours, different credit terms, 
and the lack of predictive financial analytics frequently cause 
working capital issues and delay management responses. The focus of this research is on MFG360, an AI-driven ETL solution that utilizes the Spindle Finance module as a tool for 
assessing accounts receivable risks at the transaction level in 
manufacturing settings. Predictive models are built on the basis 
of past billing records, payment histories, delay trends, and 
contract details to help users estimate receivable collection

health and ongoing operations of small manufacturing 
businesses. Even companies with consistent production and 
steady order flow can face cash flow challenges due to late 
customer payments, lengthy billing cycles, and unpredictable 
trends in accounts receivable. These issues are particularly 
evident in manufacturing, where variations in credit terms, 
contract arrangements, and customer payment habits create 
uncertainty in the timing of cash inflows. Although recent 
studies indicate that digital financial tools and predictive 
analytics can enhance forecasting precision, many small and 
medium-sized manufacturing enterprises still lack adequate 
analytical 
resources. 
Conventional 
accounts 
receivable 
management relies mainly on descriptive reports and static 
ageing assessments, which offer limited insight into anticipated 
cash inflows. From a data science perspective, these methods 
fail to fully leverage the growing volume of transactional data 
generated by contemporary digital processes. Disparate data 
sources, such as daily operational logs and outdated financial 
documents, often hinder finance teams from obtaining a 
cohesive understanding of receivable risks. Consequently, 
financial responses tend to be reactive, occurring only after 
Liquidity issues have begun to disrupt business activities. To address these challenges, this research introduces 
MFG360, a comprehensive ETL and predictive analytics 
framework tailored for finance in manufacturing. Utilising 
actual billing and payment data from a manufacturing unit in 
Pune, this system integrates diverse data sources into a single 
analytical framework. By employing temporal feature 
engineering and analysing invoicing and payment behaviours at 
the deal level, the framework uncovers trends in customer 
payment dependability and receivable risks. MFG360 
transforms raw transactional data into predictive financial

A. Traditional Methods for Cash-Flow and Receivable Management 
Financial management of small and medium manufacturing 
enterprises has traditionally used descriptive reporting methods, 
including static aging reports, manual spreadsheet tracking, and 
periodic financial summaries. The usual way in which these 
methods operate is to divide outstanding receivables into 
specific time frames, such as 30-day, 60-day or 90- day aging 
buckets. Although they provide a general overview of pending 
payments, these reports primarily describe past financial activity 
rather than forecasting future cash flows. 
Deployed systems like manual trackers, CSV files, or isolated 
accounting software are commonly used by SMEs to store 
billing and transaction records. Financial teams often rely on 
retrospective analysis and intuition when making decisions 
regarding liquidity. This is the case. Consequently, they are 
unable to detect behavioral payment patterns or predict delays in 
accounts receivable due to the absence of integrated analytics. 
Therefore, companies that have high production output and 
satisfied customers may face financial difficulties due to delayed 
payments and unpredictable cash inflows. B. Challenges with Traditional Financial Analysis 
Models

decisions are frequently made manually, rather than through 
data-driven insights.

METHODOLOGY This study proposes MFG360, an integrated data engineering 
and predictive analytics framework that can improve the 
visibility of cash-flow and reduce risk in manufacturing 
small enterprises. It transforms disorganized financial 
trecords into actionable insights by utilizing data ingestion, 
temporal feature engineering, predictive modeling, and 
visualization. A. Preparation of Dataset and Preprocessing 
 During phase I, firstly, financial data is taken from a 
manufacturing environment; this includes billing records, 
invoice information, payment transactions, and deal-level 
customer data extracted from operational systems and 
historical CSV files. Manual trackers, digital billing records, 
and payment systems are all necessary to process the data 
provided. This involves removing duplicate or incomplete 
entries, standardizing the format of these tables, converting 
dates into time-series variables, and normalizing payment 
values to ensure that data is clean (or well-structured) and 
ready for predictive analysis. B. Feature Engineering 
An ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) process combines 
dispersed financial data sources into a cohesive pipeline. 
The data is retrieved from operational trackers and legacy 
CSV records, processed through cleaning, normalization, 
and feature generation, before being loaded into a 
centralized PostgreSQL data warehouse All items are then 
stored in XML-based databases. C. Temporal Feature Engineering 
Patterns are extracted from past billing to be used in 
analyzing customer payment behavior using temporal 
feature engineering. The main components of the system are 
payment delay timeframe, invoice age, deal size, payment 
frequency, customer payment consistency, and historical 
delay patterns. 
The inclusion of these features enables the analysis at the 
deal-level and enhances the predictability of payment risks.

The inclusion of these features enables the analysis at the deal-level and enhances the predictability of payment risks. D. Predictive Modeling for Cash-Flow Forecasting 
The analysis of past financial data is used to create predictive 
models that estimate receivable timelines and forecast cash 
flow. Identifying payment trends and possible delays is 
achieved through the use of time-series forecasting 
techniques, such as moving averages and exponential 
smoothing, weighted delay scoring, and trend analysis. By 
using these models, businesses can better anticipate payment 
dues and manage liquidity risks. E. Financial Performance Metrics 
Financial analytics models, such as Accounts Receivable 
Aging, Days Sales Outstanding (DSO), and the Cash 
Conversion Cycle (CCC), are used to evaluate payment 
behavior and working capital efficiency. These models can 
categorize invoices based on payment delays or orderly 
processing of invoice payments. The measurement of 
receivable risk and liquidity performance is facilitated by 
these metrics. F. Interactive Dashboard and Visualization 
Through the use of an interactive Streamlit dashboard, 
analytical findings are presented in the form of cash-flow 
trends, payment delay predictions at the deal level, risk 
categorization (including buyer preference), and key KPIs

Abstract. Millions of people it is very difficult to apply for important government documents like income certificates, caste certificates, and proof of domicile, especially if they live in rural areas or have limited digital skills in India. Dispersed portals, unclear instructions, inconsistent state-by-state procedures, and district level these all factors complicate the process. These problems often result in process errors, frequent office visits, and the exclusion of less technical expertized individuals. GovGuideBot has been developed, an AI-powered chatbot that explains government documentation procedures, to address this issue. It provides easy-to-use, location based, step-by-step assistance. In order to understand user intent, the system uses a Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline that is optimized with transformer models like BERT. Named [NAME] (NER) is used to identify crucial information such as document type, state, and district. These specifics are arranged in structured JSON workflows that enable region specific instructions. GovGuideBot also uses location entered by user query to adapt procedures for user locations, links to official government websites to guarantee accuracy, and uses the YouTube Data API to offer visual tutorials which are particularly useful for users who might have literacy issues or are using these services for the first time. With a precision of 91%, a recall of 93%, and an overall F1-score of 92% for identifying intents and entities, GovGuideBot performs well when tested on actual citizen questions. About half of the planned features were successfully implemented in the working prototype we created for Maharashtra, which includes work-flows for income, caste, and domicile certificates. By supporting multiple languages and media formats, GovGuideBot demonstrates how chatbot technology can improve access for more people, decrease needless visits to service sites, and reduce procedural errors. Keywords: AI Chatbot, Government Services, NLP, E-Governance, Digital Assistance

Introduction Background and Motivation In India, access to essential government documents such as income certificates, caste certificates, domiciliary proofs, is also a primary and essential requirement for getting public benefits, school admissions and legal acquiescence. However, the process of acquiring these documents is a tedious ordeal, i.e., long, cumbersome and harrowing, especially for the countrymen and the digitally illiterate sections [1] in the country. Even the government efforts under Digital India and E-Governance schemes have resulted in creating a gap between availability of the services and the actual service. The cause of this malaise is mainly the obfuscatory policies of the government, vagueness and vagaries of the state level procedures and the fragmented digital infrastructure [6]. The information is available on several portals of the government, is written in technical jargon i.e., undecodable language, is not clear and often stale. The citizens are, therefore, left with only to rely on random You Tube tutorials, unverified blogs or the services of middlemen, often at exorbitant prices and incorrect guidance [14]. As a result, in the process the citizens waste their time in going to offices again and again because of improper submission of documents required and sycophancy of the dependents, creating an atmosphere of exasperation both for the applicants and the government. Need for an AI-Based Citizen Assistance System While digitization has simplified many aspects of administration, the usability gap between citizens and complex digital systems remains wide. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and conversational chatbots have shown remarkable success in domains such as healthcare, education, and customer service by enabling real-time, context-aware, and personalized assistance [22]. Applying these capabilities to government documentation can address accessibility, accuracy, and inclusion challenges in public services. The need is clear: a unified, intelligent system that can understand citizen queries in natural language, offer personalized guidance based on region and document type, and link users directly to verified government portals. Such a system can drastically reduce dependency on manual processes, improve efficiency, and enhance citizen trust in e-governance mechanisms [23]. Need for an AI-Based Citizen Assistance System

Results and Discussion The GovGuideBot system was tested on a dataset comprising by a total of 250 actual citizen queries and 15 verified government workflows derived from various states like Maharashtra, Delhi, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka in India. The test queries were framed to represent real citizen queries for certificates like income, cast, birth and residence certificate, assuring both urban and rural settings. The experiment proves that the hybrid NLP, fuzzy-matching and rule-based approaches have worked effectively in the area of intension detection, entities extraction and delivery of workflows for e-governance documentation. The high precision in intent classification (93%) suggests that the BERT and DistilBERT models are effective at deducing context even in short or unstructured user queries such as “apply income cert Pune”. The slightly reduced recall in fuzzy intent-matching (85%) indicates that some ambiguities in abbreviations or heavily misspelled words might have been origin for mismatches, but the application of RapidFuzz allowed for significantly more tolerance than the generative or exact-match comparison algorithms. The workflow retrieval accuracy (95%) shows the strength of JSON-structured linking of data and result sets particular to a specific advisory location above personalization and consistency of response. The added hybrid architecture of machine-led learning with rule-based or template-generative logic permitted accuracy and trustworthiness of results, important for a governance related application. Conclusion The paper presents an AI-enabled conversational agent, called GovGuideBot, to support the process of applying for government documentation on Income, Caste or Domicile Certification via one-on-one support based on location and process, natural language processing (NLP), and machine learning. GovGuideBot demonstrates awareness of the difficulties faced by citizens, particularly for example those in rural communities and with the lowest levels of digital literacies, attempting to access basic governments services. The evaluation findings show that GovGuideBot had a very high accuracy of intent recognition (92%), an average response time of 1.4 seconds across 651 different intents, and a 35% reduction in the number of mistakes across applications compared to self-guidance processes. In addition, anecdotal feedback from participants indicated that GovGuideBot: provided enhanced clarity, reduced the stove piping of legal documentation, and improved avoidance of reliance on informal agents or blogs for further information.

Introduction Deepfakes are digitally altered images and videos created using advanced AI techniques, and they often look so realistic that it becomes very hard to tell whether the content is real or fake. With the increasing use of social media and the easy availability of AI tools, deepfakes are now being misused for spreading false information, committing cyber fraud, misusing identities, and manipulating digital content. Detecting such fake media manually is no longer reliable because of its high visual quality, and many existing automated systems fail to provide accurate results or clear explanations for their decisions. To overcome these limitations, this project presents a web-based Deepfake Detection System that uses a Hybrid CNN–ViT model along with Explainable AI, making the detection process more accurate, transparent, and suitable for real-world use.

2. Literature Review Deepfake detection research has evolved from basic CNN-based models that identify visual and texture inconsistencies to advanced approaches using Vision Transformers (ViT) for better global image understanding. Hybrid CNN–Transformer models combine local and global feature analysis, resulting in improved detection accuracy. Some studies also use frequency-domain analysis to detect hidden deepfake artifacts. Explainable AI methods like Grad-CAM help make model decisions more transparent, but most existing solutions are limited to research experiments and are not implemented as real-world, user-friendly applications. 2.1 Recent High-Impact Deepfake Misuse Case Studies A. Deepfake Financial Fraud Using AI Voice Cloning (India, 2023) In a major cyber fraud incident in India, attackers used AI-generated deepfake voice technology to impersonate a senior company executive during a phone call. The finance department, believing the voice to be authentic, transferred a large sum of money to a fraudulent account. The fraud was detected only after internal verification failed. B. Political Deepfake Video Circulation During Elections (India, 2024) During a regional election campaign, a manipulated video surfaced on social media showing a political leader making inflammatory statements. The video went viral before it was proven to be a deepfake created using face-swapping and lip-syncing techniques. Although later debunked, the video caused public confusion and reputational damage. This incident demonstrated how deepfakes can influence public opinion and the urgent need for automated detection systems to counter misinformation. C. Celebrity Deepfake Image Abuse on Social Media (Global, 2022) Several celebrities became victims of deepfake image manipulation where their faces were digitally inserted into inappropriate or misleading content. These images spread rapidly across social media platforms, leading to emotional distress and legal challenges for the victims. The case revealed how easily accessible AI tools can be misused and how manual moderation fails to control deepfake propagation at scale. D. Corporate CEO Deepfake Video Scam (Europe, 2019) In a well-known corporate fraud case, cybercriminals used a deepfake video of a company CEO to convince employees during a virtual meeting to share sensitive internal information. Tjhe realistic facial expressions and voice synchronization made the video convincing. This incident exposed the vulnerability of video-based authentication systems and emphasized the need for deepfake detection in enterprise communication platforms. E. Many followers were deceived, resulting in financial losses. The videos were difficult to identify as fake by viewers, highlighting the risk of identity misuse and the absence of accessible deepfake verification tools for common users. 3. Research Gaps and Future Directions A. Lack of Real-Time Detection Most existing deepfake detection methods work on offline data and are not suitable for real-time scenarios such as live video streams or social media platforms. Future systems should support real-time and adaptive detection. B. Limited Feature Diversity Many models rely only on spatial image features and ignore frequency-based or contextual information. Integrating multi-domain features can improve detection reliability. C. Scalability Issues Transformer-based models are computationally expensive, making large-scale deployment difficult. There is a need for efficient and scalable hybrid architectures. D. Lack of Explainability Most systems provide predictions without explaining the decision process. Integrating Explainable AI techniques like Grad-CAM is essential to improve transparency and user trust.
