There is a need for a robust, transparent, and scalable solution that can effectively detect deepfake media and clearly explain the reasons behind its predictions.

5. Objectives The primary objectives of the proposed project are: A. To design a deepfake detection system using a hybrid CNN–ViT architecture. B. To detect both local facial artifacts and global inconsistencies in media. C. To integrate frequency-domain analysis for identifying hidden manipulation patterns. D. To apply Grad-CAM based Explainable AI for visual interpretation of predictions. E. To develop a user-friendly web-based application for real-world use. 6. Methodologies 6.1 Algorithms and Models • 
Convolutional Neural Network (CNN): Used to extract local and spatial features from images such as facial textures and inconsistencies. • 
Vision Transformer (ViT): Applied to capture global context and long-range dependencies across facial regions. • 
Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): Utilized for frequency-domain analysis to detect hidden artifacts introduced during deepfake generation. • 
Grad-CAM: Implemented as an Explainable AI technique to visually highlight important regions influencing the model’s decision. 6.2 Tools and Technologies ➢ Programming Language: Python ➢ Deep Learning Frameworks: TensorFlow / PyTorch ➢ Explainable AI: Grad-CAM ➢ Web Framework: Flask / Firebase Studio ➢ Datasets: FaceForensics++, Celeb-DF

6.3 System Architecture: Fig 1 : Deepfake Detection System Architecture. 6.4 Data Collection and Analysis ➢ Real and fake images/videos are collected from standard benchmark datasets. ➢ Preprocessing steps include face detection, normalization, and frame extraction. ➢ The hybrid CNN–ViT model is trained using labeled data. ➢ Model performance is evaluated using accuracy and confidence scores. ➢ Grad-CAM heatmaps are generated to provide visual explanations for predictions. 6.5 Project Timeline 6. Expected Results and Discussions The proposed system is expected to accurately classify real and deepfake media with higher reliability than single-model approaches. The integration of Grad-CAM will provide visual explanations highlighting manipulated regions, thereby increasing transparency and user trust. The web-based implementation ensures practical usability for academic and real-world cybersecurity applications.

7. Conclusion This project addresses the growing threat of deepfakes by proposing a hybrid deep learning-based detection system with explainable AI. By combining CNN, Vision Transformer, frequency analysis, and Grad-CAM, the system improves detection accuracy while ensuring transparency. The proposed approach fills key research gaps and offers a practical, scalable, and trustworthy solution for modern digital security challenges.

Introduction to Fruit Crop Disease Classfication Using Quantum Machine Learning In modern agriculture, early detection of fruit crop diseases is vital to minimizing yield loss and improving farm productivity. However, conventional methods often rely on large datasets and high-performance computing resources, which may not be practical in rural or low-resource settings. This project introduces an intelligent, resource-efficient disease classification system for fruit crops using Quantum Machine Learning (QML) on IBM Quantum Cloud. By analyzing grayscale images of fruit leaves, the system classifies them as healthy, wilting, or nematode-infected. It leverages PCA for dimensionality reduction, encodes features into quantum circuits, and uses a Quantum Neural Network (QNN) for accurate classification. With a user-friendly frontend built using Streamlit, the system enables farmers and researchers to upload leaf images and receive instant health predictions. This quantum-powered solution offers faster training, low compute dependency, and early disease detection—making it ideal for real-time agricultural diagnostics. Motivation In today’s agriculture-driven economy, early detection of crop diseases is essential for safeguarding fruit yield, ensuring food quality, and minimizing financial losses. Traditional methods for diagnosing plant diseases often rely on manual inspection or conventional machine learning models, which demand large datasets, extended training times, and high computational power—resources that are not always accessible to farmers, especially in remote or low-infrastructure regions.
This project is motivated by the need for a faster, lightweight, and intelligent disease classification system that overcomes these limitations. By leveraging Quantum Machine Learning (QML) through IBM Quantum Cloud, the system uses compact grayscale images of fruit leaves and Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce data complexity. The use of a Quantum Neural Network (QNN) enables accurate classification of leaf health status— Healthy, Wilting, or Nematode-Infected—using fewer resources and faster training cycles.
Furthermore, the integration of a user-friendly Streamlit interface allows farmers and researchers to access predictions directly via web or mobile browsers without requiring technical expertise or high-end computing setups. By combining the power of quantum computing with the practicality of remote diagnostics, this project offers a scalable and forward-looking tool for modern agriculture, enabling smarter, faster, and more accessible crop health management.

Traditional [NAME] like CNNs and MobileNetV2 work well but often require large datasets, high computing power, and can overfit on small agricultural datasets. To overcome these challenges, our project explores a hybrid quantum–classical approach for fruit crop disease classification. By combining classical feature extraction with quantum-inspired models, we aim to build a lightweight, efficient system that can achieve high accuracy on small datasets and demonstrate the potential of Quantum Machine Learning in agriculture

ABSTRACT The inevitable realization of large-scale quantum computers is a threat to the integrity of classical biometric systems, which mainly rely on encryption standards that may soon be broken. Current databases face the risk of “Store Now, Decrypt Later” attacks, necessi- tating a shift in security architecture. This paper presents QuMetric, a privacy-preserving biometric verification framework that uses the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics to secure digital identities. While biometric authentication systems, especially finger-based, provide better security than earlier systems, they face a new generation of threats like template stealing and the rising capabilities of quantum computers. As described in the current research, quantum algorithms threaten classical cryptosystems like RSA while current quantum biometric schemes require storing sensitive biometric templates in raw forms in quantum states for protection. To overcome these limitations, this paper focuses on the development of a secure, privacy-preserving, and quantum-safe biometric authentication system, which we name QuMetric. Our strategy involves a hybrid classical-quantum approach and uses powerful preprocessing and dimension reduction techniques for lightweight feature extraction. The obtained feature vectors are encoded in quantum states with the use of angle and amplitude encoding techniques. The scheme performs quantum-assisted similarity calculation to obtain fidelity based similarity for verification, keeping the raw biometric data in neither transmitted nor stored in any form. LITERATURE SURVEY Preamble This chapter presents a review of existing research related to biometric authentication, biometric template protection, and the use of quantum computing in secure authentica- tion systems. The main objective of this survey is to study previously proposed methods, understand their advantages and limitations, and identify the research gaps that motivate the proposed work. The literature survey is divided into three major sections: (i) classical biometric au- thentication and template protection, (ii) quantum computing techniques for similarity computation and pattern matching, and (iii) quantum-assisted biometric authentication systems. Classical Biometric Authentication and Template Protection Traditional fingerprint authentication systems mainly relied on minutiae-based match- ing techniques. Jain et al. proposed a fingerprint verification model that achieved high accuracy under controlled conditions. However, these systems generally store raw bio- metric templates directly in databases, making them vulnerable to data breaches and unauthorized access. To improve security, Ratha et al. introduced the concept of cancellable biometrics, where biometric templates are transformed using non-invertible functions. This approach al- lows templates to be revoked and replaced if compromised. Although the method im- proves security, its effectiveness depends on keeping the transformation parameters se- cret. Another important development was the introduction of biometric cryptosystems such GHRCEM, [NAME], A.Y [PHONE] [NAME] as the fuzzy vault scheme proposed by Juels and Sudan. In this approach, cryptographic keys are securely bound with biometric features. These systems can tolerate small vari- ations in biometric inputs, but they may still suffer from helper-data leakage and corre- lation attacks. Researchers also proposed hash-based biometric protection methods, where only hashed versions of biometric templates are stored. These methods provide strong irreversibility and better protection of sensitive biometric data. However, because biometric samples naturally vary during each scan, exact hash matching becomes difficult, creating the need for similarity computation techniques within protected environments. Several studies have explored techniques such as quantum cosine similarity, SWAP test-based fidelity estimation, and quantum kernel methods for comparing feature vectors. Image Preprocessing Fingerprint images captured from sensors often contain noise, uneven lighting, and dis- tortions. To fix these problems, a multi-stage preprocessing pipeline improves image quality and prepares it for feature extraction. At the start of preprocessing, each image is resized to a consistent size to keep unifor- mity in the dataset. Next, Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) is used to improve local contrast. This makes the ridge patterns clearer and easier to analyze. After that, a Gaussian filter helps reduce high-frequency noise and smooth the image while keeping important structural details. Once noise reduction is complete, adaptive thresholding turns the grayscale image into a binary image. Finally, morpho- logical operations like closing fill small gaps in ridge structures and improve continuity. 4.5
Skeletonization and Ridge Refinement After preprocessing, the binary image becomes a skeleton representation, where ridges are thinned to a single-pixel width. This process keeps the topological structure of the fingerprint while simplifying its look. However, skeletonization may create small unwanted branches due to noise or segmen- tation errors. To fix this, a pruning algorithm removes false ridge endings and short GHRCEM, [NAME], A.Y [PHONE] [NAME] branches. This step enhances the accuracy of the next minutiae detection by making sure only meaningful ridge structures remain. 4.6

These values are grouped into discrete bins using: • 16 radial bins • 8 angular bins This results in a 128-dimensional feature vector, which captures the spatial distribution of minutiae points. Minutiae points in fingerprints are where the ridges end or bifurcate. These are distinctive to an individual’s fingerprint. points. Minutiae points in fingerprints are where the ridges end or bifurcate. These are distinctive to an individual’s fingerprint. The initial step is the preprocessing stage, where the fingerprint is resized, filtered to reduce noise and transformed into a binary image where the ridges stand out and are very clear. The ridges are then skeletonised so that their width is reduced to a single pixel. Information is not lost during this step. Minutiae detection occurs at this stage by examining the neighbors of each pixel in the skeletonized image. A crossing number is calculated for each pixel and if: • the crossing number is 1 then the minutiae point is an ending • the crossing number is 3 then the minutiae point is a bifurcation The identified minutiae points are saved and noises and boundary artefacts are then filtered. 7.3.2
Algorithm 2 – Secure Feature Encoding and Hashing Algorithm The minutiae points obtained after the minutiae extraction process is then converted into a secure and structured form. The fingerprint image is divided into equal regions, and the number of minutiae points for each region is count, which is then normalized to the binary feature vector through predefined thresholds. The binary feature vector is then secured by a hybrid mechanism based on cryptographic hashing and simulated quantum key. The feature vector is concatenated with the key and hashed using SHA- 256 algorithm and produced secure bitstream. ABSTRACT This project presents a privacy-preserving cyber threat detection system using Federated Learning and Random Forest-based hybrid models. Traditional intrusion detection systems rely on centralized architectures where sensitive network data is transmitted to a central server, increasing risks of data breaches, privacy violations, and system failures. To overcome these challenges, the proposed system introduces a decentralized approach where data remains locally on devices while only model updates are shared across the network. The system integrates [NAME] (FL) with hybrid model combining Random Forest and Decision Tree algorithms, enabling efficient detection of cyber threats such as Denial of Service (Dos), Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks, and abnormal network patterns. The use of FL ensures data privacy, reduces communication overhead, and enhances scalability. Experimental results show that the system achieves high accuracy (~95%+) while maintain strong privacy preservation. This project demonstrates that decentralized intelligence can effectively replace centralized systems in cybersecurity, offering improved performance, scalability, and data protection.  The proposed system follows a well-defined and structured

methodology to detect cyber threats while ensuring data privacy. 
The process begins with data collection and preprocessing, where 
raw network traffic data is gathered from multiple distributed nodes 
such as enterprise systems, IoT devices, or cloud environments. This 
raw data often contains noise, missing values, and redundant 
information. Therefore, preprocessing techniques such as data 
cleaning, normalization, and feature selection are applied to improve 
data quality and consistency. By selecting only the most relevant 
features, the system reduces computational complexity and enhances 
the efficiency of the learning process. 
 Once the data is preprocessed, the next step involves local model training at each participant node. In this stage, each node 
independently trains a machine learning model using its own local 
dataset. This decentralized approach ensures that sensitive data 
never leaves its source, thereby maintaining privacy and complying 
with data protection requirements. Each node learns patterns and 
behaviors specific to its environment, which contributes to a more 
comprehensive understanding of network activities across the 
system. 
 After local training, the models generate parameter updates (weights) instead of sharing raw data. These updates are securely 
transmitted to a central server known as the aggregator. The 
aggregator plays a crucial role in combining the knowledge gained 
from all participating nodes. It uses the Federated Averaging 
(FedAvg) algorithm to merge these updates and create a global 
model. This process ensures that the system benefits from collective 
learning while preserving data confidentiality. 
 The training process is iterative, meaning that the updated global model is redistributed back to all nodes for further training. With 
each iteration, the model becomes more accurate and robust, as it 
continuously learns from diverse data sources. This iterative process 
helps the system adapt to new and evolving cyber threats, improving 
its detection capability over time. 6

The [NAME] algorithm begins by initializing a global model at the 
central server. This model serves as the starting point for all participating nodes.

 Each node trains the model locally using its own dataset. This ensures that 
sensitive data remains within the local system and is not shared with other nodes. 
Local training allows the model to adapt to specific network conditions. 
 After training, each node generates model updates in the form of weights or 
parameters. These updates represent the learning achieved from the local data. 
Instead of sending raw data, only these updates are transmitted to the central 
server.

(FedAvg) algorithm. This involves calculating a weighted average of all updates 
to create a new global model. This ensures that all nodes contribute to the 
learning process.

repeated for multiple iterations until the model converges and achieves high 
accuracy.

Traditional Methods for IoT Security Legacy IoT security architectures have traditionally depended on signature-based intrusion detection systems (IDS), rule- based firewalls, and centralized monitoring consoles. These techniques mainly protect against recognized threats by comparing network traffic against memorized attack signatures. Though effective in protecting regular enterprise systems, it is insufficient in IoT environments where devices are heavily heterogeneous, resource-scarce, and are constantly exposed to changing cyberattacks. Moreover, traditional IDS implementations typically produce a high volume of false positives that flood administrators and slow response to incidents. Challenges with Classical Security Models There are a number of fundamental limitations of traditional IoT defense systems. First, these systems are reactive, in the sense that they respond only after a pattern of attack is realized, leaving devices open to zero-day attacks. Second, IoT devices with limited resources are incapable of performing intensive encryption or heavy intrusion detection calculations, causing performance bottlenecks. Third, centralized monitoring solutions introduce single points of failure, exposing networks to mass-scale disruption. Lastly, the "black-box" feature of conventional ML-based models diminishes interpretability, hindering system administrators and end-users from relying on security warnings or mitigation actions. Here, the CICIDS 2017 dataset was chosen to be the standard benchmark. It is developed by the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity in order to have a realistic view of benign and malicious network traffic. Compared to older data sets like KDD99 or NSL-KDD, CICIDS 2017 depicts current attack scenarios and is consequently extremely relevant for the assessment of ML, XAI, and blockchain-based IDS models.

Compared to older data sets like KDD99 or NSL-KDD, CICIDS 2017 depicts current attack scenarios and is consequently extremely relevant for the assessment of ML, XAI, and blockchain-based IDS models. The dataset contains a mix of benign traffic (≈2.27 million) and several categories of attacks (≈557K flows), including DoS, DDoS, Port Scans, Brute Force, Web Attacks, Botnets, and Infiltration. With more than 84 statistical traffic features (time- based, packet-based, flag, and flow features), the data set is heavy and demanding, particularly because of its class imbalance. Preparation of the data set for both traditional machine learning models and sophisticated NetDefend IoT modules involved the following preprocessing steps: Data Cleaning Inconsistent, duplicate, or invalid records were eliminated. Missing values in numerical attributes were imputed with median values in order to avoid bias in training. Normalization Because network features (e.g., packet size, flow duration, byte rate) can be very disparate in scale, min–max normalization was utilized to rescale values to the [0,1] range. This helped stabilize training of the model and provide compatibility between features. Dimensionality Reduction using PCA There are 84 features in the dataset, a good number of which are correlated. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projected high-dimensional data onto lower-dimensional space with maximum variance, minimizing computational overhead. Feature Encoding Categorical attributes (for example, protocol type and service type) were encoded numerically in one-hot encoding form to remain compatible with ML and deep learning. Data Partitioning The data was split into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) sets. Stratified sampling was used to maintain rare attack categories (for example, Heartbleed and Infiltration) in all splits. Imbalance Handling

METHODOLOGY In this paper, we introduce NetDefend IoT as a hybrid system integrating Machine Learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), blockchain, and self-healing intelligence for end-to-end security of IoT. The approach is divided into six phases: dataset preparation, feature engineering, training of the ML model, integration of explainability, blockchain-secured logging, and self-healing response. Preparation of Dataset and Preprocessing IoT traffic datasets like CICIDS2017, UNSW-NB15, and Bot- IoT are preprocessed via cleaning, normalization, and dimensionality reduction (explained in Section III). This ensures the input data is uniform, balanced, and ideal for training detection models. Feature Engineering Traffic data with high dimensions was cleaned with Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and correlation-based feature removal. This eliminated duplicate attributes while preserving discriminative characteristics like packet rate, protocol type, duration of the connection, and flow-based statistics. The feature vectors are used as inputs for both traditional ML models and deep neural networks. Machine Learning for Intrusion Detection Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were used as baseline models to be trained for benchmarking detection accuracy. Deep learning models like CNN-LSTM hybrids were utilized to model both spatial and temporal attack behavior. Performance was compared using metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. Explainable AI (XAI) Integration To break the black-box problem of ML models, XAI methods like LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) and SHAP (Shapley Additive explanations) were used. These allow interpretable explanations regarding why a specific connection or device was identified as malicious, which raises transparency and trust for network administrators. Attention- based visualization methods were also used to indicate the most significant features in intrusion detection. Blockchain for Secure Logging

Blockchain for Secure Logging In order to maintain data integrity and tamper-proof storage, a light-weight blockchain was embedded within the framework. Intrusion notification and anomaly logs provided by the ML- XAI module were stored in the blockchain ledger, so security incidents cannot be modified or deleted by attackers. For efficiency, a consortium blockchain architecture was implemented, whereby only authorized IoT gateways validate blocks, resulting in less latency than public blockchains. Self-Healing Intelligence One of the major innovations of NetDefend IoT is its self- healing feature. The moment an intrusion is discovered, the system automatically quarantines the affected node, redirects communication to clean devices, and starts automated patching or reconfiguration. Recovery mechanisms are directed by a reinforcement learning agent that chooses the best response based on attack intensity and system condition. This provides minimal downtime and resistance to attacks that repeat themselves. Fig 4.1 System Architecture Flow Diagram

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Experimental Setup The experiments were run on benchmark IoT intrusion datasets, namely CICIDS2017 and UNSW-NB15. Preprocessing involved normalization, dimensionality reduction, and class balancing (as outlined in Section III). The models were coded in Python (TensorFlow/Keras for ML, SHAP and LIME for XAI, Hyperledger Fabric for blockchain), and run on a workstation with 16 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX GPU, and Intel i7 processor. Two categories of models were compared: Classical ML Models – SVM, Random Forest (RF), CNN. NetDefend IoT Hybrid Models – ML + XAI + Blockchain + Self-Healing. The performance was evaluated based on accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, false positive rate (FPR), and recovery time after attacks. Performance of Classical ML Models Classical ML methods obtained decent detection accuracy but were poor in terms of interpretability and false positives. SVM and RF obtained accuracy ranging between 82– 85%, but the performance degrades on high- dimensional data. CNN fared best among traditional models with 90– 91% accuracy but needed enormous training resources and limited interpretability. Implications for IoT Security Applications The findings bring to the fore that although traditional ML techniques are still effective for detection, NetDefend IoT comes with a complete, robust, and clear defense mechanism. Its combination of ML, XAI, blockchain, and self-healing not only provides threat detection but also post-attack restoration, making it appropriate for mission-critical areas like smart healthcare, industrial IoT, and smart cities.

CONCLUSION This project introduced NetDefend IoT, a converged platform that enhances IoT security with Machine Learning (ML), Explainable AI (XAI), blockchain, and self-healing intelligence. More advanced than traditional intrusion detection systems bounded by detection or prevention only, it offers reliable threat detection, visible reasoning, and self-recovery. Experiments with benchmark IoT intrusion datasets revealed increased detection accuracy, reduced false positives, and quicker recovery compared to standard ML approaches. XAI enhanced interpretability and trust, blockchain provided secure and tamper-proof logging, and the self-healing module ensured service continuity by containing and recovering affected nodes. Drawbacks persist, such as blockchain-related latency, self- healing resource limitations, and limited testing beyond controlled environments. Future directions consist of edge–cloud convergence for efficiency, cross-domain validation across domains such as healthcare and transportation, adaptive reinforcement learning– based recovery, and testbed deployment in the real world. NetDefend IoT represents a significant step toward robust, explainable, and resilient IoT security, ensuring future-proof cyber defense.

Abstract In today’s healthcare system, patients often struggle with scattered medical records, missed medications, and limited access to timely medical consultations. To address these issues, MediSync+ is introduced as a smart, all-in-one digital healthcare platform that allows users to upload scanned medical reports, which are processed using AI-driven Optical Character Recognition (OCR) to extract and analyze health data. The system then suggests medications, sets automated reminders, and maintains a digital prescription log. Users can also consult certified doctors via real-time chat or video calls, with doctors having access to the patient’s complete health history through a dynamic digital profile. Diagnostic labs are directly integrated through APIs, enabling instant report uploads and automatic analysis. The platform enhances treatment adherence with timely notifications and is offered under a secure, subscription-based model. Combining AI, web technologies, and real-time communication, MediSync+ bridges the gap between patients, doctors, and labs—transforming the traditional healthcare experience into a smarter, connected digital ecosystem. Keywords: Digital Healthcare, OCR, AI in Healthcare, Virtual Consultation, Medical Report Analysis, Health Data Management, Medication Reminder System, Telemedicine, Patient Health Profile, Diagnostic Lab Integration, WebRTC, Secure Cloud Storage

Introduction Healthcare is a fundamental aspect of human life, and in today's digital era, there is a growing need to make medical services more accessible, efficient, and personalized. Despite the technological advancements in other industries, the healthcare sector in many regions — particularly in developing countries — still relies heavily on manual, paper-based processes. Patients often misplace important medical reports, forget medication schedules, and face difficulties in reaching doctors for follow-ups or consultations. These gaps in the healthcare system can lead to poor diagnosis, delayed treatments, and deteriorating health outcomes. To solve these challenges, we introduce MedSync+, a digital healthcare platform designed to streamline the management of medical records, medications, doctor consultations, and diagnostic reports — all in a single web-based system. This platform empowers patients to upload their manual or scanned reports, which are automatically processed using AI-based OCR to extract meaningful health data. The data is then analyzed to provide detailed insights, suggest medications, and enable remote access to doctors through real-time video or chat consultations. The platform also maintains a dynamic digital health profile for every user — similar to a social media profile — that stores the patient’s health timeline, reports, prescriptions, and consultation history. It acts as a medical reference point that doctors can easily access before prescribing or diagnosing. Furthermore, by integrating diagnostic laboratories directly into the system, test results can be uploaded instantly and securely, removing the dependency on physical copies or patient follow-up. One of the most essential features of MedSync+ is its medication reminder system, which helps patients stick to their treatment plans through scheduled push notifications or SMS alerts. This ensures better adherence to prescribed therapies, especially for elderly patients or those with chronic illnesses. This project lies at the intersection of web development, AI/ML, and healthcare technology, and aims to provide a scalable, secure, and intelligent solution that bridges the gap between patients, doctors, and diagnostic labs. Offered as a subscription-based service, MedSync+ not only enhances the patient experience but also promotes the digital transformation of the healthcare ecosystem.

Problem Statement Laboratory test reports are often lengthy and complex, making it challenging for patients to understand their health condition and the implications of abnormal results. Misinterpretation or neglect of these reports can lead to medication errors, such as drug overdose, or untreated conditions that may escalate into serious complications. Our system aims to automate the interpretation of blood and urine test reports using AI, providing simplified, actionable insights to patients and doctors. Additionally, it monitors medication schedules and alerts users to avoid unnecessary or harmful drug intake, thus preventing potential health risks. Goals of the Project: To digitize medical records using OCR and store them in a centralized system. To provide AI-driven analysis of medical data for faster diagnosis. To enable virtual consultations with doctors through chat or video calls. To automate prescription tracking and medication reminders. To integrate diagnostic lab reports directly into the platform. To ensure secure, scalable, and user-friendly digital healthcare access. Project intends to achieve: A smart and centralized digital healthcare system. Faster, AI-supported diagnosis and health insights. Easy access to doctors from anywhere, anytime. Better medication adherence through automated alerts. Reduced reliance on paper-based health records. Improved treatment efficiency and patient outcomes

ABSTRACT This project addresses the growing cyber-physical threats in smart cities by simulating and mitigating network-based and sensor-level attacks such as Denial of Service (DoS), Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks, and ARP spoofing. The Raspberry Pi 5 is used as the smart city control module to emulate the communication and sensor interfaces typically found in real-world systems. Tools like hping3, Scapy, and ARP Spoof are utilized to perform these intrusions in a controlled environment. Since smart cities rely heavily on continuous communication with cloud servers, control units, and GPS data for safe navigation and automation, these pathways become potential points of vulnerability for malicious attackers. The project not only evaluates the impact of these cyberattacks on network integrity and performance but also implements real-time mitigation strategies to enhance system resilience. AI-based and rule-based defensive techniques are developed using iptables to detect and counteract ongoing intrusions. Both supervised and unsupervised learning models are employed to achieve adaptive and intelligent threat response. This integrated approach provides a practical, low-cost, and scalable framework for analyzing and defending smart city infrastructures against real-time cyber threats. The simulation results highlight critical technical vulnerabilities and demonstrate effective prevention strategies, contributing to the development of more secure, reliable, and intelligent smart city ecosystems capable of withstanding evolving cybersecurity challenges. It continuously monitors network traffic, detects irregularities, and automatically blocks malicious IPs without depending on complex machine learning models. SmartDefend’s proactive and modular design strengthens the foundation of smart city networks by offering scalable and adaptable security. The integration of rule-based intelligence and automated response mechanisms enables early detection and immediate mitigation of threats. With clear reporting, minimal resource usage, and compatibility with existing IoT frameworks, SmartDefend enhances the reliability, transparency, and resilience of connected urban systems. 4.1 System Architecture 4.1.1 System Architecture of SmartDefend: Fig. 6 System Architecture Diagram The architecture of the DoS and MITM Detection System is designed as a modular and efficient pipeline that ensures real-time threat detection, classification, and mitigation in smart city sensor networks. The system captures both normal and malicious network traffic, preprocesses the data for feature extraction, and then applies machine learning techniques for intelligent attack identification and prevention. The process begins with two traffic sources — the Normal Traffic Source and the Attacker Device, which generate benign and malicious packets respectively. These are fed into the Traffic Capture module, where tools such as Wireshark or tcpdump collect raw packet data in .pcap format. The captured traffic is then passed to the Feature Extraction unit, which processes the packets to derive statistical and behavioural features (such as packet rate, flag counts, and byte patterns) [37], [38], [41]. Input network traffic data from live capture or pre-collected dataset. 2. Extract numerical features — packet rate, flag ratio, byte count, and inter-arrival time. 3. Preprocess the data (normalize, remove duplicates, handle missing values). 4. Train the Random Forest Classifier on labeled traffic samples (Normal vs DoS). 5. Compute metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score to optimize the model. 6. During live deployment, classify packets based on learned behavior. 7. If a packet stream exceeds the confidence threshold, trigger the mitigation module. Output: Predicted label (“Normal” or “Attack”) with associated probability and timestamp. 6.3.2 Algorithm 2 – Rule-Based MITM Detection Logic Flow: 1. 8.1 Conclusion The AI-Powered Network Defence framework represents a significant advancement in autonomous cybersecurity, particularly for modern networks that rely heavily on IoT and edge-level devices. By combining Artificial Intelligence with rule-driven logic, the system offers a practical and responsive method for identifying and countering DoS and MITM attacks. A key feature of this design is the deployment of a lightweight Random Forest Algorithm (RFA) tailored specifically for Raspberry Pi, enabling fast processing and efficient operation even in environments with limited computational capacity. This work highlights how machine learning models and traditional rule-based techniques can complement each other to create a stronger, more reliable defence mechanism. The integration of these two approaches allows the system to detect threats more quickly while maintaining consistency in real-world network settings. Through continuous observation of traffic patterns and automated decision-making, the system ensures that anomalies are recognized early, preventing prolonged exposure to malicious activities. Overall, the project demonstrates the potential of adaptive AI systems in reinforcing cybersecurity at the network edge. By reducing delays in threat detection and improving the precision of mitigation actions, it helps minimize service interruptions and strengthens the overall security posture. The system ultimately serves as a strong example of how compact, optimized, and intelligent AI solutions can be leveraged to protect modern digital infrastructures from evolving attack vectors. Introduction to NetDefend IoT: A smarter way to detect & heal from threats using ML, XAI, blockchain & self-healing intelligence The Problem
•
IoT device growth has increased the potential for cyberattacks, raising risks of malware, DDoS, and unauthorised access. •
Traditional security systems do not adapt in real time, lack transparency, and cannot recover automatically. •
Current solutions operate alone, which makes IoT environments susceptible to changing cyber threats. Our Solution
•
Detects threats in real time using ML. •
Provides transparency with Explainable AI. •
Ensures tamper-proof alert logging with blockchain. •
Recovers on its own through self-healing mechanisms. •
Delivers scalable protection for smart cities, critical infrastructure, and enterprise IoT networks. Motivation •
With billions of IoT devices installed in homes, industries, and smart cities, even one hacked device can lead to malware attacks, system failures, or large-scale disruptions. Traditional security tools often cannot detect these threats in real time, fail to explain their decisions, and do not offer automated recovery, which leaves IoT networks exposed and reliant on manual fixes. •
These issues led us to create a smarter, unified solution. NetDefend IoT aims to change standard IoT systems into intelligent, self-protecting environments. These environments can spot threats immediately, use machine learning and explainable AI to classify risks, validate alerts through blockchain, and automatically repair compromised devices. Our goal is to use technology to not only secure devices but also create safer and more resilient IoT ecosystems. •
As cyber threats keep changing quickly, organizations need security systems that learn continuously and adjust without human help. By including explainability, decentralized trust, and self-repairing intelligence, NetDefend IoT aims to reduce downtime, improve decision transparency, and provide a dependable protection for next-generation IoT networks. This project is driven by the vision of building technology that protects itself and the world that relies on it.

Problem Statement In today's IoT-driven environments, millions of connected devices operate without strong security, which makes them vulnerable to cyberattacks. While better technologies exist, most IoT systems still rely on manual monitoring and traditional security tools. These tools often cannot detect threats in real time or explain strange behavior. This situation causes delayed responses, unnoticed intrusions, and a higher risk of system compromise. Consequently, even with modern infrastructure, we still struggle to prevent evolving attacks because we lack smart, automated, and self-repairing IoT security solutions. 1.
IoT devices are growing quickly, which increases the attack surface and makes networks more vulnerable to malware, DDoS, and unauthorized access. 2.
Current security systems do not offer real-time detection, transparency, or automated recovery. This makes manual monitoring slow and unreliable. 3.
Without a unified, smart, and self-repairing system, compromised IoT devices stay vulnerable. This allows attacks to spread and disrupt the whole system. 4.
Existing tools struggle to classify risks correctly or explain why an alert was triggered. This causes confusion, delays, and poor decisions about threats. 5.
There is no secure way to validate alerts or ensure tamper-proof logging. This reduces trust and raises the chances of unnoticed or manipulated cyber incidents.

securely, and automatically initiates self-healing actions to keep the system safe.
1. Real-Time Monitoring and Detection:
•
The system continuously monitors live IoT network traffic from connected devices. A Machine Learning
detection engine, which is a combination of Random Forest and XGBoost, analyzes packet flows in real time to
spot anomalies and potential intrusions. Incoming data goes through preprocessing with a feature pipeline that
uses datasets like CICIDS 2017 and NSL-KDD.
2. Threat Identification:
•
When suspicious activity is found, the classification module identifies the type of threat, such as DDoS, Port
Scan, Botnet behavior, or unauthorized access. Explainable AI tools like SHAP and LIME help interpret why the
model flagged the traffic as malicious. This ensures transparency for administrators.
3. Risk Assessment:
•
The system performs Risk Classification to understand the seriousness of the detected intrusion.
4. Alert & Management:
•
Depending on the risk level, the system initiates an Alert Mechanism that logs the intrusion securely using
blockchain for tamper-proof validation. The Self-Healing Engine isolates compromised nodes, reconfigures
routes, or resets affected modules automatically to contain the attack.
•
All real-time detections, risk levels, explanation graphs, and blockchain records are shown on the Admin
Dashboard for ongoing monitoring.

Methodology 1. Live IoT Traffic Monitoring
•
All incoming packets stream into the preprocessing and analysis pipeline. 
•
Traffic features like packet size, duration, flow count, and protocol type are extracted for analysis. 
•
This helps spot suspicious behavior patterns early, even before an attack is fully underway. 2. ML Detection Module (Random Forest)
•
Traffic frames, or feature vectors, are processed using a hybrid ML model for real-time anomaly detection. 
•
Random Forest handles strong feature selection and makes the initial prediction. 
•
XGBoost improves classification with high accuracy and low false positives. •
3. Explainable AI Module (SHAP + LIME)
•
For each detected intrusion, the system generates detailed interpretability outputs. SHAP values reveal which 
features contributed most to the detection.
•
LIME points out local behavior patterns for specific alerts. 
•
This allows security teams to understand: Why the ML model flagged an alert Which feature influenced the 
threat classification Whether the alert is justified or a false alarm

Methodology 4. Risk Level Classification
•
Based on model confidence and observed anomaly patterns, the system assigns a risk levels.
•
Risk scores help prioritize which IoT nodes need urgent attention. 5. Blockchain Alert Validation
•
Every critical alert (Yellow/Red) is stored on a lightweight blockchain network. 
•
A block includes the timestamp, device ID, alert type, severity, and ML confidence scores. 
•
This ensures logs are secure, tamper-proof, and verifiable at any time. It helps maintain transparent and 
trustworthy incident records. 
6. Autonomous Self-Healing Engine
•
Isolating the compromised device from the network. 
•
Resetting the service or reconfiguring routes.
•
Restoring normal operation without human intervention.
•
This achieves over a 95% recovery success rate in simulations. Algorithms & Technologies Used 1. Machine Learning Algorithms
•

without human involvement.

Conclusion In this project, we developed an IoT security framework by combining machine learning for threat detection, XAI (SHAP/LIME) for understanding, blockchain for secure logging, and self-healing intelligence for automatic recovery. This layered approach tackles key weaknesses in traditional IoT security systems, providing real-time, clear, and flexible protection. We effectively handled challenges like imbalanced data, ensuring explainability, and enabling automatic responses. The system shows strong potential for use in smart cities, healthcare, and industrial IoT settings. Moving forward, we will explore further improvements, such as optimizing lightweight models, integrating with cloud platforms, and fine-tuning self-healing triggers to enhance scalability and practical use. NetDefend IoT establishes a solid foundation for resilient, trustworthy, and smart IoT systems.

Future Scope 1. Integration of Deep Learning Models Future versions can implement CNNs, LSTMs, Autoencoders, and Graph Neural Networks to detect zero-day attacks, complex traffic patterns, and new cyber threats more accurately. 2. Deployment Using Federated Learning A federated learning setup will let IoT devices train models locally without sharing raw data. This ensures privacy and reduces bandwidth needs across large networks. 3. Real-Time Edge AI Acceleration By using NVIDIA Jetson, Coral TPU, or edge-optimized inference engines, the system can process traffic faster, lower latency, and handle high-volume IoT networks in industries and smart cities. 4. Expansion to Multimodal Threat Detection The system can include data from sensors, logs, audio, and video feeds. This enables better detection of combined physical and digital threats, such as tampering and physical intrusion.

Introduction ❖
Rapid urbanisation has led to a significant increase in public safety concerns, such as missing persons and criminal activities. Traditional surveillance systems are outdated—they rely heavily on manual monitoring, making them inefficient and prone to human error, fatigue, and delayed responses. These limitations severely affect timely threat detection and effective intervention by law enforcement agencies. ❖
 The Smart Surveillance System for Missing Person & Criminal Detection with Real-Time Alerting leverages modern technologies like artificial intelligence, computer vision, and blockchain. Using object detection and facial recognition, the system automatically scans live video feeds to detect individuals that match profiles from a centralised database of missing persons or known offenders. Once a match is identified, the system immediately notifies authorities and securely logs the incident. It enhances traditional CCTV surveillance by enabling real-time, automated detection and alerting, reducing reliance on human operators. The use of blockchain ensures secure, transparent, and tamper-proof event logging, fostering trust and accountability. By empowering law enforcement with intelligent tools, this system aims to significantly improve public safety, accelerate investigations, and support quicker recoveries and crime prevention in urban areas. This system aims to address the inefficiencies of conventional CCTV setups by leveraging modern technologies such as YOLOv7 for high-speed object detection, OpenCV for real-time camera input handling, and TensorFlow/PyTorch for facial recognition. ❖

Problem Statement Public spaces are increasingly equipped with CCTV cameras for security monitoring, yet the vast amount of video footage generated daily is mostly underutilized due to the reliance on manual observation. Security personnel are tasked with monitoring multiple feeds simultaneously, which often leads to fatigue, oversight, and missed critical incidents—especially when identifying missing individuals or tracking known criminals.  Traditional surveillance systems are passive, meaning they only record and store data without providing any intelligent decision-making capabilities. There is no real-time detection or alert mechanism integrated into the system. As a result, identifying persons of interest from live feeds requires either human memory or post-event video analysis, both of which are inefficient and delay timely action. Moreover, even when such identifications are made, current systems lack secure and verifiable logging mechanisms, which raises concerns about accountability and evidence integrity. The situation becomes even more complex when dealing with dynamic and populated areas such as airports, railway stations, or public gatherings, where rapid detection and response are crucial. Additionally, surveillance data is susceptible to manipulation if not securely stored, reducing its credibility in investigations or audits

ABSTRACT In the era of intelligent systems, interacting with structured databases remains a challenge for 
non-technical users who lack proficiency in SQL (Structured Query Language). To address this 
limitation, the project “Neuro Linguistic Voice Interface Semantic Query Synthesis” presents 
an innovative Python-based web application designed to bridge the gap between human speech 
and database interaction. Developed using the Flask framework, the system enables users to 
communicate with databases using natural voice commands, transforming spoken language into 
semantically accurate SQL queries. The proposed system integrates secure authentication 
features including user registration, login, and password recovery. Upon logging in, users can 
explore two specialized modules—Crime Data and E-Commerce Data—to perform voice-
driven data retrieval. Speech input is captured through the Google Speech Recognition API, 
converted to text, and processed using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and rule-based 
semantic mapping techniques to generate precise SQL queries. These queries are executed on 
backend databases such as SQLite or MySQL, and results are dynamically displayed in a 
structured tabular format within the web interface. What distinguishes this project is its domain-
specific adaptability and lightweight, modular design, enabling efficient operation even in low-
resource environments. By simplifying complex database querying into intuitive voice 
commands, the system empowers law enforcement officers, business analysts, and general 
users to access data seamlessly. This innovation advances the field of voice-based data 
analytics, providing a scalable and accessible framework for natural language-driven database 
interaction. Domain: Artificial Intelligence, Natural Language Processing, Web Technology Keywords: Speech Recognition, Natural Language Processing (NLP), SQL Query Generation, 
Flask Web Application, Voice-Based Data Retrieval, Semantic Query Synthesis, Human–

System Overview The project “Neuro Linguistic Voice Interface Semantic Query Synthesis” is an 
innovative web-based system designed to simplify data interaction by enabling 
users to communicate with structured databases through natural voice commands. 
The system bridges the gap between human language and database query 
languages by leveraging Speech Recognition and Natural Language Processing 
(NLP) to generate semantically accurate SQL queries. Built using the Python 
Flask framework, the application provides an intelligent, domain-specific solution 
that empowers non-technical users to retrieve and analyze data effortlessly. Core Components: 1. Voice-Based Query Input

The system captures the user’s voice input through a microphone interface, 
utilizing the Google Speech Recognition API to convert spoken commands 
into textual form. 
Example Input: A user might ask, “Show me all theft cases reported in 
Pune last month,” or “List all products priced above 1000 rupees.” 
Processing: 
Once converted to text, the input is processed through NLP techniques to 
identify key linguistic structures—such as entities, conditions, and 
attributes—relevant to database queries. 
Output: 
The recognized text is semantically analyzed and transformed into a 
structured SQL query that the database can execute. 2. Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Semantic Query Synthesis

Conclusion 
The project Neuro Linguistic Voice Interface Semantic Query Synthesis marks a 
major step forward in simplifying the way users interact with databases. By 
integrating speech recognition and natural language processing (NLP) with 
database technologies, it enables non-technical users to access and analyze data 
effortlessly through voice commands. This system eliminates the need for manual 
SQL query writing, offering a more natural and intuitive form of communication 
with structured datasets. 
Developed using Python, Flask, and the Google Speech Recognition API, the 
system ensures fast, accurate, and secure data retrieval while maintaining a 
lightweight design suitable for low-resource environments. The inclusion of 
features like user authentication, responsive result display, and multi-domain 
support (crime and e-commerce datasets) enhances usability and accessibility. 
Overall, this project demonstrates how neuro-linguistic principles can be 
effectively combined with computational intelligence to create a user-friendly, 
intelligent, and efficient database querying platform. It bridges the gap between 
human language and machine-level data retrieval, empowering users across 
domains to make data-driven decisions with ease.

system holds significant potential for growth, innovation, and broader

implementation across various domains. The following aspects highlight key

to improve semantic understanding and query precision. These models can

Continuous research can focus on refining rule-based and hybrid NLP 
approaches, optimizing performance, and enhancing response accuracy.

specific corpora, will enable the system to evolve into a more general-
purpose speech-to-database interface suitable for multiple fields. 3. Cloud and IoT Integration

distributed and concurrent multi-user access. Integration with IoT-enabled 
devices could allow real-time data querying and reporting from connected 
systems, extending its use cases to areas like smart cities, logistics, and 
industrial monitoring.

Incorporating text-to-speech (TTS) and conversational AI features can 
transform the system into an interactive assistant capable of holding real-time 
dialogues with users. This will make it more engaging, accessible, and

The system’s modular architecture allows future support for various domains 
beyond crime and e-commerce, such as healthcare, education, finance, and 
agriculture. Users could upload custom datasets, and the system could 
dynamically adapt its query generation rules for different schema structures.

Abstract With the rapid growth of digital financial services and stateless web applications, secure 
authentication has become a critical challenge in modern cybersecurity systems. JSON Web 
Tokens (JWT), widely used for stateless authentication, rely on mathematically generated 
pseudo-random keys that may become vulnerable to future quantum computing attacks. Such 
predictability enables threats like “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later,” where attackers collect 
encrypted data today and exploit it once quantum capabilities mature. Additionally, static or 
infrequently rotated JWT signing keys increase the risk of large-scale compromise in zero-trust 
and microservices architectures. To address these challenges, this project proposes a Quantum-
Seeded Dynamic JWT Authentication Framework that enhances authentication security using 
quantum-derived entropy and adaptive key management. The system integrates a quantum 
entropy source, generated through quantum simulation, to produce high-entropy, non-
deterministic signing keys for JWTs. An entropy pooling mechanism is introduced to mitigate 
quantum latency by pre-fetching and buffering quantum randomness, ensuring authentication 
performance remains within practical limits. A Redis-based key vault enforces automatic key 
expiration and rapid rotation, significantly reducing the attack window in the event of key 
compromise. Furthermore, the framework incorporates an adaptive quantum rotation strategy 
driven by a threat-scoring engine, dynamically adjusting token validity based on real-time risk 
assessment. A hybrid fail-safe mechanism ensures uninterrupted service availability by 
seamlessly switching to classical entropy during quantum source outages. Experimental 
evaluation demonstrates improved entropy quality, reduced exposure to replay and brute-force 
attacks, and negligible authentication latency overhead. The proposed framework provides a 
scalable, future-ready, and practical post-quantum authentication solution suitable for FinTech 
applications, cloud APIs, and zero-trust environments. Keywords: Post-Quantum Authentication, Quantum Entropy, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), [NAME], Zero-Trust Security, Quantum-Safe Cryptography, Stateless Authentication, FinTech Security

ABSTRACT Millions of people it is very difficult to apply for important government documents like income certificates, caste certificates, and proof of domicile, especially if they live in rural areas or have limited digital skills in India. Dispersed portals, unclear instructions, inconsistent state-by-state procedures, and district-level these all factors complicate the process. These problems often result in process errors, frequent office visits, and the exclusion of less technical expertized individuals. We have developed GovGuideBot, an AI-powered chat-bot that explains government documentation procedures, to address this issue. It provides easy-to-use, location-based, step-by-step assistance. In order to understand user intent, the system uses a Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline that is optimized with transform-er models like BERT. Named Entity Recognition (NER) is used to identify crucial information such as document type, state, and district. These specifics are arranged in structured JSON workflows that enable region-specific instructions. GovGuideBot also uses location entered by user query to adapt procedures for user locations, links to official government websites to guarantee accuracy, and uses the YouTube Data API to offer visual tutorials which are particularly useful for users who might have literacy issues or are using these services for the first time. With a precision of 91%, a recall of 93%, and an overall F1-score of 92% for identifying intents and entities, GovGuideBot performs well when tested on actual citizen questions. About half of the planned features were successfully implemented in the working prototype we created for Maharashtra, which includes workflows for income, caste, and domicile certificates. By supporting multiple languages and media formats, GovGuideBot demonstrates how chatbot technology can improve access for more people, decrease needless visits to service sites, and reduce procedural errors. Evolution of Chatbots Chatbots have evolved from simple rule-based systems to advanced AI-driven conversational models. Early chatbots like ELIZA (1966) and ALICE (1995) relied on keyword matching and handcrafted rules to generate responses. However, they lacked contextual understanding and adaptability. With the introduction of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL), modern chatbots began to leverage large datasets and neural architectures to understand user intent and maintain conversation context. The emergence of transformer-based models such as BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) by Google and GPT (Generative Pre-trained Transformer) by OpenAI marked a major breakthrough in language comprehension and text generation, leading to more natural, coherent, and human-like interactions. Chatbots in Public Service and E-Governance Recent years have seen increasing adoption of chatbots in the public sector to simplify citizen-government interactions. Gov.sg WhatsApp Bot (Singapore) – Used to share verified government updates and information with citizens. ABSTRACT Academic credential verification is fundamental to admissions, employment, and professional licensing across institutions and industries worldwide. Traditional verification methods — including manual checks, centralized databases, and direct institutional communication — are slow, costly, and critically vulnerable to document forgery, unauthorized modification, and administrative delays. The growing global mobility of students and professionals has further amplified the urgency for a reliable, fast, and trust-independent verification infrastructure. This project presents Vardox, a public-blockchain anchored academic credential verification architecture. Vardox leverages cryptographic hashing (SHA-256), Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA), Ethereum smart contracts written in Solidity, and distributed off-chain storage via the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) to deliver a complete credential lifecycle management system. Issuing authorities digitally sign documents, generate SHA-256 cryptographic hashes, and anchor these proofs immutably on the Ethereum blockchain. The original documents are stored off-chain via Pinata's IPFS pinning service, while the blockchain serves as the permanent, tamper-proof source of truth for authenticity verification. A file-upload-based verification interface abstracts blockchain complexity for non-technical verifiers, enabling instant document authenticity checks without blockchain knowledge or direct contact with the issuing institution. The system introduces a dual account model — organisations (issuers) and individuals (recipients) — each with distinct dashboard functionalities. An npm SDK (@yashodeep/vardox-sdk) and a versioned REST API (GET /api/v1/verify) enable seamless programmatic integration for external employers, HR systems, and regulatory bodies. Experimental evaluation on 200 test cases demonstrates 100% tamper detection accuracy, zero false positive rate, average end-to-end verification time of 2.8 seconds (compared to 3-7 days for traditional methods), and blockchain hash retrieval latency of 1.2 seconds on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet. CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION 1.1 Overview Academic credential verification plays a critical role in admissions, recruitment, and professional validation globally. As student and professional mobility increases across institutions and national boundaries, the demand for reliable, timely, and trust-independent cross-institutional verification has grown significantly. Institutions, employers, and regulatory bodies require fast, accurate confirmation that academic credentials presented by individuals are genuine, unaltered, and issued by recognized authorities. Traditional verification practices rely on manual processes, centralized databases, or direct communication with issuing institutions — approaches that are slow, expensive, and inefficient. These methods are further compromised by vulnerability to document forgery, unauthorized modification, and administrative delays. Even where digital certificates and hashing techniques have been introduced, most systems store verification records in centralized repositories, requiring verifiers to trust the database administrator and creating single points of failure that undermine verification integrity. Vardox is a public-blockchain anchored academic credential verification architecture that addresses all of these challenges. By anchoring cryptographic document proofs immutably on the Ethereum blockchain, Vardox eliminates the need for any centralized authority in the verification process. Any verifier — employer, university, regulatory body — can independently confirm a document's authenticity by checking the blockchain, which is publicly auditable, tamper-proof, and permanently accessible without institutional permission. 1.2 Motivation The global prevalence of counterfeit academic certificates has caused enormous damage to institutions, employers, and legitimate credential holders. The International Qualifications Assessment Service estimates that credential fraud costs economies billions of dollars annually through misplaced hiring decisions, compromised academic integrity, and fraudulent professional licensing. Traditional verification methods fail in several critical dimensions. Manual verification through institutional communication typically takes 3–7 business days or longer for international credentials. Centralized digital verification portals, while faster, remain single points of failure: a database breach, administrative error, or institutional shutdown can permanently compromise verification capability. PKI-based digital signatures improve document integrity but still require verifiers to trust the issuing institution's key management infrastructure — an assumption that is difficult to guarantee across borders and over time.

CHAPTER 2: LITERATURE SURVEY The literature survey examines four categories of prior work: (i) traditional academic document verification systems, (ii) blockchain-based credential management frameworks, (iii) decentralized identity and verifiable credential systems, and (iv) privacy-preserving and scalability-focused approaches. 2.1 Traditional Academic Document Verification Systems Early academic credential verification systems relied exclusively on centralised databases maintained by universities or third-party agencies. While effective in controlled institutional environments, such systems suffer fundamentally from single points of failure, delayed verification, and complete dependence on the issuing authority's continued operation and cooperation. To reduce fraud, several studies introduced digital signatures and Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) for certificate authentication. Digitally signed PDFs significantly reduce tampering risks at the document level; however, these systems still require verifiers to trust the issuing institution's key management and database integrity, making them vulnerable to insider threats and database manipulation. Rifat and Hossain (2025) demonstrated that SHA-256 and ECDSA based certificate generation systems provide strong tamper-evidence at the document level but fail to guarantee global verifiability without an immutable public ledger — the verification record itself remains mutable. Hash-based verification methods were subsequently introduced, where document hashes are stored in centralized databases. Mehta and Kulkarni (2025) demonstrated that although hashing ensures document integrity at the time of issuance, centralized hash storage does not prevent unauthorized modification by database administrators and lacks global verifiability. An administrator with database access could silently alter or delete hash records, destroying verification integrity. Casino et al. CHAPTER 3: RESEARCH GAP A systematic review of the literature reveals five critical gaps that collectively motivate the design and implementation of the Vardox system. These gaps are not isolated shortcomings of individual systems but represent recurring, systemic limitations across the majority of existing academic credential verification approaches. 3.1 Predominance of Centralized Verification Systems The most fundamental gap in the existing literature is the persistent reliance on centralized databases for credential verification. Despite the well-documented vulnerabilities of centralized systems — single points of failure, insider manipulation risk, data breach exposure, and service unavailability — the majority of academic document verification solutions continue to depend on institution-controlled databases. This design creates an inherent dependency: verifiers must trust not only the issuing institution's integrity but also the security and availability of its database infrastructure indefinitely into the future. Singh et al.'s centralized repositories, while effective in controlled environments, immediately fail when the institution undergoes organizational change, experiences a data breach, or simply becomes unavailable. The verification record can be silently altered or deleted by any administrator with database access, yet no external party can independently detect such manipulation. Gap: There is a critical absence of trust-independent verification mechanisms that allow any third party to verify academic credentials without relying on, contacting, or trusting any centralized authority. Vardox Response: Vardox anchors all verification proofs immutably on the Ethereum public blockchain. No entity — including the issuing institution — can alter or delete an anchored record. Verification is permanently available to any party with internet access, independent of institutional availability. 3.2 Limited Trust and Transparency in Hash-Based Verification Approaches Hash-based verification methods represent a meaningful improvement over purely database-driven approaches, as cryptographic hashing provides strong tamper-evidence at the document level. However, when document hashes are stored in centralized databases — as in all non-blockchain hash-based systems reviewed — the verification process still depends entirely on the security and honesty of the database owner.

CHAPTER 6: METHODOLOGY Vardox is developed using a phased methodology progressing from requirement analysis and architectural design through incremental implementation of cryptographic, blockchain, storage, and API components. The methodology ensures structured development with clear milestones at each review stage.

6.1 System Architecture The Vardox architecture comprises three primary actors connected through a shared blockchain network and off-chain storage system: Academic Institution / Organisation (Issuer): Creates and manages an organisation account with a dedicated Ethereum wallet. Uploads documents, captures metadata, and initiates issuance — triggering hash generation, IPFS pinning, and blockchain anchoring in a single workflow. Public Blockchain Network (Ethereum — Sepolia Testnet): Stores document hashes and issuer metadata immutably via a Solidity smart contract. Acts as the permanent, publicly auditable, and tamper-proof source of truth. No entity can modify or delete anchored records. Verifier (Employer / University / External System): Uploads the original document file on the Verify page, or submits a pre-computed hash via the SDK/API. Receives a verification result showing registry status, blockchain confirmation, issuer address, and IPFS link. Off-chain IPFS storage (via Pinata) holds the actual document files, linked to on-chain records through the document hash and IPFS Content Identifier (CID). The Node.js/Next.js backend orchestrates all interactions between the React frontend, PostgreSQL database (Prisma ORM), IPFS pinning service, and Ethereum blockchain. Registry Recording: Document metadata, hash, and recipient association are recorded in the PostgreSQL database via Prisma ORM. Blockchain Anchoring: The document hash and metadata are submitted to the Ethereum smart contract via a signed transaction. The contract records H = SHA-256(D + S) immutably and returns a transaction reference Tx. IPFS Pinning: The document file is uploaded to IPFS via Pinata's server-side pinning API. The resulting Content Identifier (CID) is stored in the database alongside the document record. The cryptographic hash formula used is H = Hash(D + S), where D is the document content and S is the issuer's digital signature. This binds both document integrity and issuer identity into a single on-chain proof. 6.3 Blockchain Hash Anchoring — Smart Contract Design The Vardox smart contract is written in Solidity and deployed on the Ethereum Sepolia testnet. The contract maintains an immutable mapping from document hashes to issuance records: mapping(bytes32 => DocumentRecord) public documents; Each DocumentRecord contains: the document hash (bytes32), issuer Ethereum address, issuance timestamp (block timestamp), and a boolean validity flag. The contract exposes two primary functions: issueDocument(bytes32 hash, string metadata): Called by the organisation's wallet to anchor a new document proof. Emits a DocumentIssued event on success. Reverts if the same hash is submitted twice (preventing duplicate issuance). verifyDocument(bytes32 hash): View function returning the DocumentRecord for a given hash, or indicating absence. No gas fee is required for verification queries.

Store these in the OnchainProof database table linked to the document record. Return the issuance success response to the client, including the transaction hash as a Sepolia Etherscan link for independent verification. 7.2.4 Dual-Layer Verification System The verification engine implements a dual-layer check providing stronger assurance than single-source approaches. CHAPTER 8: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION The Vardox system was evaluated through comprehensive testing across four performance dimensions: verification accuracy, verification time, resistance to tampering, and scalability. Experimental results confirm that Vardox meets all defined functional and non-functional requirements. 8.1 Verification Accuracy The system was tested on 200 document test cases comprising 100 legitimately issued documents and 100 tampered, forged, or unissued documents. Results: True Positive Rate (correctly verified): 100% — all 100 legitimately issued documents were correctly identified as valid. True Negative Rate (correctly rejected): 100% — all 100 tampered/forged/unissued documents were correctly identified as invalid. False Positive Rate: 0% — no tampered or unissued document was incorrectly verified as valid. False Negative Rate: 0% — no legitimately issued document was incorrectly rejected. Tampering test scenarios included: single-byte content modification, metadata-only changes (document name, dates), pixel-level image modification, PDF metadata tampering, re-encoding with identical visual appearance but different binary content, and unauthorized hash substitution attempts. All scenarios were detected through SHA-256 hash mismatch. Digital signature validation confirmed issuer authenticity in all valid credential scenarios — the smart contract verifyDocument() function returned the correct issuer Ethereum address in all 100 valid test cases. 8.2 Verification Time End-to-end verification time was measured from file upload initiation to verification result display for 50 verification operations: Average end-to-end verification time: 2.8 seconds (compared to 3-7 business days for traditional manual verification — an improvement of several orders of magnitude). Blockchain hash retrieval latency on Ethereum Sepolia testnet: average 1.2 seconds per query (range: 0.8s – 2.1s depending on testnet load). Client-side SHA-256 hash computation: < 200ms for documents up to 10MB. Registry database query: < 50ms average on PostgreSQL. IPFS CID retrieval and gateway link construction: < 100ms. 8.3 Resistance to Tampering

The immutability of the Ethereum blockchain record ensured that even with full database access (simulated insider threat scenario), verification integrity could not be compromised — the smart contract returned the original anchored hash, which differed from the tampered document's computed hash, producing a correct 'Invalid' result. CHAPTER 9: CONCLUSION This project presented Vardox — a public-blockchain anchored academic credential verification architecture that directly addresses the critical limitations of centralized credential management systems identified throughout the literature. By anchoring SHA-256 cryptographic hashes of academic documents immutably on the Ethereum blockchain via Solidity smart contracts, Vardox delivers permanent, tamper-proof, and trust-independent verification that no centralized system can match. The three-phase review implementation demonstrated a disciplined, incremental development approach. Review 1 (15%) established the cryptographic foundation through client-side SHA-256 hash generation, Google OAuth authentication, PostgreSQL schema design, and a responsive document issuance interface. Review 2 (50%) integrated the Ethereum blockchain through smart contract development and deployment, organisation-level wallet management, on-chain document anchoring, and dual-layer registry-plus-blockchain verification. Review 3 (100%) completed the platform with IPFS document storage via Pinata, a published TypeScript npm SDK, a versioned REST API with API key management, and an in-application SDK test interface. Experimental evaluation on 200 test cases confirmed 100% tamper detection accuracy, zero false positives, and an average end-to-end verification time of 2.8 seconds — a reduction from 3-7 business days for traditional manual verification of several orders of magnitude. The dual-layer verification approach — checking both the application registry and the Ethereum blockchain — proved particularly valuable in insider threat scenarios, where database manipulation was correctly detected through blockchain consistency checking. The Vardox SDK and REST API represent a significant contribution toward practical adoption. By abstracting all blockchain complexity behind a simple URL plus API key interface, Vardox enables any employer, HR platform, or university admissions system to integrate blockchain-grade credential verification into existing workflows without blockchain expertise or infrastructure. The zero-dependency TypeScript SDK, published on npm at @yashodeep/vardox-sdk, is immediately installable and usable by any Node.js developer.
