CHAPTER 10: FUTURE SCOPE While Vardox achieves all defined project objectives, the architecture is designed for extensibility and several significant enhancements are planned or recommended for future development: 10.1 Decentralized Identity (DID) Integration Integration with W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DID) and Verifiable Credentials (VC) standards would enable true cross-border interoperability. Under a DID architecture, Vardox-issued credentials could be verified by any W3C-compliant verifier globally without requiring interaction with the Vardox platform. This would position Vardox within the broader Decentralized Identity ecosystem alongside systems like OpenCerts, EduCTX, and national digital identity frameworks. 10.2 Zero-Knowledge Proof Selective Disclosure Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) would enable recipients to selectively prove specific credential attributes — such as 'I graduated from a recognized university' or 'My GPA is above 8.0' — without revealing the complete certificate to the verifier. ZKP-based selective disclosure is particularly valuable for privacy-sensitive employment and immigration scenarios where full document revelation is inappropriate. Implementation would likely use zk-SNARKs on Ethereum via libraries such as snarkjs or Circom. 10.3 On-Chain Credential Revocation A credential revocation mechanism would allow issuing organisations to invalidate compromised, expired, or incorrectly issued credentials on-chain while preserving the complete audit trail. The revocation record would be anchored on the blockchain (setting a 'revoked' flag in the smart contract), ensuring that revocation is as tamper-proof and permanent as the original issuance. Verification would then check both the issuance record and the revocation status. 10.4 Layer 2 Gas Optimization for Mainnet Deployment Ethereum mainnet gas fees make high-volume credential issuance expensive. Migration to Layer 2 solutions — Polygon, Base (Coinbase), or Optimism — would reduce transaction costs by 10-100x while maintaining Ethereum-equivalent security guarantees. Base in particular offers EVM compatibility, institutional backing, and growing adoption that would benefit Vardox's institutional deployment path. 10.5 Mobile Application Development

Abstract—Crack formation inside pipeline networks is a ma-
jor safety concern in industries that rely on continuous fluid
transport. Pipelines carrying water, oil, gas, and industrial
chemicals are exposed to sustained internal pressure, corrosion,
and mechanical fatigue that initiate surface defects over time.
Traditional methods of inspecting pipes from the inside are slow,
risky for workers, and often impractical in confined or chemically
hazardous spaces. This paper describes an inspection system
in which a small wheeled robot carries a camera through the
pipeline and transmits live images to a computer for automatic
defect analysis. A two-stage deep learning approach is adopted:
YOLOv8 first draws bounding boxes around suspected crack or
corrosion areas, and an [NAME] then produces pixel-
level segmentation maps within those regions. Once a crack
mask is obtained, morphological skeletonization gives the crack
length and area as actual numbers that engineers can use to
decide on repairs. Testing on 1,777 annotated images yielded an
accuracy of 98.21%, Dice coefficient of 0.6886, IoU of 0.5305,
precision of 0.9714, recall of 0.9621, and F1-score of 0.9667. A
three-way ablation study confirmed that combining both models
outperforms either one working alone. The complete setup is
low-cost and does not require shutting down the pipeline during
inspection. Index Terms—YOLOv8, [NAME], crack detection,

INTRODUCTION Pipelines are among the most critical pieces of infrastructure in modern industry. Water distribution networks, oil and gas transmission lines, and chemical processing plants all depend on pipes that remain structurally sound over decades of contin-
uous use. The combination of cyclic pressure loading, internal
corrosion, and temperature variation gradually weakens pipe
walls and produces small surface cracks. These cracks do
not stay small; under repeated stress they grow, eventually
leading to leakage, environmental pollution, service interrup-
tion, and sometimes catastrophic rupture [8]. The financial and
safety consequences of such failures are well documented,
yet catching defects early remains a persistent operational
challenge [10]. The fundamental difficulty is access. Many pipelines run
underground, underwater, or through hazardous industrial
zones where a human inspector cannot enter safely. Even in
accessible pipes, manual inspection is slow and results depend
heavily on the individual doing the work. Established non-
destructive testing (NDT) techniques such as magnetic flux
leakage, acoustic emission sensing, and eddy-current probing
address some of these problems, but they require expensive
dedicated equipment, need the pipe to be taken out of service,
and still require an expert to interpret the raw data [2].
For large pipeline networks spread over wide areas, this is
economically and logistically very difficult to sustain. Camera-based inspection with automated image analysis
has attracted growing interest as a cheaper and more flexible
alternative [8], [9]. Deep learning models, particularly convo-
lutional neural networks, have shown strong results on crack
detection in laboratory experiments. The practical limitation is that real pipeline images suffer from uneven illumination,
motion blur, surface rust, and a narrow field of view [5]. A
system that performs well in the lab often fails in the field. This work addresses that gap directly. The contributions are
as follows.

LITERATURE REVIEW Work on automated pipeline inspection divides broadly into two streams: building robots that travel inside pipes, and developing algorithms that identify defects in the images those robots collect. Most published systems address one stream; few combine both. On the robotics side, Kandil et al. [1] built a swarm of small
robots that cooperate over IoT communication and classify
cracks using a VGG16 network, with ultrasonic sensors added
for ranging. The system is restricted to horizontal empty
pipes, and the ultrasonic hardware gives unreliable readings
on curved or corroded surfaces. Daniyan et al. [2] produced a
compact inline robot with embedded sensors and a camera
monitored remotely by a technician. It reduces hazard to
workers but has no learned crack classifier; detection still
depends on a person watching the video feed. Mohammed
et al. [3] designed a modular robot that adjusts its width
for different pipe diameters. The mechanical design is well
conceived, but defect detection is limited to simple threshold-
based image checks with no segmentation. Subha et al. [4]
concentrated on navigation and obstacle avoidance inside
confined pipelines. Navigation performance is good, but the
paper does not address crack detection. On the detection side, Colvalkar et al. [5] applied classical
edge-detection and thresholding operators to find cracks and
corrosion. These methods are fast but break down whenever
lighting conditions change. Alex et al. [6] added multi-sensor
fusion to improve detection reliability. Alkhedher et al. [10]
demonstrated an intelligent robotic inspection system capable
of autonomous navigation and structural condition reporting.

image collection by the robot, frame preprocessing, bounding-
box detection with YOLOv8, pixel-level segmentation with the
[NAME], quantitative crack measurement, and result
visualisation. Each stage is described below. A. Data Collection The dataset contains 1,777 annotated images covering two
defect classes: crack and corrosion. Images came from two
complementary sources. First, publicly available labeled crack
datasets supplied diverse sample images with verified ground-
truth annotations. Second, the robotic platform described in
Section III-F was used to record additional frames directly
inside pipe-like test tunnels. The robot moved slowly while the
ESP32-CAM captured frames showing all the visual problems
seen in real pipes: rust patches, wall shadows, varying crack
angles, and surface staining. Combining both sources gave the
training set a much broader range of conditions than either
alone could provide. B. Image Preprocessing and Augmentation

Image Preprocessing and Augmentation Images taken inside dark, dirty pipes are rarely usable
straight from the camera. They tend to be underexposed,
brighter on one side than the other, and blurred where the
robot moved quickly. Several preprocessing steps were applied
to every frame before passing it to the models. All images were resized to 640 × 640 pixels so that model
input dimensions stayed fixed. Contrast Limited Adaptive His-
togram Equalization (CLAHE) was applied with a clip limit
of 2.0 on an 8 × 8 tile grid, sharpening local contrast in small
image regions and making hairline cracks visible without over-
brightening noisy areas. Non-Local Means (NLM) denoising
then reduced random sensor noise while preserving crack
edges. For training, the dataset was further expanded through
stochastic augmentation: random in-plane rotation up to ±15◦,
brightness and contrast scaling over [0.7, 1.3], additive Gaus-
sian noise with σ ∈[5, 25], and motion-blur simulation using
linear kernels of width k ∈{3, 5, 7} at random orientations.
These transforms collectively approximate the image degrada-
tions encountered during real in-pipe inspection. C. Crack Detection Using YOLOv8 Each preprocessed frame is analyzed by YOLOv8 [8],
an anchor-free single-stage detector that handles small and
irregularly shaped objects well. For every suspected defect

Robotic Platform The robot is built on a commercial RC-car chassis approxi-
mately 26 cm long and 18 cm wide, giving sufficient clearance
for pipes with inner diameters above 100 mm. A 10,000 mAh
portable power bank supplies both the drive motors and the
ESP32-CAM, providing roughly four hours of continuous
operation per charge. The camera is mounted coaxially with
the pipe axis. During a test run it streams compressed JPEG
frames over a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi link to a laptop running the
inference pipeline. Wireless delay averaged below 80 ms, and
model inference takes approximately 120 ms per frame on a
GPU, supporting around five inspection frames per second
end-to-end. IV. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE The end-to-end architecture is illustrated in Fig. 1. The
mobile robotic platform captures images and transmits them
over Wi-Fi to the processing host. A shared convolutional
backbone performs multi-scale feature extraction; its feature
pyramid feeds two parallel heads. The YOLOv8 detection
head produces bounding boxes with confidence scores, while
the [NAME] decoder generates dense probability maps
at pixel level. Post-processing derives binary masks and nu-
merical crack metrics, which are assembled into a structured
visual report comprising bounding-box overlays, probability
heatmaps, and a crack-metrics dashboard. Fig. 1.

Experimental Setup The 1,777 annotated images were partitioned into training
(70%), validation (15%), and test (15%) subsets using a
stratified split to preserve class balance. YOLOv8 was fine-
tuned for 80 epochs with an initial learning rate of 1×10−3 and
cosine annealing decay, with a batch size of 16. The Attention
U-Net was trained for up to 100 epochs using the Adam
optimiser at 5 × 10−4, with early stopping if validation loss
failed to improve for 15 consecutive epochs. All experiments
were conducted on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 GPU
(12 GB VRAM). B. Training Performance Loss vs. Epoch: Fig. 2 tracks training loss across 80 epochs.
Starting at 1.46 in the first epoch, the loss drops sharply
through epoch 10 as the network learns the dominant crack and
corrosion features. The rate of decrease slows between epochs
10 and 30, where minor oscillations are visible around the
0.40–0.45 range, reflecting the model adapting to harder, more
ambiguous samples introduced by the augmentation strategy.
From epoch 30 onward the curve resumes a gradual but
consistent downward trend, reaching approximately 0.27 by
epoch 80. There are no signs of divergence or runaway loss,
which indicates that the chosen learning rate schedule and
batch size were appropriate for this dataset. Accuracy vs. Epoch: Fig. 3 shows how validation accuracy

ABSTRACT The unexpected growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has changed how we collect and 
share data, but it has also created a significant target for cyber-attacks. These devices lack the 
computing resources and security features needed to defend against evolving threats, making 
them vulnerable. Traditional security methods can no longer handle these dynamic challenges. NetDefend IoT offers an intelligent, adaptive security system that combines machine learning 
(ML), explainable AI (XAI), blockchain, and self-healing intelligence to provide a 
comprehensive defense for IoT systems. The design not only detects threats in real-time but 
also responds and recovers automatically, ensuring continuous protection. The system uses ML 
algorithms to monitor device behavior and identify anomalies, while XAI explains the 
reasoning behind threat detection, helping managers understand the decisions made. Blockchain technology ensures secure, tamper-proof communication between IoT devices to 
prevent tampering and guarantee reliable collaboration. Additionally, the self-healing 
component enables the system to automatically patch vulnerabilities or reconfigure itself 
during an attack, reducing downtime and human intervention. This solution marks a significant 
step forward in IoT security by integrating cutting-edge technologies into one unified, effective 
system for seamless operation. The innovation is based on combining explainability, secure 
collaboration, and automated recovery, addressing the needs of resource-limited IoT devices. Domain: IOT, ML, Cyber-Security Keywords: IoT, AI, ML, XAI, Blockchain, Self-healing intelligence v Table of contents Section

INTRODUCTION Preamble The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has changed modern systems. However, it has also raised security risks because of device weaknesses and limited protection options. IoT botnets and DDoS attacks are increasing, so real-time threat detection is essential. NetDefend IoT aims to tackle this problem by creating a lightweight, efficient, and smart anomaly detection system that operates at the network edge. This project offers a practical way to identify harmful traffic, spot compromised devices, and improve the overall security and strength of IoT environments.

1.1 Problem Statement The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices across industries has introduced unprecedented convenience and connectivity but has also exposed significant vulnerabilities in network security. Due to limited computational capabilities and inadequate built-in defense mechanisms, IoT systems are highly susceptible to cyberattacks, including data breaches, malware infiltration, and unauthorized access. Despite progress in cybersecurity technologies, the lack of an intelligent, adaptive, and scalable protection framework continues to challenge the safe deployment of IoT ecosystems. Existing security solutions are often static, resource-intensive, and fail to address the dynamic nature of IoT environments. Moreover, there is a lack of integrated platforms that utilize Machine Learning (ML) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) for real-time threat detection, interpretation, and response. This gap limits transparency and trust in automated security systems. Therefore, there is a pressing need for an advanced IoT security framework capable of autonomously detecting, analyzing, and mitigating evolving threats while maintaining interpretability and resource efficiency. Addressing these challenges through an intelligent and explainable security model would significantly enhance IoT resilience, safeguard critical infrastructures, and contribute to a more secure and trustworthy connected ecosystem. This multi-layered approach aims to detect and respond to IoT network threats effectively. It also ensures transparency, data integrity, and automated recovery in limited-resource environments like Raspberry Pi. 3.1 Research / Development framework The development of NetDefend IoT uses a hybrid research method that combines data- driven machine learning techniques with smart self-healing and blockchain-based security mechanisms. The framework focuses on four key phases: data acquisition, model development, blockchain integration, and self-healing automation. The overall design flow is structured as follows: • Requirement Analysis and Problem Definition: Identify cybersecurity gaps in IoT environments, especially in intrusion detection, response flexibility, and data integrity. • Dataset Selection and Preprocessing: We use publicly available IoT intrusion datasets such as CICIDS 2017, NSL-KDD, and TON_IoT for training and testing. Preprocessing steps include normalization, feature selection, and attack label encoding. [1], [3], [4], [12] • Machine Learning-Based Detection: We implement multiple classifiers, including Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Networks. The integrity of the chain is checked by recalculating hashes and examining previous-hash links. Each alert is stored as a block that includes an index, timestamp, alert data, the hash of the previous block, and the block's own SHA-256 hash. When a full Ethereum network is not needed for proof-of-concept deployments or local testing, this straightforward on-chain structure guarantees immutability and offers auditable provenance for alerts. The is_chain_valid() method provides a fast integrity check to identify corruption or tampering, and the module is designed to be integrated with the NetDefend pipeline. Alerts are hashed and appended to the ledger.Functionality: Each alert triggers a smart contract transaction that stores a hashed record in the blockchain ledger. 6.3.5 Self-Healing Intelligence Module When an intrusion is detected, the Self-Healing Intelligence Module automatically isolates the compromised devices and resumes normal operation. Device health and anomaly signals from the IDS are continuously monitored. When a device is identified as compromised, the module initiates containment measures (such as blocking or quarantining the device), initiates automated reconfiguration processes to safely restore connectivity, and optionally records post- recovery telemetry to retrain models for better detection in the future.[6] The module allows operators to review, approve, or reverse corrective actions by supporting human-in-the-loop overrides and logging all actions for auditability.These modules together make NetDefend IoT a self-adjusting, resilient IoT security framework that not only detects attacks but also explains and recovers from them autonomously. 1. Introduction The EcoGrid project is founded on the principles of the circular economy, aiming to dismantle the traditional "take-make-dispose" model that currently dominates modern consumerism. This linear approach results in significant resource underutilization and environmental degradation, as durable household goods often sit idle for the majority of their functional lifespans. Research confirms that sharing economy participants are initially motivated by sustainability and economic gains, though long-term engagement is driven by the social gratification of community interaction. EcoGrid addresses these challenges by creating a peer-to-peer (P2P) marketplace where neighborhood resources are kept in active use through renting, lending, or donating. By maximizing the utility of every item, the platform directly contributes to waste reduction and promotes a more sustainable lifestyle for urban residents. A primary innovation of EcoGrid is its strict focus on hyper-local optimization, which is essential for reducing the environmental impact of modern logistics. Most global marketplaces fail to address the "carbon footprint of logistics," as shipping goods over long distances often negates the ecological benefits of buying second-hand or sharing. By keeping resource loops within a narrow geographic radius of 5-10 kilometers, EcoGrid ensures that transportation emissions are kept to an absolute minimum. This localized approach not only benefits the environment but also strengthens community bonds by encouraging physical interactions between neighbors. The platform functions as a decentralized warehouse, allowing the community to effectively manage its own collective inventory without the need for high-cost, centralized infrastructure.

Abstract With the rapid growth of cyber-attacks, maintaining the integrity and authenticity of security logs has become a major challenge. Traditional logging systems can be modified or deleted by attackers, and future advancements in quantum computing may further weaken existing cryptographic protections. To address these issues, this project proposes a Quantum Safe [NAME] Honeypot Logging System. In this system, a honeypot is deployed to attract attackers and capture real cyber-attack activities such as IP addresses, login attempts, and attack commands without affecting the actual system. The collected logs are processed and secured using quantum-resistant cryptographic hashing techniques to ensure long-term security against quantum threats. Only the hash values of the attack logs are stored on a blockchain, providing immutability, transparency, and reliable time-stamping. The original logs are stored securely off-chain to reduce storage overhead. Log integrity is verified by recalculating and comparing hash values with the blockchain records. Any modification in the logs can be easily detected. The system also includes an admin dashboard that allows security analysts to monitor attack logs and verify their integrity status. This approach ensures a tamper-proof, future-ready, and trustworthy cyber-attack logging system, making it suitable for modern cybersecurity and forensic applications. Keywords: Honeypot, Blockchain, Quantum-Resistant Cryptography, Cyber Attack Logging, Log Integrity, Tamper-Proof System, Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics.

ABSTRACT In the digital age, networking plays a crucial role in professional development, particularly for students transitioning from academia to industry. "RAISONI CONNECT" is a dedicated platform designed exclusively for students of Raisoni College, facilitating meaningful connections, collaboration, and career opportunities. This project aims to bridge the gap between students, alumni, and potential employers, fostering a vibrant community that enhances professional growth and knowledge sharing. The significance of "RAISONI CONNECT" lies in its tailored approach to meet the unique needs of our college community. By providing a space for students to showcase their skills, share projects, and seek mentorship, the platform empowers users to build their professional identities and expand their networks. The methodology employed in this project includes a combination of user-centered design principles, agile development practices, and the integration of social networking features. The platform will utilize a robust database to manage user profiles, connections, and job postings, ensuring a seamless user experience. The novelty of this work lies in its focus on a specific academic community, allowing for a more personalized and relevant networking experience compared to broader platforms like LinkedIn. By fostering a sense of belonging and collaboration among students, "RAISONI CONNECT" aims to enhance employability and create a supportive ecosystem for future professionals. Although platforms like LinkedIn and other global networks provide avenues for professional interaction, they are often too broad and fail to cater to the localized needs of students, alumni, and faculty from a single institution. As a result, students struggle to identify relevant mentors, collaborate on academic or technical projects, or access internship and placement opportunities that are directly associated with their college network. At G. H. Raisoni College, communication between students, alumni, faculty, and recruiters remains largely unstructured and fragmented across multiple channels such as emails, social media groups, and informal messaging platforms. This lack of a unified system limits collaboration, mentorship opportunities, and effective sharing of achievements or research initiatives. Moreover, recruiters often find it difficult to reach potential candidates who possess the right skills and interests within the college. Therefore, there is a pressing need for a centralized networking platform that brings together all stakeholders of the Raisoni community—students, alumni, faculty, and recruiters—on a single, secure, and interactive platform. Such a system will not only enhance professional collaboration but also promote mentorship, streamline internship, and job opportunities, and strengthen the overall academic ecosystem of the institution. 1.2 Project Objectives 1. The system verifies whether the email domain (e.g., @raisoni.net [EMAIL]) matches the predefined whitelist of approved institutional domains. 3. If the email domain is found in the whitelist, the system proceeds to send a verification code or link to the user’s email for confirmation. 4. Upon successful verification, the user is allowed to create their profile and access the platform’s features. 5. If the email domain does not match the whitelist, the system immediately denies access and displays an error message stating “Unauthorized domain — access restricted to Raisoni members only. Purpose: This algorithm ensures that only genuine members of the Raisoni ecosystem can register, thus maintaining exclusivity, data integrity, and security within the platform. Abstract— The Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System is designed to counter the primary disadvantage of conventional drones with centralized control and manual triggering. Under high-risk operations such as defense, surveillance, or disaster relief, such systems are extremely susceptible to jamming or controller breakdown. This research proposes a next-generation system where drones self-trigger based on onboard sensors (e.g., MPU6050) as soon as they are deployed or enter into free-fall. This self-initiated mode permits instant mid-air launch without human intervention, guaranteeing mission integrity even if mothership or command station is lost. After taking off, every drone stabilizes and resumes autonomous flight, applying onboard computer vision to spot and engage dynamically detected targets. Without the requirement for external instructions, the system greatly improves responsiveness and reliability in dynamic or communication-restricted environments. The project design involves an industrial-strength latch and fallout system that allows safe dropping of multiple child drones by a mother drone. The small drones are contained in latches that secure them until a programmed trigger condition (e.g., free-fall or altitude level) is achieved. When released, the drones automatically start and spread out for assigned functions. Keywords— Swarm Intelligence, Latch and Fallout Mechanism, Autonomous Mini Drones, Computer Vision

Introduction Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are emerging as crucial assets in defense, disaster management, and large-scale monitoring. Conventional drones, however, remain dependent on central ground control or continuous operator involvement, which restricts their autonomy and makes them vulnerable in signal-jammed or GPS-denied conditions. The Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System aims to overcome these limitations by creating drones that activate automatically upon release and coordinate among themselves as a swarm. Each unit is equipped with onboard sensors, real-time vision systems, and peer-to-peer communication, enabling them to share information, adapt to changing situations, and execute missions collectively without external supervision. This approach eliminates reliance on central control, thereby improving robustness, scalability, and mission efficiency. Such a system holds promise for military operations, emergency response, and civilian applications where quick, autonomous deployment is essentials. Background Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), commonly known as drones, have rapidly evolved from simple remotely piloted machines to highly sophisticated autonomous systems. Their applications now span across military, commercial, and civilian domains, including surveillance, disaster management, logistics, agriculture, and environmental monitoring. Traditionally, drone operations have relied on centralized ground control stations or human operators for navigation, mission planning, and target identification. While effective in structured environments, such dependence introduces significant vulnerabilities in contested or communication-denied regions where external signals may be jammed, lost, or deliberately disrupted. Literature Survey Recent years have seen significant progress in UAV target detection and swarm intelligence, with researchers focusing on improving both accuracy and autonomy. One line of work has enhanced the YOLOv5 framework by modifying its backbone and anchor strategies. For instance, an improved YOLOv5 model introduced an Asymmetric ResNet backbone and Asymmetric Enhanced Feature Extraction (AEFE), which boosted small-object detection accuracy and swarm coordination in aerial imagery. Building on this, Zhang (2025) proposed Drone YOLO, an efficient deep learning model optimized for drone-captured images. By integrating multistage learning and channel attention modules, the framework improved recognition of small and distant targets while remaining computationally efficient for deployment on lightweight UAV platforms. Similarly, studies in robust swarm control have redesigned network neck structures and pooling layers, replacing conventional SPP and PANet modules with more effective fusion techniques. These modifications strengthened UAVs’ ability to adapt to dynamic environments without continuous human supervision. Modified YOLOv5 models with asymmetric backbones, attention modules, and improved anchor strategies have demonstrated higher accuracy for small-object detection in aerial imagery, while Zhang’s Drone YOLO (2025) further improved efficiency through multistage learning and channel attention, making it suitable for lightweight UAV platforms.

Parallel efforts in swarm autonomy redesigned pooling and fusion structures, enabling drones to function reliably in dynamic conditions without constant human input. Xiao et al. (2023, 2024) applied reinforcement learning and curriculum-based multistage models for collaborative multi-target search, achieving improved decision-making and accuracy on UAV datasets like VisDrone2019. In trajectory optimization, Nguyen and Park (2024) introduced distributed deep reinforcement learning approaches that reduced mission time and enhanced stability, while Rani and Verma (2023) surveyed swarm intelligence algorithms such as PSO, ACO, and Boids, highlighting their potential for autonomous coordination. Communication strategies were strengthened by Choudhary and Desai (2024), who proposed multi-hop and master–slave architectures to reduce latency and support search-and-rescue operations, whereas Patel and Singh (2023) developed energy-efficient protocols that extended UAV mission endurance under resource constraints. Collectively, these studies show that although significant progress has been made in detection accuracy, trajectory optimization, and communication efficiency, there is still a pressing need for fully autonomous, self-triggered drone swarms capable of decentralized deployment and mission execution in communication-denied or GPS-restricted environments, which forms the basis of the present research.

Methodology The proposed system consists of a mothership drone equipped with an Arduino Uno, LoRa module, and servo-controlled latch to release swarm drones upon signal loss, ensuring autonomous deployment. Each child drone, powered by an Arduino Nano, brushless motors, and IMU sensors, activates mid-air through timer or accelerometer triggers and stabilizes autonomously. Computer vision using OpenCV and YOLOv5 enables real-time target detection, with drones hovering over identified objects for precise localization. Peer-to-peer communication protocols allow basic swarm behaviors such as leader–follower and synchronized movement, ensuring decentralized coordination. The system’s performance is evaluated through simulations and real-time tests measuring latch activation, hovering precision, and successful autonomous deployment under communication-denied conditions. System Overview The system is structured into two primary units: the Mothership Drone Unit and the Swarm Child Drones. The mothership serves as the launch platform, equipped with LoRa communication, GPS for altitude estimation, and a servo-based latch mechanism for controlled release. It monitors signal integrity, and in the event of communication failure, automatically triggers the release of child drones. The swarm drones, designed as compact and lightweight units, include onboard control systems, IMU-based triggering, and modular payload capacity for tasks such as target detection and environmental sensing. Each child drone is capable of autonomous stabilization, vision-based object recognition, and coordinated flight behaviors through decentralized communication with peer drones. This distributed architecture eliminates single points of failure, ensuring resilience and adaptability in mission-critical environments. The modular nature of the design also allows scalability, enabling the swarm to expand in size or adapt to various applications such as defense reconnaissance, disaster relief, and search-and-rescue operations. Conclusion The Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System represents a paradigm shift in autonomous aerial operations by eliminating dependence on centralized control and enabling drones to self-activate, self-organize, and self-execute complex missions. Through decentralized coordination, onboard computer vision, and real-time decision-making, the swarm demonstrates exceptional resilience, adaptability, and mission efficiency—even in GPS-denied or communication-compromised environments. The integration of onboard computer vision, real-time peer-to-peer communication, and decentralized intelligence allows the swarm to not only perform coordinated actions but also adapt to unforeseen challenges in real-time. This adaptability ensures that even if one or more drones are lost or disabled, the swarm as a whole continues its mission without failure. This kind of fault-tolerant behavior significantly enhances operational reliability and mission assurance. This innovation not only strengthens capabilities in high-stakes military operations but also opens up transformative applications in civilian sectors such as disaster response, environmental monitoring, and search-and-rescue missions. With its modular, energy-efficient design and scalable architecture, the system sets a strong foundation for the future of intelligent, cooperative drone technology. As autonomous swarms continue to evolve, they promise to become indispensable tools in both strategic and humanitarian missions, redefining the boundaries of what unmanned aerial systems can achieve. Looking ahead, the continued development of such systems holds immense potential. As AI, machine learning, sensor technologies, and swarm algorithms advance, these drones will become smarter, faster, and more capable of performing complex missions without human intervention.

ABSTRACT AcuPath is an AI-powered Android application developed using Java and XML with Firebase [NAME] as the backend, designed to deliver personalized exercise-based guidance for relieving common musculoskeletal pain, including back, neck, shoulder, and knee pain. The system captures user-reported pain location and intensity and conducts a structured, symptom-driven questionnaire that dynamically adapts using Agentic AI to select only the most relevant follow-up questions. Based on the collected inputs, Generative AI generates clear, user-friendly exercise routines, posture correction advice, do’s and don’ts, and safety alerts, including recommendations for medical consultation when red-flag symptoms are detected. AcuPath also integrates an AI Assistant with NLP-based intent recognition to support natural language queries and context-aware responses, along with a Video module that provides visual exercise demonstrations via embedded web content. User pain records, sessions, and recommendations are securely stored with timestamps in Firebase to enable history tracking and repeated personalized guidance, resulting in an intelligent, interactive, and accessible digital self-care solution for pain management. Keywords: AcuPath, Android Application, Body Pain Relief, Exercise Recommendation, Firebase [NAME], Generative AI, Agentic AI, NLP, AI Assistant, WebView..

INTRODUCTION Insider Musculoskeletal (MSK) pain especially low back, neck, shoulder, and knee pain is one of the most common reasons people lose productivity, avoid physical activity, and seek healthcare support[1].The problem is not that exercises don’t work; the problem is that most people don’t know which exercise is safe for their pain type, don’t follow routines consistently, and don’t get proper explanations or feedback when pain changes day-to- day[3]. Digital self-management tools (mobile apps) are now widely used for rehabilitation guidance and pain management, but many apps still suffer from generic recommendations, weak personalization, limited conversational support, and poor adherence [7]. Evidence shows mobile/telerehab approaches can be safe and useful, but results vary and need better personalization and engagement strategies. AcuPath is proposed as an Android app (Java/XML) with Firebase [NAME], designed to: i. 
capture pain location + symptom context, ii. 
run a dynamic question flow (Agentic AI) to narrow down the safest pathway, iii. 
generate clear exercise guidance + precautions (Generative AI), iv. 
answer user queries via NLP-based AI assistant, and v. 
provide a video guidance module through WebView-based content embedding. The aim is not to “diagnose diseases.” The aim is to deliver structured, safe, personalized self-care exercises and education for common non-emergency pain patterns, while clearly flagging red-flag symptoms that require professional evaluation.

MOTIVATION In today’s fast-paced digital lifestyle, a large portion of the population suffers from daily body pain such as neck pain, back pain, shoulder pain, knee pain, and headaches. These problems are mainly caused by poor posture, long sitting hours, excessive mobile and laptop usage, gym strain, lack of physical activity, and unhealthy lifestyle habits. Most people do not seek immediate professional help for such pain due to high cost, lack of time, long waiting periods, and limited access to physiotherapists or healthcare experts, especially in rural and semi-urban areas. Instead, users depend on random YouTube videos, social media reels, or Google searches, which usually provide generic exercises and advice that are not personalized to the user’s actual pain condition. This often leads to incorrect practice, delayed recovery, or even worsening of pain. Traditional acupressure and physiotherapy methods are effective and drug-free, but

Instead, users depend on random YouTube videos, social media reels, or Google searches, which usually provide generic exercises and advice that are not personalized to the user’s actual pain condition. This often leads to incorrect practice, delayed recovery, or even worsening of pain. Traditional acupressure and physiotherapy methods are effective and drug-free, but they require expert knowledge to identify the correct acupoints, sequence, pressure duration, and frequency. Without proper guidance, users are unable to apply these techniques correctly on their own. With recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence, it has become possible to analyze user symptoms, pain intensity, health conditions, and lifestyle patterns to provide personalized and intelligent recommendations. AI enables systems to move beyond one-size-fits-all solutions and deliver customized pain-relief guidance that adapts to each individual user.

PROPOSED SYSTEM The proposed system aims to develop an AI-powered personalized acupoint recommendation platform for pain relief and overall human health management. The system will analyze user-specific data such as pain type, pain location, intensity, duration, health conditions, and lifestyle habits to generate a customized acupoint sequence (AcuPath) for effective and safe pain management. The architecture will follow a client–server model, where the client interface collects user inputs through a web or mobile application, and the server processes this information using AI and machine learning algorithms. A structured acupoint knowledge base will be maintained to map pain conditions with appropriate acupoints and therapeutic sequences. To enhance accuracy and user safety, the system will move from generic exercise-based recommendations to personalized AI-driven guidance, minimizing the risk of incorrect or unsuitable therapy. Interactive guidance will be provided through visual body maps, step- by-step instructions, and time-based recommendations, enabling users to correctly apply acupressure techniques. Additionally, real-time interaction and feedback mechanisms will be integrated, allowing users to report pain improvement and clarify doubts during therapy sessions. This feedback will be utilized to continuously refine the recommendation model. Performance optimization will be considered to support multiple concurrent users while maintaining fast response times.

Introduction With the application of advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS), their focus now includes optimizing safety, traffic control, and ensuring the comfort of the users. As part of this technology shift, ADAS Level 3 is where vehicles will be able to automate most of the driving tasks with some human assistance around the full driving context. Connected vehicles are becoming more common, and thus real time data generated from onboard sensors is also rapidly rising. [7] It is projected that by 2025, more than 30% of vehicles will have Level 3 equipped, which will play an important role in reducing vehicle accidents and traffic jams. Such systems require real-time spatial awareness, reasoning, and control bound to constant incoming data. This project deals with the enhancements of ADAS Level 3 functions like automatic cruise control, lane keeping assist, automatic emergency breaking, and sign recognition. [2] The goal is to formulate efficient methods to deal with dynamic driving scenarios in regions like India, which are notoriously known for their varying complex road conditions with the help of deep learning, sensor fusion and edge computing. [8] Level 3 automation has a real-world use case which deals with unpredictable traffic patterns, erratic road signage, and dynamic latency-sensitive decision making. This project primarily aims to examine these issues and design a system architecture that is safe, adaptable, compliant with regulations, and learns from real world vehicle data. [4] While most research to date has focused on structured environments and labeled datasets, real-world deployment demands models that can learn incrementally, detect anomalies, and make context-aware decisions on-the-fly. Therefore, our objective is to implement a scalable, resource-efficient, and low-latency ADAS Level 3 framework capable of functioning under diverse road conditions. Surveys and experimental results have highlighted the need to evolve from static perception models to dynamic, continuously
learning systems. [1] Through continuous learning algorithms, real-time analytics, and the integration of hardware and software, this work advances the theoretical models for ADAS systems toward their practical and scalable incorporation into contemporary vehicles.

has grown significantly. Despite advancements in driver assistance technologies, current road safety systems—especially in regions with unstructured traffic like India—still rely heavily on human decision-making. This dependency results in delayed reactions, reduced efficiency, and a higher likelihood of accidents due to driver distraction or fatigue. ADAS Level 3 systems offer conditional automation, where the vehicle takes over control under specific conditions. However, implementing such systems poses several challenges: real-time perception from noisy environments, dynamic decision-making in mixed traffic, low-latency actuation, and seamless transition of control between the driver and the system. Moreover, existing ADAS deployments often fail to scale effectively on low-cost embedded hardware due to computational complexity, making them inaccessible to mass-market vehicles. Traditional camera-based systems (ADAS Level 2) are limited by their inability to perform full-scene analysis, sensor fusion, or proactive intervention. map that can be used to accelerate the implementation of ADAS

Introduction In today’s digital banking environment, online transactions and mobile banking services are widely used, but they also increase the risk of cyber threats such as phishing links, fraudulent OTP messages, and malicious images that target users’ personal and financial information. This project introduces [NAME], a Banking Threat Detection System designed to protect users from digital banking frauds. The system integrates URL analysis, NLP-based message classification, and image risk assessment, and presents results through a simple risk-based interface using Red (harmful), Blue (suspicious), and Green (safe) indicators in a lightweight mobile and web application. [NAME] focuses on early threat detection to help users make safer decisions before interacting with suspicious content. The system continuously analyzes incoming data and provides instant feedback in an easy-to-understand format. By combining multiple detection techniques, it improves accuracy and reduces the chances of financial loss. Overall, the project aims to enhance trust and safety in digital banking platforms. Motivation The motivation for developing [NAME] comes from the rising number of banking frauds affecting users on both mobile and web platforms. As digital banking grows, users are increasingly exposed to threats like phishing links, fake OTP messages, and malicious images that can lead to serious financial losses. Many existing security solutions focus on only a single type of threat, such as spam messages or phishing URLs, which leaves other attack paths unprotected. In addition, non-technical users often struggle to identify fraudulent content on their own, making them easy targets for cybercriminals. This lack of awareness increases the risk of accidental clicks and data leakage. This project aims to bridge these gaps by offering a simple, all-in-one security solution that detects suspicious links, fraudulent OTP messages, and harmful images in real time. By providing clear alerts and easy-to-understand feedback, [NAME] helps users stay informed, improves cybersecurity awareness, and reduces financial losses caused by digital banking frauds.

Problem Statement Digital banking security has become a serious concern as more users depend on mobile and web platforms for everyday financial transactions. Despite this growth, many existing security systems still have noticeable limitations, such as: No single solution that can jointly detect malicious links, fake OTP messages, and misleading images.
Delayed or unclear risk alerts that are difficult for non-technical users to understand.
Limited ability to keep up with constantly evolving digital banking fraud techniques. To overcome these issues, this project introduces [NAME], a lightweight and user-friendly threat detection system that examines links, messages, and images and delivers clear, real-time risk indicators to help users stay safe. [NAME] successfully achieves this objective by integrating URL analysis, NLP-based message classification, and image threat assessment into a single platform. The system presents clear, color-coded risk indicators that enhance user understanding and enable quick responses to potential threats. By providing real-time alerts and intuitive guidance, it empowers users to make safer online decisions. ABSTRACT The fast development of quantum computing is expected to challenge the security of many traditional cryptographic systems, especially in areas that deal with highly sensitive information such as healthcare. The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) plays a crucial role in modern healthcare by allowing continuous monitoring of patients through connected devices. These devices generate large amounts of real-time data, which must be securely transmitted and stored to protect patient privacy.In this paper, we present a secure web-based IoMT system that incorporates Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) techniques to enhance data protection. The system uses CRYSTALS-Kyber for secure key exchange and CRYSTALS-Dilithium for digital signatures, while AES-256 is applied for efficient data encryption. It is developed using modern web technologies, with React and TypeScript for the frontend and Supabase for backend services.The proposed architecture supports real-time data monitoring, secure file management, and data integrity verification. This makes the system suitable for future healthcare applications where security requirements are expected to be even more demanding. INTRODUCTION Preamble This chapter provides the foundational context for the project, highlighting the need for proactive insider threat detection in modern organizations. It introduces core challenges, project objectives, and the motivations driving the development of an advanced, explainable monitoring system that bridges practical security and technological innovation.

1.1 
Introduction Insider threats—malicious or careless behavior by trusted individuals—continue to be among the most destructive and most difficult-to-detect threats facing today's enterprises. In contrast to malicious outsiders who need to penetrate a perimeter, insiders 2 take advantage of approved avenues, integrate perfectly with normal organizational processes, and can adapt their techniques according to prevailing security measures. This presents an intricate security problem where the attacker is already inside the trusted environment, making many common defenses moot. The urgent need is not just for better algorithms, but for unified, deployable systems that can ingest massive real time data streams and deliver actionable, trusted insights. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a novel engineering and analytical framework that moves beyond fragmented algorithms to deliver a complete, production-ready solution. Our primary contribution lies in the synergistic integration of hybrid detection, dynamic contextualization, multi-layered explainability (XAI), and enterprise governance controls (privacy and real-time performance) into a single, cohesive Insider Threat Detection System.

1.2 
Problem Statement Existing and modern methods for insider threat detection are usually unsuccessful because they possess four habitual shortcomings that confine their functional efficiency: a. Inflexibility to CBIR-Based Rules. Signature-based systems and fixed ahead-of- time predetermined rules are inherently reactive. They cannot generalize and A Behavior-Driven Approach to Insider Threat Detection in Organizational Systems 2 
GHRCEM, Department of CSE (Cyber Security), 2025-26 discover new, unknown, or complex malicious activity that doesn't conform to predetermined pat terns. b. Inadequate Contextualization. Behavior is often reviewed in a vacuum, without con sideration for the effect that the obligations of the user, peer group networking, or the underlying organizational paradigm may have. This inadequate contextualization accounts for much incorrect risk assessment and generates an intolerably high level of false positives, thereby inundating security analysts. c. 
Limited Real-Time Capability. Most solutions are dependent on batch processing of logs, thus introducing a notable delay between a malicious activity and its detection. The delay gives insiders a grace period during which they are able to fulfill their objectives and inflict a great amount of damage before a response is initiated. d. Offered Limited Explainability. Among the crucial obstacles for real-world practical use of most machine learning systems is that they are "black boxes." Without a simple, comprehensible explanation available for human users when an alert is produced, that diminishes analysts' confidence, slows investigation triage effectiveness, and complicates auditing the system. 1.3

Conclusion The Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System represents a significant advancement in the field of organizational cybersecurity and security operations. By seamlessly integrating hybrid machine learning models with explainable AI technologies, it offers continuous behavioral monitoring and flexible threat detection methods, empowering security analysts to take proactive steps in safeguarding organizational assets. This innovative system bridges the gap between complex machine learning capabilities and practical security operations, allowing for early insider threat detection, ultimately reducing data breach incidents and financial losses. The real-time insights, analyst-friendly dashboard interface, and transparent explainability features provided by the system have the potential to revolutionize intelligent, data-driven security operations. The hybrid detection approach combining Isolation Forest for statistical analysis, Autoencoder for behavioral patterns, and Graph Analytics for contextual relationships achieves superior accuracy while maintaining low false positive rates. The system's sub-100ms latency and throughput exceeding 1,000 events per minute demonstrate its capability for enterprise-scale deployments. In conclusion, the Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System is not just a solution but a stepping stone towards the future of intelligent security operations and early threat intervention. Introduction Cyber-attacks are becoming more frequent, complex, and difficult to trace. Organizations face
constant threats such as unauthorized access, malware injections, and brute-force attacks, making
effective attack monitoring and forensic analysis critical. Although security systems generate large
volumes of attack logs, traditional logging mechanisms are centralized and vulnerable to tampering,
allowing attackers to erase or modify evidence. 
 Moreover, with the emergence of quantum computing, existing cryptographic techniques used to
protect logs may become insecure in the future. To address these challenges, this project proposes a
Quantum-Safe Blockchain-Based Honeypot Logging System that combines real-time attack capture
using honeypots, tamper-proof log verification using blockchain, and future-ready security through
quantum-resistant cryptographic hashing. This integrated approach ensures secure, transparent, and
reliable cyber-attack logging for next-generation cybersecurity systems. Motivation Cyber-attacks are increasing rapidly, making accurate and reliable attack logging essential for security
analysis and forensics.
Traditional centralized logging systems are vulnerable to tampering, deletion, and manipulation by
attackers.
Honeypot systems can capture real attacker behavior, but lack secure and tamper-proof storage for the
collected logs.
Blockchain technology provides immutability and transparency, making it ideal for securing security
logs.
Existing blockchain and logging systems rely on classical cryptography, which may become insecure
in the era of quantum computing.
There is a need for a future-ready security solution that combines attack capture, tamper-proof
logging, and quantum-safe cryptography.

Problem Statement Traditional logging systems store data in centralized environments, which allows attackers to modify
or delete logs after gaining access, thereby hiding their activities. While honeypot systems are effective
in capturing attacker behavior, they do not guarantee tamper-proof storage of collected logs. Moreover,
most existing secure logging mechanisms rely on classical cryptographic algorithms that may become
vulnerable with the advent of quantum computing. Therefore, there is a strong need for a secure, future-
ready system that integrates honeypot-based attack capture with blockchain-based immutable logging
and quantum-safe cryptography.

ABSTRACT The rising complexity and frequency of cybercrimes highlight a critical challenge: most victims lack the technical knowledge and legal awareness required to collect admissible digital evidence and prepare clear, structured reports. As a result, incidents are underreported, crucial data is mishandled, and investigations experience unnecessary delays. To address these limitations, we introduce JusticeAssist — an intelligent, jurisdiction-aware platform designed to guide users through incident identification, evidence preservation, and complaint formulation. The system processes multiple evidence formats, extracts and organizes content using OCR and parsing techniques, and classifies incidents through LLM-based and fallback machine learning models. It further generates legally compliant complaint documents tailored for submission to cybercrime authorities. JusticeAssist prioritizes data security through JWT authentication, hashed credentials, and optional encryption for sensitive information, while asynchronous processing with Redis queues ensures responsive and scalable operation. Testing on both simulated and real-world inputs demonstrates that JusticeAssist enhances report completeness, reduces documentation errors, and accelerates evidence analysis; however, OCR and AI performance remain influenced by input quality and external API constraints. By integrating usability, forensic intelligence, and legal accuracy, JusticeAssist empowers victims to submit actionable cybercrime complaints and supports more efficient, reliable investigations. ABSTRACT Insider threats remain a critical challenge in organizational cybersecurity, given the trusted access insiders possess and the subtle nature of their malicious or negligent actions. This paper presents “A Behaviour-Driven Approach to Insider Threat Detection in Organizational Systems”, which leverages behavioural analytics to identify anomalies in user activity that may indicate potential insider threats. The proposed system establishes dynamic behavioural baselines for individual users by monitoring patterns such as access frequency, file usage, login times, and resource interactions. Any significant deviation from these baselines is flagged through a risk-scoring mechanism that aids security teams in assessing and responding to threats in real time. Unlike traditional rule-based systems, this behaviour-driven model adapts continuously to evolving user behaviour, thereby reducing false positives and enhancing detection reliability. The study includes a detailed evaluation of real-world insider threat incidents, with a focus on Indian organizations, and compares the effectiveness of current detection techniques across key metrics such as accuracy, false positive rate, and operational success. The integration of machine learning techniques further strengthens the system’s predictive capabilities and supports automated threat mitigation strategies. By aligning behavioural intelligence with adaptive detection mechanisms, this approach provides a scalable and proactive solution to safeguard organizational systems against insider threats.

INTRODUCTION The Crack formation in critical infrastructure has emerged as a major engineering concern due to aging materials, prolonged operational loads, corrosion, and harsh environmental conditions. Among various infrastructure elements, pipelines play a vital role in the transportation of water, oil, gas, and industrial fluids, making their structural integrity extremely important. Cracks in pipelines often initiate as micro-defects and gradually propagate under internal pressure and environmental stress, leading to leakage, contamination, economic loss, and in severe cases, catastrophic failure. In addition to pipelines, similar crack-related issues are also observed in roads, bridges, tunnels, and concrete structures, further emphasizing the need for reliable inspection systems. Traditional pipeline crack inspection methods largely depend on manual surveys, shutdown-based inspection, or contact-based sensing techniques, which are expensive, time-consuming, and sometimes unsafe. Pipelines located underground, underwater, or in hazardous industrial environments pose significant challenges for human inspectors. Moreover, manual inspection may fail to identify fine surface cracks or early-stage defects, and inspection outcomes often vary based on operator experience and visibility conditions. While automated inspection techniques such as ultrasonic and acoustic methods have been used, they require specialized equipment and are not always suitable for continuous monitoring. In recent years, image-based crack detection using computer vision and deep learning has gained attention as a non-contact and cost-effective alternative. However, many existing approaches rely on high-resolution images captured under controlled lighting and static conditions, limiting their effectiveness in real-world pipeline environments. Factors such as motion blur, uneven illumination, surface rust, and noise significantly reduce detection accuracy in practical scenarios. The proposed project addresses these limitations by developing an image-based pipeline crack detection system deployed on a mobile robotic platform. A low-cost camera is used to capture real-time images of pipeline surfaces during inspection. Deep learning models are employed to automatically detect, localize, and segment crack regions from captured images. The system is designed to operate under realistic field conditions and does not require manual image acquisition or shutdown of pipeline operations.

LITERATURE SURVEY SCOPE The scope of Internal Pipeline Crack Detection Using Artificial Intelligence and Robot project is to design and develop a system that can detect internal cracks in pipelines using a mobile robotic platform. The system focuses on identifying cracks at an early stage so that damage can be prevented before it becomes severe. The project covers the use of a camera-mounted robot to capture images from inside the pipeline without stopping pipeline operation. These images are analyzed to detect the presence and location of cracks, reducing the need for manual inspection in unsafe or confined environments. The system is intended to work under real conditions where lighting may be uneven and pipeline surfaces may be corroded or noisy. It aims to provide clear visual output showing crack locations along with basic crack measurements such as length and width. The scope of the project is limited to surface crack detection using image data and does not include depth measurement or material strength analysis. The proposed approach is suitable for small to medium pipelines and can be further extended to other infrastructure structures like tunnels, bridges, and concrete surfaces in the future. MOTIVATION Pipelines are a critical component of industrial and public infrastructure, yet their internal condition is difficult to inspect using conventional methods. Over time, internal cracks develop due to corrosion, pressure variations, and material fatigue, which may lead to leakage, system failure, or safety hazards if not detected early. Existing inspection techniques often require manual intervention, pipeline shutdowns, or expensive equipment, making the process inefficient and risky. These challenges highlight the need for an automated and reliable inspection mechanism. The motivation of this final-year project is to design a practical solution that combines robotics and intelligent image-based analysis to improve pipeline inspection. By enabling real-time internal crack detection using a mobile robotic platform, the system reduces human risk and enhances inspection accuracy. This project aims to apply theoretical knowledge of computer vision and machine learning to a real-world engineering problem, providing a cost-effective and scalable approach suitable for modern infrastructure monitoring.

PROPOSED SYSTEM The project introduces an automated approach for detecting internal cracks in pipelines using a mobile robotic platform and image-based analysis. The system is designed to inspect pipeline interiors without requiring shutdown or manual intervention, making the inspection process safer and more efficient. A compact robot equipped with an ESP32-CAM module moves inside the pipeline and continuously captures images of the internal surface under real operating conditions. The captured images are transmitted wirelessly to a processing unit, where image preprocessing techniques such as resizing, noise reduction, and contrast enhancement are applied to improve crack visibility. Deep learning–based models are then used to analyze the images. An object detection model identifies and localizes crack regions, while a segmentation model performs pixel-level extraction to accurately outline crack patterns. Further image analysis is carried out to estimate crack length and width, providing quantitative information for condition assessment. The system generates annotated visual outputs that assist in monitoring pipeline health and support timely maintenance decisions, offering a practical and scalable solution for infrastructure inspection.

IMPLEMENTATION The implementation of the internal pipeline crack detection system was carried out in a structured manner to ensure reliable performance and ease of integration. The development process was divided into multiple stages, focusing on hardware setup, image acquisition, model integration, and result visualization. System Setup and Hardware Integration Initially, the mobile robotic platform was assembled using an RC car–based chassis. An ESP32-CAM module was mounted on the robot to capture images of the internal pipeline surface. The ESP32-CAM was configured for wireless image transmission, enabling real-time data transfer without physical connections. Basic movement control of the robot was tested to ensure stable navigation inside confined spaces. Image Acquisition and Preprocessing During inspection, the ESP32-CAM continuously captures images of the pipeline interior. These images are transmitted to the processing unit, where preprocessing operations are applied. Image resizing, noise reduction, and contrast enhancement are performed to improve crack visibility and reduce the effects of low lighting, corrosion, and motion blur caused by movement. Crack Detection and Segmentation After preprocessing, the images are passed through deep learning models for crack analysis. An object detection model is used to identify and localize crack regions by generating bounding boxes. The detected regions are then processed using a segmentation model to extract cracks at the pixel level. This two-stage approach improves detection accuracy and ensures that even fine and thin cracks are properly identified. Crack Measurement and Analysis The segmented crack regions are further analyzed using image processing techniques to estimate crack length and width. These measurements provide quantitative information about crack severity, which is essential for maintenance planning and structural assessment. Output Visualization and Testing The final output is displayed as annotated images showing detected cracks, bounding boxes, segmentation masks, and crack dimensions. Initial testing was performed using sample datasets and captured images to verify detection accuracy and system stability. The implementation phase successfully demonstrates the feasibility of combining robotics and artificial intelligence for automated internal pipeline inspection.

CONCLUSION This project demonstrates a practical approach to automated crack detection and measurement using deep learning and a mobile robotic platform. By combining image preprocessing with parallel detection and segmentation models, the system accurately identifies cracks under real-world conditions. The proposed solution offers a reliable and cost-effective alternative to manual inspection, supporting efficient infrastructure monitoring and maintenance.

text: Introduction In today’s digital age, government services are increasingly being moved online to improve accessibility and transparency. While this transformation is a step in the right direction, many citizens still struggle to navigate these online platforms. Applying for basic documents like income certificates, caste certificates, or domicile proofs often becomes a tedious and confusing experience. People are required to search through multiple websites, understand complex application processes, identify relevant documents, and follow region-specific procedures—all without any centralized guidance. This situation leads to delays, errors, multiple visits to government offices, and a poor user experience, especially for first-time applicants and those from rural or semi-urban areas. The need of the hour is a digital assistant that not only provides accurate information but also guides users through the process in a clear, step-by-step manner. To address this gap, we propose GovGuideBot—an AI-powered chatbot designed to simplify the government document application process. This system will use Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) to understand user queries and provide region-specific procedures, document checklists, official website links, and relevant YouTube tutorials. The chatbot will allow users to move through the process step by step, ask questions at any point, and receive contextual help. Additionally, the system will be scalable and may include IoT-based integrations such as real-time office queue monitoring and document delivery tracking. The overall aim is to make public service navigation as easy as chatting with a friend—intuitive, interactive, and informative. This project not only addresses a real-world problem faced by millions but also aligns with the broader goals of Digital India by promoting inclusive, transparent, and citizen-friendly governance.

text: Literature Review The literature review focuses on existing chatbot technologies, AI-powered public service tools, and how governments are currently delivering digital services. Several platforms offer automated customer support and basic FAQ bots, but most lack the ability to provide personalized, step-by-step guidance for government-related tasks. Studies have shown that Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) can significantly enhance user experience when applied to conversational interfaces. However, when it comes to government documentation assistance, there is still a gap in creating region-specific, easy-to-follow systems. This project aims to bridge that gap by learning from existing tools and improving upon their limitations. Table 1: Literature Survey

text: Problem Statement Government documentation plays a critical role in every citizen’s life—whether it’s for availing social benefits, proving identity or residence, or applying for education and jobs. However, the process of applying for essential government documents like income certificates, caste certificates, domicile proofs, and more is often anything but smooth. Citizens, especially those unfamiliar with digital systems, face multiple hurdles in the form of unclear instructions, fragmented websites, region-specific processes, and a lack of personalized assistance. The situation becomes even more challenging when people are unaware of which documents are required, what steps they need to follow, or where to apply. Currently, individuals either rely on friends or relatives for guidance, visit cyber cafes, or search through unreliable sources like outdated blogs or random YouTube videos. Even official websites can be difficult to navigate, filled with technical jargon or missing the localized steps needed for specific districts or states. As a result, citizens often make errors during application, miss required documents, or have to visit government offices multiple times—leading to frustration and a loss of time and productivity. This project aims to solve these issues by developing GovGuideBot, an intelligent AI-powered chatbot that acts as a virtual assistant for citizens applying for government documents. The chatbot will allow users to ask their questions in simple natural language, understand what they need using machine learning and NLP, and then walk them through the entire process—step-by-step—based on their location and the specific certificate required. The chatbot will also provide direct links to official websites, required document checklists, and recommend relevant YouTube tutorials for better understanding. Optional IoT integration will allow features such as real-time queue monitoring at government offices or document delivery tracking—making the experience even more seamless.

text: Methodology The development of GovGuideBot will follow a modular and structured methodology that blends conversational AI, machine learning, and (optionally) IoT technologies to provide a smooth and intelligent user experience [1]. The system will be designed in such a way that it can understand what a user wants, provide accurate, region-specific information in simple language, and guide them step-by-step through the government documentation process. 4.1 System Overview The entire project will be built around three main layers: User Interaction Layer (Frontend) Processing Layer (Backend + AI/ML Models) Data & Integration Layer (Databases, APIs, IoT Devices) 4.2 Step-by-Step Working Process User Input: The user interacts with the chatbot via a simple and intuitive chat interface. They can type queries like: "How do I apply for an income certificate in Pune?" or "What documents are needed for a domicile certificate in Maharashtra?" Intent Recognition Using NLP and Machine Learning: The chatbot uses Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning models to understand the user’s intent. For example, it identifies that the user is interested in “applying for an income certificate” and that the location is “Pune, Maharashtra.” Location-Based Flow Fetching: Once the intent and location are known, the system fetches the exact step-by-step application procedure for that region [2]. This data will be pre-fed into a database collected from official government sources. Step-by-Step Chat Flow: Instead of dumping all the information at once, the chatbot will guide the user one step at a time [5]. The user can type “Next” to move ahead or ask follow-up questions like “Where can I upload the documents?” or “Do I need an Aadhaar card?” The system will handle these queries using its FAQ logic. YouTube Video Recommendation (ML-Based): To make the experience even more helpful, the chatbot will suggest YouTube videos related to the document process. A content similarity model will be used to recommend the most relevant videos based on the user’s query and location. Smart FAQs & Dynamic Question Answering:

Abstract As part of our security training program, the VR Cybercrime Scene Investigation Lab will be an innovative educational project that aims to make the journey from theory to practice easier and more seamless. The so-called “traditional” approach to teaching digital forensics will involve giving lectures and carrying out case studies. However, in reality, these methods will not provide much investigation practice. The Cybercop Project will aim to address that deficiency. We will build an integrated virtual reality environment where students will act as investigators, facing off against a new class of high-tech criminals: cybercrime. Our project will utilize virtual reality to create an immersive environment that will enable students to acquire the necessary forensic training. In the simulation, users will explore crime scenes such as the office of a hacker workspace or a previously breached office to collect and analyse digital evidence (such as a USB device), phishing emails, suspicious server logs, and more, all while performing forensic work with live-mode forensic kit maintenance and feedback. The

methodology of the project will include VR environment design, interactive asset content management, content creation, and scenario-based learning to provide a cost-efficient, scalable, and engaging training tool. Keywords: Virtual Reality, Cybercrime Investigation, Digital Forensics, Cybersecurity Education, Immersive Training

Introduction EcoGrid is a hyper-local marketplace that fosters a sustainable circular economy by allowing neighbors to borrow, rent, or trade household items like tools and electronics. By extending product lifecycles and reducing waste, the platform encourages resource efficiency within local communities. The system leverages GPS and Google Maps integration to seamlessly connect users within a specific radius, such as 5km, ensuring logistical ease. To maintain safety and reliability, it incorporates a specialized "Trust Score" algorithm that verifies the reputation of participants in every peer-to-peer transaction..E Motivation Modern consumer culture encourages buying new items for temporary needs (e.g., a drill used once a year), leading to massive environmental waste.
There is a growing global movement towards Sustainability and ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) goals.
Existing marketplaces like eBay or Craigslist are designed for shipping and selling, not for local, temporary sharing or borrowing.
Building strong, resilient local communities requires tools that foster interaction and mutual aid.

Problem Statement Despite a willingness to share, communities waste money and resources buying new household items because functional, idle assets remain hidden due to local discovery gaps and difficult handover logistics. Furthermore, without built-in trust verification or clear gamified incentives to motivate users, people hesitate to lend to strangers, leaving valuable resources significantly underutilized.
