Dynamic Frontend Rendering The choice of EJS (Embedded JavaScript Templates) for front-end rendering over client-side frameworks such as React or Vue.js is deliberate and grounded in the user demographics of EcoGrid’s target deployment. Urban Indian communities in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities exhibit median mobile data speeds of 8–15Mbps on 4G networks, with significant variability during peak commute hours. A React single-page application carries a minimum JavaScript bundle of approximately 130– 150KB (gzipped) before any application-specific code; on a 4G connection encountering packet loss, this translates to a perceptible blank-screen interval before first content paint. EJS partials are rendered on the server before transmission. The HTTP response carries complete, pre-populated HTML that browsers can begin painting immediately upon receipt of the first TCP segment. There is no hydration step, no clientside router initialization, and no initial API fetch waterfall. For authenticated feeds—where the visible listing set is determined by the user’s geolocation and trust tier—server-side rendering also avoids the pattern where client code must make two serial requests (first for the page shell, then for user-specific data), a common React architecture that doubles perceived load time on high-latency connections. EJS partials are organized into a component-like directory structure (views/partials/) covering the navigation bar, listing card, trust badge, and modal containers. The template engine renders at approximately 8,000 partials per second under single-core load, a throughput that is not the bottleneck at expected concurrent user levels. The tropical-tech visual theme—combining dark green, amber, and cream color variables—is implemented entirely in CSS custom properties, ensuring zero JavaScript dependency for visual styling. E. Hyper-Local Geofencing Logic The geofencing subsystem is the architectural feature that most directly implements EcoGrid’s environmental thesis. When a user registers, their home coordinates are stored in the Geolocations table. Every subsequent listing retrieval request passes through the geofenceMiddleware function, which appends the user’s coordinates and the configured radius threshold to the request context before the route handler executes. The route handler passes these parameters to the proximity query module, which applies a bounding-box prefilter followed by precise Haversine refinement. The bounding box is computed from the user’s latitude and longitude by adding and subtracting a latitude degree offset equal to radius_km / 111.32 and a longitude degree offset equal to radius_km / (111.32 * cos(lat_rad)). This rectangular pre-filter leverages the SPATIAL index on the Geolocations table and reduces the candidate row set before the more expensive per-row trigonometric calculation. Only rows surviving the boundingbox filter are passed through the Haversine function, which computes exact great-circle distance and excludes candidates outside the true radial boundary. The geofence radius defaults to 5km but is stored as a community-level configuration parameter in the Communities table, allowing administrators to tighten it to 1km for dense urban neighborhoods or relax it to 10km for peri-urban zones where population density is lower. This configurability also enables pilot deployments where adjacent communities can be given overlapping radii during onboarding phases to accelerate the initial supply-demand bootstrap. F. Security and Authentication Flow User passwords are hashed using bcrypt with a work factor of 12 before storage. Bcrypt’s adaptive cost function means that as compute hardware improves, the work factor can be increased without changing the algorithm or the stored hash format, preserving forward resistance against offline bruteforce attacks on the Users table. Session tokens are generated using crypto.randomBytes(32) and stored server-side in the session table, with only a session ID transmitted to the client. The session ID cookie is set with the HttpOnly flag (preventing JavaScript access), the Secure flag (transmitting only over TLS), and SameSite=Lax (mitigating cross-site request forgery from third-party navigations). This session architecture was preferred over stateless JWT for EcoGrid because it allows immediate token invalidation on logout or account suspension—a property that stateless JWT cannot provide without a server-side token blacklist.

I. Selective Structure, Processing and Evaluation The evaluation methodology employs a simulated coordinate testing phase to validate the geofencing logic independent of real-world address data. A grid of synthetic user coordinates is generated at 100-meter intervals across a 12km × 12km bounding box centered on a reference point in Pune, Maharashtra (latitude 18.5204◦N, longitude 73.8567◦E). For each synthetic user, a set of listing coordinates is generated at known distances from 0.5km to 10km in 0.5km increments, providing 20 distance classes per user and enabling granular assessment of boundary behavior around the 5km threshold. The test harness instruments the geofence middleware to record, for each query, the pre-filter candidate count, the postHaversine inclusion count, and the delta against the groundtruth label set. Boundary cases—listings whose true distance falls within 50m of the 5km threshold—are analyzed separately, as floating-point precision in DECIMAL(10,8) coordinate storage introduces sub-meter rounding that can produce a 0.001% boundary misclassification rate. This is acknowledged as an acceptable tolerance for a marketplace application, where the practical consequence of a boundary misclassification is the inclusion or exclusion of a listing at 4.999km versus 5.001km from the user, a difference imperceptible in any real exchange scenario.

V.CONCLUSION EcoGrid demonstrates that a hyper-local circular economy marketplace is architecturally feasible, environmentally motivated, and technically competitive on the metrics that matter for its deployment context. The strict geographic enforcement mechanism—implemented via Haversine-based radial exclusion with SPATIAL-indexed bounding-box pre-filtering— achieves 97.3% matchmaking accuracy while adding less than 3ms of computation overhead per request. This overhead is absorbed within the overall API latency budget and does not degrade user-perceived response times relative to a nongeofenced baseline. The decision to use EJS server-side rendering rather than a client-side single-page application framework is validated by the render times—consistently below 15ms—and by the architectural simplicity it affords. Eliminating the front-end build pipeline, hydration step, and client-side router reduces the attack surface, lowers operational complexity for communitymanaged deployments, and produces pages accessible on midtier devices without JavaScript-heavy bundle parsing. For the Tier-2 Indian urban context EcoGrid targets, these are not incidental advantages; they are prerequisites for meaningful adoption.

From an environmental standpoint, the platform’s core contribution is the elimination of inter-district logistics from the re-commerce supply chain. By structurally preventing listings from being visible beyond the configured community radius, EcoGrid removes the mechanism through which platformmediated exchange generates parcel delivery emissions. If applied at scale across a mid-sized Indian city of 500,000 households, and assuming that 5% of annual household goods purchases are re-commerce transactions that currently involve intra-city shipping, the substitution of hyper-local exchange could avoid an estimated 1.2 million vehicle-kilometers per year—a figure derived by applying the per-transaction distance estimates from Mehrotra and Lal [1] to the household count.

The EcoBot AI assistant, currently implemented as a stateless relay to an LLM completion endpoint, could be extended with retrieval-augmented generation over the community’s active listing inventory, enabling natural-language product discovery without traditional keyword search. EcoGrid represents a narrow but deliberately scoped contribution: it proves that a trustworthy, performant, and geographically constrained marketplace can be built on a conventional, well-normalized relational stack and server-side rendering, without distributed infrastructure, machine learning recommenders at inference time, or blockchain-based trust anchoring. The simplicity is intentional. A platform whose environmental value depends on consistent operation benefits from an architecture whose failure modes are predictable and recoverable by a small development team.

ABSTRACT Insider threats, particularly those exploiting legitimate credentials, are a leading cause of organizational security breaches worldwide. Early detection and continuous monitoring of user behavior play a pivotal role in reducing the associated risks. In response to this challenge, we introduce a Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System, an innovative Machine Learning project that seamlessly integrates with Explainable AI to provide a comprehensive solution for organizational security management. The system continuously monitors user activities by utilizing endpoint and application event sensors. Real-time data are processed to notify security analysts of behavioral anomalies, distinguishing between normal user patterns and suspicious activities that may indicate insider threats. The system's real strength emerges in its hybrid detection capabilities, driven by AI. It leverages statistical analysis through Isolation Forest, behavioral modelling via Autoencoders, and graph-based relationship analysis to predict insider threats. What sets this system apart is its versatility, as it allows analysts to detect threats using statistical anomalies, behavioral deviations, or a combination of both, harnessing the power of Isolation Forest for statistical analysis, Autoencoders for behavioral patterns, and Graph Analytics for contextual relationships. The system achieves 89% accuracy with an 8% false positive rate, processing over 1,000 events per minute with sub-100ms latency. To make security management accessible and user-friendly, the system offers a dedicated real-time dashboard application built with Next.js. This application enables analysts to monitor risk scores and behavioral patterns continually, granting them the ability to gauge organizational security posture. Should analysts suspect an anomaly, the system's Explainable AI features step in to provide transparent insights into threat predictions. If insider threats are detected, the application facilitates seamless investigation and triage with security teams, ensuring timely intervention. 1. INTRODUCTION 1.1 Overview In the modern healthcare ecosystem, timely access to accurate and well-organized patient data is essential for effective diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. Despite the ongoing digital transformation in hospitals, diagnostic centres, and clinics, a significant portion of medical communication especially laboratory reports remains paper-based. These reports are often scanned or manually entered, leading to fragmented health records, data duplication, and delays in interpretation. For healthcare professionals, this creates additional administrative burdens and increases the potential for human error. Patients, on the other hand, struggle to understand complex medical terminology, interpret abnormal values, and maintain their long-term health records. This disconnects between clinical data and patient comprehension often results in poor medication adherence, delayed treatments, and inefficient decision-making. Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Optical Character Recognition (OCR), and Large Language Models (LLMs) have the potential to transform how healthcare data is processed and interpreted. OCR technology can automatically convert scanned or handwritten medical reports into structured, machine- readable text, while LLMs such as Gemini AI or GPT-4 can analyze and simplify this data into patient-friendly summaries. When integrated within a secure cloud-based architecture, these technologies can create a seamless digital healthcare environment that benefits both clinicians and patients. To address these challenges, the proposed system MediSync: AI-Based Medical Report Analytics and [NAME] combine OCR-based report digitization, AI- driven report analysis, cloud-based data storage, and interactive dashboards. Introduction The rapid growth of audio and video-based communication platforms such as online lectures, virtual meetings, call recordings, and voice notes has resulted in the generation of large volumes of unstructured multimedia data [1][2]. These recordings frequently contain critical academic, professional, and personal information, including sensitive content such as passwords, OTPs, banking credentials, and confidential discussions [3]. However, traditional multimedia players and recording systems do not provide efficient mechanisms to search for specific spoken content within long recordings, forcing users to manually browse timelines, which is time-consuming and error-prone [4]. Additionally, the unintentional disclosure of sensitive spoken information in public or shared environments poses serious privacy and cybersecurity risks [5]. Existing speech-to-text systems primarily focus on transcription accuracy but fail to incorporate security-aware mechanisms such as data leakage prevention and controlled access to confidential content [6][7]. The envisioned project proposes SonicSearch, a secure AI-powered audio and video content search system that enables timestamp-level retrieval of spoken information while integrating sensitive keyword detection and user-controlled disclosure mechanisms. By combining speech recognition, natural language processing, and cybersecurity principles, the system aims to provide a scalable, privacy-aware, and efficient solution for secure multimedia information management [2][8][9].

Literature Review The advancement of speech recognition and multimedia analytics has led to the development of several systems for audio transcription, indexing, and retrieval. However, the integration of cybersecurity mechanisms within such systems remains limited. This section reviews existing literature related to speech-to-text processing, bilingual NLP, sensitive data detection, and secure multimedia systems. 2.1 Recent Research and Case Studies [NAME] and Audio Indexing Systems Recent research demonstrates that deep learning-based speech recognition models can accurately convert spoken language into text and support keyword-based search with timestamp alignment [1][2]. While these systems improve usability, they largely ignore security concerns related to sensitive information embedded in spoken content [6]. ii. Bilingual and Hinglish Speech Processing Studies indicate that conversational speech in the Indian context is predominantly bilingual, combining English and Hindi (Hinglish) [7][8]. Existing multilingual NLP models support code-mixed speech transcription; however, most focus on linguistic accuracy rather than secure retrieval or privacy preservation [9]. iii. Sensitive Information Exposure in Audio and Video Content A Several real-world incidents highlight the risks of verbally sharing confidential data during calls and meetings, particularly when recordings are replayed in public environments [3][5]. These cases emphasize the necessity of data leakage prevention mechanisms in speech-based systems. iv. Keyword-Based Security Monitoring Techniques Keyword detection approaches are widely used in cybersecurity for identifying sensitive information in textual logs and communications [4][10]. However, their application to audio and video content remains underexplored, especially in user-facing multimedia retrieval systems. Existing automated techniques are expensive and not suitable for continuous monitoring. Existing inspection methods are costly, time-consuming, and unsafe, often requiring shutdowns and manual intervention. Hence, there is a need for an automated internal crack detection system to enable early fault identification, improve safety, and reduce maintenance costs.

ABSTRACT Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a life-threatening hematological malignancy characterized by the overproduction of immature lymphocytes in the bone marrow. Early and accurate identification of its progression stages—beginner, early, pre-leukemic, and pro-leukemic—is critical for timely intervention and improved prognosis. Traditional diagnostic approaches that rely on manually looking at microscopic blood smear images take a long time and can vary from person to person.. In this project, we propose a deep learning-based framework for automated white blood cell (WBC) classification and confidence estimation to identify the stages of ALL from microscopic images. The methodology involves preprocessing a publicly available dataset of labeled microscopic WBC images, followed by the implementation of (CNNs) for feature extraction and stage classification. To ensure reliability in clinical decision-making, our approach incorporates confidence estimation techniques using softmax probability calibration and uncertainty quantification via [NAME] or Bayesian networks. This enables the system not only to classify the stages but also to provide confidence levels for each prediction, aiding in trust and interpretability. Performance metrics will be evaluated to validate the model. This study aims to assist medical professionals with a robust, interpretable, and reliable tool for ALL diagnosis, ultimately contributing to faster and more accurate clinical workflows in hematopathology. The project will be developed using Python and deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow. Future scope includes expanding the model to multi-class cancer detection and real-time clinical deployment. Keywords: Tensorflow, Python, Confidence estimation, softmax probability, Image Classification.

INTRODUCTION Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a cancer that affects lymphoid progenitor cells. It mainly impacts the bone marrow and blood. While it occurs in children 80% of the time, adults generally face a tougher outlook. In the U.S., the rate is 1.6 per 100,000 people and shows a bimodal age distribution—one peak in childhood and another around age 50. ALL results from the clonal growth of immature lymphoid cells. Certain genetic syndromes, including Down syndrome and Fanconi anemia, as well as environmental influences such as radiation, pesticides, and viruses like EBV and HIV, may increase the risk.However, most cases arise without any prior conditions. The current approach has limited effectiveness due to poor confidence in estimates, and this project aims to address that issue. Patients may show signs like fatigue, fever, bleeding, infections, and bone pain. Common indicators of marrow failure include anemia and low platelet counts, along with organ enlargement and central nervous system involvement in 5–8% of patients. Identifying all subtypes early and with precision is essential for choosing the most effective treatment. Misdiagnosis or delays in classification can lead to wrong therapies, higher medical costs, and worsening health. The differences in the appearance of ALL at various stages are often subtle and hard for the human eye to distinguish, especially in the early stages.

Preprocessing: Images are resized, normalized, and converted to a format compatible with the deep learning model. Image augmentation techniques are applied to improve model generalization. Image Segmentation: Segmented datasets (if available) are used to focus the learning on cell regions, removing background noise and enhancing feature extraction. Data Rescaling & Augmentation: All pixel values are rescaled (typically normalized to a 0–1 range) to stabilize and accelerate training. Additionally, data augmentation techniques are used to increase data diversity and reduce the risk of overfitting. Model Architecture (Transfer Learning): A pre-trained CNN model is used with its top layers modified for leukemia classification. The model leverages learned features from ImageNet and adapts them to medical image features. Model Training & Tuning: The model is trained using the optimizer, loss function, and early stopping based on validation loss. Hyperparameter tuning is performed to improve performance. Evaluation & Testing: The trained model is evaluated using Performance metrics on the test set. Confidence metrics post-temperature scaling are also analyzed. Training Support: Training uses Adam optimizer, [NAME], and Data Augmentation to improve model performance and generalization. Confidence Estimation: To enhance the interpretability and reliability of predictions, a post-training calibration method known as temperature scaling is applied. CONCLUSION The project titled “Confidence Estimation Techniques For White Blood Cell Classification in Healthcare” gives a full and creative technique to use white blood cell (WBC) images to automatically classify the phases of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL). By leveraging the power of deep learning, particularly transfer learning with CNN architectures such as ResNet, the system is designed to accurately identify the subtle morphological changes that occur across the four critical stages of ALL — beginning, early, pre, and pro. The model uses advanced training methods such as data augmentation, optimization strategies, and confidence calibration through techniques such as temperature scaling to enhance prediction accuracy. Abstract: Ectrinex is a clever AIoT-powered system that addresses important issues including energy loss, coil misalignment, and overheating in order to maximize wireless EV charging. With the help of an ESP32 microcontroller and a number of sensors, the system continuously checks real-time variables like temperature and voltage. Machine learning is then used to dynamically modify power levels for optimal effectiveness and security. Ectrinex, in contrast to conventional static systems, uses cloud-based IoT for remote monitoring and predictive analytics, guaranteeing proactive defect identification and lower maintenance. Its scalable, modular design makes it a future-ready smart city solution that can be easily integrated with autonomous car systems and renewable energy sources to offer a high-performance, sustainable, and smooth charging experience. Keywords —: AIoT, machine learning, smart infrastructure, wireless charging, electric vehicles, and charging optimization. ----------------------------------------************************----------------------------------

INTRODUCTION In addition to efficient charging systems, the rapid use of electric vehicles (EVs) has raised demand for safe, intelligent, and user-friendly ones. Traditional cable charging methods have several disadvantages, including human handling, safety risks, physical connector deterioration, and a lack of real-time monitoring. Although wireless charging has emerged as a practical answer to these issues, misalignment losses, overheating, low user intelligence, and insufficient monitoring capabilities are still issues with existing wireless charging systems. This project, "Ectrinex: Smart AIoT-Driven Wireless Charging Infrastructure for Electric Vehicles," proposes an intelligent wireless EV charging system that integrates artificial intelligence (AI), the Internet of Things (IoT), RFID-based access control, and real-time monitoring to enhance charging efficiency, safety, and usability. The proposed system employs a systematic process that starts with the arrival of the vehicle and RFID-based authorization. Infrared and ultrasonic sensors are then used to confirm alignment. Once safe battery conditions and proper alignment are confirmed, the charging procedure begins automatically. While charging, the gadget continuously checks electrical and thermal parameters, detects abnormal conditions like overvoltage, overtemperature, or misalignment, and immediately cuts off power if any safety concern is discovered.

LITERATURE REVIEW wireless power transfer (WPT) research has progressed from simple inductive coupling to intricate smart systems. although early models demonstrated that charging without a connection was feasible, they lacked the intelligence to control coil misalignment, which can cause an efficiency drop of more than 25%. remote monitoring is possible with current IOT-enabled stations, but the majority are "static"—they only record data and are unable to respond on their own to safety threats like thermal runaway. additionally, there is a gap in the way ai-driven safety logic and RFID security are integrated. The majority of systems concentrate on either software or hardware separately. Ectrinex fills this gap by fusing IOT visualization with real-time ai decision-making to produce a safe, self-optimizing charging infrastructure. OBJECTIVE • To develop a wireless charging system for electric vehicles that safely and contactless delivers power using inductive coupling techniques. • To install an AIoT-based monitoring and control system that continuously evaluates charging parameters, including alignment, temperature, voltage, current, and battery state of charge. • To integrate RFID-based access control and session management for secure user authentication and automated charging session initiation. • To employ a decision engine driven by AI for safety assessment, charging time estimation, charging optimization, and automated cut-off in odd situations. • To develop a real-time dashboard and reporting system that displays charging status, alerts, historical data, and session reports for effective monitoring and future scalability. 1. Introduction In today’s digital world, cyber-attacks are increasing rapidly in both number and complexity [6],[5],[10]. Organizations face constant threats such as unauthorized access, malware attacks, and brute-force login attempts [5],[10]. To investigate these attacks and improve system security, attack logs play a very important role [4],[1]. These logs help security analysts understand how attacks happen and how systems are being targeted [5],[10]. However, traditional logging systems have a major weakness. If an attacker gains access to the system, they may delete or modify logs to hide their activities [6],[4]. This makes incident investigation and digital forensics difficult [1],[4],[10]. In addition to this, current cryptographic methods used to protect logs may become insecure in the future due to the development of quantum computers, which can potentially break existing encryption and hashing techniques [2],[7],[8],[9]. To overcome these challenges, this project introduces a Quantum Safe Blockchain Based Honeypot Logging System. A honeypot is a decoy system designed to look like a real target and attract attackers [5],[10]. Instead of protecting against attacks, it allows attackers to interact with the system so that their actions can be safely monitored and recorded [5],[10]. Once the attack data is collected, it is secured using quantum-resistant cryptographic hashing, to ensure long-term data integrity [7],[9]. To further enhance security, the hash values of the logs are stored on a blockchain, which provides immutability and time-stamping [1],[2],[4]. This ensures that any tampering with logs can be easily detected [1],[4],[5]. By combining honeypot technology, blockchain, and quantum-safe security, this project provides a reliable, tamper-proof, and future-ready solution for cyber-attack logging and analysis [1],[2],[5],[7],[9],[10].

4. Problem Statement Existing cyber attack logging systems are vulnerable to tampering and do not provide guarantees of long-term security against emerging quantum computing threats. This makes attack logs unreliable for forensic analysis, compliance, and legal evidence. Therefore, there is a need for a secure logging system that can capture real cyber attacks, ensure tamper-proof storage, and remain resilient to future cryptographic threats.

4.1 Objectives: To build a secure and future-ready system that captures cyber attacks and stores logs immutably using quantum-safe blockchain technology. A. To ensure integrity, transparency, and immutability of cyber attack logs. C. To incorporate quantum-safe cryptographic principles to protect logs from future quantum threats. D. To prevent log manipulation and insider attacks in cybersecurity monitoring systems. To support reliable digital forensics and incident investigation through trusted attack records. E. 5.1 System Architecture: The proposed Quantum Safe Blockchain Based Honeypot Logging System follows a structured methodology to capture, secure, and verify cyber-attack logs. The complete working is divided into the following steps: Fig 5.1: Secure and Tamper-Proof Honeypot Logging System Using Quantum-Resistant Blockchain I. 
Honeypot Deployment A honeypot server is deployed to act as a decoy system that looks like a real target to attackers. It exposes selected services such as SSH or web services to attract unauthorized access attempts. The honeypot is isolated from the actual system to ensure safety. II. 
Attack Capture and Log Collection When an attacker interacts with the honeypot, all activities are recorded. This include: • 
Attacker IP address • 
Login attempts • 
Timestamp • 
Commands executed III. 
Log Processing and Structuring The collected logs are cleaned and structured into a standard format. Unnecessary or duplicate entries are removed, and important fields are organized for further processing and analysis. IV. 
Quantum-Resistant Hash Generation Each structured log is passed through a quantum-resistant hashing algorithm such as SHA-3 or hybrid hashing. This generates a fixed-length hash value that uniquely represents the log content. Any change in the log will produce a different hash. V. 
Blockchain Storage of Hash Values Only the hash values of the logs are stored on a blockchain network. The blockchain provides: • 
 Immutability • 
 Decentralization • 
 Secure time-stamping Storing hashes instead of full logs reduces storage overhead and improves system performance. VI. 
Secure Off-Chain Log Storage The original attack logs are stored securely in off-chain storage such as a protected database or file system. This allows efficient access while keeping the blockchain lightweight. VII. 
Log Integrity Verification Whenever log verification is required, the system recalculates the hash of the stored log and compares it with the corresponding hash stored on the blockchain: • 
If hashes match → Log is authentic and untampered • 
If hashes do not match → Log is modified or corrupted VIII.

IntroductionIntroduction to Advanced Military Equipment Detection using Satellite Imagery (AMED) AMED (Advanced Military Equipment Detection) is a modular AI-based system designed to detect hidden, camouflaged, or partially visible military equipment in satellite images.The project combines advanced preprocessing techniques (cloud masking, shadow enhancement), AI-based detection (YOLOv11, autoencoders, CNNs), and geometric analysis to identify military objects using direct and indirect visual cues.
This system leverages multimodal data RGB, Infrared, and radar along with anomaly detection methods to enhance accuracy, especially under camouflage or occlusion. Motivation In modern defense and surveillance ecosystems, satellite imagery plays a pivotal role in monitoring critical infrastructures, border areas, and military activities. However, identifying military equipment from satellite images is a significant challenge due to factors like camouflage, environmental occlusions, and limited visibility. Traditional object detection systems often underperform in such scenarios as they depend heavily on direct visual cues. This project is driven by the growing need for a more intelligent and adaptable detection pipeline that can operate even under adversarial conditions. By integrating deep learning models such as YOLOv8, autoencoders, and anomaly detection techniques with preprocessing steps like cloud masking, shadow enhancement, and vegetation segmentation, this system aims to deliver accurate and explainable predictions. The ability to analyze shadows and geometry further allows for indirect inference of object presence, enabling detection even when equipment is not fully visible. The motivation lies in building a hybrid and modular system that uses visual, geometric, and spectral information to detect hidden or camouflaged military assets, which can be a game-changer for defense surveillance, disaster response, and strategic planning.

Conclusion In this phase of the project, a strong foundation has been laid with the successful implementation of the initial modules in the data acquisition and preprocessing pipeline. Key accomplishments include setting up the project environment, integrating cloud masking using U-Net models, enhancing shadow visibility through CLAHE and gamma correction, and automating patch extraction for large satellite images. The pipeline has been structured to support modularity and future extensions, with configurations managed via YAML and outputs visualized for validation. While challenges such as cloud occlusion simulation, high-resolution data handling, and image enhancement consistency were encountered, they were mitigated through preprocessing techniques and iterative testing. With the ability to ingest, process, and visualize satellite image patches now established, the groundwork has been prepared for the integration of AI-based detection modules such as YOLOv8, CNN-based camouflage detection, and geometric shadow analysis.

The AMED system is well-positioned to deliver a powerful tool for military surveillance, offering accurate detection even in visually challenging environments.

ABSTRACT With the rapid growth of multimedia content across digital platforms, efficiently extracting and searching information from audio and video data has become a significant challenge. Traditional systems do not allow users to directly search within spoken content, making information retrieval time-consuming and inefficient. To address these issues, this project proposes SonicSearch, an intelligent multimedia transcription and search system. In this system, users can upload audio or video files or provide links from platforms such as YouTube or Instagram, which are then processed to extract meaningful textual data. The system utilizes advanced speech recognition technologies, for fast and scalable cloud-based transcription, with OpenAI Whisper for accurate deep learning-based speech processing. The generated transcripts are stored efficiently and indexed to enable keyword-based searching within the content. Sensitive keyword detection mechanisms are also implemented to identify critical or flagged terms within the transcript. The system ensures optimized performance by handling large media files and minimizing processing delays. Users can verify search results instantly by locating keywords within the transcript, improving accessibility and usability. The system also includes an intuitive dashboard that allows users to upload files, view transcripts, perform searches, and analyze detected keywords. This approach provides an efficient, scalable, and user-friendly solution for multimedia content analysis, making it highly suitable for modern applications such as content moderation, digital forensics, and educational resource management. LITERATURE SURVEY Several studies have explored speech recognition and audio processing techniques for multimedia content analysis and information retrieval. Conformer architectures have improved speech recognition performance by combining convolutional and transformer-based learning approaches [1]. Deep audio representation techniques have also enhanced audio understanding and feature extraction capabilities [2]. Baevski et al. proposed wav2vec 2.0 for self-supervised speech representation learning, improving transcription accuracy while reducing dependency on labeled datasets [3]. Radford et al. developed OpenAI Whisper for robust multilingual speech recognition and transcription in noisy environments [4]. Traditional multimedia systems mainly focus on playback and storage and lack advanced features such as intelligent search and content analysis [9]. Research on keyword spotting and multimedia indexing techniques has enabled efficient retrieval of information from long audio recordings and large multimedia datasets [9][14]. Audio intelligence systems have further improved keyword detection and multimedia search capabilities [15]. Recent advancements in natural language processing have enhanced semantic understanding of transcribed content [19], while AI-based summarization models have improved usability by generating concise summaries from large textual data [13]. Several studies have also emphasized the importance of detecting sensitive information in voice-based communication systems. Venkataraman et al. proposed NLP-based techniques for identifying confidential information in spoken content [5]. Conti et al. analyzed voice phishing and social engineering threats in communication systems [6]. Machine learning approaches for sensitive content detection in speech signals have also been explored to improve multimedia security and monitoring [7][8]. Despite these advancements, most existing systems focus on individual functionalities such as transcription, keyword spotting, or sensitive information detection independently, rather than integrating them into a unified multimedia analysis framework [11][12][16]. Introduction AcuPath is an AI-powered Android application developed using Java/XML with Firebase [NAME], designed to help users reduce common body pain such as back, neck, shoulder, and knee pain through personalized exercise guidance. The app first identifies the pain area, then asks a short set of targeted questions to understand pain severity, duration, triggers, and mobility limitations. Using Agentic AI, the system dynamically chooses the next relevant question and selects a safe recommendation pathway. After analysis, the app provides a structured plan including warm-up, recommended exercises, precautions, and do’s/don’ts, supported with a video tab (WebView) for demonstrations. Users can also ask doubts through an AI Assistant that uses NLP + Generative AI to answer queries and guide safe self-care. Motivation Many people suffer from daily body pain due to poor posture, long sitting hours, gym strain, and lifestyle habits. Most users rely on random YouTube videos or Google searches, which are often generic and may not match the user’s pain condition. Access to physiotherapy or expert guidance is not always available due to time, cost, and location limitations. Users need a simple tool that can understand their pain situation, guide them with safe exercises, and explain everything clearly. AI makes it possible to provide personalized recommendations + interactive doubt solving, improving user confidence and consistency.

Problem Statement Many people who have body pain do not know which exercises are safe for their pain. Most existing apps give the same exercises to everyone and do not consider how serious the pain is, what causes it, or how much the person can move. This can confuse users and sometimes make the pain worse. Therefore, there is a need for an Android app that understands the user’s pain by asking simple and relevant questions, then suggests the right exercises with proper safety tips. With AI support, exercise videos, and saved user history, the app can help people manage their pain better and more safely over time.

ABSTRACT Internal cracks in pipeline systems pose serious risks to industrial safety, environmental protection, and operational reliability, particularly in aging pipelines used for transporting oil, gas, water, and chemicals. Manual inspection of internal pipelines is often unsafe, time-consuming, and unreliable due to confined spaces, low visibility, and hazardous conditions. To address these challenges, this work presents an autonomous robotic system for internal pipeline crack detection using artificial intelligence. The proposed system utilizes a mobile in-pipe robotic platform equipped with a low-cost vision sensor to capture internal surface images during inspection. An image-based hybrid deep learning framework is employed, where YOLOv8 is used for real-time crack detection and localization, and an Attention U-Net model performs pixel-level crack segmentation for precise visualization. Image-processing techniques are further applied to estimate crack length and width, enabling quantitative defect assessment. The system is designed to operate reliably under practical internal pipeline conditions such as low illumination, surface noise, motion blur, and limited visibility. Experimental results demonstrate effective detection of small and fine internal cracks, along with structured visual outputs and measurements to support maintenance decisions. By integrating autonomous robotic mobility with robust AI-based vision models, the proposed approach provides a cost-effective, scalable, and reliable solution for automated internal pipeline inspection. Domain: AI, Structural Health Monitoring KeyWords: Internal Pipeline Inspection, Crack Detection, Autonomous Robotics, Artificial Intelligence, Deep Learning, YOLOv8, Attention U-Net. INTRODUCTION The Crack formation in critical infrastructure has emerged as a major engineering concern due to aging materials, prolonged operational loads, corrosion, and harsh environmental conditions. Among various infrastructure elements, pipelines play a vital role in the transportation of water, oil, gas, and industrial fluids, making their structural integrity extremely important. Cracks in pipelines often initiate as micro-defects and gradually propagate under internal pressure and environmental stress, leading to leakage, contamination, economic loss, and in severe cases, catastrophic failure. In addition to pipelines, similar crack-related issues are also observed in roads, bridges, tunnels, and concrete structures, further emphasizing the need for reliable inspection systems. Traditional pipeline crack inspection methods largely depend on manual surveys, shutdown-based inspection, or contact-based sensing techniques, which are expensive, time-consuming, and sometimes unsafe. Pipelines located underground, underwater, or in hazardous industrial environments pose significant challenges for human inspectors. Moreover, manual inspection may fail to identify fine surface cracks or early-stage defects, and inspection outcomes often vary based on operator experience and visibility conditions. While automated inspection techniques such as ultrasonic and acoustic methods have been used, they require specialized equipment and are not always suitable for continuous monitoring. In recent years, image-based crack detection using computer vision and deep learning has gained attention as a non-contact and cost-effective alternative. However, many existing approaches rely on high-resolution images captured under controlled lighting and static conditions, limiting their effectiveness in real-world pipeline environments. Factors such as motion blur, uneven illumination, surface rust, and noise significantly reduce detection accuracy in practical scenarios. The proposed project addresses these limitations by developing an image-based pipeline crack detection system deployed on a mobile robotic platform. A low-cost camera is used to capture real-time images of pipeline surfaces during inspection. Deep learning models are employed to automatically detect, localize, and segment crack regions from captured images. The system is designed to operate under realistic field conditions and does not require manual image acquisition or shutdown of pipeline operations. 1.1 Overview

Image Preprocessing and Augmentation Images taken inside dark, dirty pipes are rarely usable straight from the camera. They tend to be underexposed, brighter on one side than the other, and blurred where the robot moved quickly. Several preprocessing steps were applied to every frame before passing it to the models. All images were resized to 640 ×640 pixels so that model input dimensions stayed fixed. Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) was applied with a clip limit of 2.0 on an 8×8 tile grid, sharpening local contrast in small image regions and making hairline cracks visible without over brightening noisy areas. Non-Local Means (NLM) denoising then reduced random sensor noise while preserving crack edges. For training, the dataset was further expanded through stochastic augmentation: random in-plane rotation up to ±15◦, brightness and contrast scaling over [0.7, 1.3], additive Gaussian noise with σ ∈ [5, 25], and motion-blur simulation using linear kernels of width k ∈ {3,5,7} at random orientations. These transforms collectively approximate the image degradations encountered during real in-pipe inspection. Robotic Platform The robot is built on a commercial RC-car chassis approximately 26cm long and 18cm wide, giving sufficient clearance for pipes with inner diameters above 100mm. A 10,000mAh portable power bank supplies both the drive motors and the ESP32-CAM, providing roughly four hours of continuous operation per charge. The camera is mounted coaxially with the pipe axis. During a test run it streams compressed JPEG frames over a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi link to a laptop running the inference pipeline. Wireless delay averaged below 80ms, and model inference takes approximately 120ms per frame on a GPU, supporting around five inspection frames per second end-to-end.

LITERATURE SURVEY Survey The detection and analysis of cracks in pipelines and structural systems have gained significant attention due to increasing infrastructure failures and safety concerns. Modern inspection systems utilize a combination of image processing, deep learning, and robotic technologies to improve the accuracy and efficiency of crack detection. These systems rely on various data inputs such as pipeline surface images, sensor data, and real-time video streams to identify structural defects. 2.1.1 A Machine-Learning-Based and IoT-Enabled Robot Swarm System for Pipeline Crack Detection (Ayman Kandil et al., 2024) Observation Summary: This study presents an advanced pipeline inspection system based on an IoT-enabled swarm robotics framework integrated with a deep learning model. The system utilizes a VGG16-based Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for crack detection and severity classification. Multiple robots collaboratively inspect pipelines and communicate using long-range LoRa technology, enabling large-scale monitoring with minimal human intervention. Additionally, ultrasonic sensors are incorporated to enhance defect detection capabilities. 2.1.2 Design and Development of an In-Pipe Mobile Robot with AI Defect Detection (Kenzhekhan et al., 2023) Observation Summary: This work presents a robotic platform designed for in-pipe inspection using video-based monitoring and planned integration of AI-based defect detection. The system aims to automate inspection and improve defect identification through visual data analysis. However, the system has limited experimental validation, and the performance of the deep learning model is not clearly evaluated. This reduces confidence in its reliability and effectiveness for real-world deployment. 2.1.3 A New Approach to Design and Development of In-Pipe Inspection Robots (Mohammed et al., 2020)

The system aims to automate inspection and improve defect identification through visual data analysis. The modular design allows flexibility and adaptability to different pipeline diameters and conditions, making it suitable for a range of inspection scenarios. Despite its mechanical advantages, the system lacks intelligent data processing capabilities. It does not incorporate machine learning or deep learning techniques for crack detection, classification, or segmentation. 4.1 System Architecture The proposed Internal Pipeline Crack Detection System Architecture is designed to provide an efficient and automated solution for detecting, analyzing, and reporting cracks in pipeline structures. Mobile Platform and Image Acquisition The system uses a mobile robotic platform equipped with an ESP32-CAM module. As the robot moves along or inside the pipeline, the camera continuously captures images of the internal surface. This robotic setup allows inspection in confined, hazardous, or inaccessible environments where manual inspection is unsafe or impractical. 2. Image Preprocessing The captured images are first passed through a preprocessing stage to enhance image quality and ensure consistency. Preprocessing operations include resizing, noise reduction, contrast enhancement, and brightness normalization. These steps improve crack visibility and reduce the impact of motion blur and varying lighting conditions caused by robot movement. 3. Shared CNN Backbone The preprocessed images are fed into a shared convolutional neural network backbone responsible for extracting meaningful visual features. Crack Segmentation Using U-Net In parallel, the shared features are processed by a U-Net-based segmentation module. This module performs pixel-level segmentation to generate a crack mask that accurately outlines the crack shape, including thin and micro-cracks that may not be fully captured by bounding boxes [8]. 6. It processes the entire image in a single pass and predicts bounding boxes along with confidence scores. The model takes an input image and divides it into regions, detecting cracks based on learned features. YOLOv8 is highly efficient and suitable for real-time applications due to its fast inference speed and high accuracy. It reduces computational complexity while maintaining reliable detection performance, making it ideal for integration with robotic inspection systems. 6.3.2 Algorithm 2 U-Net (Segmentation):

The model takes an input image and divides it into regions, detecting cracks based on learned features. YOLOv8 is highly efficient and suitable for real-time applications due to its fast inference speed and high accuracy. It reduces computational complexity while maintaining reliable detection performance, making it ideal for integration with robotic inspection systems. 6.3.2 Algorithm 2 U-Net (Segmentation): U-Net is a convolutional neural network specifically designed for image segmentation tasks. In this project, it is used to extract pixel-level information of crack regions after detection. The architecture consists of an encoder-decoder structure, where the encoder captures features and the decoder reconstructs the segmented output. U-Net helps in accurately identifying the shape and spread of cracks by separating them from the background. This improves the precision of crack analysis and enables further measurements. 6.3.3 Algorithm 3 Image Processing for Measurement : After segmentation, image processing techniques are applied to calculate crack dimensions such as length, width, and area. The segmented crack region is analyzed using pixel-based calculations and converted into meaningful measurements. This step is essential for evaluating the severity of cracks and supports decision-making for maintenance and repair. The combination of segmentation and measurement ensures both qualitative and quantitative analysis of pipeline defects.

Table 7.6: Performance Comparison of Models on Test Set The above table presents the performance of different model configurations evaluated on the test dataset. The YOLOv8 model alone (M1) achieves an accuracy of 94.60% with strong precision and recall values; however, it is limited to bounding box detection and cannot accurately capture thin and irregular crack patterns. On the other hand, the Attention U-Net model (M2) achieves a slightly higher segmentation capability, reflected in a marginally better IoU score, but shows lower overall accuracy of 93.10% due to the absence of detection guidance, which causes the model to process irrelevant background regions. The proposed hybrid model (M3), which combines YOLOv8 for detection and U-Net for segmentation, significantly outperforms both individual models across all evaluation metrics. It achieves the highest accuracy of 98.21%, along with superior precision, recall, F1-score, and IoU values. The hybrid model shows an improvement of 3.61 percentage points over YOLOv8 and 5.11 percentage points over U-Net in terms of accuracy. This clearly demonstrates that integrating detection-guided region localization with pixel-level segmentation enhances overall performance. Abstract The rapid growth of audio and video-based communication has resulted in a large volume of unstructured multimedia data containing critical information, including sensitive and confidential content. However, existing systems lack effective mechanisms to search, retrieve, and protect such information at a granular level. This paper presents “SonicSearch: Secure AI-Powered Audio and Video Content Search with Sensitive Information Protection”, an intelligent web-based system designed to enable timestamp-level search and retrieval of spoken content while preventing unintended disclosure of security-sensitive information. The proposed system leverages speech-to-text conversion and natural language processing to transform audio and video inputs into searchable textual transcripts, supporting bilingual communication in English and Hinglish. A keyword-based search mechanism allows users to instantly locate important notes, questions, or discussions within long recordings, with highlighted timestamps for precise navigation. To align with cybersecurity principles, the system integrates a sensitive keyword detection module that identifies confidential terms such as passwords, OTPs, and banking details, and enforces user-controlled disclosure through security alerts and access confirmation. This approach supports data leakage prevention by minimizing the risk of exposing sensitive information in public or shared environments. The system architecture emphasizes usability, privacy awareness, and scalable design, making it suitable for academic, professional, and organizational use cases. By combining intelligent audio retrieval with contextual security controls, SonicSearch provides a practical and proactive solution for secure multimedia information management. Keywords: Audio Search, Speech-to-Text, Sensitive Keyword Detection, Data Leakage Prevention, Cyber Security, Hinglish NLP, Multimedia Information Retrieval.

make data-driven decisions. To address this, we introduce Mon-
goTalk, a novel web-based system that bridges this usability chasm.
MongoTalk offers a unified conversational interface, powered by a
locally-hosted [NAME] (LLM), enabling users
to perform a full range of database interactions—from schema cre-
ation and data manipulation to complex querying, automated visual-
ization, and scheduled reporting entirely through natural language.
The system’s architecture includes a robust intent-classification
pipeline, a rule-based engine for selecting visualizations, and a se-

we conducted a user study comparing MongoTalk against Mon-
goDB Compass. The results were compelling: MongoTalk reduced
task completion time by an average of 65% and error rates by 78%.
It also achieved a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 88.5 ("Excel-
lent"), significantly outperforming Compass’s score of 65.2 ("Okay").
Our work demonstrates a significant step towards the true democra-
tization of NoSQL data by providing a comprehensive, secure, and
highly usable paradigm for natural language database interaction. Keywords Natural Language Interface to Database (NLIDB), MongoDB, Large

Figure 1: Growth of MongoDB Towards AI (2020–2025). 2.1 Evolution of Database Interfaces The earliest interactions with databases were conducted through
low-level, procedural command-line interfaces (CLIs), which de-
manded deep technical expertise. The invention of SQL and the
relational model marked a significant leap forward, offering a declar-
ative language that allowed users to specify what data they wanted,
rather than how to retrieve it [5, 55]. However, SQL itself remains
a formal language that requires training and an understanding of
the underlying database schema, posing a barrier to casual and
non-technical users [6]. In response, researchers and developers
created higher-level interfaces, such as form-based interfaces and
visual query builders [7]. These systems, like Query-by-Example
[8], aimed to simplify query construction by providing graphical
representations of the database schema and allowing users to build
queries through direct manipulation. While an improvement, these
visual systems often struggle to express highly complex or ad-hoc
queries and still require users to understand database concepts like
joins and relations. 2.2
Natural Language Interfaces for Databases
(NLIDB) The pursuit of a true natural language interface for databases has
a long history, with early systems relying on brittle, manually-
engineered linguistic rules [5, 9, 54]. The recent advent of Large
Language Models (LLMs) has revolutionized the field, driving a
paradigm shift towards deep learning-based approaches. This new
wave has predominantly focused on the Text-to-SQL task, aiming
to translate natural language questions into executable SQL queries,
with significant success attributed to transformer architectures and
large benchmark datasets [10, 11, 20].

Methodology MongoTalk is a multi-component web application designed to serve
as a comprehensive conversational gateway to MongoDB. This
section provides a detailed technical description of its architecture
and the core modules that enable its functionality. Figure 2: Pipeline Overview Diagram. I. Frontend: A modern, responsive web interface built using the React framework. It provides a simple chat-style input for
users to enter their natural language commands. The inter-
face is responsible for rendering query results, which can be
raw JSON data, formatted tables, or interactive visualizations
generated by a library such as Chart.js. II. Backend Orchestrator: A Python-based server built with the FastAPI framework. This component is the brain of the
system, responsible for managing user sessions, receiving
natural language input from the frontend, and coordinat-
ing the workflow between the other modules. It houses the
Natural Language Understanding (NLU) module, the Secure
Execution Engine, the Automated Visualization Engine, and
the Automated Reporting Module.
III. LLM Service: The system leverages a locally-hosted LLM served via Ollama. This approach ensures data privacy, as
no user prompts or database schemas are sent to third-party
APIs, and provides full control over model selection and con-
figuration. For the task of generating MQL, a code-specialized
model such as codellama:34b is employed, chosen for its
strong performance in code generation and understanding
context across multiple files [13].
IV. MongoDB Instance: The target database that the user wishes to interact with. The backend orchestrator connects to this
instance using a standard MongoDB driver.Rather than open-
ing a new connection for every single user request, the sys-
tem typically maintains a connection pool—a cache of open,
reusable database connections. When the Secure Execution
Engine approves a query, the orchestrator borrows a connec-
tion from this pool, serializes the validated MQL into BSON
(Binary JSON), and transmits it securely over the network
(encrypted via TLS/SSL).

The process initiates at the frontend interface, where the user en-
ters a command or query in plain natural language, effectively
abstracting away the complexity of database syntax. This input is
immediately transmitted to the backend orchestrator, which serves
as the system’s central control unit. Upon receipt, the orchestra-
tor leverages a specialized Natural Language Understanding (NLU)
module to parse the user’s text, rigorously classifying the intent
and extracting relevant entities. Based on this analysis, the system
constructs a highly detailed, context-aware prompt optimized for
the integrated [NAME] (LLM). The LLM pro-
cesses this prompt to translate the human-readable request into
precise, syntactically correct MQL code, bridging the gap between
natural language and technical database logic. Once the MQL code is generated, it is returned to the orchestrator,
which initiates a rigorous safety phase rather than executing the
code immediately. The code is passed through a Secure Execution
Engine that validates the syntax and permissions to ensure system
integrity before running the query. Upon successful execution,
the retrieved data is forwarded to the Automated Visualization
Engine. This intelligent component analyzes the shape and nature
of the results to dynamically determine the most effective visual
representation—whether that be a specific chart type, graph, or

Once the in- tent is classified, the orchestrator dynamically constructs a highly specific and context-rich prompt for the main codellama:34b model. This process of prompt engineering is crucial for guiding the LLM to generate accurate and safe MQL. The prompt is assembled from several key components: • Role Definition: The prompt begins by assigning a persona
to the LLM, priming it for the specific task. For example: "You
are an expert MongoDB database administrator. Your task
is to convert the user’s request into a single, syntactically
correct MongoDB Query Language (MQL) command" [14].
• Schema Injection: To ground the LLM in the specific con-
text of the target database, the system retrieves the relevant
schema information (collection names, field names, and data
types) and injects it into the prompt. This provides the model
with the necessary information to generate a valid query
that references existing fields. For a CRUD_FIND intent, the
instruction might be: “Generate a !db.collection.find()! or
!db.collection.aggregate()! query to answer the user’s ques-
tion.”
• Few-Shot Examples: For particularly complex tasks, such
as generating multi-stage aggregation pipelines, the prompt
is augmented with two or three curated examples. Each
example consists of a sample natural language question and
the corresponding correct, complex MQL. This technique,
known as few-shot prompting, significantly improves the
model’s ability to handle nuanced and difficult requests by
demonstrating the desired pattern [11]. 3.2

The Secure Execution Engine is a non-negotiable component of the MongoTalk architecture, designed to mitigate these risks through a multi-layered defense strategy. 3.2.1
Static Analysis and Validation. Before execution, every gen-
erated MQL query is subjected to a static analysis validator. This
layer uses a combination of regular expressions and abstract syntax
tree (AST) parsing to enforce a strict security policy. It explicitly
disallows potentially destructive commands (e.g., ‘dropDatabase()‘,
‘drop()‘, ‘remove()‘) and flags queries that could lead to excessive resource consumption. This pre-execution check acts as a first line
of defense against malicious or poorly formed queries. 3.2.2
Sandboxed Execution. Validated queries are not executed in
the main application environment. Instead, they are run within a
secure, isolated sandbox. MongoTalk utilizes short-lived Docker
containers for this purpose [17]. For each query, a new container is
spun up, executes the single MQL command, and is then destroyed.
This ephemeral environment ensures that even if a malicious query
bypasses the validation layer, it has no access to the host system’s
filesystem or network resources. Furthermore, the database connec-
tion string used within the sandbox is provisioned with a role that
adheres to the principle of least privilege [18]. For FIND queries,
the role is strictly read-only. For INSERT or UPDATE queries, the
role grants write permissions only to the specific collection being
targeted. This strategy minimizes the potential "blast radius" of a
malicious operation, preventing it from affecting other parts of the
database or the application itself. 3.3

difficult to interpret. The Automated Visualization Engine addresses
this by transforming query results into meaningful and contextually
appropriate visual representations, following principles of effective
data visualization [34, 51]. The engine uses a set of heuristic rules,
inspired by pioneering work in automatic graphical presentation
[37], to select the most effective chart type: • If the result contains a temporal field (date/timestamp) and
a numerical metric, a line chart is chosen to show trends
over time.
• If the result contains a categorical dimension and a numerical
metric, a bar chart is selected for comparison.
• If the result shows parts of a whole (e.g., percentages), a pie
chart is used.
• If the result contains geospatial coordinates, a map visual-
ization is rendered. These rules allow the system to automatically generate insightful
visualizations without requiring any input from the user, further
lowering the cognitive barrier to data analysis [35]. 3.4

conducted a formal user study involving 20 non-technical domain
experts, primarily recruited from business intelligence, marketing,
and product management roles. These participants were selected
to represent the system’s target demographic: professionals who
possess deep semantic knowledge of the business data but lack the
technical proficiency to author complex MongoDB Query Language
(MQL) scripts. 5.1

consisted of 20 professionals recruited from a mix of local private
enterprises and university administrative departments, ensuring a
representative cross-section of non-technical data users. The spe-
cific role distribution included Marketing Analysts (n=6), Project
Managers (n=5), Sales Operations Specialists (n=4), and Financial

ticipants engaged in a series of representative data interaction tasks
designed to simulate real-world workflows, such as filtering com-
plex datasets, aggregating financial figures, and retrieving specific
project milestones. The analysis was multi-dimensional, triangu-
lating quantitative performance metrics, such as task completion
time and error rates, with qualitative user feedback. This included
standardized usability scoring and subjective assessments of cogni-

performance but also enhances the user experience by making data
interaction feel more intuitive and less intimidating. 5.4

analysis of the few task failures is instructive. The 4% of failures pri-

fell into two categories: 1) misinterpretation of highly ambiguous
natural language, where the user’s phrasing could plausibly map to
multiple different queries, and 2) failure to generate a correct query
for requests involving complex, multi-step logical reasoning that ex-
ceeded the single-shot capabilities of the LLM. For instance, a query
like "Show me the top 3 product categories by sales growth this
quarter compared to last quarter, but only for categories that have at
least 100 unique customers" requires multiple stages of aggregation
and comparison. These failures highlight the current limitations of
the technology and underscore the importance of the future work
on conversational context and iterative query refinement. 6
Discussion The results of our user study strongly suggest that a holistic, con-
versational interface can significantly lower the barrier to entry for
interacting with complex NoSQL databases. The stark contrast in
performance and success rates between MongoTalk and MongoDB
Compass, particularly on complex tasks, highlights the limitations
of traditional GUI-based tools for non-technical users. While GUIs
provide a visual representation of the data, they often still require
a conceptual understanding of database operations that domain
experts may not possess. MongoTalk, by contrast, allows users to
operate in their own domain language, offloading the cognitive bur-
den of query construction, result interpretation, and visualization
selection to the AI. The high SUS score of 88.5 for MongoTalk is Figure 6: SUS Score.

The high SUS score of 88.5 for MongoTalk is Figure 6: SUS Score. particularly noteworthy. This "Excellent" rating, based on a well-
established usability scale [62], indicates that users found the sys-
tem not only effective but also easy to learn and satisfying to use.
This is a critical factor for adoption in enterprise environments,
where tools that are perceived as difficult or frustrating are often abandoned, regardless of their theoretical capabilities. The "Okay"
rating for Compass (65.2) is typical for specialized tools and reflects
the learning curve associated with its more technical interface. Our
work suggests that the true "cost" of a data tool is not just its li-
cense fee, but also the cognitive overhead it imposes on its users;
by minimizing this overhead, systems like MongoTalk can deliver
substantial productivity gains. The democratization of data access, while operationally trans-
formative, introduces a paradox: as the technical barrier to entry
lowers, the cognitive burden of interpretation rises. Empowering
a broader demographic of users to interact with data directly in-
creases the potential for misinterpretation and erroneous conclu-
sions, even when the underlying data retrieval is technically flaw-
less. While MongoTalk effectively abstracts away the complexity
of MQL syntax, it cannot automate the domain expertise required
to understand the context of that data. There is a tangible risk
of “blind trust,” where users accept the LLM-generated output as
absolute truth without scrutinizing the logic used to derive it. A
non-technical user may not recognize if a query accidentally omits
a crucial filter or aggregates averages in a way that skews the sta-
tistical reality, leading to business decisions based on “hallucinated”
or contextually inappropriate insights.

date a strategic audit of core business processes, mapping
them against the Precision/Productivity framework. The goal
is to identify the top 3-5 highest-impact initiatives for each
category. For Precision AI, this might be automating quality
control on a manufacturing line or developing a proprietary
fraud detection model. For Productivity AI, it could be de-
ploying a conversational interface for sales analytics or HR
data management. This structured approach moves beyond
ad-hoc AI adoption to a deliberate, portfolio-based strategy.
• Develop Industry-Specific Data Consortiums: To over-
come the "Data Provenance" imperative for building world-
class Precision AI, industry bodies should consider forming
consortiums to create, share, and govern high-quality, un-
biased datasets. By pooling anonymized data resources, an
entire industry (e.g., banking, insurance, manufacturing) can
accelerate the development of robust AI models that benefit
all members, overcoming the data scarcity that can limit
individual firms. 7 • Develop a Bifurcated Regulatory Framework: A one-
size-fits-all approach to AI regulation is destined to fail. Poli-
cymakers should develop a bifurcated framework that distin-
guishes between high-risk and low-risk applications. High-
risk Precision AI, particularly in domains like healthcare,
justice, and critical infrastructure, requires stringent, domain-
specific regulations focused on safety, efficacy, transparency,
and bias mitigation. In contrast, lower-risk Productivity AI
applications can be governed by lighter-touch guidelines
that foster innovation while enforcing strong standards for
data privacy and security, as exemplified by the principles
of Sovereign AI. 8

dialogue state tracking and coreference resolution will be critical
for achieving this more natural, multi-turn interaction. Another promising direction is the expansion of the system to

an NLU module, a secure execution engine, and a visualization

Conclusion This paper introduced MongoTalk, a novel conversational system
that abstracts the entire lifecycle of interaction with a MongoDB
database. By leveraging a locally-hosted LLM, our system enables
non-technical users to perform complex data retrieval, manipula-
tion, visualization, and automated reporting tasks using natural
language. The results from our user study provide strong empirical
evidence for the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating sig-
nificant improvements in task completion time, success rate, and
user satisfaction compared to a traditional GUI tool. MongoTalk
offers a viable path toward true data democratization, empowering
domain experts to directly engage with their data without the need
for specialized technical skills. By providing a secure, intuitive, and
comprehensive interface, our work lays the foundation for a new
generation of data interaction tools that are not only powerful but
also accessible to all. The authors would like to express their sincere gratitude to their

Introduction In the evolving era of intelligent aerial technologies, autonomous drones are playing a transformative role in high-stakes operations such as surveillance, reconnaissance, and precision strike missions. Traditional drone systems typically depend on centralized control or ground-based human operators to navigate and perform their tasks. While effective in controlled settings, this architecture introduces critical vulnerabilities during real-world deployments—especially in hostile or communication-denied environments—due to its reliance on external commands and data links [5]. To overcome these limitations, this project introduces an innovative Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System. In this design, individual drones are capable of autonomous activation immediately after ejection, without the need for any remote instruction. Once deployed in the air, the drones organize themselves into a swarm, establishing peer-to-peer communication and dynamically coordinating their actions to complete the mission at hand [1,3]. Each drone is equipped with onboard computer vision, enabling it to detect, analyse, and track targets in real time. The swarm collectively shares information, adapts to new conditions, and executes complex strategies without requiring any central controller. This decentralized, distributed approach enhances system resilience, allowing the swarm to function seamlessly even in GPS-denied or jammed environments [2]. The scalability and robustness of the Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System make it suitable for a wide range of applications. In military scenarios, it ensures continued performance despite adversarial attempts to disrupt communication networks. In civilian domains, it can support disaster relief, search-and-rescue operations, and environmental monitoring. By reducing reliance on external control and increasing operational autonomy, this system represents a significant leap forward in the development of next-generation drone swarms [4]. Furthermore, the design prioritizes energy efficiency and modular adaptability, allowing drones to carry different sensor payloads based on mission requirements. Whether deployed individually or as a large collective unit, the swarm remains flexible, self-sustaining, and capable of reconfiguration mid-mission. These features collectively enhance the operational versatility and mission-readiness of the system across a broad range of scenarios.

3. Problem Statement 3.1 Dependency on Centralized Control Conventional drone systems are heavily dependent on either manual operation or centralized control architectures. This reliance creates a significant vulnerability: if the communication infrastructure is jammed, disrupted, or otherwise compromised—such as in electronic warfare scenarios or remote environments—the entire system can fail. These control dependencies limit operational range, introduce single points of failure, and restrict drones from performing missions in contested or communication-denied zones [3]. 3.2 Inability to Deploy Autonomously Traditional drones often require some form of manual intervention, external triggering, or pre-programmed launch protocols. Such reliance on external input severely restricts their deployment speed and adaptability, particularly in high-stakes missions where rapid response is crucial. In hostile or unpredictable environments—such as during natural disasters, battlefield situations, or surveillance missions in enemy territory—human involvement may be impractical or dangerous. Therefore, a shift toward fully autonomous deployment is critical for ensuring operational continuity and tactical advantage [5]. 3.3 Target Identification Without Ground Control One of the pressing challenges in modern drone technology is the ability to detect, classify, and respond to targets independently, without relying on continuous human supervision or ground-based computer vision systems. To be truly autonomous, drones must be equipped with onboard intelligence capable of real-time scene analysis, object recognition, and dynamic decision-making. Such capabilities would enable drones to carry out reconnaissance, surveillance, or precision strikes even in GPS-denied or communication-impaired conditions, greatly enhancing their usefulness in complex missions [1,3].

4.1 System Architecture The system consists of two major units: Mothership Drone Unit: Built with an Arduino Uno and LoRa SX1278 module for communication, it houses a servo-controlled latch system that releases swarm drones based on signal conditions. It includes a GPS module for height estimation and an RC receiver for manual control. Swarm Child Drones: Each child drone is equipped with a self-contained flight system powered by brushless motors, ESCs, and an onboard Pixhawk FC. Once released, they are activated by a sensor-based or timer-based trigger to stabilize mid-air and hit the target. A fixed-ground LoRa transmitter communicates continuously with the mothership drone, and signal failure triggers automatic latch deployment, releasing the child drones. The drones then execute visual recognition and hover above assigned targets and act accordingly as per the mission planner. 4.2 Algorithms Latch Activation Logic: A custom Arduino sketch continuously checks for LoRa signal input. If signal drops for more than a defined timeout (e.g., 2–5 seconds), the servo motor opens the latch. Child Drone Auto-Start Logic: Upon free fall, either a timer or an accelerometer sensor triggers motor activation. Target Hovering Algorithm: Using OpenCV or YOLOv5 (on PC simulation), the drone processes downward video frames to detect letters A or B and adjusts motor thrust to centre above the target [1].
