8. Conclusion The Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System represents a paradigm shift in autonomous aerial operations by eliminating dependence on centralized control and enabling drones to self-activate, self-organize, and self-execute complex missions. Through decentralized coordination, onboard computer vision, and real-time decision-making, the swarm demonstrates exceptional resilience, adaptability, and mission efficiency—even in GPS-denied or communication-compromised environments. The integration of onboard computer vision, real-time peer-to-peer communication, and decentralized intelligence allows the swarm to not only perform coordinated actions but also adapt to unforeseen challenges in real-time. This adaptability ensures that even if one or more drones are lost or disabled, the swarm as a whole continues its mission without failure. This kind of fault-tolerant behavior significantly enhances operational reliability and mission assurance. This innovation not only strengthens capabilities in high-stakes military operations but also opens up transformative applications in civilian sectors such as disaster response, environmental monitoring, and search-and-rescue missions. With its modular, energy-efficient design and scalable architecture, the system sets a strong foundation for the future of intelligent, cooperative drone technology. As autonomous swarms continue to evolve, they promise to become indispensable tools in both strategic and humanitarian missions, redefining the boundaries of what unmanned aerial systems can achieve. Looking ahead, the continued development of such systems holds immense potential. As AI, machine learning, sensor technologies, and swarm algorithms advance, these drones will become smarter, faster, and more capable of performing complex missions without human intervention. Furthermore, as ethical frameworks and regulatory systems evolve to accommodate autonomous technologies, such swarms can be deployed more confidently in both defence and civilian sectors. In essence, the Self-Triggered Swarm Drone System is not just an innovation in drone technology—it is a foundation for the future of fully autonomous, resilient, and intelligent aerial systems capable of redefining strategic operations across domains. It represents a convergence of autonomy, collaboration, and adaptability, setting a new benchmark for what drone systems can accomplish in the age of intelligent machines.

ABSTRACT Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a serious blood cancer that causes too many immature lymphocytes to form in the bone marrow. Detecting its stages early—beginner, early, pre-leukemic, and pro-leukemic—is important for timely treatment and better outcomes. Traditional methods, which involve manually examining blood smear images under a microscope, can be slow and may lead to different results depending on who is looking. In this project, we propose a deep learning-based framework for automated white blood cell (WBC) classification and confidence estimation to identify the stages of ALL from microscopic images. The methodology involves preprocessing a publicly available dataset of labeled microscopic WBC images, followed by the implementation of (CNNs) for feature extraction and stage classification. To ensure reliability in clinical decision-making, our approach incorporates confidence estimation techniques. This enables the system not only to classify the stages but also to provide confidence levels for each prediction, aiding in trust and interpretability. Performance metrics will be evaluated to validate the model. This study aims to assist medical professionals with a robust, interpretable, and reliable tool for ALL diagnosis, ultimately contributing to faster and more accurate clinical workflows in hematopathology. Future scope includes expanding the model to multi-class cancer detection and real-time clinical deployment. INTRODUCTION B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is a frequent type of leukemia with an age-independent incidence in people but is still more often diagnosed in children [4,5]. Timely diagnosis of malignant lymphoblasts provides an essential opportunity for the best possible treatment and prognosis, so timely identification is crucial. Although these techniques provide reliable diagnostic analysis at a high standard of care there are many difficulties associated with process including discomfort for the patient, the amount of time taken from a professional, and finances that require significant costs of healthcare resources. In recent years, advancements in (AI) and, more recently, in deep learning (DL) methods, have produced promising candidates for analyzing medical images. By utilizing convolutional neural networks (CNNs), a certain class of DL algorithms, we have found promising applications in hematological malignancies. These DL algorithms have automated the task of learning and discriminating salient features from features of an image without the need for handcrafted descriptors [10,11]. In hematological malignancies, CNNs have identified leukemia blasts with accuracy that exceeds those of trained professionals. However, still, the majority of studies remain either experimental or proof-of-concept, and little evidence can be found of these studies translating into practical clinical or point-of-care applications. In order to overcome these obstacles, this study presents a lightweight CNN-based model for the classification of blood smear images into benign (hematogones) and malignant classes, in addition to identifying B-ALL subtypes (Early Pre-B, Pre-B, and Pro-B). One main contribution of this study is the deployment of the trained model This providing a quick and reliable classification in real-time, thus reducing its reliance on invasive diagnostic options and associated delays with respect to diagnosis. 1.1 Overview This project is an innovative healthcare project that integrates advanced deep learning and image processing techniques to automate the detection and classification of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) from microscopic blood smear images. The system focuses on accurately identifying leukemia subtypes — Benign, Early Pre-B, Pre-B, and Pro-B — while providing calibrated confidence scores for each prediction to assist clinicians in making reliable diagnostic decisions. Graphical and textual representation of predictions such as: “Predicted: Pre-B with 82% confidence — Highly reliable.” Motivation Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a rapidly progressing and life-threatening blood cancer primarily affecting children but also present in adults. It disrupts normal blood cell formation by producing immature lymphocytes, leading to severe health complications if not diagnosed and treated early. The urgency for early and accurate diagnosis cannot be overstated, as treatment protocols and patient outcomes are highly dependent on correctly identifying the stage of disease progression. Traditionally, the diagnosis and staging of ALL rely on the manual examination of microscopic images of blood or bone marrow smears by trained hematologists. While effective, this process is inherently time-consuming, labor-intensive, and subject to inter-observer variability, especially in the early stages where morphological differences between subtypes are extremely subtle. These limitations can lead to delayed treatment, misclassification, and suboptimal care.

However, traditional diagnostic methods rely heavily on manual examination of microscopic blood smear images by pathologists, which can be time-consuming, subjective, and prone to human error. Differences in staining techniques, lighting conditions, and image quality make it difficult for human experts to maintain consistent accuracy. Furthermore, existing automated systems often focus only on classification accuracy, ignoring the confidence or reliability of their predictions. In medical applications, knowing how confident an AI model is in its decision is just as important as the prediction itself. A misclassified sample with high confidence can mislead clinicians, whereas a well-calibrated confidence estimation system can alert them to uncertain cases needing further review. Therefore, the problem addressed in this project is the development of an efficient, interpretable, and confidence-aware deep learning model capable of accurately detecting and classifying Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia from microscopic blood smear images. The model should not only predict the subtype of leukemia but also quantify its confidence level, ensuring trustworthy and explainable AI-based diagnosis. 1.3.2 Objective

Each image contains different types of white blood cells with varying shapes, sizes, and color intensities. The dataset was divided into three parts for effective training and testing: Training Set (80%) – used for model learning Validation Set (10%) – used for tuning hyperparameters Testing Set (10%) – used for final performance evaluation All images were resized to a fixed dimension of 224×224 pixels to match the input requirements of pre-trained convolutional neural networks (CNNs).

Introduction of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are advanced deep learning models inspired by the visual processing system of the human brain. They are widely used in image recognition, pattern detection, and medical diagnosis tasks. A CNN is employed to classify microscopic blood cell images into different subtypes of Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) — Benign, Early Pre-B, Pre-B, and Pro-B. Instead of training from scratch, Transfer Learning is used to improve accuracy and reduce training time. The model uses pre-trained ImageNet weights from architectures like EfficientNetB0, which have already learned general visual features (edges, shapes, colors, textures) from millions of natural images. These learned features are then fine-tuned on the leukemia dataset to detect specific patterns of lymphoblast cells. Image Segmentation in the this System In this project, image segmentation plays a key role in identifying the Region of Interest (ROI), i.e., the lymphoblast cells that are critical for diagnosing Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL). The main goal of segmentation is to remove unnecessary components such as plasma, and background noise so that the CNN can focus only on the leukemia-affected cells. To achieve this, the RGB images are first converted into the L*a*b* color space, which separates the color information into three components: L* — Lightness (brightness level), a* — Green to Red color range, b* — Blue to Yellow color range. This color model better represents how humans perceive color differences and enhances the separation between the blast cells and the background. Confidence Estimation and Calibration In medical diagnosis, it is not enough for a model to be accurate — it must also be reliable. Therefore, this project includes a confidence estimation module to evaluate how sure the model is about its predictions. Two major techniques were implemented: Temperature Scaling (TS): A post-processing calibration technique that adjusts the model’s output probabilities, ensuring that predicted confidence aligns with actual accuracy. Monte Carlo Dropout (MCD)(optional for this Project): This method estimates uncertainty by performing multiple predictions with dropout layers active during inference, helping to identify cases where the model is uncertain or confused. This approach ensures the model provides both predictions and a confidence score, allowing users and clinicians to interpret results more responsibly. These metrics collectively assess how well the model distinguishes between leukemia subtypes. Additionally, the model’s calibration quality was analyzed through reliability plots and confidence histograms. Its baseline model is our entry point, which takes in an input image using 224 ×224 x 3 dimensions. The model then extracts features throughout the layers by using multiple convolutional layers using a 3 ×3 receptive field and the mobile inverted bottleneck Conv (MBConv). Compared to other DCNNs, EfficientNetB0 scales each dimension using a fixed set of scaling coefficients. This approach surpassed other state-of-the-art models trained on the ImageNet dataset. In this stage, the ROI areas are segmented by depicting the important parts of the model. In this study, segmentation aimed to extract and display areas that are clinically significant to the clinical specialist and, therefore, the ML model. One of the goals of segmentation in this study was to eliminate and ignore unnecessary parts that are insignificant for learning models and disrupt the learning process as noise. As a way to sensitize the network to lymphoblast cells and enhance the model’s precision and reliability, the input images were segmented using a unique method, that separated the blast cells from other blood parts (erythrocytes and plasma). For blast cells’ segmentation, we used an approach based on color interval separation and color thresholding that was both successful and cost-efficient. By default, blood microscopic images in the RGB space contain three channels of red, green, and blue. Image segmentation under the clustering paradigm was employed herein. This segmentation method utilizes a robust clustering algorithm in the L*a*b color space of pixels. In this method, image segmentation is performed directly by adjusting each pixel to the corresponding cluster. This color space was originally defined by CAE and specified by the International Commission on Illumination. A lab color space is a color- opponent space with dimension L for lightness and a and b for the color opponent dimensions, based on nonlinearly compressed CIE XYZ color space coordinates. The coordinates of the Hunter 1948 L, a, b color space are L, a, and b. The nonlinear relations for L*, a*, and b* are intended to mimic the nonlinear response of the eye. Furthermore, uniform changes of components in the L*a*b* color space aim to correspond to uniform variations in perceived color, so the relative perceptual differences between any two colors in L*a*b* can be approximated by treating each color as a point in a three-dimensional (3D) space (with three components L*, a*, b*) and taking the Euclidean distance between them [8,9]. The blast cells were segregated by using this mask on the input pictures. This procedure is depicted in Fig. 7.1 for a sample.

The research integrates advanced computer vision, deep learning, and confidence calibration techniques to support medical professionals in the early and accurate detection of leukemia. The project successfully demonstrated that deep learning-based image analysis can significantly improve the speed and precision of leukemia diagnosis compared to traditional manual methods. In particular, the implementation of transfer learning models such as EfficientNetB0, ResNet50, VGG19, and MobileNetV2 allowed the system to leverage pre-trained knowledge from large-scale image datasets (ImageNet) and adapt it to specialized medical imaging data. Among these architectures, EfficientNetB0 showed the best performance in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency, making it suitable for real-time clinical applications. A major contribution of the project is the segmentation module, which isolates the region of interest (ROI) using color space conversion (LAB model) and clustering (K-means algorithm). This segmentation improves the visibility of lymphoblast cells, enabling the neural network to focus on diagnostically significant features while removing unnecessary background noise. The segmentation process not only enhances model performance but also helps in reducing computational load and training time.

Another important innovation in this project is the integration of confidence estimation techniques, such as Temperature Scaling and Monte Carlo Dropout, to assess the reliability of model predictions. Overall, the project successfully combines medical image analysis, machine learning, and interpretability techniques to develop an efficient, transparent, and clinically meaningful leukemia detection framework. It bridges the gap between automated systems and clinical diagnostics by ensuring that predictions are not only accurate but also supported by measurable confidence levels. This system can serve as a valuable tool for medical professionals, providing quick and reliable diagnostic assistance while reducing the dependency on time-consuming manual assessments. PROPOSED SYSTEM The proposed system aims to simulate and prevent external attacks—such as Denial of Service (DoS), SYN/ICMP flood, and spoofing—on sensors deployed in smart city infrastructures. Using Raspberry Pi as a lightweight testbed and [NAME] for attack simulation, the system will monitor sensor traffic in real time and detect abnormal patterns. The architecture will follow a node-based model, where sensor nodes are actively monitored for intrusion signs using network sniffing tools and detection scripts. To enhance security, the system will focus on identifying high-frequency or malformed packets using tools like hping3 and tcpdump, which will help in flagging potential DoS attacks. A Random Forest algorithm will be integrated to classify network traffic and detect SYN and ICMP flood attempts effectively. This machine learning approach will provide better detection accuracy compared to basic rule-based intrusion methods. By combining real-time traffic analysis with a lightweight Random Forest-based detection mechanism, the proposed system offers a low-cost, scalable solution for securing sensor communication in AVs and smart city environments. It ensures that even resource-constrained devices can maintain operational integrity under attack conditions, contributing to safer and more resilient smart systems.

IMPLEMENTATION 1. Data collection Collected a dataset named big data attack.csv with ~100,000 labeled samples covering four classes: ICMP_FLOOD, ICMP_NORMAL, TCP_FLOOD, and TCP_NORMAL. The dataset captures real and simulated traffic traces for robust classification across ICMP and TCP protocols. 2. Data preprocessing Cleaned the dataset by removing missing entries and outliers. Categorical fields were label-encoded and numeric features standardized using StandardScaler so all features share comparable ranges for training. 3. Feature engineering Created the crucial realtime feature rate_sec (packets per second) from packet timestamps to capture volumetric behavior. Implemented a lightweight Pi-side routine that computes rate_sec in real time from tcpdump output so the model receives live-ready features. 4. Train–test split Performed a stratified split with 85% train (≈85k) and 15% test (≈15k) to preserve class balance between attacks and normal traffic across protocols. 5.Model training Trained a RandomForestClassifier as the baseline detection model. Extracted feature-importance scores to confirm rate_sec, packet_size, and src_ip_rate as top contributors. 6. Communication & runtime program Built a lightweight communication program that runs on the Raspberry Pi and on the backend: it (a) does realtime feature extraction, (b) queries the model for predictions, and (c) sends results/alerts to the frontend UI and local mitigation module (iptables/nft/ebtables). The program is resilient to intermittent connectivity and logs all decisions. 7. Model evaluation & results On the held-out test set the model achieved ~99% accuracy with precision, recall, and F1 ≈ 0.99 across main classes. Confusion-matrix analysis shows excellent Flood vs Normal separation; distinguishing protocol specifics (TCP vs ICMP subtle cases) required additional contextual features but was acceptable for mitigation purposes. 8. Key observations & deliverables Real-time rate_sec proved decisive for volumetric attack detection. End-to-end pipeline (tcpdump → feature engine → model → mitigation) was deployed and validated in a closed testbed (Kali → Raspberry Pi).

Problem Statement Modern IoT systems like [NAME] are commonly deployed on local networks with minimal built-in security. These networks often rely on the ARP protocol for IP-to-MAC resolution, which lacks authentication. This makes them highly vulnerable to Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks via ARP spoofing, where an attacker silently intercepts communication by sending forged ARP replies. Such attacks can compromise sensitive data, redirect traffic, or inject malicious responses without detection. Traditional networks fail to identify these intrusions in real time, increasing the risk of data theft, tampering, or device manipulation — especially in critical setups like smart homes, industry, or remote monitoring environments.

Methodology The proposed system employs a multi-stage architecture integrating live network traffic monitoring, machine learning-based intrusion detection, automated alert generation, and secure event logging. The methodology focuses on simulating multiple types of network attacks (DoS and ARP spoofing) on a [NAME] and building an AI-driven defense pipeline that can detect these anomalies in real-time. Traffic data is captured during controlled attack simulations and used to train classification models using supervised machine learning. These models are then deployed on the [NAME] to continuously analyze live packets and identify deviations from normal traffic patterns. Upon detection, the system generates immediate alerts via a connected dashboard or notification system and securely logs the incident using cryptographic hash mechanisms to maintain data integrity and auditability.

Introduction Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a rapidly progressing blood cancer that mostly affects children but can also occur in adults. It leads to the overproduction of immature lymphocytes, weakening the immune system and causing serious health issues. Traditional diagnosis of ALL relies on manual examination of microscopic blood or bone marrow smear images by experts. Abstract - Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) is a serious blood cancer that causes too many immature lymphocytes to form in the bone marrow. Detecting its stages early—beginner, early, pre-leukemic, and pro-leukemic—is important for timely treatment and better outcomes. Traditional methods, which involve manually examining blood smear images under a microscope, can be slow and may lead to different results depending on who is looking. In this project, we propose a deep learning-based framework for automated white blood cell (WBC) classification and confidence estimation to identify the stages of ALL from microscopic images. The methodology involves preprocessing a publicly available dataset of labeled microscopic WBC images, followed by the implementation of (CNNs) for feature extraction and stage classification. To ensure reliability in clinical decision-making, our approach incorporates confidence estimation techniques. This enables the system not only to classify the stages but also to provide confidence levels for each prediction, aiding in trust and interpretability. Performance metrics will be evaluated to validate the model. This study aims to assist medical professionals with a robust, interpretable, and reliable tool for ALL diagnosis, ultimately contributing to faster and more accurate clinical workflows in hematopathology. Future scope includes expanding the model to multi-class cancer detection and real-time clinical deployment. Keywords— Tensorflow, Python, Confidence estimation, softmax probability, Image Classification.

Introduction B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) is a frequent type of leukemia with an age-independent incidence in people but is still more often diagnosed in children [7,8]. Timely diagnosis of malignant lymphoblasts provides an essential opportunity for the best possible treatment and prognosis, so timely identification is crucial. Invasive diagnostic analysis of the bone marrow with bone marrow aspiration (BMA) and additional analysis with bone marrow biopsy (BMB) are recognized as the gold standard in the diagnosis of leukemia, followed by immunophenotyping and analysis with flow cytometry . Although these techniques provide reliable diagnostic analysis at a high standard of care there are many difficulties associated with process including discomfort for the patient, the amount of time taken from a professional, and finances that require significant costs of healthcare resources. The invasive nature of performing procedures also adds further complications to diagnosis for each of these patients (physical discomfort for the individual and psycho-social distress) to consider, especially given that most patients affected by B-ALL are children. The microscopic examination of peripheral blood smears as a primary, non-invasive, diagnostic tool has significant drawbacks. Peripheral blood smears are comprised of many cells that must be examined individually, making the process labor intensive and susceptible to human error . Fatigue and the variability of expertise of laboratory personnel and morphology of malignant lymphoblasts compared to benign hematogones increases the chances of misclassification. Hematogones are normal B cell precursors and very similar morphologically to malignant B-ALL cells, but they are benign and require no treatment. The fact that they are indistinguishable with only morphology generally leads to confirmatory testing via flow cytometry in order to differentiate between the two cell types. This step does not only lengthen the time of diagnosis, it increases healthcare costs and dependence on resources.

Conclusion This study describes a comprehensive and sophisticated diagnostic system for automatically classifying (ALL) phases using (WBC) pictures. The method is intended to precisely detect the minute morphological shifts that take place throughout the four crucial stages of ALL—beginning, early, pre, and pro—by utilizing the abilities of deep learning, especially transfer learning with CNN architectures. To increase prediction reliability, the model uses sophisticated training tactics including data augmentation, optimization approaches like SGD with momentum, and confidence calibration utilizing techniques like temperature scaling. This improves the model's generalizability across various imaging conditions and patient demographics in addition to guaranteeing excellent accuracy and sensitivity in early-stage identification. ABSTRACT The contemporary urban landscape is currently trapped in a wasteful cycle of consumption where household goods are frequently discarded or left idle, despite having significant remaining value. This problem is worsened by a lack of trust and connectivity within local neighbourhoods, forcing residents to rely on global delivery platforms that incur high carbon footprints. EcoGrid addresses these challenges by creating a digital infrastructure that enables a community to function as a self-sustaining circular economy. By facilitating the sharing of tools, goods, and skills within a strictly hyper-local radius, the platform transforms idle assets into community resources, significantly reducing environmental impact. The technical architecture is built on a high-performance Node.js and Express.js backend, utilizing a hybrid database approach with PostgreSQL and MongoDB for seamless geospatial discovery. To move beyond traditional listing sites, EcoGrid integrates a sophisticated intelligence layer powered by Python-based Flask microservices. A Collaborative Filtering Recommendation Model built with Scikit-Learn analyses user preferences and proximity to suggest relevant items, while an autonomous AI Agent—integrated via Lang Chain and OpenAI's GPT-4o—serves as a specialized facilitator to streamline negotiations and automated item categorization. Central to the platform’s success is a Proprietary Trust Score Algorithm, which utilizes Random Forest Regressors to digitize social reliability by evaluating transaction history, verification status, and peer reviews. This model, coupled with TensorFlow-based anomaly detection for fraud prevention, creates a secure environment where users feel confident engaging in peer-to-peer exchanges. By serving the frontend via EJS and rewarding sustainable behavior with gamified Eco-Credits, the project demonstrates how modern web frameworks and machine learning can be harmonized to revive neighborly sharing. Introduction 1.1 Overview The modern economy is witnessing a significant paradigm shift from ownership to access. The sharing economy, fueled by the proliferation of smartphones, real-time location services, and digital payment systems, has demonstrated that underutilized assets can be monetized effectively between individuals without the involvement of traditional intermediaries. While global platforms like Airbnb and Uber popularized this concept in accommodation and transportation, the application of peer-to-peer sharing to everyday household items remains largely untapped, especially in the Indian context. EcoGrid is a hyper-local Consumer-to-Consumer (C2C) circular economy marketplace designed specifically for Indian users. The platform enables residents within a defined geographical radius to rent items from each other, post items available for lending, and donate unused possessions — all facilitated through a secure, smartphonefriendly web application. The application leverages the GPS capabilities of modern browsers to surface listings within a user-defined search radius (1 to 50 kilometres), allowing neighbourhood-level discovery that global platforms fail to address. The platform operates on three fundamental transaction types: Lend: A user who owns an item (e.g., a power drill, camera, or tent) lists it for rental at a price per day or per week, earning passive income from an otherwise idle asset. Rent Request (Wanted): A user who needs a specific item posts a request, signaling to nearby lenders what is needed. This creates a demand-driven discovery mechanism. Donate: A user who wishes to give away an item for free lists it as a donation for anyone nearby to claim, supporting the circular economy principle of extending product life. This model directly supports the circular economy principle — where resources are kept in use for as long as possible and the generation of waste is minimized. Instead of purchasing a power drill for a one-time home renovation project, a user can rent one from a neighbour for two days. Instead of discarding a tent after a camping trip, it can be rented out to someone planning a trek to Lonavala or Mahabaleshwar. This reduces consumption, saves money, and builds community connections.

The system is built as a full-stack MERN application with MongoDB handling geospatial data persistence, Express.js managing the REST API layer, React 18 powering the frontend SPA, and Node.js running the backend server. Socket.io provides real-time bidirectional communication for user-to-user messaging, and the Browser Geolocation API enables automatic GPS-based location detection. 1.2 Motivation The motivation for building EcoGrid stems from several converging trends and real-world problems observed in urban India: The Idle Asset Problem: Research indicates that the average Indian household owns several tools, appliances, and equipment that are used fewer than five times per year. A power drill may be purchased for one home renovation and then remain unused for years. This represents a significant economic waste when the item could be generating rental income for the owner. Affordability in Tier-2 Cities: In cities like Pune, Nagpur, and Indore, a large student and working-class population frequently needs expensive equipment — DSLR cameras for college events, projectors for presentations, camping gear for weekend trips — but cannot justify the purchase price. Rental platforms that require expensive storefronts or delivery logistics are not economically viable at this scale. Lack of Trust in P2P Transactions: The biggest barrier to peer-to-peer lending is trust. Without a reputation system, identity verification, and legal accountability, most people are reluctant to lend their belongings to strangers. EcoGrid directly addresses this through its Trust Score Algorithm, KYC verification, and legally structured digital rental agreements. Environmental Impact: Manufacturing one kilogram of consumer electronics generates approximately 70 kilograms of CO2 equivalent. By extending the useful life of existing products through sharing and reducing unnecessary new purchases, EcoGrid contributes meaningfully to environmental sustainability goals.

While individuals are willing in principle to lend or borrow items from community members, the absence of digital identity verification, formal rental agreements, payment accountability, and reputation systems makes such transactions risky and uncomfortable. Existing classified advertisement platforms like OLX allow users to post items for sale or rent, but provide no framework for agreements, payments, or accountability. There is no mechanism to verify that the renter will return the item in good condition, that the payment will be processed securely, or that either party has a history of reliable transactions. Furthermore, location-based discovery in existing platforms is rudimentary, relying on city-level filtering rather than precise GPS-based proximity search. A user in Wagholi, Pune has no way to discover items available within 2 kilometres of their home on current platforms. Therefore, the problem addressed in this project is the design and development of a comprehensive, secure, and trust-enabling C2C marketplace that provides: Real-time geolocation-based listing discovery with configurable search radius Multi-factor trust and reputation scoring that updates based on user behavior

Implement Real KYC Verification: Develop a 4-step [STUDENT_ID] that collects and validates Aadhaar numbers (using the Verhoeff checksum algorithm), PAN numbers, age, gender, and address to authenticate user identity. Create Digital Rental Agreements: Design a legally structured agreement flow with date selection, total cost calculation, e-signature support, and a full lifecycle from creation through payment, return, and review. Develop a Recommendation Algorithm: Build a weighted scoring system that ranks nearby listings based on lender trust score, listing recency, and inverse popularity to surface the most relevant and reliable options.

Express.js provides a minimal, flexible Node.js web framework with excellent middleware support for authentication (JWT), file upload (Multer), and rate limiting. React 18 with Vite offers component-based UI architecture, Context API for global state (AuthContext, MapContext), and React-Leaflet for map integration without heavy dependencies. Literature Survey 2.1 Survey Overview The domain of peer-to-peer sharing economy platforms and their enabling technologies has been extensively studied. EcoGrid draws insights from multiple research areas: trust frameworks, geospatial computing, digital identity verification, cybersecurity, and recommendation systems. 2.1.1 Peer-to-Peer Sharing Economy Platforms (2023) Observation Summary: Studies on global P2P platforms reveal three critical success factors: identity verification, reputation mechanisms, and dispute resolution infrastructure. Platforms lacking any of these three pillars consistently show lower user adoption and higher fraud rates. Research shows that KYC-verified platforms achieve 3.2× higher transaction completion rates compared to anonymous platforms. Research Gap: P2P sharing principles applied to everyday household tools and consumer electronics at the neighbourhood level in India — particularly with Aadhaar/PANbased identity verification — remain largely undocumented in academic literature. Relevance to EcoGrid: EcoGrid addresses all three success factors with KYCbased identity (Aadhaar + PAN + OTP), the Trust Score algorithm as the reputation mechanism, and digital agreements as the dispute resolution framework. 2.1.2 Reputation Systems in Online Marketplaces (2023) Observation Summary: Research on eBay’s feedback system and Airbnb’s reviews demonstrates that multi-dimensional trust scores aggregating multiple behavioral signals are significantly more resistant to manipulation than single-metric ratings. Eventdriven reputation updates (triggered by specific platform actions) outperform solicited post-transaction ratings in accuracy. Research Gap: A proactive trust score that updates in real-time based on behavioral events (return timeliness, payment speed, KYC completion) rather than only solicited reviews is not widely implemented in existing P2P platforms. Relevance to EcoGrid: The EcoGrid Trust Score is event-driven and multi-factor (11 behavioral signals), updating automatically as users complete transactions, pay, return items, and finish KYC. 2.1.3 Geospatial Search for Location-Based Services (2022)

Automated credential stuffing tools submit keystrokes in under 20ms — physically impossible for human typists whose average inter-keystroke interval is 150–200ms. Research Gap: Keystroke timing analysis as a lightweight bot detection mechanism on login forms, without requiring server-side processing or visual CAPTCHAs, is an emerging frontend security pattern. Relevance to EcoGrid: EcoGrid measures inter-keystroke intervals on the password field. Average intervals below 20ms trigger a bot flag. CHAPTER 8 Conclusions 8.1 Conclusions EcoGrid has been successfully designed, developed, and tested as a comprehensive Consumer-to-Consumer circular economy marketplace. The project demonstrates that it is technically feasible to build a hyper-local goods rental platform for India that addresses the fundamental trust, identity, and accountability challenges inherent in peerto-peer transactions. The Trust Score Algorithm proved to be the most innovative contribution, creating a dynamic, multi-factor reputation system that evolves continuously with user behavior rather than relying solely on post-transaction ratings. Eleven behavioral signals produce a holistic score that effectively captures user trustworthiness across multiple dimensions of platform participation. The KYC [STUDENT_ID] with Verhoeff Aadhaar validation and PAN format checking establishes a meaningful identity layer that distinguishes EcoGrid from anonymous classified platforms. Identity verification before platform participation creates accountability that traditional P2P platforms lack. The geospatial discovery system leveraging MongoDB’s 2dsphere indexing enables sub-100ms radius searches with multi-filter support, demonstrating the practical superiority of native database geospatial features over application-level filtering approaches. The security architecture incorporating paste-disabled passwords, keystroke timing bot detection, math CAPTCHA, and account lockout addresses modern web authentication threats comprehensively within a student project scope. The Digital Rental Agreement System formalizes informal borrowing relationships with legally structured contracts, e-signatures, payment audit trails, and condition documentation — providing a framework for dispute resolution that informal lending entirely lacks. Overall, EcoGrid represents a complete, production-ready foundation for a circular economy marketplace tailored to India’s digital identity infrastructure (Aadhaar/PAN), payment ecosystem (UPI), and mobile-first internet access patterns. The platform successfully demonstrates that everyday sharing — from a power drill to a camera to a camping tent — can be made safe, accountable, and rewarding for both parties. 8.2 Future Work SMS Gateway Integration: Integrate Fast2SMS, MSG91, or Twilio for actual OTP delivery to phones. Introduction 1.Why Insider Threats are the Most Dangerous 
Insider threats arise when a trusted employee or partner
compromises the confidentiality of the organization.
They are uniquely difficult to detect because attackers act with
legitimate credentials.
Attackers often use adaptive behaviors that circumvent static,
signature-based rules. 2.The Failure of Traditional Security 
Traditional security measures are often insufficient or ineffective
at mitigating this problem.
This necessitates a complete monitoring system that can detect
and alert on this type of intrusion in real time. 3. Increasing Organizational Risk 
There has been a significant increase in organizational insider threats over the years.
Negligent Insiders continue to be the largest threat category, though Malicious Insiders are steadily increasing.
(This chart shows the trend from 2020 to 2025).

Problem Statement Inflexibility to
Predetermined Rules Inadequate Contextualization (High FPR) Limited Real-Time Capability Offered Limited Explainability Signature-based systems and fixed predetermined rules are inherently reactive. They cannot generalize and discover new, unknown, or complex malicious activity that doesn't conform to patterns set in advance. Behavior is often reviewed in a vacuum. This review lacks consideration for the user's role, peer group networking, or the underlying organizational paradigm. This inadequate context leads to incorrect risk assessment and generates an intolerably high level of false positives (FPR), which inundates security analysts. Most solutions depend on batch processing of logs. This introduces a notable delay between a malicious activity and its detection. This delay gives insiders a grace period to fulfill their objectives and inflict damage before a response is initiated. Most machine learning systems are "black boxes". Without a simple, comprehensible explanation available for human users when an alert is produced, it diminishes analysts' confidence. This also slows investigation triage effectiveness and complicates auditing the system.

ABSTRACT AcuPath is an AI-powered Android application developed using Java and XML with Firebase Realtime Database as the backend, designed to deliver personalized exercise-based guidance for relieving common musculoskeletal pain, including back, neck, shoulder, and knee pain. The system captures user-reported pain location and intensity and conducts a structured, symptom-driven questionnaire that dynamically adapts using Agentic AI to select only the most relevant follow-up questions. Based on the collected inputs, Generative AI generates clear, user-friendly exercise routines, posture correction advice, do’s and don’ts, and safety alerts, including recommendations for medical consultation when red-flag symptoms are detected. AcuPath also integrates an AI Assistant with NLP-based intent recognition to support natural language queries and context-aware responses, along with a Video module that provides visual exercise demonstrations via embedded web content. User pain records, sessions, and recommendations are securely stored with timestamps in Firebase to enable history tracking and repeated personalized guidance, resulting in an intelligent, interactive, and accessible digital self-care solution for pain management. 8.1 Conclusion Musculoskeletal (MSK) pain, particularly affecting the lower back, neck, shoulder, and knee, represents a significant global health challenge, leading to diminished productivity, restricted physical activity, and increased healthcare burdens. While therapeutic exercises are widely recognized for their efficacy in managing these conditions, individuals frequently encounter difficulties in identifying appropriate routines, maintaining consistency, and adapting to fluctuating pain levels. Existing digital self-management tools, despite their potential, often fall short in delivering truly personalized experiences, fostering meaningful user interaction, and sustaining long-term engagement, thereby contributing to inconsistent therapeutic outcomes. In response to these critical gaps, AcuPath has been conceptualized and developed as an intelligent, Android-based application designed to revolutionize self-management for common non-emergency MSK pain conditions. Leveraging a robust architecture built with Java/XML and supported by Firebase Realtime Database, AcuPath integrates an advanced agentic AI- driven dynamic question flow. This system meticulously assesses a user's specific pain characteristics and contextual symptoms, enabling the generation of highly personalized exercise recommendations and essential safety precautions. ABSTRACT In the face of increasing urban crowd density, rising numbers of child disappearance cases, and the limitations of conventional surveillance systems, the need for intelligent and responsive safety solutions has never been more urgent. AI Lost Tech is a real-time, AI-powered surveillance and alert system designed to assist in the rapid identification and recovery of lost or unattended children in public spaces. By integrating computer vision, facial recognition, and automated risk analysis into a single unified platform, the system enhances the responsiveness and reliability of child safety infrastructure. The primary objective of AI Lost Tech is to bridge the gap between passive surveillance and active intervention by using existing CCTV feeds and advanced AI algorithms to detect, identify, and assess the presence of lost children. Through real-time object detection and face matching with missing children databases, the system can quickly flag high-risk situations and alert security personnel with precise visual and location data. The application also offers a parent-initiated alert feature, enabling families to submit missing child information directly, initiating an immediate system-wide search. To improve reliability and reduce false positives, the platform classifies cases based on context and behavior, using a simple but effective rule-based risk engine. Designed for flexibility and scalability, AI Lost Tech can operate on local servers, edge devices, or cloud infrastructure, making it suitable for deployment in railway stations, shopping malls, festivals, and smart city ecosystems. Its intuitive dashboard and real-time alert mechanism ensure that critical information reaches the right people at the right time. More than just a technical tool, AI Lost Tech strives to become a trusted safety companion in urban environments providing families, law enforcement, and public agencies with the confidence and capability to protect children through proactive, intelligent, and compassionate technology. Keywords: Lost Child Detection, Real-Time Surveillance, Face Recognition, YOLO Object Detection, Risk Classification, Automated Alert System, Smart City Security.

The longer it takes to recognize that a child is missing, the greater the risk becomes and sadly, in many cases, by the time action is taken, the opportunity for a swift and safe recovery has already passed. While most of these public places are under surveillance through CCTV camera networks, the current systems often lack the intelligence to distinguish between a child who is simply wandering alone and one who is genuinely lost and in need of immediate help. This inability to accurately assess risk can lead to two major problems: delays in response when action is urgently needed, or unnecessary panic when a child is actually safe. Both situations highlight the critical gaps in our current approach to real-time monitoring and incident classification. To address these shortcomings, we propose a smart, AI-powered system that enhances traditional surveillance infrastructure. Our platform is designed to detect lost or unattended children in real- time, analyze behaviour patterns, and classify potential risks more accurately. Our platform is designed to detect lost or unattended children in real- time, analyze behaviour patterns, and classify potential risks more accurately. By leveraging advanced computer vision techniques and facial recognition algorithms, the system can not only identify if a child appears to be lost but also compare their image with a central database of reported missing children. If a match or high-risk situation is identified, it instantly notifies on- ground security personnel with detailed alerts including location, time, and images enabling rapid and effective intervention. The motivation behind this project stems from a shared concern for child safety and the belief that technology, when used responsibly, can be a powerful force for good. Our mission is to transform passive surveillance into an active guardian capable of making intelligent decisions, reducing human error, and most importantly, saving lives.

PROPOSED SYSTEM Firstly, the system will be able to identify the child as well as the risk at real time instead of reviewing the whole CCTV footage. This system’s work will not be limited to identify the lost children but also to monitor the whole children at a particular place. And it aims that if it identifies someone to be lost then to send the alert to the local authority immediately. Second, by using the facial recognition and behaviour detection, the system can identify the child is missing or not in the database. And if someone from the crowd reports the missing report then it will provide a priority search for that person or child on basis of clothing facial recognition. Another one is to send the alert at the right time and to send the location or exact location to the local authority or security. For example, a child is identified as lost at a mall and the system has flagged then the system should give an instant alert to the admin with the particular location. One of the key features that sets this system apart from others is its risk classification mechanism, which uses a three-color signal system to indicate the safety status of a child in real time. • A Green signal appears when the system identifies that the child is accompanied or clearly safe. • A Yellow signal is displayed when the child is detected to be alone, but behavior analysis suggests that the child is calm and not in immediate danger. • A Red signal is triggered when the system detects that the child is both alone and potentially unsafe, showing signs of distress or confusion.

Abstract— Both patients and professionals alike, the growing dependence on paper-based laboratory reports poses problems, such as disjointed medical records, delayed interpretation, and trouble tracking longitudinal health data. The AI-powered healthcare platform MediSync is presented in this study. Its event-driven architecture automates the digitization and analysis of medical records. Tesseract OCR is used for dependable text extraction, and a Node.js Event Emitter pipeline is used to modularly and asynchronously coordinate sequential processing operations. GPT-4 is used for the analysis of extracted data, producing summaries that are easy for patients to understand, highlighting anomalous findings, and producing contextual insights. Users may monitor trends, track health scores, and get customized prescription reminders thanks to interactive dashboards that display processed data that are safely saved in Supabase. A useful and expandable system for connecting unprocessed medical records with useful digital health insights, MediSync combines cloud-native storage, massive language model reasoning, and established OCR technology into a single framework. Personalized medicine reminders, trend analysis, and health score tracking is all made possible by the interactive dashboards that display processed data, which are safely saved in Supabase. MediSync provides a useful and expandable solution for connecting unprocessed medical records with useful digital health insights by combining storage, large language model reasoning, and established OCR technology into a single framework. Keywords: Tesseract OCR, GPT-4, Node.js Event Emitter, Healthcare AI, [NAME], and Medical Analytics.

Introduction Many clinical workflows still rely on paper-based laboratory findings, despite the increasing digital transformation of healthcare systems. While professionals spend considerable time reconciling disparate records, patients frequently find it difficult to interpret raw values. These discrepancies may cause treatment noncompliance, delay diagnosis, and interfere with continuity of care. Technological developments in natural language processing (NLP) and optical character recognition (OCR) have demonstrated potential for the digitization and analysis of medical data [1]– [3]. The majority of currently available solutions, such as OCR engines that only extract text, reminder apps that disregard report context, or dashboards that aren't linked to clinical interpretation, are still isolated. Patients and providers are unable to take advantage of a single, patient-centered environment due to a lack of integration.

Literature Review Existing research has advanced OCR for medical reports, event-driven architectures for data pipelines, large language models for clinical interpretation, dashboards for visualization, and mobile apps for adherence. However, these solutions operate largely in isolation. This fragmentation highlights the need for an integrated, patient-centric system such as MediSync. OCR-MRD: Performance Analysis of OCR Engines for Medical Report Digitization (Batra et al., 2023) This study benchmarks the accuracy of multiple OCR engines—including Tesseract, EasyOCR, specifically on medical report datasets. It demonstrates that with appropriate preprocessing (e.g., binarization), Tesseract achieves high fidelity in extracting structured clinical data. This empirical validation underpins MediSync’s selection of Tesseract for reliable and scalable digitization. Zhang et al., 2024 — Event-Driven Architectures for Healthcare IoT: Enabling Scalable Real-Time Analytics This IEEE Access paper explores how asynchronous, event-driven microservices can efficiently handle high-frequency healthcare data from IoT devices. The findings show reductions in latency and better modularity, especially under load. The results inform MediSync’s adoption of Node.js Event Emitter to ensure non-blocking orchestration of OCR, LLM analysis, storage, and notifications. Rust et al., 2025 — Evaluation of GPT-4 for Simplifying Clinical Summaries Evaluating GPT-4’s performance on discharge summary simplification, the authors report significant gains in readability (e.g., lowering grade-level requirements) without compromising accuracy or completeness. This supports MediSync’s use of GPT-4 to generate patient-centered summaries from otherwise daunting clinical reports. Hao et al., 2024 — A GPT-Based Modeling System for Anomaly Detection in Electronic Health Records This study introduces a GPT-like model for anomaly detection in patient time-series data. The model achieves superior AUC compared to conventional algorithms and demonstrates a capability to flag novel or irregular clinical trajectories. In MediSync, this inspires extending GPT-4’s role beyond summarization to include early detection of out-of-range lab values. To ensure interpretability and early warning functionality. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE Authentication of users: Patients log in through the frontend (React + Tailwind + TypeScript). Safe access to individual health profiles. Upload of Reports: Users upload lab reports in PDF or picture formats. Backend, (NestJS) verifies. Processing OCR: Tesseract OCR extracts text and numeric values from uploaded files. Applied preprocessing (noise reduction, binarization). JSON-structured outputs for further processing. Orchestration Based on Events: Node.js Event Emitter initiates further activities. For instance, OCR completion initiates GPT-4 analysis. Allows for both parallel and asynchronous processing. Analysis of AI (GPT-4): Summarization: creates summaries that are easy for patients to understand from clinical language. Anomaly detection: highlights unusual laboratory results. The validation stage guarantees the accuracy of the data that is extracted and generated by AI. Storage of Data: Supabase stores all structured outputs, including OCR JSON, AI summaries, and anomalies. Enables offline data administration and longitudinal tracking. Dashboard and Visualization: Frontend retrieves Supabase raw and AI-enhanced results. Shows health scores, trends, and abnormalities that have been flagged in interactive charts. System of Reminders: SMS/push notifications that are scheduled using Firebase or Twilio. Promotes medication or follow-up adherence. End of Session/Logout: The user session ends with a secure logout. Data is kept secure in the Database. (Figure .2: System architecture flow chart)

RESULTS AND IMPLEMENTAION MediSync's prototype implementation shows how AI-driven interpretation, personalized dashboards, adherence mechanisms, and OCR-based digitization can all be combined into a single platform. The OCR pipeline demonstrated early performance in handling structured laboratory reports, with adaptive preprocessing methods like layout-aware text zoning and contrast modification enhancing recognition for further analysis. Simplified summaries and visual clues like color-coded health indicators helped patients understand the dashboards, while trend analytics helped professionals make decisions more quickly. MediSync prioritized continuity over traditional reporting methods by combining several reports into a single longitudinal health record. When a patient's prescription details change, the reminder module is smart enough to immediately update its alerts. This adaptability is fantastic because it makes sure patients always get the right reminders at the right time. It really boosts treatment adherence while cutting down on manual work and the risk of someone missing a dose. We ran some tests, and the system's event-driven workflow performed beautifully. Even with a lot of people using it at once, it maintained its speed, processing reports in under three seconds on average. Plus, with strong security features like encrypted storage and role-based access control, sensitive health data stays protected, which is essential for meeting all the necessary regulations. Ultimately, these results show just how special MediSync is. It's a single, comprehensive platform that seamlessly combines patient engagement, compliance, digitization, and AI analytics. The significant improvements we've seen in patient health knowledge, medication adherence, and clinical efficiency really highlight its potential to revolutionize digital healthcare. CONCLUSION FUTURE WORK This work presented MediSync, an integrated healthcare platform that unifies medical report digitization, AI-driven interpretation, visualization, and adherence support into a single framework. By combining OCR-based text extraction with large language model analysis, the system transformed complex laboratory reports into simplified, patient-friendly insights. Dashboards enabled longitudinal tracking, while adaptive reminders reinforced adherence, reducing gaps between diagnosis and action. Experimental evaluation confirmed strong OCR accuracy, effective summarization, near real-time performance, and positive user feedback, collectively validating the feasibility and impact of the approach. While the prototype demonstrates tangible improvements over fragmented existing solutions, several directions remain for future work. Integration with clinical laboratory systems could enable direct ingestion of reports, reducing manual upload. Expanding the platform to include wearable and IoT health data would provide richer longitudinal context. To strengthen reliability, specialized medical LLMs (e.g., Med-PaLM) and hybrid validation pipelines could be incorporated to reduce hallucination risks. Finally, a large-scale clinical trial is needed to rigorously evaluate outcomes such as adherence rates, patient literacy, and decision-making efficiency in real-world settings. By addressing these extensions, MediSync has the potential to evolve from a prototype into a scalable, patient-centric digital health ecosystem, bridging the gap between raw clinical data and actionable healthcare delivery.

INTRODUCTION 01 This project presents an advanced mothership–child drone system designed for autonomous target detection and strike operations. The mothership carries multiple child drones and deploys them automatically based on mission triggers. Once released, each child drone stabilizes mid-air, performs real-time target detection using onboard AI, and executes assigned actions with minimal human intervention. The system leverages swarm coordination and decentralized decision-making, ensuring mission continuity even in communication loss or adverse conditions. The approach integrates low-cost, edge-computing modules with resilient communication links to achieve practical, testable prototypes suitable for real-world scenarios.

PROBLEM STATEMENT 02 Limited Autonomy in Existing Systems:Most current drones or swarms rely heavily on manual control or centralized operation, reducing reaction speed and mission continuity during communication loss.
Lack of Integrated Mothership–Child Deployment: While DARPA, naval, and academic projects demonstrate mothership launches or swarm coordination separately, few systems combine self-triggered deployment, autonomous swarm operation, and edge-based target detection in a single, practical system.
Edge Intelligence & Resilient Operation Under Constraints: Global research emphasizes either high-cost AI platforms or simulation-based swarms. Compact, low-cost drones capable of autonomous decision-making, resilient operation under signal loss, and real-time target detection remain largely untested outside lab environments. [NAME] 03 The proposed system is an integrated aerial network designed for autonomous deployment and mission execution using a coordinated swarm mechanism. To understand its functioning clearly, the entire operation can be divided into three interconnected phases: Mothership Phase Latch System Phase Child Drone Phase 3.1 Mothership Phase Serves as the central aerial platform carrying and controlling child drones. It maintains stable flight, monitors mission parameters, and autonomously triggers the latch release upon signal loss or command input — ensuring intelligent, fail-safe drone deployment with coordinated execution. 3.2 Latch System Phase Acts as the secure intermediary between the mothership and child drones. Powered by a microcontroller and servo mechanism, it locks drones safely during flight and intelligently releases them upon trigger or signal loss — ensuring precise, automated deployment without affecting mothership stability. 3.3 Child Drone Phase Each child drone autonomously stabilizes after release, detects and tracks targets using onboard vision and sensors, and executes mission objectives such as surveillance or data capture. Designed for self-reliant operation, it ensures real-time adaptability and intelligent task completion even without mothership control.

Introduction In the age of digital transformation, government services are increasingly becoming available online. However,
navigating these services remains a significant challenge for many citizens, particularly those from rural areas
or with limited digital literacy. Applying for essential documents like income certificates, caste certificates, or
domicile proofs often involves complex procedures that vary by state and district. Information is scattered
across multiple sources, often outdated, and written in technical language that is difficult to understand.
To solve this problem, we propose GovGuideBot—an AI-powered chatbot designed to assist users in a simple
and conversational way. Using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML), the chatbot
can understand user queries, detect intent, and deliver personalized, step-by-step guidance based on the user’s
location. In addition to providing official links and document checklists, it also recommends helpful YouTube
tutorials to make the process even easier.
GovGuideBot is designed to reduce confusion, save time, and improve access to public services. It supports the
broader goal of Digital India by promoting inclusive, citizen-friendly, and transparent governance through the
power of AI. GovGuideBot: AI Chatbot for Government Document Assistance Motivation Despite the push for digital governance, many citizens still struggle to access government services effectively—
especially when applying for documents like income, caste, or domicile certificates. The lack of a centralized
platform, unclear procedures, and region-specific variations force people to rely on outdated blogs, random
YouTube videos, or repeated visits to government offices. This results in confusion, wasted time, and
frustration. The motivation behind GovGuideBot is to create a smart, AI-powered solution that simplifies this process. By
using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML), the chatbot can guide users step-by-
step through the documentation process in a conversational, user-friendly manner. It aims to reduce
dependency on intermediaries, improve digital inclusion, and support the vision of transparent and citizen-
centric governance under Digital India.

Problem Statement Citizens face difficulty in applying for government certificates due to lack of clear and
reliable information. Information varies by region and is not presented in a user-friendly way. There is no real-time assistant that can understand user queries in natural language and
provide step-by-step help. This leads to time loss, incorrect applications, and user frustration. Objective Simplify Access to Government Services – Provide citizens with an easy-to-use chatbot that
explains the process of applying for various government documents step by step.
Automate Query Understanding – Use Natural Language Processing (NLP) for intent
classification and entity recognition to automatically understand user queries without
manual keyword mapping.
Ensure Accurate and Reliable Guidance – Deliver consistent, up-to-date, and structured
responses with official links, required documents, and procedural steps for each government
service.
Enhance User Experience through Context Handling – Maintain conversation context
(intent + entities) so users can ask follow-up questions and receive personalized, continuous
assistance. Sr.

The overall workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1 and consists of seven stages... A. Fingerprint Preprocessing The input fingerprint image is first resized to a fixed
resolution of 256 × 256 pixels to ensure consistency across
samples. Contrast enhancement is performed using Contrast
Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) with clip
limit 2.0 and an 8 × 8 tile grid [22]. Gaussian smoothing
with a 5 × 5 kernel is applied to reduce sensor noise and
minor acquisition artifacts. Adaptive Gaussian thresholding
(block size 17, constant C = 4) is then employed to generate
a binary ridge map, enabling robust ridge separation under
varying illumination and contrast conditions. A 3×3 elliptical
morphological closing kernel fills small ridge gaps. Finally,
morphological skeletonization [23] is applied to reduce ridge
structures to a single-pixel width, facilitating accurate minutiae
detection [1]. B. Rotation-Invariant Minutiae Feature Extraction Minutiae points, specifically ridge endings (crossing number
CN= 1) and bifurcations (CN= 3), are extracted from the
skeletonized fingerprint image using the crossing number
method. For each ridge pixel, the number of transitions be-
tween foreground and background pixels in its 8-connected
neighborhood is computed. Minutiae points within a 10-pixel
border margin are discarded to reduce edge artifacts. To overcome the spatial sensitivity of grid-based approaches
under finger rotation and translation, the detected minutiae are
encoded using a rotation-invariant radial-angular histogram.

VI. SECURITY ANALYSIS This section analyzes the security properties of the pro- posed QuMetric framework with respect to biometric template protection, resistance to classical and quantum attacks, and potential attack surfaces. A. Biometric Template Irreversibility A fundamental requirement of secure biometric systems is
template irreversibility, ensuring that original biometric traits
cannot be reconstructed from stored data. In the proposed
framework, fingerprint minutiae are transformed into a radial-
angular histogram, binarized, and subsequently protected using
SHA-256 hashing combined with secret key binding. Since
cryptographic hash functions are one-way, recovering the
original biometric features from the stored protected represen-
tation is computationally infeasible. As a result, even if the
database of protected templates is compromised, an attacker
cannot reconstruct the original fingerprint image or minutiae
pattern [2], [3]. B. Resistance to Template Leakage Attacks Traditional biometric systems often store feature vectors
or transformed templates that may leak sensitive biometric
information. The proposed approach stores only a hashed
and key-bound representation. The implementation of key
binding also guarantees that the same biometric inputs do not
generate identical stored representations when distinct keys
are employed, reducing cross-matching assaults across several
databases and improving user privacy [2]. C. Security Against Quantum-Capable Adversaries The suggested framework is developed based on the premise
of a quantum-enabled opponent equipped with polynomial-
time quantum access algorithms. Instead of relying on classical
public-key cryptography, which may be vulnerable to quantum
attacks [5], the system assumes secure key generation via QKD
or a post-quantum key exchange mechanism [6]. The crypto-
graphic hash function used for template protection remains
secure against known quantum attacks, providing a quadratic
rather than exponential speedup for brute-force attempts [6]. D. Protection of Quantum Encoded States

Instead of relying on classical public-key cryptography, which may be vulnerable to quantum attacks [5], the system assumes secure key generation via QKD or a post-quantum key exchange mechanism [6]. The crypto- graphic hash function used for template protection remains secure against known quantum attacks, providing a quadratic rather than exponential speedup for brute-force attempts [6]. D. Protection of Quantum Encoded States The quantum states used for similarity evaluation are gen-
erated dynamically during authentication and are not perma-
nently stored. Even if an adversary intercepts the quantum-
encoded states, the no-cloning theorem prevents perfect du-
plication of unknown quantum states [9]. Furthermore, the
encoded quantum states represent compressed and protected
biometric features rather than raw biometric data, limiting the
potential impact of quantum state leakage. E. Hardware IP Core Security The FIR filter activation key is derived from the biometric
key κ and is never stored in hardware. Physical access to
the device without successful biometric authentication yields
only 0xERROR_LOCKED. This extends logic locking [12]
and active hardware metering [21] with the additional prop-
erty that the activation credential is biometric and quantum-
authenticated, rather than a static design-time secret. F. Attack Surface and Limitations The proposed security analysis assumes trusted fingerprint
acquisition hardware and does not address sensor-level attacks
such as spoofing or presentation attacks. Additionally, while
the framework ensures strong template protection and post-
quantum security, the current implementation relies on clas-
sical simulation of quantum operations. Practical deployment
on real quantum hardware may introduce noise-related vulner-
abilities that require additional error mitigation strategies [10].
These aspects are identified as important directions for future
work. VII. LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK While the proposed QuMetric framework demonstrates
strong authentication performance on the SOCOFing dataset,
several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the QKD key
distribution is simulated; integration with a physical QKD
channel over fiber or free-space optical link is required for
deployment. The BB84 protocol and its successors have been
demonstrated over metropolitan fiber networks, providing a
clear path toward physical integration [24].

WORK While the proposed QuMetric framework demonstrates strong authentication performance on the SOCOFing dataset, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the QKD key distribution is simulated; integration with a physical QKD channel over fiber or free-space optical link is required for deployment. The BB84 protocol and its successors have been demonstrated over metropolitan fiber networks, providing a clear path toward physical integration [24]. Second, the current implementation employs fixed block-
averaging compression to accommodate qubit constraints.
Even though this method permits execution utilizing 12 qubits,
adaptive and learning-oriented compression techniques could
enhance differentiation at the expense of increased quantum
resource usage.Third, the security analysis assumes trusted
fingerprint acquisition hardware and does not address presen-
tation attacks or sensor spoofing. Integrating liveness detection
and multimodal biometric fusion within the proposed frame-
work represents an important direction for future research. Finally, although the proposed approach is designed for
NISQ devices, all experiments are performed using classical
simulation. Future work will focus on deploying the frame-
work on real quantum hardware and analyzing the impact
of noise, decoherence, and gate imperfections on biometric
similarity evaluation. Replacing the crossing-number minutiae extractor with NIST NBIS mindtct [28] is expected to
further reduce EER toward the sub-5% range. VIII. CONCLUSION This paper presented QuMetric, a hybrid post-quantum
fingerprint authentication framework that integrates classical
biometric template protection with quantum-assisted similarity
computation and hardware IP core locking. Unlike exist-
ing approaches that directly encode raw biometric data into
quantum states, the proposed method emphasizes template
irreversibility and post-quantum security by applying QKD-
derived key binding prior to quantum processing. A rotation-
invariant radial-angular minutiae histogram addresses the spa-
tial sensitivity of prior grid-based approaches under realistic
finger placement variation. To address the constraints of cur-
rent quantum hardware, protected biometric representations
are compressed and encoded using a 12-qubit angle-based
quantum circuit.

ABSTRACT Quantum computing is updating from theory toward practical capability, and that shift was direct consequences for how we can protect digital systems especially in healthcare, where data is sensitivity is high and device lifespans are long. The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) is now a core part of real life modern clinical workflows: wearables, bedside monitors, and implantable devices continuously stream patient vitals to remote servers. Most of these systems still depend on RSA or Elliptic Curve Cryptography for securing that traffic, which is not secure right now. Both schemes can be broken by Shor's algorithm [1] once a sufficiently large quantum computer exists, which makes the current trust model in IoMT a temporary one. This project responds to that gap. We have built a hybrid cryptographic framework for IoMT in which post quantum primitives sit alongside conventional symmetric encryption [3], [4] rather than replacing it outright. CRYSTALS Kyber [3] used to handles the key exchange step as a lattice based KEM, CRYSTALS Dilithium [4] signs for every outgoing packet for authenticity, and AES 256 GCM [7], [8] does the bulk encryption for security, the latter is chosen because symmetric ciphers remain practical even on small size microcontrollers. The hardware side is runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico W [19] with attached pulse oximeter and temperature sensors to get readings. Rather than forcing each medical device to perform Kyber and Dilithium operations directly, we do route everything through a secure gateway that takes load of the cryptographic. This way, hospitals do not have chance to swap out existing devices to gain quantum resistant protection. A React + TypeScript dashboard, backed by Supabase[18], handles cloud storage, real time visualization, and user access control. Test is runs on the prototype show that signed encrypted packets are travel end to end without breaking real time monitoring, and the added latency from the PQC layer stays within a few milliseconds per session. The result is a working proof of quantum safe IoMT to achievable today, on cheap hardware and software, without waiting for the next threat to mature.

1.2 Problem Statement IoMT has changed patient care dramatically, but this convenience comes with a hidden cost. Most devices today still rely on RSA or ECC, which work fine against current attackers. The trouble is, a future quantum computer could crack these algorithms [1] in seconds. In healthcare, a patient's records can stay sensitive for decades, so an attacker could "harvest now and decrypt later" using quantum hardware that experts say may arrive in the next ten to fifteen years. To make matters worse, medical sensors are tiny, power starved, and have barely enough memory to run their basic functions they cannot handle heavy crypto on their own. You simply cannot drop a full post quantum library onto a wearable that already struggles to last a week on a coin cell battery. This project solves that problem with a hybrid approach. I moved the hard post quantum work (Kyber for key exchange and Dilithium for signatures [4] ) to a simple Raspberry Pi Pico W [19] gateway, while the sensor itself only does lightweight AES GCM encryption. The gateway handles the heavy lifting, so the existing medical devices do not need any hardware upgrades or costly re certification. The secured data then goes to a cloud dashboard built with React and Supabase[18], giving clinicians real time visibility. The result is a practical, quantum safe IoMT system that can be deployed today without ripping out the sensors that hospitals already rely on.

This helped us see why moving to post-quantum cryptography is not just a fancy idea but a real necessity for keeping patient data safe in the long run. Design a gateway-centric intermediary layer that offloads all the heavy post-quantum work. Since updating the firmware on medical devices that are already deployed in hospitals is almost never practical, we made the gateway do the heavy lifting. It runs a lightweight Python service that handles Kyber encapsulation/decapsulation, Dilithium signing and verification, [3], [4] and AES-GCM encryption/decryption. The endpoint sensors see a simple, legacy-compatible interface, so no firmware updates or expensive re-certification are needed. This gives the whole network a quantum-resistant security perimeter without touching the existing hardware. Build a secure cloud backend that stores authenticated data safely and can handle multiple users querying it at the same time.
