Traditional manual audits are costly, time-consuming, and error-prone, while enterprise compliance tools are often inaccessible due to high costs and technical complexity. This gap has created a clear need for an efficient, accessible, and scalable compliance solution. Project COMPASS aims to address this need by providing an AI-powered, web-based platform that automates clause-level analysis of privacy policies against GDPR requirements. Built on a FastAPI microservices architecture, it leverages Legal-BERT NLP models and rule-based logic to deliver comprehensive compliance scores, risk assessments, and human-readable explanations mapped directly to GDPR articles. Users can easily upload privacy policies in various formats (PDF, URL, or text) and receive real- time analysis without data persistence, preserving their own data protection standards. The project democratizes compliance verification by identifying missing mandatory disclosures, vague language, and potential compliance gaps—empowering organizations to conduct preliminary assessments without needing specialized legal expertise. With its privacy-by-design approach, semantic analysis, and modular architecture, COMPASS also supports future expansion to frameworks like India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act and other sector-specific regulations. It introduces core challenges, project objectives, and the motivations driving the development of an advanced, explainable monitoring system that bridges practical security and technological innovation.

Introduction Insider threats—malicious or careless behavior by trusted individuals—continue to be among the most destructive and most difficult-to-detect threats facing today's enterprises. In contrast to malicious outsiders who need to penetrate a perimeter, insiders 2 take advantage of approved avenues, integrate perfectly with normal organizational processes, and can adapt their techniques according to prevailing security measures. This presents an intricate security problem where the attacker is already inside the trusted environment, making many common defenses moot. The urgent need is not just for better algorithms, but for unified, deployable systems that can ingest massive real time data streams and deliver actionable, trusted insights. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a novel engineering and analytical framework that moves beyond fragmented algorithms to deliver a complete, production-ready solution. Our primary contribution lies in the synergistic integration of hybrid detection, dynamic contextualization, multi-layered explainability (XAI), and enterprise governance controls (privacy and real-time performance) into a single, cohesive Insider Threat Detection System.

Problem Statement Existing and modern methods for insider threat detection are usually unsuccessful because they possess four habitual shortcomings that confine their functional efficiency: Inflexibility to CBIR-Based Rules. Signature-based systems and fixed ahead-of-time predetermined rules are inherently reactive. They cannot generalize and discover new, unknown, or complex malicious activity that doesn't conform to predetermined pat terns. Inadequate Contextualization. Behavior is often reviewed in a vacuum, without con sideration for the effect that the obligations of the user, peer group networking, or the underlying organizational paradigm may have. This inadequate contextualization accounts for much incorrect risk assessment and generates an intolerably high level of false positives, thereby inundating security analysts. Limited Real-Time Capability. Most solutions are dependent on batch processing of logs, thus introducing a notable delay between a malicious activity and its detection. The delay gives insiders a grace period during which they are able to fulfill their objectives and inflict a great amount of damage before a response is initiated. Offered Limited Explainability. Among the crucial obstacles for real-world practical use of most machine learning systems is that they are "black boxes." Without a simple, comprehensible explanation available for human users when an alert is produced, that diminishes analysts' confidence, slows investigation triage effectiveness, and complicates auditing the system. Project Objectives The main goals of this study are to: Create a hybrid, behavior-based pipeline that captures complementary aspects of insider risk by blending statistical, pattern-based, and contextual anomaly detection models. Provide real-time scoring and alerting with dynamic, peer-group-based thresh olds that adjust according to organizational norms and sharply cut down false positive rates. Offer multi-layer explainability that renders all risk decisions open, auditable, and actionable for security analysts by revealing feature attributions, graph insights, and peer comparisons. Integrate privacy, security, and governance controls into the whole data lifecycle, from collection to storage and analysis. Autoencoder (Behavioral Pattern Detection): Autoencoders are neural network architectures designed to learn compressed representations of input data. In the Insider Threat Detection System, Autoencoders are used for detecting behavioral anomalies by learning normal user activity patterns and identifying deviations through reconstruction error. Input: The Autoencoder receives input as sequential behavioral event data representing user activity patterns over time windows. Features include event types, frequencies, temporal characteristics, and resource access patterns. Operation: The Autoencoder learns to compress and reconstruct normal behavioral patterns through its encoder-decoder architecture. During inference, it attempts to reconstruct incoming behavioral sequences. High reconstruction error indicates that the observed behavior significantly deviates from learned normal patterns. Output: The output of the Autoencoder is the reconstruction error metric, which quantifies how well the model can recreate the observed behavior. Higher reconstruction error signals anomalous behavior that doesn't match normal user patterns. The preprocessing pipeline feeds sequential behavioral data representing user activity patterns over temporal windows to the Autoencoder model. This deep learning architecture specializes in learning compressed representations of normal user behavior through its encoder-decoder structure. The encoder layers progressively compress input behavioral sequences into a lower-dimensional latent space that captures essential activity patterns. The decoder layers then attempt to reconstruct the original sequence from this compressed representation. During training on normal user activities, the model learns to accurately recreate typical behavioral patterns. However, when presented with anomalous insider threat behaviors during inference, the reconstruction quality deteriorates significantly. The reconstruction error—measured as the difference between input and reconstructed sequences—serves as the primary anomaly signal. High reconstruction error indicates that the observed behavior deviates substantially from learned normal patterns. Results are transmitted to the risk fusion layer, a component that further refines threat detection through integration with statistical and contextual signals. Finally, the dashboard delivers these behavioral anomaly scores to analysts in an easily interpretable format with detailed explanations. This architecture empowers security teams to detect non-linear behavioral deviations that traditional rule-based systems miss, promoting early identification of insider threats and proactive organizational security management. Conclusion The Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System represents a significant advancement in the field of organizational cybersecurity and security operations. By seamlessly integrating hybrid machine learning models with explainable AI technologies, it offers continuous behavioral monitoring and flexible threat detection methods, empowering security analysts to take proactive steps in safeguarding organizational assets. This innovative system bridges the gap between complex machine learning capabilities and practical security operations, allowing for early insider threat detection, ultimately reducing data breach incidents and financial losses. The real-time insights, analyst-friendly dashboard interface, and transparent explainability features provided by the system have the potential to revolutionize intelligent, data-driven security operations. The hybrid detection approach combining Isolation Forest for statistical analysis, Autoencoder for behavioral patterns, and Graph Analytics for contextual relationships achieves superior accuracy while maintaining low false positive rates. The system's sub-100ms latency and throughput exceeding 1,000 events per minute demonstrate its capability for enterprise-scale deployments. In conclusion, the Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System is not just a solution but a stepping stone towards the future of intelligent security operations and early threat intervention. Its future scope promises broader accessibility, continuous improvement in detection algorithms, and integration with enterprise security ecosystems, empowering organizations to proactively manage insider risks and reduce the burden of security incidents on enterprise operations worldwide.

Future Scope The future of the Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System holds strong potential for both technical and organizational growth: Scalability, Enterprise Adoption & Integration: Expanding deployment to organizations of all sizes—including multi-tenant large enterprises and MSSP partners—will be supported by optimizing for cloud-native platforms (AWS, Azure, GCP) and offering flexible APIs for integration with SIEM, IAM, and SOAR systems. Ongoing improvements in scalability (distributed processing, GPU acceleration) and adaptive architecture (auto-scaling microservices, role-based dashboard access) will enable seamless, efficient operation across both small and global enterprises. Advanced Models, Analytics & Multi-Modal Signals: Continuous research and development will further enhance detection capabilities. Future efforts include training on larger and more diverse behavioral datasets, integrating advanced methods like transformer models and graph neural networks, and leveraging federated learning for collaborative security across organizations. Enriching the system with threat intelligence feeds, predictive analytics, and multi-modal event signals (such as email, code repository, and physical access data) will support comprehensive and proactive risk management. Adaptive Learning & Continuous Improvement: Integrating adaptive and continuous learning mechanisms—such as automatic model updating based on analyst feedback, policy changes, or organizational restructuring—will maintain effectiveness as insider tactics and business environments evolve. Feedback loops and reinforcement learning will ensure models remain responsive, accurate, and aligned with real-world security priorities.

ABSTRACT The Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Authentication System is a cryptographic solution 
designed to verify user identities without revealing any sensitive information, such as 
passwords or personal data, during the authentication process. This system leverages the 
principles of zero knowledge proofs to enhance both security and privacy in digital 
communication and access control mechanisms. Traditional authentication systems often rely on password-based verification, which poses 
significant security risks, including phishing, credential stuffing, and data breaches. With the 
increasing concern over data privacy and the rising number of cyber-attacks, there is a 
growing demand for authentication methods that ensure high security while preserving user 
privacy. Zero-Knowledge Proofs, a concept from theoretical cryptography, provide a solution 
by allowing one party to prove to another that a statement is true without conveying any 
additional information. The primary purpose of the ZKP Authentication System is to develop a robust and privacy 
preserving authentication mechanism that eliminates the need for transmitting or storing 
sensitive user credentials. This system significantly reduces the attack surface for hackers 
and enhances user trust in digital platforms. Its significance lies in its potential application 
across various domains, including secure banking, blockchain-based systems, secure voting, 
and privacy-focused web applications. Keywords : Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) ,Secure Authentication ,Privacy-Preserving 
Protocols , Cryptographic Security, Identity Verification

INTRODUCTION This project aims to implement a Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Authentication System that 
allows users to log in securely without revealing their password to the server. The system 
generates a random number and combines it with the password to create a proof, which is 
then verified by the server using a simple mathematical challenge. Traditional login systems require users to send and store passwords on the server, which 
exposes them to risks like hacking, phishing, and data breaches. Zero Knowledge Proof is a 
cryptographic method where a user can prove they know a secret without actually revealing it, 
making it a promising solution for secure authentication. The purpose of this project is to build a secure and privacy-preserving authentication 
mechanism. It removes the need to store sensitive information on the server, reduces the risk 
of password theft, and enhances user trust. By using simple random numbers and mathematical 
operations, this system is easy to implement and demonstrates the core idea of ZKP in a 
practical way. This project implements a basic version of ZKP authentication for educational and 
demonstration purposes. A random number is generated, combined with a password (locally), 
and a challenge is sent to the server. The server verifies the user's identity without storing or 
knowing the original password. This innovation aligns with the growing need for passwordless login systems, preserving 
privacy while maintaining strong authentication.

PROPOSED SYSTEM The proposed system introduces a Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) based authentication 
mechanism that allows a user to log in without sending or storing their password on the 
server. This is achieved through a challenge-response process using a randomly generated 
number and simple mathematical operations. In the system, the user enters their password on the client side. A random number (also 
known as a nonce) is generated by the system during each login attempt. This password and 
random number are combined using a simple logic (e.g., addition) to generate a ZKP proof, 
which is then sent to the server. The password is never transmitted or stored, ensuring 
privacy and security. The server receives the proof and issues a challenge to the client — such as verifying the

result of a mathematical operation based on the same random number. If the user correctly 
responds to the challenge (based on their original secret and the random number), the server 
grants access. Otherwise, access is denied. This system demonstrates the core idea of zero-knowledge proof — proving knowledge of 
a secret without revealing the secret itself. It is simple, educational, lightweight, and 
highly relevant in the context of modern, secure authentication systems.

ABSTRACT Secure authentication has become a critical concern in modern cybersecurity systems due to the rapid growth of digital financial services and stateless web application technologies. JSON Web Tokens (JWTs), widely used for stateless authentication, rely on pseudo-random keys generated through mathematical algorithms. These keys may become vulnerable to future quantum computing attacks, particularly under the “Harvest Now, Decrypt Later” threat model, where adversaries collect encrypted data today and decrypt it once quantum capabilities mature. The predictability of classical key generation methods increases exposure to large-scale attacks, especially in microservices-based and zero-trust architectures. To address these challenges, a Quantum Seeded Dynamic JWT Authentication Framework is proposed. The framework integrates a quantum entropy source generated through a quantum simulation technique to produce high-entropy, non-deterministic signing keys for JWTs. This approach enhances randomness and significantly reduces predictability compared to classical pseudo-random generators. To mitigate quantum generation delays and maintain authentication response times, an entropy pooling mechanism is introduced, ensuring continuous availability of secure keys without performance degradation. The architecture further incorporates a Redis-based key vault system that enables rapid and automated key rotation, thereby minimizing the exposure window in the event of key compromise. An adaptive quantum rotation mechanism dynamically adjusts token validity based on a calculated threat score, strengthening resilience in high-risk scenarios. Additionally, a hybrid fail-safe strategy ensures uninterrupted service by seamlessly switching to classical entropy sources if the quantum source becomes unavailable. Introduction 1.1 Overview In the contemporary landscape of distributed systems, microservices, and cloud- native applications, robust identity verification and session management have become the most critical pillars of cybersecurity. Traditional stateful authentication models, which rely on server-side session data, have largely been superseded by stateless authentication mechanisms. Among these, JSON Web Tokens (JWT) have emerged as the de facto standard for transmitting trusted, verifiable claims between interacting parties across a network. A standard JWT comprises a header, a payload containing user claims, and a signature that ensures the data's integrity. However, the foundational security of any cryptographic system including JWT relies heavily on the unpredictability and absolute secrecy of the keys used to sign the tokens. Modern authentication frameworks predominantly generate these cryptographic keys using Classical Pseudo-Random Number Generators (PRNGs). PRNGs rely on deterministic algorithms and systemic entropy sources (such as CPU temperature or keystroke timings) to simulate randomness. While sufficient for rudimentary security, these mathematically generated sequences are not fundamentally unpredictable. Furthermore, existing JWT ecosystems often default to utilizing long-lived, static secrets or rely on infrequent programmatic key rotation, leaving the underlying architecture susceptible to brute-force techniques, key-guessing attacks, and sophisticated side-channel vulnerabilities. 1.2 Motivation The rapid advancement in computational power, exacerbated by the looming advent of usable quantum computers, poses a severe threat to classical cryptographic paradigms. If malicious actors acquire high-performance computing capabilities or algorithms capable of deciphering pseudo-randomly generated secrets, standard JWT architectures can be trivially compromised. Furthermore, human error remains one of the largest attack vectors in modern software engineering. Static signing secrets are frequently hardcoded, accidentally pushed to public version-control repositories, or poorly managed by centralized secret managers. It is implemented as a Python-based service that communicates with IBM Quantum systems through Qiskit APIs to generate true random values using quantum circuits. In case quantum resources are unavailable, it automatically switches to a secure classical random generator to ensure uninterrupted key production. 2. Entropy Pool Management Module: The Entropy Pool Management Module is responsible for maintaining a Redis-based pool of cryptographic keys. It operates using a FIFO approach where keys are inserted and consumed in sequence using Redis commands. The module monitors pool capacity using predefined thresholds to ensure optimal availability. When Redis is unavailable or empty, a local in-memory fallback mechanism ensures continuity. This design guarantees that token generation processes do not experience delays or interruptions. 3. Ephemeral Key Lifecycle Management Module: The Ephemeral Key Lifecycle Management Module manages short-lived keys used for signing JWTs. Each key is stored in Redis with a unique identifier and an expiration time aligned with the token’s validity. Once the time-to-live expires, Redis automatically removes the key, preventing reuse. This ensures that keys exist only for a limited duration, enhancing security. Introduction Security Operations Center (SOCs) play a critical role in monitoring and responding to cybersecurity threats using tools such as SIEM, IDS/IPS, firewalls, and endpoint security solutions. These tools generate a large volume of alerts on a daily basis, many of which are false positives or low-risk events. As a result, security analysts are often overwhelmed, leading to alert fatigue and delayed threat response. The proposed system focuses on introducing an intelligent alert prioritization mechanism that assists SOC analysts by automatically classifying and ranking alerts based on risk. By applying artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques, the system aims to improve alert visibility, reduce noise, and enhance SOC operational efficiency. Motivation With the rapid increase in cyberattacks and digital infrastructure complexity, SOC teams are facing an unprecedented volume of security alerts. Traditional rule-based alerting mechanisms rely primarily on static severity levels, which are insufficient to accurately represent real-world risk. Manual alert triage is time-consuming, prone to human error, and does not scale with increasing alert volume. This motivates the need for an intelligent, data-driven approach that can automatically prioritize alerts and assist analysts in focusing on high-risk security incidents.

Problem Statement Modern SOC environments generate thousands of alerts daily from multiple security tools. A significant portion of these alerts are repetitive, false positives, or low-priority events. Investigating every alert manually leads to alert fatigue, reduced analyst productivity, and delayed response to genuine threats. Existing alert prioritization techniques are mostly rule-based and lack adaptability. Therefore, there is a need for an intelligent system that can analyze alert patterns, assign risk-based priorities, and reduce alert noise to enhance threat monitoring in SOCs.

1. Introduction
Privacy-Preserving Cyber Threat Detection using Federated Learning aims to design a secure and cooperative cybersecurity system capable of identifying cyber threats without revealing sensitive organizational data. With the increasing frequency of cyberattacks such as malware infections, phishing scams, ransomware incidents, and network intrusions, there is a growing demand for intelligent and adaptive threat detection mechanisms.
Traditional cybersecurity solutions rely heavily on centralized data collection and analysis, which poses significant risks related to data privacy, security breaches, and regulatory non-compliance. Organizations are often reluctant to share raw security data due to confidentiality concerns and legal restrictions.
Federated Learning offers a decentralized machine learning approach where multiple organizations collaboratively train a shared detection model while retaining their data locally. In this framework, each organization trains the model on its own cybersecurity data and shares only encrypted model updates rather than sensitive raw information. This ensures that confidential data such as system logs, network traffic, and user activity remains protected within local environments.
The proposed system focuses on achieving high detection accuracy while maintaining strong privacy guarantees. By incorporating privacy-preserving techniques, the framework supports compliance with data protection regulations such as GDPR. Overall, the project promotes trusted collaboration among organizations to strengthen cyber defense without compromising data security. Key Features:

ABSTRACT Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental condition that requires early and accurate detection for timely intervention and improved quality of life. Traditional diagnostic procedures are time-consuming, subjective, and require continuous expert evaluation, making them less scalable for large populations. This project proposes an intelligent Deep Learning based Autism Prediction System that integrates multimodal data sources including questionnaire responses, speech audio, facial video expressions, and textual behavioral descriptions to provid9e accurate and automated autism risk assessment. The proposed system utilizes advanced deep learning architectures to extract and learn meaningful behavioral patterns from diverse modalities. Transformer-based BERT models are employed to analyze textual inputs and questionnaire narratives, enabling contextual understanding of behavioral symptoms. Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks (CRNN) are applied to speech audio signals to detect vocal anomalies associated with autism, while CNN-based deep vision models analyze facial expressions and micro-movements from video inputs to identify visual behavioral markers. These multimodal features are fused to form a unified representation, which is further processed using deep neural networks to classify individuals into autism risk categories such as Low, Medium, and High Risk. The system not only delivers high predictive accuracy but also provides probability-based confidence scores to support clinical decision-making. By automating multimodal autism screening, the proposed framework significantly reduces manual dependency, improves early detection capability, and enables scalable deployment in healthcare and educational environments. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of multimodal deep learning models in enhancing autism prediction and contributes towards the development of reliable, accessible, and intelligent healthcare diagnostic solutions. System Architecture of CareAI The CareAI system is a multimodal deep learning–based healthcare framework designed to predict autism risk by analyzing diverse behavioral inputs. It integrates Deep Learning, Multimodal Analysis, and Dynamic Fusion Intelligence into a unified system. Figure. 6.1. CareAI System Architecture Diagram Overall System Overview The architecture consists of five main layers that work together in a coordinated way: i. User Input & Data Collection Layer This layer collects behavioral data from users through the web interface. It includes questionnaire responses, speech recordings, facial images, short videos, and textual inputs. The data can be either uploaded or captured using devices such as a webcam and microphone. ii. Data Preprocessing Layer This layer processes raw multimodal data to improve quality and consistency. It includes tasks such as noise removal, normalization, feature extraction, encoding of categorical values, and conversion of raw inputs into model-compatible formats such as Mel-spectrograms for audio and tensors for images. iii. Deep Learning Analysis Layer This layer consists of multiple specialized deep learning models: CNN models analyze facial images CRNN and LSTM models process speech signals BERT transformer models analyze textual inputs CRNN models analyze video sequences MLP models process questionnaire data Each model independently extracts meaningful behavioral features from its respective modality. iv. Dynamic Fusion Layer This layer integrates features from all deep learning models using a fusion neural network. It assigns importance weights to each modality and combines them into a unified feature representation. The system is designed to handle missing inputs by adapting weights dynamically. v. Prediction & Web Interface Layer The final layer generates autism risk predictions (Low, Medium, High Risk) along with confidence scores. The results are displayed through a user-friendly web interface built using Flask, enabling real-time and remote screening. Conclusion The increasing prevalence of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and the critical importance of early diagnosis have created a strong need for intelligent, scalable, and accessible screening solutions. Traditional diagnostic methods rely heavily on manual clinical evaluations, behavioral observations, and expert interpretation, which are often time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale across large populations, especially in rural and resource-constrained environments. To address these challenges, the CareAI framework integrates Deep Learning, Multimodal Behavioral Analysis, and Dynamic Fusion Intelligence to create a more advanced and adaptive autism screening system. The platform not only predicts autism risk by analyzing diverse behavioral inputs such as text, speech, facial expressions, video patterns, and questionnaire responses using models like CNN, CRNN, LSTM, and BERT, but also combines these insights through a dynamic fusion network to improve overall prediction reliability. The system is designed to handle real-world scenarios through missing-modality awareness, ensuring that predictions can still be generated even when some inputs are unavailable. Additionally, the deployment of the system as a web-based platform enables real-time and remote screening, making it accessible to parents, caregivers, and healthcare professionals. Together, these capabilities demonstrate how combining intelligent prediction, multimodal understanding, adaptive fusion, and scalable deployment can significantly enhance the effectiveness and accessibility of autism screening systems, moving toward a more reliable, data-driven, and inclusive digital healthcare approach. 8.2 Major Findings and Outcomes From the experimental evaluation and system implementation, the following findings emerged: i. 8.3 Future Scope While CareAI achieved strong performance across multimodal datasets, there are several areas for future improvement and expansion: • Integration with Explainable AI (XAI): Incorporating techniques such as SHAP and LIME can enhance transparency by explaining how different features contribute to autism risk predictions. • Advanced Deep Learning Models: Using architectures such as Vision Transformers (ViT), Graph Neural Networks (GNN), or multimodal transformers can further improve detection of complex behavioral patterns. • Real-Time Edge Deployment: Deploying CareAI on edge devices like smartphones or embedded systems can enable faster and offline screening capabilities. • Federated Learning Implementation: Applying federated learning can allow model training across distributed datasets while preserving user privacy and reducing data-sharing risks. • Expanded Dataset Diversity: Incorporating larger and more diverse datasets from different age groups, languages, and regions can improve model generalization and reliability. • User Interface Enhancement: Developing interactive dashboards and detailed reporting systems can improve usability and support better clinical decision-making. Summary: In summary, CareAI represents a significant advancement in autism screening by integrating Deep Learning, Multimodal Analysis, and Dynamic Fusion into a unified intelligent healthcare framework. By accurately analyzing diverse behavioral inputs, providing reliable predictions, and enabling real-time remote screening, the system enhances both early detection and accessibility. This integrated approach not only improves diagnostic support but also promotes scalability, adaptability, and inclusiveness—key factors required for the next generation of intelligent and data-driven healthcare systems.

Abstract— Both patients and professionals alike, the growing dependence on paper-based laboratory reports poses problems, such as disjointed medical records, delayed interpretation, and trouble tracking longitudinal health data. The AI-powered healthcare platform MediSync is presented in this study. Its event-driven architecture automates the digitization and analysis of medical records. Tesseract OCR is used for dependable text extraction, and a Node.js Event Emitter pipeline is used to modularly and asynchronously coordinate sequential processing operations. GPT-4 is used for the analysis of extracted data, producing summaries that are easy for patients to understand, highlighting anomalous findings, and producing contextual insights. Users may monitor trends, track health scores, and get customized prescription reminders thanks to interactive dashboards that display processed data that are safely saved in Supabase. A useful and expandable system for connecting unprocessed medical records with useful digital health insights, MediSync combines cloud-native storage, massive language model reasoning, and established OCR technology into a single framework. Personalized medicine reminders, trend analysis, and health score tracking is all made possible by the interactive dashboards that display processed data, which are safely saved in Supabase. MediSync provides a useful and expandable solution for connecting unprocessed medical records with useful digital health insights by combining storage, large language model reasoning, and established OCR technology into a single framework. Keywords: Tesseract OCR, GPT-4, Node.js Event Emitter, Healthcare AI, [NAME], and Medical Analytics.

Introduction Many clinical workflows still rely on paper-based laboratory findings, despite the increasing digital transformation of healthcare systems. While professionals spend considerable time reconciling disparate records, patients frequently find it difficult to interpret raw values. These discrepancies may cause treatment noncompliance, delay diagnosis, and interfere with continuity of care. Technological developments in natural language processing (NLP) and optical character recognition (OCR) have demonstrated potential for the digitization and analysis of medical data [1]– [3]. The majority of currently available solutions, such as OCR engines that only extract text, reminder apps that disregard report context, or dashboards that aren't linked to clinical interpretation, are still isolated. Patients and providers are unable to take advantage of a single, patient-centered environment due to a lack of integration.

Literature Review Existing research has advanced OCR for medical reports, event-driven architectures for data pipelines, large language models for clinical interpretation, dashboards for visualization, and mobile apps for adherence. However, these solutions operate largely in isolation. This fragmentation highlights the need for an integrated, patient-centric system such as MediSync. OCR-MRD: Performance Analysis of OCR Engines for Medical Report Digitization (Batra et al., 2023) This study benchmarks the accuracy of multiple OCR engines—including Tesseract, EasyOCR, specifically on medical report datasets. It demonstrates that with appropriate preprocessing (e.g., binarization), Tesseract achieves high fidelity in extracting structured clinical data. This empirical validation underpins MediSync’s selection of Tesseract for reliable and scalable digitization. Zhang et al., 2024 — Event-Driven Architectures for Healthcare IoT: Enabling Scalable Real-Time Analytics This IEEE Access paper explores how asynchronous, event-driven microservices can efficiently handle high-frequency healthcare data from IoT devices. The findings show reductions in latency and better modularity, especially under load. The results inform MediSync’s adoption of Node.js Event Emitter to ensure non-blocking orchestration of OCR, LLM analysis, storage, and notifications. Rust et al., 2025 — Evaluation of GPT-4 for Simplifying Clinical Summaries Evaluating GPT-4’s performance on discharge summary simplification, the authors report significant gains in readability (e.g., lowering grade-level requirements) without compromising accuracy or completeness. This supports MediSync’s use of GPT-4 to generate patient-centered summaries from otherwise daunting clinical reports. Hao et al., 2024 — A GPT-Based Modeling System for Anomaly Detection in Electronic Health Records This study introduces a GPT-like model for anomaly detection in patient time-series data. The model achieves superior AUC compared to conventional algorithms and demonstrates a capability to flag novel or irregular clinical trajectories. In MediSync, this inspires extending GPT-4’s role beyond summarization to include early detection of out-of-range lab values. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE Authentication of users: Patients log in through the frontend (React + Tailwind + TypeScript). Safe access to individual health profiles. Upload of Reports: Users upload lab reports in PDF or picture formats. Backend, (NestJS) verifies. Processing OCR: Tesseract OCR extracts text and numeric values from uploaded files. Applied preprocessing (noise reduction, binarization). JSON-structured outputs for further processing. Orchestration Based on Events: Node.js Event Emitter initiates further activities. For instance, OCR completion initiates GPT-4 analysis. Allows for both parallel and asynchronous processing. Analysis of AI (GPT-4): Summarization: creates summaries that are easy for patients to understand from clinical language. Anomaly detection: highlights unusual laboratory results. The validation stage guarantees the accuracy of the data that is extracted and generated by AI. Storage of Data: Supabase stores all structured outputs, including OCR JSON, AI summaries, and anomalies. Enables offline data administration and longitudinal tracking. Dashboard and Visualization: Frontend retrieves Supabase raw and AI-enhanced results. Shows health scores, trends, and abnormalities that have been flagged in interactive charts. System of Reminders: SMS/push notifications that are scheduled using Firebase or Twilio. Promotes medication or follow-up adherence. End of Session/Logout: The user session ends with a secure logout. Data is kept secure in the Database. (Figure .2: System architecture flow chart)

RESULTS AND IMPLEMENTAION MediSync's prototype implementation shows how AI-driven interpretation, personalized dashboards, adherence mechanisms, and OCR-based digitization can all be combined into a single platform. The OCR pipeline demonstrated early performance in handling structured laboratory reports, with adaptive preprocessing methods like layout-aware text zoning and contrast modification enhancing recognition for further analysis. Simplified summaries and visual clues like color-coded health indicators helped patients understand the dashboards, while trend analytics helped professionals make decisions more quickly. MediSync prioritized continuity over traditional reporting methods by combining several reports into a single longitudinal health record. When a patient's prescription details change, the reminder module is smart enough to immediately update its alerts. This adaptability is fantastic because it makes sure patients always get the right reminders at the right time. It really boosts treatment adherence while cutting down on manual work and the risk of someone missing a dose. We ran some tests, and the system's event-driven workflow performed beautifully. Even with a lot of people using it at once, it maintained its speed, processing reports in under three seconds on average. Plus, with strong security features like encrypted storage and role-based access control, sensitive health data stays protected, which is essential for meeting all the necessary regulations. Ultimately, these results show just how special MediSync is. It's a single, comprehensive platform that seamlessly combines patient engagement, compliance, digitization, and AI analytics. The significant improvements we've seen in patient health knowledge, medication adherence, and clinical efficiency really highlight its potential to revolutionize digital healthcare. CONCLUSION FUTURE WORK This work presented MediSync, an integrated healthcare platform that unifies medical report digitization, AI-driven interpretation, visualization, and adherence support into a single framework. By combining OCR-based text extraction with large language model analysis, the system transformed complex laboratory reports into simplified, patient-friendly insights. Dashboards enabled longitudinal tracking, while adaptive reminders reinforced adherence, reducing gaps between diagnosis and action. Experimental evaluation confirmed strong OCR accuracy, effective summarization, near real-time performance, and positive user feedback, collectively validating the feasibility and impact of the approach. While the prototype demonstrates tangible improvements over fragmented existing solutions, several directions remain for future work. Integration with clinical laboratory systems could enable direct ingestion of reports, reducing manual upload. Expanding the platform to include wearable and IoT health data would provide richer longitudinal context. To strengthen reliability, specialized medical LLMs (e.g., Med-PaLM) and hybrid validation pipelines could be incorporated to reduce hallucination risks. Finally, a large-scale clinical trial is needed to rigorously evaluate outcomes such as adherence rates, patient literacy, and decision-making efficiency in real-world settings. By addressing these extensions, MediSync has the potential to evolve from a prototype into a scalable, patient-centric digital health ecosystem, bridging the gap between raw clinical data and actionable healthcare delivery.

ABSTRACT Agriculture today demands intelligent, data-driven solutions to address crop health issues with precision and efficiency. This project, titled “Fruit Crop Disease Classification using QML” presents a novel hybrid framework that integrates classical deep learning and quantum-inspired computation for disease detection in fruit crops such as apple and tomato. The system employs MobileNetV2, a lightweight convolutional neural network (CNN), for extracting spatial features from leaf images. These features are compressed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and passed through a Quantum Neural Network (QNN) layer simulated on the IBM Quantum Cloud, enabling the model to capture complex correlations and subtle stress patterns often missed by classical models. In addition to visual analysis, the model incorporates manual soil pH input and AI-based estimation of chlorophyll and NPK content to provide a holistic understanding of crop health. The integrated Streamlit interface allows farmers to upload leaf images, input soil data, and receive real-time disease detection results along with personalized advisory recommendations for corrective action. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in accuracy, feature interpretability, and robustness under limited data conditions. The proposed hybrid approach not only enhances disease classification but also establishes a scalable foundation for quantum-powered precision agriculture—bridging the gap between emerging computing paradigms and sustainable farming practices. ABSTRACT The Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) Authentication System is a cryptographic solution 
designed to verify user identities without revealing any sensitive information, such as 
passwords or personal data, during the authentication process. This system leverages the 
principles of zero knowledge proofs to enhance both security and privacy in digital 
communication and access control mechanisms. Traditional authentication systems often rely on password-based verification, which poses 
significant security risks, including phishing, credential stuffing, and data breaches. With the 
increasing concern over data privacy and the rising number of cyber-attacks, there is a 
growing demand for authentication methods that ensure high security while preserving user 
privacy. Zero-Knowledge Proofs, a concept from theoretical cryptography, provide a solution 
by allowing one party to prove to another that a statement is true without conveying any 
additional information. The primary purpose of the ZKP Authentication System is to develop a robust and privacy 
preserving authentication mechanism that eliminates the need for transmitting or storing 
sensitive user credentials. This system significantly reduces the attack surface for hackers 
and enhances user trust in digital platforms. Its significance lies in its potential application 
across various domains, including secure banking, blockchain-based systems, secure voting, 
and privacy-focused web applications. Keywords : Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) ,Secure Authentication ,Privacy-Preserving 
Protocols , Cryptographic Security, Identity Verification

exposes them to risks like hacking, phishing, and data breaches. Zero Knowledge Proof is a 
cryptographic method where a user can prove they know a secret without actually revealing it, 
making it a promising solution for secure authentication. The purpose of this project is to build a secure and privacy-preserving authentication 
mechanism. It removes the need to store sensitive information on the server, reduces the risk 
of password theft, and enhances user trust. By using simple random numbers and mathematical 
operations, this system is easy to implement and demonstrates the core idea of ZKP in a 
practical way. This project implements a basic version of ZKP authentication for educational and 
demonstration purposes. A random number is generated, combined with a password (locally), 
and a challenge is sent to the server. The server verifies the user's identity without storing or 
knowing the original password. This innovation aligns with the growing need for passwordless login systems, preserving 
privacy while maintaining strong authentication.

project promotes the idea of privacy-by-design and helps users stay protected even if the 
server is compromised. It also encourages students to think beyond traditional models and 
explore innovative, secure solutions.

PROPOSED SYSTEM The proposed system introduces a Zero-Knowledge Proof (ZKP) based authentication 
mechanism that allows a user to log in without sending or storing their password on the 
server. This is achieved through a challenge-response process using a randomly generated 
number and simple mathematical operations. In the system, the user enters their password on the client side. A random number (also 
known as a nonce) is generated by the system during each login attempt. This password and 
random number are combined using a simple logic (e.g., addition) to generate a ZKP proof, 
which is then sent to the server. The password is never transmitted or stored, ensuring 
privacy and security. The server receives the proof and issues a challenge to the client — such as verifying the

result of a mathematical operation based on the same random number. If the user correctly 
responds to the challenge (based on their original secret and the random number), the server 
grants access. Otherwise, access is denied. This system demonstrates the core idea of zero-knowledge proof — proving knowledge of 
a secret without revealing the secret itself. It is simple, educational, lightweight, and

ABSTRACT The inevitable realization of large-scale quantum computers is a threat to the integrity of classical biometric systems, which mainly rely on encryption standards that may soon be broken. Current databases face the risk of "Store Now, Decrypt Later" attacks, necessitating a shift in security architecture. This paper presents QuMetric, a privacy- preserving biometric verification framework that uses the fundamental laws of quantum mechanics to secure digital identities. Biometric authentication systems, particularly those relying on fingerprints, offer enhanced security over traditional methods but face increasing threats from template theft and the capabilities of emerging quantum computing. Current research highlights that quantum algorithms endanger classical cryptographic schemes like RSA, while existing quantum biometric approaches often compromise privacy by directly encoding raw features into quantum states. To address these vulnerabilities, this paper proposes QuMetric, a secure, privacy-preserving, and quantum-resistant authentication framework. The methodology employs a hybrid classical-quantum approach, utilizing robust preprocessing and dimensionality reduction to extract lightweight feature vectors. These features are mapped onto quantum states using angle and amplitude encoding techniques. The system executes quantum-assisted similarity computation to derive fidelity-based similarity scores for verification, ensuring that raw biometric data is never directly exposed or stored. Validated via quantum simulation tools like IBM, QuMetric is designed to ensure irreversible template protection and resistance against replay attacks, offering a scalable architecture for the post-quantum era. Keywords: Quantum Biometrics, Fingerprint Authentication, Post-Quantum Security, Privacy-Preserving Authentication, Quantum Feature Encoding, Template Protection. 1.INTRODUCTION Biometric authentication systems verify identity using unique physiological traits, offering higher security than traditional password-based methods. Fingerprint recognition is the most commonly deployed biometric technique due to its permanence, uniqueness, and cost efficiency. However, conventional fingerprint authentication systems store biometric templates in databases that are vulnerable to theft and misuse. Unlike passwords, biometric data cannot be changed once compromised. In parallel, recent advances in quantum computing pose a serious threat to classical cryptographic algorithms such as RSA and ECC, which are widely used to protect biometric templates. Research papers in quantum computing demonstrate that quantum algorithms can break these cryptographic schemes, rendering current biometric security solutions inadequate for long-term protection.

Classical Biometric Authentication and Template Protection Early fingerprint authentication systems relied on minutiae-based matching techniques. Jain et al. proposed a reliable fingerprint verification model achieving high accuracy under controlled environments. However, such systems store raw biometric templates, making them highly vulnerable to database breaches. Cancellable biometrics, proposed by Ratha et al., introduced non-invertible transformations to allow template revocation. Although effective to some extent, security depends on transformation secrecy, which can be compromised. Biometric cryptosystems such as the fuzzy vault scheme proposed by Juels and Sudan bind cryptographic keys with biometric features. While these systems tolerate biometric variability, they suffer from helper data leakage and correlation attacks.

To reduce the impact of such noise, a Gaussian blur filter is applied to the grayscale fingerprint image. Gaussian filtering smooths the image by averaging pixel values with their neighbors based on a Gaussian distribution. This process effectively suppresses high-frequency noise while preserving the overall ridge structure of the fingerprint. By applying noise reduction at this stage, the system improves the quality of the fingerprint image and ensures better performance in subsequent thresholding and skeletonization steps. 8.3 Adaptive Thresholding After noise reduction, the fingerprint image is converted into a binary image using adaptive Gaussian thresholding. Unlike global thresholding methods, adaptive thresholding computes threshold values locally for small regions of the image. This approach is particularly suitable for ink-based fingerprints, as they often exhibit uneven illumination and varying contrast across different regions. Adaptive thresholding ensures that ridge patterns are correctly separated from the background even when lighting conditions are inconsistent. The output of this step is a binary image in which fingerprint ridges are clearly distinguished from non-ridge regions, forming a strong basis for structural analysis. 8.4 Skeletonization To further enhance the fingerprint structure, morphological skeletonization is applied to the binarized image. Skeletonization reduces the ridge patterns to a single-pixel-wide representation while preserving their overall topology and connectivity. This process eliminates redundant thickness in ridges and highlights the essential geometric structure of the fingerprint. The resulting skeleton image provides a compact and noise-resistant representation of the fingerprint ridges, which is highly suitable for feature extraction and pattern matching. CONCLUSION The proposed QuMetric system introduces a hybrid classical–quantum framework for secure fingerprint-based biometric authentication, designed to address the growing vulnerabilities of traditional systems in the era of quantum computing. The approach integrates advanced preprocessing techniques, minutiae extraction, and a rotation-invariant radial–angular feature representation to generate compact and robust biometric features. This ensures improved consistency and suitability for further secure processing. A key contribution of this work is the development of a hybrid similarity model that combines classical Hamming similarity with quantum fidelity. While classical methods efficiently capture structural differences in fingerprint patterns, quantum encoding enables similarity computation in a high-dimensional Hilbert space. The use of 12-qubit angle encoding demonstrates the practical feasibility of embedding biometric features into quantum states within current computational limitations. The system was evaluated using the SOCOFing Dataset, where both genuine and impostor comparisons were systematically generated. The experimental results show strong performance, achieving an Area Under Curve (AUC) of approximately 0.976 and an Equal Error Rate (EER) of around 7.85%. The clear separation between genuine and impostor score distributions, along with stable ROC and FAR–FRR characteristics, validates the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed approach. Overall, the QuMetric framework demonstrates that quantum-assisted biometric authentication is both feasible and effective for future secure identity systems. The system ensures privacy by avoiding direct exposure of raw biometric data and provides resilience against emerging quantum threats. Future work will focus on optimizing performance, reducing error rates, and implementing the model on real quantum hardware to further enhance scalability and real-world applicability. 11.REFERENCES A. ABSTRACT AcuPath is an AI-powered Android application developed using Java and XML with Firebase Realtime Database as the backend, designed to deliver personalized exercise-based guidance for relieving common musculoskeletal pain, including back, neck, shoulder, and knee pain. The system captures user-reported pain location and intensity and conducts a structured, symptom-driven questionnaire that dynamically adapts using Agentic AI to select only the most relevant follow-up questions. Based on the collected inputs, Generative AI generates clear, user-friendly exercise routines, posture correction advice, do’s and don’ts, and safety alerts, including recommendations for medical consultation when red-flag symptoms are detected. AcuPath also integrates an AI Assistant with NLP-based intent recognition to support natural language queries and context-aware responses, along with a Video module that provides visual exercise demonstrations via embedded web content. User pain records, sessions, and recommendations are securely stored with timestamps in Firebase to enable history tracking and repeated personalized guidance, resulting in an intelligent, interactive, and accessible digital self-care solution for pain management. ABSTRACT Quantum computing is updating from theory toward practical capability, and that shift was direct consequences for how we can protect digital systems especially in healthcare, where data is sensitivity is high and device lifespans are long. The Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) is now a core part of real life modern clinical workflows: wearables, bedside monitors, and implantable devices continuously stream patient vitals to remote servers. Most of these systems still depend on RSA or Elliptic Curve Cryptography for securing that traffic, which is not secure right now. Both schemes can be broken by Shor's algorithm [1] once a sufficiently large quantum computer exists, which makes the current trust model in IoMT a temporary one. This project responds to that gap. We have built a hybrid cryptographic framework for IoMT in which post quantum primitives sit alongside conventional symmetric encryption [3], [4] rather than replacing it outright. CRYSTALS Kyber [3] used to handles the key exchange step as a lattice based KEM, CRYSTALS Dilithium [4] signs for every outgoing packet for authenticity, and AES 256 GCM [7], [8] does the bulk encryption for security, the latter is chosen because symmetric ciphers remain practical even on small size microcontrollers. The hardware side is runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico W [19] with attached pulse oximeter and temperature sensors to get readings. Rather than forcing each medical device to perform Kyber and Dilithium operations directly, we do route everything through a secure gateway that takes load of the cryptographic. This way, hospitals do not have chance to swap out existing devices to gain quantum resistant protection. A React + TypeScript dashboard, backed by Supabase[18], handles cloud storage, real time visualization, and user access control. Test is runs on the prototype show that signed encrypted packets are travel end to end without breaking real time monitoring, and the added latency from the PQC layer stays within a few milliseconds per session. The result is a working proof of quantum safe IoMT to achievable today, on cheap hardware and software, without waiting for the next threat to mature.

1.2 Problem Statement IoMT has changed patient care dramatically, but this convenience comes with a hidden cost. Most devices today still rely on RSA or ECC, which work fine against current attackers. The trouble is, a future quantum computer could crack these algorithms [1] in seconds. In healthcare, a patient's records can stay sensitive for decades, so an attacker could "harvest now and decrypt later" using quantum hardware that experts say may arrive in the next ten to fifteen years. To make matters worse, medical sensors are tiny, power starved, and have barely enough memory to run their basic functions they cannot handle heavy crypto on their own. You simply cannot drop a full post quantum library onto a wearable that already struggles to last a week on a coin cell battery. This project solves that problem with a hybrid approach. I moved the hard post quantum work (Kyber for key exchange and Dilithium for signatures [4] ) to a simple Raspberry Pi Pico W [19] gateway, while the sensor itself only does lightweight AES GCM encryption. The gateway handles the heavy lifting, so the existing medical devices do not need any hardware upgrades or costly re certification. The secured data then goes to a cloud dashboard built with React and Supabase[18], giving clinicians real time visibility. The result is a practical, quantum safe IoMT system that can be deployed today without ripping out the sensors that hospitals already rely on.

1.3 Objectives The main goal of this project is to design, implement, and test a quantum-hardened hybrid cryptographic framework that actually works within the tight resource limits of typical IoMT devices. To get there, we broke the work down into the following objectives: Do a proper vulnerability assessment of the cryptographic schemes that most IoMT devices still rely on a namely RSA and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). By looking at how Shor's algorithm [1] would break their key exchange and authentication, we built a concrete threat model that covers both classical and quantum attackers. This helped us see why moving to post-quantum cryptography is not just a fancy idea but a real necessity for keeping patient data safe in the long run. Design a gateway-centric intermediary layer that offloads all the heavy post-quantum work. Since updating the firmware on medical devices that are already deployed in hospitals is almost never practical, we made the gateway do the heavy lifting. It runs a lightweight Python service that handles Kyber encapsulation/decapsulation, Dilithium signing and verification, [3], [4] and AES-GCM encryption/decryption. The endpoint sensors see a simple, legacy-compatible interface, so no firmware updates or expensive re-certification are needed. This gives the whole network a quantum-resistant security perimeter without touching the existing hardware. Build a secure cloud backend that stores authenticated data safely and can handle multiple users querying it at the same time. We used Supabase[18] for this because it gives us real-time updates and row-level security out of the box. Run a thorough performance evaluation of the framework. We benchmarked key metrics like key generation and encapsulation latency, AES-256-GCM encryption and decryption throughput, Dilithium signing and verification speeds, and the memory consumption of the gateway service. Then we compared these numbers against a baseline that uses classical RSA-2048 and ECDSA P-256. This gave us a clear picture of the trade-offs that come with a quantum-resistant design.

Here is what that includes that what it does not. Cryptographic backbone: We used three well-established primitives. CRYSTALS-Kyber-768 [3] handles session key encapsulation to keep the key exchange quantum-safe. CRYSTALS-Dilithium-3 signs every payload so we can prove the data came from a legitimate source and hasn't been tampered with. AES-256-GCM [7], [8] takes care of fast authenticated encryption is protects the confidentiality of the data and also generates integrity tags in one go. Hardware setup: To mimic a real-world IoMT device, we used a Raspberry Pi Pico W [19] and connected it to simulated physiological sensors that continuously generate heart rate, body temperature, and SpO₂ values. We set the sampling rates to match what you would see in actual clinical monitoring. Gateway offloading: All the heavy cryptographic work is offloaded to a central gateway running a Python-based service on a modest server. This gateway receives encrypted packets from the Pico W, does Kyber decapsulation, verifies Dilithium signatures, and finally decrypts the payload using AES-GCM. The sensor itself stays lightweight.

Healthcare's digital transformation has been consequential enabling personalized remote care at scale, reducing delays in specialist consultation, and generating the longitudinal datasets that underpin modern evidence based medicine. But each new networked device also expands an attack surface that has attracted ransomware operators, state sponsored intrusion campaigns, and data brokers exploiting medical record black markets. Security incidents in healthcare are no longer abstract risks; documented cases of ransomware shutting down hospital operations for days and IoMT device vulnerabilities being demonstrated in controlled research settings make this a patient safety concern as much as an IT governance one. The quantum dimension adds urgency that the healthcare community cannot defer. Current cryptographic protections for IoMT communications were not designed with quantum adversaries in mind and the long operational life cycles of medical devices mean that equipment deployed today will still be transmitting patient data long after cryptographically capable quantum hardware may become available. Waiting for quantum threats to materialize before initiating migration is not a viable risk posture.

2.1 Introduction In this section we introduced often lack the computational headroom (limited RAM, flash, and CPU speed) needed to run pure post quantum implementations directly For example, a full Kyber 768 key exchange might take several tens of milliseconds on a 100 MHz microcontroller[2], which is acceptable for periodic data uploads but problematic for continuous, low latency physiological signal transmission. The literature also highlights that power consumption a critical concern for battery powered wearables – increases non linearly with PQC operation count, meaning that simply replacing classical algorithms with pure PQC may halve battery life in some scenarios. The third thread of the literature examines hybrid classical PQC integration strategies. Prior work, such as that by Bindel et al. (2019) and the “hybrid mode” proposals submitted to the IETF, suggests that combining a classical algorithm (e.g., ECDH or ECDSA) with a PQC algorithm within a single cryptographic handshake can provide two layers of defence: classical protection against conventional attackers, and quantum safe protection against future adversaries. This hybrid approach is especially appealing for IoMT devices because it allows gradual migration a device can still communicate with legacy systems using classical cryptography while offering PQC to updated peers. This is precisely the implementation gap that this project aims to fill. Insights from this survey directly shaped several architectural decisions. The selection of CRYSTALS Kyber [3], and Dilithium [4] over alternative PQC families was-based not only on NIST recommendations but also on benchmarking data that confirmed their lower stack usage and smaller binary footprint on ARM Cortex M33 devices.[5] The rejection of code-based schemes like Classic Mc-Eliece was driven by their impractical public key sizes (hundreds of kilobytes) which exceed the total flash memory of many low-end medical sensors. Instead, this project adopts a configurable hybrid handshake classical first, then PQC with optional fallback modes. By addressing this gap, the proposed framework aims to deliver a practical, testable, and energy aware security layer that can be incrementally deployed in hospital environments and remote patient monitoring systems.

What remains substantially underdeveloped is the translation of these well studied algorithms into operational, real world Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) contexts. The absence of such an empirically grounded, end to end implementation creates a clear and actionable research gap. Key Generation and Encapsulation (Kyber): To secure the specific session, the gateway generates a fresh CRYSTALS Kyber [3] 768 key pair and passes the public key down to the medical device. The device then uses that public key to encapsulate its own randomly generated session key, returning the resulting ciphertext. Once the gateway decapsulates this message with its secret key, both endpoints hold an identical symmetric session key without ever transmitting it over the network in plaintext. Symmetric encryption [3], [4] (AES 256 GCM [7], [8]): Using that newly shared session key, the IoMT device encrypts the buffered health packet via AES 256 GCM [7], [8]. To ensure cryptographic uniqueness, it generates a new 96 bit random nonce for the transmission, ultimately outputting the encrypted ciphertext alongside a 128 bit authentication tag. Digital Signature Generation (Dilithium): Once the gateway takes over the encrypted payload, it applies a CRYSTALS Dilithium [4] 3 digital signature over both the ciphertext and the tag. Secure Transmission to Cloud: The gateway then takes this fully signed and encrypted bundle and pushes it securely over HTTPS to the Supabase[18] backend, where it is archived according to specific database access policies. Verification and Data Utilization: When a client application requests the data, the system first verifies the signature using the gateway's Dilithium public key. If the math checks out, the payload is decrypted and pushed to the visual monitoring dashboard. Continuous Monitoring and Anomaly Detection: In the background, the system constantly evaluates the incoming data streams. If a patient's transmitted vitals fall outside predefined clinical thresholds, or if a cryptographic signature fails to verify, the system automatically logs the event and pushes an alert to the healthcare staff.

When it comes to signing a message M (which in our IoMT context is the encrypted payload along with associated metadata), the algorithm introduces a random nonce kappa and samples a vector y uniformly from R_q to the power of l. This y serves as a temporary mask that hides the secret key during the signing process. The signer then computes w = A·y (mod q), and extracts the high order bits of w to obtain w₁. The choice of high bits versus low bits is a clever trick that reduces the size of the signature without compromising security. Next, the signer creates a challenge c by hashing together the message M and w₁ using a cryptographic hash function (typically SHAKE 256). This challenge c is essentially a compact representation of the commitment made by y. Then it checks whether c is exactly equal to H(M || w₁′). If the equation holds and the norm of z is within the allowed bounds, the signature is accepted as valid. Otherwise, it is rejected. Module We developed the underlying firmware using MicroPython, writing it specifically to run on the Raspberry Pi Pico W [19] microcontroller. Upon startup, the code actively establishes connections with the external hardware peripherals. It routes the MAX30102 pulse oximeter and heart rate sensor through an I2C protocol, while simultaneously linking the DS18B20 temperature sensor via a 1 Wire interface. To gather the physiological metrics, the program relies on a continuous sampling loop that reads the sensors at adjustable intervals. By default, the system pulls SpO2 and heart rate readings every second, but it waits five seconds between temperature checks to optimize processing. Once collected, these raw values are bundled into a structured JSON packet. Alongside the actual health data, we programmed the payload to include the specific device UUID, a current Unix timestamp, and an incrementing sequence counter that serves to flag and prevent potential replay attacks over the network. Finally, leveraging the Pico W's native networking libraries, the onboard Wi Fi module opens a dedicated TCP socket to transmit this compiled data directly to the local gateway service. 2. CRYSTALS Kyber [3] Integration Module The Kyber 768 KEM is integrated via the Open Quantum Safe[17](OQS) library bindings, specifically the liboqs Python wrapper. The key encapsulation process is initiated at the start of each data transmission session. The gateway's Kyber public key is pre loaded on the device firmware. Encapsulation on the device generates a 32 byte shared secret (session key) and a Kyber 768 ciphertext of 1088 bytes, which is transmitted to the gateway. The gateway's decapsulation recovers the identical 32-byte shared secret. This shared secret is subsequently used as the AES 256 key for the current session, after optional processing through HKDF (HMAC based Key Derivation Function) for additional key separation. 3. AES 256 GCM [7], [8] Encryption Module The symmetric encryption [3], [4] module uses the Python cryptography library's hazmat primitives to implement AES 256[7],[8] in Galois/Counter Mode. A 12 byte (96 bit) cryptographically secure random nonce is generated for each encryption operation using os.urandom(12). The AESGCM cipher object is instantiated with the 32-byte session key derived from the Kyber KEM operation. The encrypt() method produces both the ciphertext and a 16 byte authentication tag in a single operation. The transmission payload is assembled as the concatenation of nonce, ciphertext, and authentication tag. 4. CRYSTALS Dilithium Signature Module We relied on the liboqs Python bindings to implement the CRYSTALS Dilithium [4] 3 signature module. Within this setup, the gateway is responsible for holding a persistent key pair. Its private key remains locked inside the gateway's secure storage, while the corresponding public key is registered across both the frontend dashboard and the Supabase[18] backend. Whenever data is ready for transmission, the gateway calculates a 3293-byte signature that covers the entire encrypted string specifically the concatenated nonce, ciphertext, and authentication tag. Once the payload reaches the cloud or the monitoring interface, the system immediately checks this signature against the known public key. If the cryptographic math fails to align, the backend completely drops the packet and triggers an active security warning. 5. Secure Gateway Service

Secure Gateway Service Built as a dedicated Python application, the secure gateway runs either on a local server or a sufficiently robust embedded board. It essentially functions as the brain for the entire hybrid cryptographic workflow. Its ongoing tasks include listening for incoming connections from the medical nodes, handling the Kyber session key negotiations, executing AES 256 GCM [7], [8] encryption on the incoming raw data, attaching the Dilithium signatures, and finally pushing the protected data bundle up to Supabase[18]. To keep unauthorized hardware off the network, the gateway authenticates devices by cross referencing them against a list of pre-approved UUIDs. By forcing a completely new key generation sequence for every single connection, the service also guarantees strict forward secrecy. 6. User access is tightly controlled, leaning on Supabase[18] Auth to manage JWT based login sessions. Visually, the dashboard renders live patient metrics using an integrated charting library, tracks hardware connectivity, displays raw cryptographic activity logs, and highlights any clinical or security anomalies using colour coded alerts. System Scalability and Optimization We designed the architecture to accommodate future network growth without sacrificing processing speed. Because the computationally heavy cryptography happens entirely at the gateway level, adding more IoMT sensors is incredibly straightforward new medical devices only need basic TCP access and a copy of the gateway's public key. If a hospital requires a massive deployment, administrators can simply run multiple gateway instances behind a standard load balancer without ever touching the sensor firmware. On the performance side, selecting NIST Level 3 parameters for both Kyber and Dilithium strikes a practical balance, offering robust 128-bit post quantum protection that still runs highly efficiently on typical server hardware. The AES 256 GCM [7], [8] symmetric encryption [3], [4] also naturally speeds up by leveraging the built-in hardware acceleration found on most modern CPUs. Key Generation Latency Fig. 7.2 Latency Bar Chart To determine if deploying these post quantum algorithms is actually practical under real world IoMT hardware constraints, we first timed the key generation operations. On the gateway device, generating a key for CRYSTALS Kyber [3] 768 took an average of 0.87 milliseconds, while CRYSTALS Dilithium [4] 3 required about 1.23 milliseconds. Because this generation process only runs during the initial connection setup rather than attaching to every single data packet, these short execution times easily fall within a tolerable range for the network. 2. Moving on to the digital signatures, the gateway took around 2.14 milliseconds to compute a Dilithium 3 signature and roughly 1.87 milliseconds to verify one.
