8.1 Conclusion Through the design, deployment, and rigorous testing phases, this research delivered a fully functional Hybrid Cryptographic Framework tailored specifically for Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) networks. By doing so, it establishes a robust, quantum resistant shield for highly sensitive patient health records. Traditional encryption algorithms are already exhibiting well documented vulnerabilities when measured against emerging quantum computing capabilities, posing a massive long-term threat to healthcare data infrastructure. The architecture developed here directly neutralizes that fundamental risk. The most significant technical achievement of this project is the practical blending of newly standardized NIST post quantum primitives with proven symmetric encryption [3], [4]. Specifically, the system utilizes CRYSTALS Kyber [3] 768 to safely encapsulate keys and relies on CRYSTALS Dilithium [4] 3 for generating digital signatures. It then pairs these advanced protocols with the highly efficient AES 256 operating in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) to handle the actual data payload encryption. To make this hybrid approach deployable, we utilized a gateway centric architectural model. This specific design choice is crucial because it shifts the heavy computational demands of post quantum cryptography away from the actual medical sensors. Consequently, healthcare facilities can deploy this advanced security without having to modify, replace, or upgrade their existing resource constrained device hardware, drastically lowering the barrier to entry. compliance standards as global quantum computing hardware continues to mature. What this project ultimately proves is that the medical sector does not need to wait for fully realized quantum computers to arrive before taking defensive action. Post quantum cryptographic methods can be practically and effectively integrated into live IoMT deployments right now. By adopting this hybrid framework, healthcare facilities can establish a highly scalable, standard compliant security foundation that is genuinely prepared for the next generation of connected medical devices.

8.2 Future Scope 1. AI Enhanced Anomaly Detection and Threat Intelligence Looking ahead, integrating machine learning into the system offers a major area for improvement. By training deep learning models specifically LSTMs or Transformer architectures on the framework's historical health data and encryption logs, the network could learn to independently spot the subtle warning signs of both medical emergencies and active cyberattacks. Additionally, adopting a federated learning approach would allow different hospitals to share threat intelligence with each other without ever exposing sensitive patient records, helping build a broader, collaborative defence network for medical IoT devices. 2. Edge Computing Integration Another promising direction involves shifting toward edge computing. Instead of relying heavily on a single central node, future versions of this architecture could distribute the intense cryptographic processing across multiple localized edge devices, such as NVIDIA Jetson Nanos or high-performance ARM embedded processors. Pushing the post quantum workload closer to the actual medical sensors would cut down on network latency and improve overall system resilience. This localized processing would be especially useful in environments with spotty internet connections, such as rural clinics or active ambulances relying on mobile telemedicine. 3. Blockchain Integration for Immutable Audit Trails To strengthen data accountability, the framework could eventually incorporate distributed ledger technology. By tying the architecture into a permissioned blockchain like Hyperledger Fabric, every single data access request and cryptographic event would generate a permanent, tamper proof audit trail. From a regulatory perspective, utilizing smart contracts could automatically enforce patient consent and access control policies. This would make it much easier for healthcare facilities to comply with strict HIPAA or GDPR rules, while also providing clear forensic evidence if a security breach actually occurs. 4. Zero Trust Security Architecture The system's current security posture could also be upgraded to a strict Zero Trust model. In this type of setup, the network never assumes a device or user is safe just because they are already connected. Instead, every individual data request requires continuous authentication. Implementing this concept would involve adding hardware security primitives, like Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs), for ongoing device attestation. 5. ABSTRACT Children with dyslexia face persistent challenges in recognizing alphabets, developing phonemic awareness, and connecting letters with corresponding sounds and visual cues. This paper introduces an interactive prototype that integrates Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) technologies to support dyslexic learners. The proposed system provides a multisensory learning environment that encourages engagement through visual, auditory, and interactive elements. The VR module allows learners to type alphabets, visualize the corresponding letters in three dimensions, hear accurate pronunciations,
and
view
representative
images.
This
immersive
experience strengthens letter-sound associations and reinforces memory retention. The AR module, developed using a custom Android application, enables users to scan printed book images, overlay 3D objects on them, play relevant audio cues, and display concise textual descriptions. A pilot study was conducted with dyslexic children to evaluate the usability and educational impact of both modules. Results indicate that the VR module fostered greater engagement, focus, and faster alphabet recognition, while the AR module enhanced real-world contextual understanding and reading motivation. Observations revealed
that
both environments improved learners’ confidence and enthusiasm toward literacy activities. The combined AR and VR approach effectively utilizes multisensory stimulation to accommodate diverse cognitive needs and learning preferences. Overall, this research highlights the potential of immersive technologies in supporting inclusive education. The developed prototype demonstrates how AR and VR can transform traditional alphabet learning into an engaging, adaptive, and effective experience for dyslexic children. INTRODUCTION 1.1 Overview The project titled “Exploring Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality for Dyslexic Students in Education” aims to develop an interactive, immersive, and assistive learning platform using Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) technologies to support students with dyslexia—a learning disorder that affects reading, writing, and spelling abilities. The project focuses on enhancing learning outcomes through multisensory engagement, where students can see, hear, and interact with educational content in real time. By leveraging the immersive potential of AR and VR, the system intends to create a stimulating environment that improves word recognition, memory retention, and comprehension skills for dyslexic learners. The AR component of the project allows students to scan educational markers or QR codes using a mobile device or tablet to visualize 3D objects and animations related to alphabets, animals, or vocabulary words. This feature helps bridge the gap between

abstract symbols and their real-world meanings, making learning more concrete and enjoyable. On the other hand, the VR module offers a fully immersive virtual classroom, where learners can manipulate 3D shapes, grab objects, and listen to phonetic sounds associated with letters or words. This hands- on approach encourages active participation, which is known to significantly benefit learners with dyslexia by improving focus and reinforcing visual-auditory connections. The system is developed using Unity 3D as the main development engine, integrated with Vuforia SDK for AR functionality and Unity XR Toolkit for VR development. The project also employs Firebase as a backend database for storing user profiles, learning progress, and performance analytics. The interface is designed to be dyslexia-friendly, incorporating accessible fonts, high- contrast visuals, and voice guidance to ensure ease of understanding. The ultimate goal of this project is to demonstrate how technology can create an inclusive educational environment where dyslexic students can learn at their own pace, gain confidence, and overcome traditional literacy barriers through immersive and engaging experiences. 1. Introduction Medical imaging is a critical component of modern healthcare, supporting the diagnosis and monitoring of various diseases through modalities such as X-rays and MRI scans. Traditional diagnostic processes rely heavily on manual interpretation by medical experts, which can be time-consuming, subjective, and prone to error due to increasing workloads and image complexity. Recent advancements in deep learning, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have shown strong potential in automated medical image analysis. However, most existing AI-based diagnostic systems are limited to identifying a single disease, making them unsuitable for real-world clinical scenarios where multiple conditions may coexist. Additionally, many deep learning models operate as black-box systems, providing limited interpretability, which reduces trust and acceptance among healthcare professionals. The proposed Multi-Disease Medical Diagnosis System addresses these limitations by developing a unified framework capable of detecting multiple diseases from medical images within a single system. The project leverages CNN-based transfer learning models to extract discriminative features and accurately classify medical images into different disease categories. To improve transparency and clinical reliability, Explainable AI techniques such as heatmap visualizations are incorporated to highlight affected regions influencing the model’s predictions. Furthermore, the system integrates AI agents to intelligently manage and coordinate different stages of the diagnostic pipeline, including image preprocessing, disease classification, explainability generation, and decision support. Rather than replacing medical professionals, the system functions as a decision support tool, assisting clinicians in faster diagnosis, reducing diagnostic errors, and enabling early disease detection. This approach demonstrates how agent-based AI and deep learning can be effectively combined to enhance modern healthcare outcomes. 4

Literature Review The literature survey is organized into three categories: (i) classical biometric authentication and template protection, (ii) quantum computing in pattern matching, and (iii) quantum-assisted biometric systems. 2.1 Classical Biometric Authentication and Template Protection Early fingerprint authentication systems relied on minutiae-based matching techniques. Jain et al. proposed a reliable fingerprint verification model achieving high accuracy under controlled environments. However, such systems store raw biometric templates, making them highly vulnerable to database breaches. Cancellable biometrics, proposed by Ratha et al., introduced non-invertible transformations to allow template revocation. Although effective to some extent, security depends on transformation secrecy, which can be compromised. Biometric cryptosystems such as the fuzzy vault scheme proposed by Juels and Sudan bind cryptographic keys with biometric features. While these systems tolerate biometric variability, they suffer from helper data leakage and correlation attacks. Hash-based biometric protection techniques provide strong irreversibility by storing only hashed templates. However, due to intra-class variations in biometric data, hash-based matching becomes challenging, motivating the need for similarity computation in protected domains. 2.2 Quantum Computing and Similarity Computation Several uploaded research papers discuss quantum similarity measures such as quantum cosine similarity, SWAP test–based fidelity estimation, and quantum kernel methods. These techniques demonstrate theoretical and experimental advantages in computing similarity between high-dimensional vectors. Quantum machine learning algorithms such as Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVM) have been applied to classification tasks and show competitive accuracy on small datasets. However, most studies assume direct access to raw feature vectors, which is unsuitable for sensitive biometric data. 5 2.3 Quantum-Assisted Biometric Authentication Recent works specifically explore quantum fingerprinting and quantum biometric matching. Papers such as those by Mogos et al. and Kipchirchir et al. demonstrate the feasibility of encoding fingerprint features into quantum states and performing matching using quantum algorithms. Research Gaps A comprehensive analysis of existing research on medical image analysis, deep learning based diagnosis, explainable AI, and agent-based systems reveals several critical gaps that motivate the proposed Multi-Disease Medical Diagnosis System. 1. Predominance of Single-Disease Diagnostic Systems Recent studies in medical image analysis largely focus on detecting individual diseases such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, brain tumors, or diabetic retinopathy using deep learning models. While these systems achieve high accuracy for specific conditions, they operate in isolation and do not reflect real-world clinical scenarios where patients may present with multiple or overlapping diseases. Gap: There is a lack of a unified diagnostic framework capable of identifying multiple diseases from medical images within a single system. 2. Limited Integration of Multi-Class and Multi-Disease Learning Several research works extend binary classification to multi-class problems; however, these approaches are often dataset-specific and lack generalizability across different disease categories and imaging modalities. Most systems are not designed to scale beyond predefined disease sets. Gap: Existing approaches do not provide a scalable and extensible multi-disease learning framework suitable for diverse medical imaging data. 3. Insufficient Explainability in Deep Learning-Based Diagnosis Although deep learning models demonstrate strong predictive performance, many operate as black boxes, offering little insight into the reasoning behind their predictions. While some studies introduce Explainable AI techniques, these are often treated as optional visualizations rather than integral components of the diagnostic process. Gap: There is no widespread adoption of tightly integrated explainability mechanisms that systematically support clinical trust and interpretability in multi-disease diagnosis systems. 4. 4. Problem Statement The rapid growth of medical imaging data in healthcare has increased the demand for accurate and timely disease diagnosis. Traditional diagnostic practices rely heavily on manual interpretation by medical professionals, which is time-consuming, subject to variability, and prone to error under high workload conditions. Although deep learning techniques have shown promising results in automated medical image analysis, most existing systems are limited to detecting a single disease and operate as black-box models with limited interpretability. Furthermore, current AI-based diagnostic solutions lack intelligent coordination across different stages of the diagnostic pipeline, such as preprocessing, disease classification, and

result interpretation. The absence of explainable outputs and decision support mechanisms reduces clinician trust and limits the practical adoption of such systems in real-world healthcare environments. Therefore, the problem is to design a unified, scalable, and explainable medical diagnosis system capable of accurately identifying multiple diseases from medical imaging data while providing transparent and clinically meaningful insights. The system must incorporate intelligent AI agent-based coordination to automate and manage the diagnostic workflow, support informed clinical decision-making, and assist healthcare professionals without replacing their expertise. 10

5. Objectives The primary objective of this project is to design an intelligent multi-disease medical diagnosis system that leverages deep learning and AI agent-based coordination to accurately identify multiple diseases from medical imaging data such as X-ray and MRI scans. The system aims to implement effective image acquisition and preprocessing techniques to enhance image quality, followed by feature extraction using Convolutional Neural Networks and transfer learning models to generate discriminative representations for reliable multi-class disease classification. Explainable AI techniques, such as heatmap- based visualizations, are incorporated to highlight clinically relevant regions influencing model predictions, thereby improving transparency and trust. AI agents are employed to autonomously manage preprocessing, diagnosis, explainability generation, and decision support, ensuring an efficient and modular diagnostic workflow while supporting clinicians without replacing medical expertise. The secondary objective of the project is to evaluate the performance and practical feasibility of the proposed framework using standard medical imaging datasets. This includes analyzing classification accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score across multiple disease categories, as well as assessing the effectiveness of explainability outputs and AI agent coordination. The project also aims to compare the proposed multi-disease, agent- driven approach with conventional single-disease diagnostic systems, study its ability to reduce diagnostic time and errors, and design a scalable architecture that can be extended to additional diseases, imaging modalities, and future intelligent healthcare applications. 11

methodology to ensure systematic design, implementation, and evaluation. Each phase addresses a specific component of the system while maintaining integration through AI agent coordination. Phase 1: Data Collection and Dataset Preparation In this phase, publicly available and clinically validated medical imaging datasets are collected, including X-ray and MRI images representing multiple disease categories. The datasets are examined for class imbalance, image quality, and labeling accuracy. The data is then organized into training, validation, and testing subsets to support reliable model development and evaluation. Phase 2: Image Preprocessing and Enhancement This phase focuses on improving the quality and consistency of input images. Preprocessing operations such as resizing, normalization, noise reduction, and contrast enhancement are applied. Data augmentation techniques, including rotation, flipping, and scaling, are used to improve model generalization. A dedicated AI preprocessing agent manages and automates these tasks to ensure standardized input across the system. Phase 3: Feature Extraction Using Deep Learning In this phase, Convolutional Neural Networks and transfer learning models such as ResNet, DenseNet, or EfficientNet are employed to extract discriminative features from medical images. Pre-trained models are fine-tuned on the medical datasets to capture disease- specific patterns while reducing training time and overfitting. The diagnosis AI agent selects and executes the appropriate model for multi-disease classification. Phase 4: Multi-Disease Classification and Prediction The extracted features are passed to a multi-class classification layer that predicts disease categories along with confidence scores. The system is designed to handle multiple disease classes within a single framework. The diagnosis agent performs inference and forwards

results to subsequent agents for interpretation and validation. Phase 5: Explainable AI Integration To address the black-box nature of deep learning models, Explainable AI techniques such as Grad-CAM are applied in this phase. Heatmaps are generated to visually highlight 12 regions in the medical images that influence the model’s predictions. An explainability AI agent is responsible for producing and managing these visual explanations, enhancing transparency and clinician trust. Phase 6: AI Agent-Based Decision Support In this phase, a decision support agent aggregates outputs from the diagnosis and explainability agents. It analyzes confidence levels, flags uncertain predictions, and presents structured diagnostic insights through the user interface. This phase ensures that the system functions as an assistive tool for clinicians rather than an autonomous decision- maker. 13

ABSTRACT In the face of increasing urban crowd density, rising numbers of child disappearance cases, and the limitations of conventional surveillance systems, the need for intelligent and responsive safety solutions has never been more urgent. AI Lost Tech is a real-time, AI-powered surveillance and alert system designed to assist in the rapid identification and recovery of lost or unattended children in public spaces. By integrating computer vision, facial recognition, and automated risk analysis into a single unified platform, the system enhances the responsiveness and reliability of child safety infrastructure. The primary objective of AI Lost Tech is to bridge the gap between passive surveillance and active intervention by using existing CCTV feeds and advanced AI algorithms to detect, identify, and assess the presence of lost children. Through real-time object detection and face matching with missing children databases, the system can quickly flag high-risk situations and alert security personnel with precise visual and location data. The application also offers a parent-initiated alert feature, enabling families to submit missing child information directly, initiating an immediate system-wide search. To improve reliability and reduce false positives, the platform classifies cases based on context and behavior, using a simple but effective rule-based risk engine. Designed for flexibility and scalability, AI Lost Tech can operate on local servers, edge devices, or cloud infrastructure, making it suitable for deployment in railway stations, shopping malls, festivals, and smart city ecosystems. Its intuitive dashboard and real-time alert mechanism ensure that critical information reaches the right people at the right time. More than just a technical tool, AI Lost Tech strives to become a trusted safety companion in urban environments providing families, law enforcement, and public agencies with the confidence and capability to protect children through proactive, intelligent, and compassionate technology. Keywords: Lost Child Detection, Real-Time Surveillance, Face Recognition, YOLO Object Detection, Risk Classification, Automated Alert System, Smart City Security.

MOTIVATION In crowded public spaces such as shopping malls, amusement parks, railway stations, and city fairs, it is alarmingly easy for children to become separated from their parents or guardians. These situations are incredibly distressing, not only for the child but also for the families involved. In those crucial initial moments of separation, every second matters. The longer it takes to recognize that a child is missing, the greater the risk becomes and sadly, in many cases, by the time action is taken, the opportunity for a swift and safe recovery has already passed. While most of these public places are under surveillance through CCTV camera networks, the current systems often lack the intelligence to distinguish between a child who is simply wandering alone and one who is genuinely lost and in need of immediate help. This inability to accurately assess risk can lead to two major problems: delays in response when action is urgently needed, or unnecessary panic when a child is actually safe. Both situations highlight the critical gaps in our current approach to real-time monitoring and incident classification. To address these shortcomings, we propose a smart, AI-powered system that enhances traditional surveillance infrastructure. Our platform is designed to detect lost or unattended children in real- time, analyze behaviour patterns, and classify potential risks more accurately. Our platform is designed to detect lost or unattended children in real- time, analyze behaviour patterns, and classify potential risks more accurately. By leveraging advanced computer vision techniques and facial recognition algorithms, the system can not only identify if a child appears to be lost but also compare their image with a central database of reported missing children. If a match or high-risk situation is identified, it instantly notifies on- ground security personnel with detailed alerts including location, time, and images enabling rapid and effective intervention. The motivation behind this project stems from a shared concern for child safety and the belief that technology, when used responsibly, can be a powerful force for good. Our mission is to transform passive surveillance into an active guardian capable of making intelligent decisions, reducing human error, and most importantly, saving lives.

For example, a child is identified as lost at a mall and the system has flagged then the system should give an instant alert to the admin with the particular location. One of the key features that sets this system apart from others is its risk classification mechanism, which uses a three-color signal system to indicate the safety status of a child in real time. • A Green signal appears when the system identifies that the child is accompanied or clearly safe. • A Yellow signal is displayed when the child is detected to be alone, but behavior analysis suggests that the child is calm and not in immediate danger. • A Red signal is triggered when the system detects that the child is both alone and potentially unsafe, showing signs of distress or confusion.

across multiple sources, often outdated, and written in technical language that is difficult to understand.
To solve this problem, we propose GovGuideBot—an AI-powered chatbot designed to assist users in a simple
and conversational way. Using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML), the chatbot
can understand user queries, detect intent, and deliver personalized, step-by-step guidance based on the user’s
location. In addition to providing official links and document checklists, it also recommends helpful YouTube
tutorials to make the process even easier.
GovGuideBot is designed to reduce confusion, save time, and improve access to public services. It supports the
broader goal of Digital India by promoting inclusive, citizen-friendly, and transparent governance through the
power of AI. GovGuideBot: AI Chatbot for Government Document Assistance Motivation Despite the push for digital governance, many citizens still struggle to access government services effectively—

frustration. The motivation behind GovGuideBot is to create a smart, AI-powered solution that simplifies this process. By

V. METHODOLOGY A. System Architecture The Vardox architecture comprises three actors: (1) the 
Academic Institution (issuer), (2) the Public Blockchain 
Network, and (3) the Verifier (employer/university). Institutions 
interact via the Vardox SDK/API which abstracts all blockchain 
operations. Document hashes are anchored on Ethereum via 
smart contracts; original documents remain in off-chain 
institutional storage. Fig. 1. High-Level Architecture of the Decentralised Academic Verification System Fig. 2. End-to-End Academic Credential Lifecycle Sequence Diagram Fig. 3. IPFS architecture Fig. 4. On-chain storage flow B. Document Issuance and Digital Signing Institutions generate certificates and apply ECDSA digital 
signatures to establish issuer authenticity. A SHA-256 hash of 
the signed document is computed: H = Hash(D + S), where D is 
the document and S is the digital signature. C. Blockchain Hash Anchoring 
The document hash and metadata are submitted to Ethereum via 
a Solidity smart contract. The contract records the hash 
immutably and returns a transaction reference Tx as proof of 
record. No entity — including the issuing institution — can alter 
the verification proof after anchoring. D. Off-Chain Document Storage 
Original documents are stored in secure institutional off-chain 
storage. A logical link is maintained between each document and 
its blockchain transaction reference Tx, enabling efficient 
retrieval without exposing sensitive content on-chain. ​

Introduction In recent years, the rapid growth of digital infrastructure and the increasing frequency of cyberattacks have significantly raised the demand for effective security monitoring within organizations. Security Operations Centers (SOCs) play a critical role in monitoring, detecting, and responding to security incidents by analyzing alerts generated from various security tools such as Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems, intrusion detection systems, firewalls, and endpoint security solutions. However, the growing number of security tools has resulted in an overwhelming volume of alerts being generated on a daily basis. A major challenge faced by modern SOC environments is alert fatigue, where security analysts are inundated with a large number of alerts, many of which are false positives or low-risk events. Manual analysis and triaging of these alerts is time-consuming, inefficient, and prone to human error. As a result, genuine security incidents may be delayed or overlooked, leading to increased organizational risk and reduced operational efficiency. The proposed project, Automated Alert Prioritization for Security Operations Centers: Reducing [NAME] AI/ML, aims to address this challenge by introducing an intelligent alert prioritization system based on artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques. The system focuses on analyzing security alerts generated from multiple sources and automatically classifying them based on their risk level. By prioritizing high-risk alerts and suppressing low-priority or repetitive alerts, the system assists security analysts in focusing on critical incidents that require immediate attention. This project is significant as it enhances the efficiency of SOC operations by reducing alert noise, improving visibility into high-risk security events, and supporting faster decision-making. The use of AI/ML techniques enables adaptive learning from historical alert patterns, making the system more effective than traditional rule-based approaches. With the increasing complexity of cyber threats and the growing workload on SOC analysts, automated alert prioritization has become an essential requirement for modern cybersecurity operations

Problem Statement Security Operations Centers (SOCs) rely on multiple security monitoring tools such as Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems, intrusion detection and prevention systems (IDS/IPS), firewalls, and endpoint security solutions to detect potential cyber threats. These tools continuously generate a large number of security alerts that require analysis and triage by security analysts. However, a significant proportion of these alerts are false positives, duplicate events, or low- severity notifications that do not require immediate action. The excessive volume of alerts results in alert fatigue, where SOC analysts become overwhelmed and are unable to effectively differentiate between critical and non-critical alerts. Manual alert triaging is time-consuming, inefficient, and highly dependent on analyst experience. As the scale and complexity of cyberattacks increase, traditional rule-based alerting mechanisms fail to adapt to evolving threat patterns, leading to delayed incident detection and response. Furthermore, existing SOC alert management approaches lack intelligent prioritization mechanisms that can automatically assess alert risk based on historical patterns, contextual information, and behavioral characteristics. This absence of automation places a heavy burden on analysts and increases the likelihood of overlooking genuine security incidents. Therefore, there is a need for an automated, intelligent alert prioritization system that leverages artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to classify and prioritize SOC alerts based on their risk level. Such a system can significantly reduce alert noise, improve analyst efficiency, and enhance the overall effectiveness of SOC operations.  Objectives of the Project The primary objective of this project is to design and implement an AI/ML-based system that automates the prioritization of security alerts in Security Operations Centers. The specific objectives of the project are as follows: 1. 
Automated Alert Ingestion To collect and process security alerts generated from multiple sources such as simulated SIEM logs, IDS/IPS alerts, firewall events, and endpoint security notifications. 2. 
Alert Preprocessing and Feature Extraction To normalize and preprocess alerts and extract meaningful features such as severity, frequency, time patterns, and source behavior for further analysis. 3. 
AI/ML-Based Alert Classification To apply machine learning techniques to classify alerts into high, medium, and low priority categories based on their risk level. 4.

Methodology The The proposed system follows a structured and modular methodology to ensure accurate alert prioritization and efficient SOC operations. The methodology is designed to simulate real-world SOC alert handling while maintaining a controlled and ethical academic environment. The overall approach consists of alert collection, preprocessing, machine learning–based analysis, prioritization, and visualization. 1. Alert Data Collection Security alerts are collected from simulated SOC environments that represent common alert sources such as SIEM systems, intrusion detection systems, firewalls, and endpoint security tools. Publicly available cybersecurity datasets are also utilized and converted into alert-style records to resemble real SOC alerts. These alerts are stored in a structured format for further processing. 2. Data Preprocessing and Normalization Collected alerts often vary in structure, severity levels, and formats. Therefore, preprocessing is performed to normalize alerts into a common schema. This step includes handling missing values, standardizing severity levels, timestamp normalization, and encoding categorical attributes. Proper preprocessing ensures consistency and improves machine learning performance. 3. Feature Extraction Relevant features are extracted from the preprocessed alerts to capture meaningful characteristics such as alert frequency, source behavior, time-based patterns, alert category, and historical occurrence. These features form the input for the machine learning models and play a crucial role in distinguishing high-risk alerts from low-priority events. 4. AI/ML-Based Alert Classification Supervised machine learning techniques are applied to classify alerts into high, medium, and low priority categories. A Random Forest classifier is used as the primary model due to its robustness and ability to handle noisy and imbalanced data. Baseline models are used for comparison to evaluate classification effectiveness. 5. Alert Risk Scoring and Prioritization Based on the output of the machine learning model, a risk score is assigned to each alert. This score is used to prioritize alerts, ensuring that high-risk alerts are escalated for analyst attention while low-risk alerts are suppressed or deprioritized. 6. Visualization and Analysis A centralized SOC-style dashboard is developed to display prioritized alerts, alert trends, and statistical insights. This visualization assists SOC analysts in monitoring critical alerts efficiently and supports faster decision-making. Technologies and Tools Software Requirements Sr. No. Technology

1. Introduction Brief Overview of the Project: Justice Assist is a cybersecurity-powered AI platform designed to simplify and streamline the process of reporting cybercrimes. It guides users through identifying the nature of the cybercrime, collecting admissible digital evidence (such as screenshots, chats, and transactions), and automatically generating a legally structured complaint report in PDF format. The platform also helps users connect with the nearest cybercrime portal or police station. Justice Assist combines technologies such as Natural Language Processing (NLP), form validation, and AI decision-making to make cybercrime reporting more accessible, especially for non-technical users. • Background Information: With the rise in digital connectivity, cybercrime has become a major threat affecting individuals, businesses, and governments. Despite the existence of reporting portals, many victims struggle with understanding how to report incidents, what qualifies as evidence, and how to present their complaints in a structured manner. Often, complaints get rejected due to poor documentation or lack of clarity. Existing systems also lack multilingual and accessibility features, making them unusable for people from regional or rural backgrounds. JusticeAssist addresses these challenges by providing step-by-step, AI-guided assistance for reporting cybercrimes. Purpose of the Project: 1. To assist cybercrime victims in accurately identifying the type of crime. 2. To guide users in collecting and structuring valid digital evidence. 3. To auto-generate a formal and complete cybercrime complaint report. 4. To bridge the gap between victims and cyber law enforcement agencies.

2. Literature Review Recent research highlights the growing use of AI and NLP in digital forensics, cybercrime reporting, and legal tech platforms. 1. AI in Digital Forensics and Evidence Handling AI and machine learning models have been used to automate the extraction and classification of digital evidence. Du et al. (2020) showed that such automation reduces investigation time and improves accuracy. 2. NLP for Legal Complaint Drafting Studies like Fernandes & Shaikh (2018) explored the use of NLP in simplifying legal complaints and user queries. NLP-driven tools help convert plain user input into structured legal formats. 3. Secure Evidence Management Blockchain-based approaches, as discussed by Dasaklis et al. (2020), ensure the integrity of digital evidence through tamper-proof logs and traceable data handling. 4. User-Centric Legal Platforms Bhargava (2022) emphasized the need for multilingual, accessible legal tech tools to support non-technical users, increasing public engagement in digital justice systems. How This Project Contributes to Existing Research Combines AI, NLP, and secure reporting into one platform. Provides multilingual, guided evidence collection. 3. Problem Statement The primary goal of this project is to develop an AI-powered platform that guides users through the process of reporting cybercrimes and compiling valid digital evidence. The system is designed to assist victims in understanding the type of crime, organizing admissible evidence, and submitting a well-structured complaint. Currently, victims face several challenges when attempting to report cybercrimes: Lack of awareness about how to file a cyber complaint properly. Unstructured or incomplete evidence leading to delays or rejection of cases. Language and accessibility barriers for users from regional or non-technical backgrounds. Limited legal understanding, making it difficult to present a valid complaint. Justice Assist aims to overcome these issues by providing AI-guided assistance for cybercrime reporting and evidence preparation. What the Project Intends to Achieve: Build a user-friendly platform that guides users step-by-step through cybercrime reporting.  Help users identify the category of cybercrime based on their inputs.  Provide structured suggestions for collecting and submitting digital evidence.  Generate legally complaint reports in PDF format.  Support multilingual and accessible interfaces to include non-technical and regional users.

Objectives:  Design a web-based platform for guided cybercrime reporting and evidence compilation.  Implement NLP to classify the type of cybercrime based on user input.  Assist users in uploading relevant evidence like chat screenshots, emails, or transaction logs.  Automate the generation of structured, formal complaint reports in PDF format.  Provide an intuitive, multilingual interface accessible to a broad user base.  Improve the efficiency of cybercrime case handling by delivering structured reports to authorities.

4. Methodology Description of Methods and Procedures: Justice Assist follows a web-based client–server architecture designed to guide users through cybercrime reporting and structured evidence building using AI and NLP techniques. The system collects inputs from users, classifies the type of cybercrime, provides relevant evidence suggestions, and generates a formal complaint report in PDF format. The process includes multilingual support and a simplified interface to ensure accessibility for non-technical users. At runtime:  The user logs into the platform and inputs basic incident details.  The system applies NLP to identify the nature of the cybercrime.  It suggests evidence types (e.g., chat screenshots, transaction logs).  The user uploads or selects appropriate evidence.  The system compiles the data into a structured, auto-generated PDF complaint.  The report is made available for download or forwarding to a relevant cybercrime unit. Data Collection and Analysis Techniques: No persistent personal data is stored; all session data is temporary. Text input is processed using NLP for classification and context extraction. Evidence uploads are verified (e.g., file type, size) for integrity. The complaint report is generated only after all validations are passed. Analytics (optional) can be used to track common crime types for system improvement (without storing PII). System Integration and Workflow Coordination All system components—frontend, backend, AI microservices, and the database—communicate through RESTful APIs. The frontend uses Axios to interact with the backend, while the backend coordinates with Python-based microservices (e.g., for classification, PDF generation). System Architecture Description Summary: - The Justice Assist system architecture integrates multiple intelligent modules to streamline cybercrime reporting and legal assistance. The AI Chatbot uses NLP and GPT-based prompt management to guide users with legal queries and case navigation. The Document Analyzer validates uploaded evidence, extracts content using OCR, and assesses relevance through NLP-based scoring. The PDF Complaint Generator organizes user inputs, validates key fields, and renders them into legally structured, downloadable complaint reports. The Suspect Guess module analyzes metadata and headers to estimate the attacker’s IP and location, providing behavioral profiling using a trained dataset. The Cyber Awareness module includes a quiz engine, trend visualizer, educational videos, and safety guides to promote digital literacy. Each module is backed by relevant datasets to support decision-making, classification, and personalization, ensuring JusticeAssist delivers a user-friendly, AI-powered reporting and awareness platform. 5. The system aims to automatically detect and classify various land categories, including buildings, roads, vegetation, water bodies, and open land, thereby reducing the need for manual analysis. A CNN-based architecture is implemented to extract meaningful spatial features and perform accurate classification. Abstract—Biometric authentication systems are extensively
utilized because of their ease and trustworthiness; nonetheless,
the enduring characteristic of biometric attributes render them
susceptible to template breaches and replay assaults. Mean-
while, developments in quantum computing present risks in
the long run. to traditional cryptographic security methods
utilized in biometrics systems. Recent research has investigated
quantum representations. For biometric matching, numerous
current methods either necessitate high-dimensional quantum
states or fail to consider biometric template safeguarding. This
paper presents QuMetric, a hybrid post-quantum fingerprint
authentication framework that combines classical biometric tem-
plate protection with low-qubit quantum similarity evaluation.
Fingerprint minutiae are extracted and transformed into a
rotation-invariant radial-angular feature representation, which
is protected using a simulated quantum key distribution (QKD)-
derived key and encoded into a quantum state using angle-based
rotation gates. A hybrid similarity score combining quantum state
fidelity with Hamming similarity enables accurate authentication
while operating with a limited number of qubits. Additionally,
a hardware intellectual property (IP) core locking mechanism
binds a DSP FIR filter to the biometric authentication outcome,
ensuring hardware functional access is gated by biometric iden-
tity. Experiments on the SOCOFing dataset using 200 subjects,
1,999 genuine pairs, and 1,000 impostor pairs yield an Equal
Error Rate (EER) of 7.85% and an Area Under the ROC
Curve (AUC) of 0.9761, demonstrating that secure and resource-
efficient quantum-assisted biometric authentication is feasible in
the current NISQ era. Index Terms—quantum cryptography, [NAME]
tion, fingerprint recognition, quantum state fidelity, quantum
key distribution, hardware IP protection, angle encoding, NISQ

platforms. In spite of its benefits, Fingerprint authentication
encounters significant security issues associated for the storage
and safeguarding of biometric templates Unlike passwords or
cryptographic keys, biometric traits cannot be revoked once
compromised, making template security a primary concern [2]. Traditional biometric systems rely on classical crypto-

Consequently, there is a growing fascination with creating biometric authentication systems that stay secure even when there is quantum-enabled opponents [6]. In parallel, quantum computing has emerged as a promising paradigm for pattern representation and similarity evalua- tion. Recent studies have explored quantum data encoding techniques and quantum similarity measures for image and
biometric recognition tasks [7], [8]. Quantum state fidelity,
in particular, provides a natural and mathematically grounded
measure for comparing quantum-encoded patterns [9]. How-
ever, many existing quantum biometric approaches focus pri-
marily on direct quantum encoding of biometric data, often
requiring a large number of qubits or overlooking biometric
template protection, which limits their practicality on noisy
intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices [10], [11]. To address these limitations, this paper presents QuMetric,
a hybrid fingerprint authentication framework that combines
classical biometric template protection with quantum-assisted
similarity computation and hardware IP core locking. Instead
of directly encoding raw fingerprint images into quantum
states, the proposed approach extracts fingerprint minutiae
and converts them into a rotation-invariant radial-angular
histogram, which is protected using QKD-derived key bind-
ing following established principles of biometric template
protection [2]. To accommodate qubit constraints in current
quantum hardware, the protected representation is compressed
and encoded using low-qubit angle-based quantum encoding,
which has been shown to be suitable for near-term quantum
devices [8]. Authentication is performed by evaluating a
hybrid score combining quantum state fidelity and Hamming
similarity. Upon successful authentication, a hardware DSP
FIR filter IP core is unlocked using a biometric-derived key,
binding hardware functionality to biometric identity [12]. The primary contributions of this work are as follows: • A hybrid post-quantum fingerprint authentication frame-
work integrating classical template protection with quan-
tum similarity evaluation and hardware IP core locking. • A rotation-invariant radial-angular minutiae histogram
providing stable feature representations under realistic
finger placement variation, overcoming the spatial sen-
sitivity of prior grid-based approaches.

cause of its capability to offer enhanced identity verification
in relation to knowledge-based and methods based on tokens.
Among different biometric modalities, fingerprints recognition
continues to be among the most developed and extensively
utilized methods due to its distinctiveness, durability, and
high user acceptance [1]. Nevertheless, traditional fingerprint
Recognition systems generally retain minutiae-oriented or feature-oriented templates in their unaltered or slightly mod-
ified state, rendering them susceptible to template breaches
and identity fraud in case of database breach [2].To reduce
these risks, various biometric template protection methods
have been suggested. Cryptographic approaches such as fuzzy
commitment schemes bind biometric features with secret keys
while allowing error tolerance during matching [3]. Dodis et
al. [14] established the information-theoretic foundations of
fuzzy extractors, which provide provably secure key derivation
from noisy biometric data. These techniques improve template
security but are primarily developed under classical crypto-
graphic assumptions, which may be insufficient against adver-
saries equipped with quantum computational capabilities [5],

The emergence of quantum computing has motivated re-
search into quantum-based pattern recognition and biometric
matching. Quantum image representations such as FRQI [15]
and NEQR [16] enable classical image data to be encoded into
quantum states, forming the foundation for quantum image
processing and analysis. Numerous surveys and experimental
research have emphasized the possibilities of these representa-
tions while also recognizing practical limitations when utilized
on NISQ tools [10], [11]. Recent research has investigated the
use of quantum methods to matching fingerprints and asso-
ciated biometric activities. Mogos [17] proposed a quantum
matching algorithm for biometric fingerprints, demonstrating
the feasibility of quantum-assisted fingerprint comparison.
Other works have investigated quantum fingerprinting pro-
tocols, which enable comparison of large classical datasets
using compact quantum states [18], [19]. While these methods
offer communication and theoretical efficiency advantages,
they are primarily designed for equality testing and do not
directly address biometric variability or template protection
requirements. A limited number of studies have attempted to integrate bio-
metric verification with quantum-secure communication prim-
itives. Ramos et al. [20] demonstrated QKD-assisted biometric
verification using quantum oblivious transfer for secure multi-
party authentication scenarios. However, such systems often
focus on secure transmission rather than irreversible biometric
template protection prior to quantum processing. Hardware
security has been addressed through logic locking [12] and
active hardware metering [21]; binding hardware access to
quantum-verified biometric identity represents a gap that this
work addresses.

The overall workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1 and consists of seven stages... A. Fingerprint Preprocessing The input fingerprint image is first resized to a fixed
resolution of 256 × 256 pixels to ensure consistency across
samples. Contrast enhancement is performed using Contrast
Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) with clip
limit 2.0 and an 8 × 8 tile grid [22]. Gaussian smoothing
with a 5 × 5 kernel is applied to reduce sensor noise and
minor acquisition artifacts. Adaptive Gaussian thresholding
(block size 17, constant C = 4) is then employed to generate
a binary ridge map, enabling robust ridge separation under
varying illumination and contrast conditions. A 3×3 elliptical
morphological closing kernel fills small ridge gaps. Finally,
morphological skeletonization [23] is applied to reduce ridge
structures to a single-pixel width, facilitating accurate minutiae
detection [1]. B. Rotation-Invariant Minutiae Feature Extraction Minutiae points, specifically ridge endings (crossing number
CN= 1) and bifurcations (CN= 3), are extracted from the
skeletonized fingerprint image using the crossing number
method. For each ridge pixel, the number of transitions be-
tween foreground and background pixels in its 8-connected
neighborhood is computed. Minutiae points within a 10-pixel
border margin are discarded to reduce edge artifacts. To overcome the spatial sensitivity of grid-based approaches
under finger rotation and translation, the detected minutiae are
encoded using a rotation-invariant radial-angular histogram.

deployment. Impostor pairs are formed by comparing real images from different subjects with the same finger position.

because it offers linear qubit scaling and low circuit depth
suitable for NISQ devices [7], [8]. The hybrid score weight
is set to α = 0.6. Quantum state fidelity combined with
Hamming similarity is used as the authentication metric [9]. D. Evaluation Protocol For each pair, both images undergo identical preprocessing,
feature extraction, protection, compression, and quantum en-

VI. SECURITY ANALYSIS This section analyzes the security properties of the pro- posed QuMetric framework with respect to biometric template protection, resistance to classical and quantum attacks, and potential attack surfaces. A. Biometric Template Irreversibility A fundamental requirement of secure biometric systems is
template irreversibility, ensuring that original biometric traits
cannot be reconstructed from stored data. In the proposed
framework, fingerprint minutiae are transformed into a radial-
angular histogram, binarized, and subsequently protected using
SHA-256 hashing combined with secret key binding. Since
cryptographic hash functions are one-way, recovering the
original biometric features from the stored protected represen-
tation is computationally infeasible. As a result, even if the
database of protected templates is compromised, an attacker
cannot reconstruct the original fingerprint image or minutiae
pattern [2], [3]. B. Resistance to Template Leakage Attacks Traditional biometric systems often store feature vectors
or transformed templates that may leak sensitive biometric
information. The proposed approach stores only a hashed
and key-bound representation. The implementation of key
binding also guarantees that the same biometric inputs do not
generate identical stored representations when distinct keys
are employed, reducing cross-matching assaults across several
databases and improving user privacy [2]. C. Security Against Quantum-Capable Adversaries The suggested framework is developed based on the premise
of a quantum-enabled opponent equipped with polynomial-
time quantum access algorithms. Instead of relying on classical
public-key cryptography, which may be vulnerable to quantum
attacks [5], the system assumes secure key generation via QKD
or a post-quantum key exchange mechanism [6]. The crypto-
graphic hash function used for template protection remains
secure against known quantum attacks, providing a quadratic
rather than exponential speedup for brute-force attempts [6]. D. Protection of Quantum Encoded States

Instead of relying on classical public-key cryptography, which may be vulnerable to quantum attacks [5], the system assumes secure key generation via QKD or a post-quantum key exchange mechanism [6]. The crypto- graphic hash function used for template protection remains secure against known quantum attacks, providing a quadratic rather than exponential speedup for brute-force attempts [6]. D. Protection of Quantum Encoded States The quantum states used for similarity evaluation are gen-
erated dynamically during authentication and are not perma-
nently stored. Even if an adversary intercepts the quantum-
encoded states, the no-cloning theorem prevents perfect du-
plication of unknown quantum states [9]. Furthermore, the
encoded quantum states represent compressed and protected
biometric features rather than raw biometric data, limiting the
potential impact of quantum state leakage. E. Hardware IP Core Security The FIR filter activation key is derived from the biometric
key κ and is never stored in hardware. Physical access to
the device without successful biometric authentication yields
only 0xERROR_LOCKED. This extends logic locking [12]
and active hardware metering [21] with the additional prop-
erty that the activation credential is biometric and quantum-
authenticated, rather than a static design-time secret. F. Attack Surface and Limitations The proposed security analysis assumes trusted fingerprint
acquisition hardware and does not address sensor-level attacks
such as spoofing or presentation attacks. Additionally, while
the framework ensures strong template protection and post-
quantum security, the current implementation relies on clas-
sical simulation of quantum operations. Practical deployment
on real quantum hardware may introduce noise-related vulner-
abilities that require additional error mitigation strategies [10].
These aspects are identified as important directions for future
work. VII. LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK While the proposed QuMetric framework demonstrates
strong authentication performance on the SOCOFing dataset,
several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the QKD key
distribution is simulated; integration with a physical QKD
channel over fiber or free-space optical link is required for
deployment. The BB84 protocol and its successors have been
demonstrated over metropolitan fiber networks, providing a
clear path toward physical integration [24].

WORK While the proposed QuMetric framework demonstrates strong authentication performance on the SOCOFing dataset, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the QKD key distribution is simulated; integration with a physical QKD channel over fiber or free-space optical link is required for deployment. The BB84 protocol and its successors have been demonstrated over metropolitan fiber networks, providing a clear path toward physical integration [24]. Second, the current implementation employs fixed block-
averaging compression to accommodate qubit constraints.
Even though this method permits execution utilizing 12 qubits,
adaptive and learning-oriented compression techniques could
enhance differentiation at the expense of increased quantum
resource usage.Third, the security analysis assumes trusted
fingerprint acquisition hardware and does not address presen-
tation attacks or sensor spoofing. Integrating liveness detection
and multimodal biometric fusion within the proposed frame-
work represents an important direction for future research. Finally, although the proposed approach is designed for
NISQ devices, all experiments are performed using classical
simulation. Future work will focus on deploying the frame-
work on real quantum hardware and analyzing the impact
of noise, decoherence, and gate imperfections on biometric
similarity evaluation. Replacing the crossing-number minutiae extractor with NIST NBIS mindtct [28] is expected to
further reduce EER toward the sub-5% range. VIII. CONCLUSION This paper presented QuMetric, a hybrid post-quantum
fingerprint authentication framework that integrates classical
biometric template protection with quantum-assisted similarity
computation and hardware IP core locking. Unlike exist-
ing approaches that directly encode raw biometric data into
quantum states, the proposed method emphasizes template
irreversibility and post-quantum security by applying QKD-
derived key binding prior to quantum processing. A rotation-
invariant radial-angular minutiae histogram addresses the spa-
tial sensitivity of prior grid-based approaches under realistic
finger placement variation. To address the constraints of cur-
rent quantum hardware, protected biometric representations
are compressed and encoded using a 12-qubit angle-based
quantum circuit.

1. Introduction: In recent years, the rise in cybercrime has made it more important than ever for students to gain practical skills in digital forensics and cybersecurity. However, most educational institutions still depend on classroom theory, which doesn’t always give learners the real-time experience they need. To manage this gap, we developed the VR Cybercrime Scene Investigation Lab, a virtual reality-based learning platform that simulates real- world cybercrime cases. This project allows students to step into the world of cyber investigators, where they can explore crime scenes, collect evidence, and analyze digital traces all within a realistic and interactive VR environment. By doing so, they not only understand how cyberattacks happen but also learn how to respond to them effectively. The goal is to make cybersecurity education more engaging, practical, and accessible, especially for institutions that may not have access to expensive forensic labs.

INTRODUCTION AcuPath is an AI-powered Android application developed using Java/XML with Firebase [NAME], designed to
help users reduce common body pain such as back, neck, shoulder, and knee pain through personalized exercise guidance. 
The app first identifies the pain area, then asks a short set of targeted questions to understand pain severity, duration,
triggers, and mobility limitations. Using Agentic AI, the system dynamically chooses the next relevant question and selects a
safe recommendation pathway.

pain. Most existing apps give the same exercises to everyone and do not consider
how serious the pain is, what causes it, or how much the person can move. This can
confuse users and sometimes make the pain worse. Therefore, there is a need for an
Android app that understands the user’s pain by asking simple and relevant
questions, then suggests the right exercises with proper safety tips. With AI support,
exercise videos, and saved user history, the app can help people manage their pain
better and more safely over time.

A robust recommendation system has been implemented, combining rule-based logic with intelligent decision-making to provide accurate and personalized

The UI/UX has been significantly enhanced, featuring improved alignment, smooth transitions, responsive design, and comprehensive input validation for better
user interaction. Additionally, the Firebase database structure has been fully optimized to securely and efficiently store user responses, assessment history, and
session data, ensuring seamless data management and retrieval.

CONCLUSION The user interface structure has been designed, including layouts for pain area selection and the questionnaire screen. The overall content framework has been

3. PROBLEM STATEMENT Managing MongoDB databases typically requires significant technical expertise in database query 
languages and system administration. This creates barriers for non-technical users and slows down 
data management processes. Current tools lack intuitive conversational interfaces and autonomous 
capabilities to simplify database management without coding. There is a need for an intelligent, 
agentic AI framework that enables users to interact with and manage MongoDB databases through 
natural language, automating complex tasks and minimizing the need for technical intervention.

3.1 Objectives: a. Develop a Conversational Interface: Create an AI-powered natural language interface that allows users to perform MongoDB operations (CRUD, queries, indexing, aggregation) through simple, intuitive conversations. b. Enable No-Code Database Management: Design the system to autonomously translate natural language commands into optimized MongoDB queries and commands, eliminating the need for users to write any code. c. Implement Autonomous Task Execution: Equip the AI agent with the ability to autonomously perform routine database management tasks such as backups, schema updates, performance monitoring, and data validation. d. Ensure Scalability and Flexibility: Build the framework to handle various MongoDB deployments, from single instances to large, distributed clusters, supporting diverse user needs. e. Incorporate User Feedback Loop: Allow the system to learn from user interactions to improve accuracy, responsiveness, and the handling of ambiguous or complex requests. f. Maintain Security and Access Control: Integrate mechanisms to ensure secure access to databases and protect sensitive data while allowing authorized operations.

4. METHODOLOGY MongoTalk is a multi-component web application designed to serve as a comprehensive 
conversational gateway to MongoDB. This section provides a detailed technical description of its 
architecture and the core modules that enable its functionality. I. 
Frontend: A modern, responsive web interface built using the React framework. It provides a 
simple chatstyle input for users to enter their natural language commands. The interface is 
responsible for rendering query results, which can be raw JSON data, formatted tables, or interactive 
visualizations generated by a library such as Chart.js. II. 
Backend Orchestrator: A Python-based server built with the FastAPI framework. This component 
is the brain of the system, responsible for managing user sessions, receiving natural language input 
from the frontend, and coordinating the workflow between the other modules. It houses the Natural 
Language Understanding (NLU) module, the Secure Execution Engine, the Automated Visualization 
Engine, and the Automated Reporting Module. III. 
LLM Service: The system leverages a locally-hosted LLM served via Ollama. This approach 
ensures data privacy, as no user prompts or database schemas are sent to third-party APIs, and 
provides full control over model selection and configuration. For the task of generating MQL, a 
code-specialized model such as codellama:34b is employed, chosen for its strong performance in 
code generation and understanding context across multiple files.[42] IV. 
MongoDB Instance: The target database that the user wishes to interact with. The backend 
orchestrator connects to this instance using a standard MongoDB driver. The typical workflow is as 
follows: a user enters a natural language command into the frontend. The command is sent to the 
backend orchestrator, which uses its NLU module to classify the user's intent and construct a 
detailed prompt for the Ollama LLM. The LLM generates the corresponding MQL code, which is 
returned to the orchestrator. The orchestrator validates and executes the code via its Secure 
Execution Engine. The results are then passed to the Automated Visualization Engine, which 
determines the best way to display the data. Finally, the processed results and visualization are sent 
back to the frontend for the user to view.  Tools & Technologies Category

Introduction The project aims to help police and law enforcement by generating facial sketches from photos using deep learning technique.
It replaces manual hand-drawn sketches with computer-generated sketches using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).
GANs are a type of deep learning model that can learn to generate realistic facial sketches based on patterns in training data.
The system is trained on a dataset of face photos and corresponding sketches to learn how to convert between the two.
This helps in identifying suspects when only a sketch or partial visual information is available, making investigations faster and more accurate.
The project brings automation, consistency, and intelligence to the sketching process, reducing human error and time. Motivation Assist Law Enforcement: To support police and investigative agencies in identifying suspects when no clear photo evidence is available, especially in cases relying on eyewitness-provided sketches. Reduce Manual Effort: To minimize dependency on forensic sketch artists, who may not always be available or consistent, by automating the sketch-to-photo conversion process using deep learning models. Save Time: To significantly reduce the time taken in generating suspect visuals, which can be crucial in early stages of investigation, especially in high-profile or time-sensitive cases.

Problem Statement To improve traditional methods, there is a need for a system that can automatically convert suspect sketches into genuine face-like images, helping investigators in faster and more reliable identification. To develop a model which will automatically transform facial sketches into genuine images using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Existing GAN models for sketch-to-photo are costly, need long training, and require powerful GPUs. 
This project aims to build an optimized GAN model that overcomes these issues for practical forensic use. To address this gap by developing a deep learning-based solution using GANs for efficient and reliable facial sketch reconstruction. INTRODUCTION Preamble This chapter provides the foundational context for the project, highlighting the need for proactive insider threat detection in modern organizations. It introduces core challenges, project objectives, and the motivations driving the development of an advanced, explainable monitoring system that bridges practical security and technological innovation.

Introduction Insider threats—malicious or careless behavior by trusted individuals—continue to be among the most destructive and most difficult-to-detect threats facing today's enterprises. In contrast to malicious outsiders who need to penetrate a perimeter, insiders 2 take advantage of approved avenues, integrate perfectly with normal organizational processes, and can adapt their techniques according to prevailing security measures. This presents an intricate security problem where the attacker is already inside the trusted environment, making many common defenses moot. The urgent need is not just for better algorithms, but for unified, deployable systems that can ingest massive real time data streams and deliver actionable, trusted insights. This paper addresses this gap by presenting a novel engineering and analytical framework that moves beyond fragmented algorithms to deliver a complete, production-ready solution. Our primary contribution lies in the synergistic integration of hybrid detection, dynamic contextualization, multi-layered explainability (XAI), and enterprise governance controls (privacy and real-time performance) into a single, cohesive Insider Threat Detection System.

Problem Statement Existing and modern methods for insider threat detection are usually unsuccessful because they possess four habitual shortcomings that confine their functional efficiency: Inflexibility to CBIR-Based Rules. Signature-based systems and fixed ahead-of-time predetermined rules are inherently reactive. They cannot generalize and discover new, unknown, or complex malicious activity that doesn't conform to predetermined pat terns. Inadequate Contextualization. Behavior is often reviewed in a vacuum, without con sideration for the effect that the obligations of the user, peer group networking, or the underlying organizational paradigm may have. This inadequate contextualization accounts for much incorrect risk assessment and generates an intolerably high level of false positives, thereby inundating security analysts. Limited Real-Time Capability. Most solutions are dependent on batch processing of logs, thus introducing a notable delay between a malicious activity and its detection. The delay gives insiders a grace period during which they are able to fulfill their objectives and inflict a great amount of damage before a response is initiated. Offered Limited Explainability. Among the crucial obstacles for real-world practical use of most machine learning systems is that they are "black boxes." Without a simple, comprehensible explanation available for human users when an alert is produced, that diminishes analysts' confidence, slows investigation triage effectiveness, and complicates auditing the system. Project Objectives The main goals of this study are to: Create a hybrid, behavior-based pipeline that captures complementary aspects of insider risk by blending statistical, pattern-based, and contextual anomaly detection models. Provide real-time scoring and alerting with dynamic, peer-group-based thresh olds that adjust according to organizational norms and sharply cut down false positive rates. Offer multi-layer explainability that renders all risk decisions open, auditable, and actionable for security analysts by revealing feature attributions, graph insights, and peer comparisons. Integrate privacy, security, and governance controls into the whole data lifecycle, from collection to storage and analysis. System Architecture Fig. 4.1 System Architecture Diagram of Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System The architecture of the Behavior-Driven Insider Threat Detection System is a comprehensive yet efficient framework that captures behavioral data from organizational endpoints, processes it through hybrid machine learning models, and delivers actionable insights to security analysts through an intuitive dashboard. The system's event telemetry is captured by endpoint agents and SIEM connectors monitoring authentication systems, file servers, USB devices, and network activities. This data is then transmitted to the FastAPI backend, which acts as the central processing engine of the system, converting raw event streams into normalized, feature-engineered data suitable for anomaly detection. The processed data flows through three parallel detection pipelines: Isolation Forest for statistical analysis, Autoencoder for behavioral pattern recognition, and Graph Analytics for contextual relationship assessment. These detection signals are then synthesized through a risk fusion layer that applies peer-group normalization and dynamic thresholds to produce accurate, context-aware risk scores. The results are persisted in a PostgreSQL database for audit trails and longitudinal analysis, while simultaneously being transmitted via WebSocket to the Next.js dashboard. The dashboard provides real-time insider threat monitoring with explainable AI insights, enabling security analysts to investigate alerts, understand threat rationale through SHAP-based feature attributions, and take informed action. This architecture allows organizations to monitor behavioral patterns proactively and make data-driven security decisions, all accessible through an analyst-friendly interface that bridges the gap between complex machine learning and practical security operations. Key Detection Methods Used in the System: The system utilizes three primary detection approaches for behavioral monitoring and insider threat identification. These methods play a crucial role in the system's ability to continuously analyze user activities and provide comprehensive risk assessment. Here's a detailed explanation of these detection methods and how they process input and provide output: Isolation Forest (Statistical Detection): Isolation Forest is an anomaly detection algorithm based on the principle that anomalies are easier to isolate than normal instances. In the context of the Insider Threat Detection System, Isolation Forest is employed to process and analyze behavioral features extracted from user events for identifying statistical anomalies.

In the context of the Insider Threat Detection System, Isolation Forest is employed to process and analyze behavioral features extracted from user events for identifying statistical anomalies. Input: The Isolation Forest model receives input from preprocessed behavioral features extracted from user events, including login timestamps, file access counts, data transfer volumes, and temporal patterns aggregated in [STUDENT_ID] windows. Operation: The algorithm isolates anomalies by randomly selecting features and split values. Normal instances require more partitions to isolate, while anomalies are isolated quickly with fewer partitions. The model calculates an anomaly score based on the average path length required to isolate each instance. Output: The output of the Isolation Forest is a normalized anomaly score ranging from 0 to 1, where higher scores indicate greater deviation from normal behavior. This score is continuously transmitted to the fusion layer for real-time risk assessment. Autoencoder (Behavioral Pattern Detection): Autoencoders are neural network architectures designed to learn compressed representations of input data. In the Insider Threat Detection System, Autoencoders are used for detecting behavioral anomalies by learning normal user activity patterns and identifying deviations through reconstruction error. Input: The Autoencoder receives input as sequential behavioral event data representing user activity patterns over time windows. Features include event types, frequencies, temporal characteristics, and resource access patterns. Operation: The Autoencoder learns to compress and reconstruct normal behavioral patterns through its encoder-decoder architecture. During inference, it attempts to reconstruct incoming behavioral sequences. High reconstruction error indicates that the observed behavior significantly deviates from learned normal patterns. Output: The output of the Autoencoder is the reconstruction error metric, which quantifies how well the model can recreate the observed behavior. Higher reconstruction error signals anomalous behavior that doesn't match normal user patterns. The system's architecture seamlessly processes behavioral sequences through an Autoencoder neural network before presenting reconstruction error metrics to the risk fusion layer. The preprocessing pipeline feeds sequential behavioral data representing user activity patterns over temporal windows to the Autoencoder model. This deep learning architecture specializes in learning compressed representations of normal user behavior through its encoder-decoder structure. The encoder layers progressively compress input behavioral sequences into a lower-dimensional latent space that captures essential activity patterns. The decoder layers then attempt to reconstruct the original sequence from this compressed representation. During training on normal user activities, the model learns to accurately recreate typical behavioral patterns. However, when presented with anomalous insider threat behaviors during inference, the reconstruction quality deteriorates significantly. The reconstruction error—measured as the difference between input and reconstructed sequences—serves as the primary anomaly signal. High reconstruction error indicates that the observed behavior deviates substantially from learned normal patterns. Results are transmitted to the risk fusion layer, a component that further refines threat detection through integration with statistical and contextual signals. Finally, the dashboard delivers these behavioral anomaly scores to analysts in an easily interpretable format with detailed explanations. This architecture empowers security teams to detect non-linear behavioral deviations that traditional rule-based systems miss, promoting early identification of insider threats and proactive organizational security management.
